District Attorney Larry Krasner.: “The charges for in each of their cases because there will be a total of 11 victims, if not more, but at this 0.11 victims and 11 cases, these charges apply to all 9. ”

text:
Science & Tech Daily | October 12, 2026

Seven developments worth tracking, from papers published October 9 to 11.

1. A high-entropy molecular contact pushed an inverted perovskite solar cell to 27.31% certified steady-state efficiency.

Three self-assembling molecules with different bonding geometries, mixed into one hole-selective layer, held 27.50% best efficiency with negligible loss after 1,300 hours at 85°C in ambient air.

It remains a peer-reviewed small-area lab cell. Large-area coating, yield and outdoor lifetime still need demonstrating.

2. A 100-qubit processor tamed chaotic quantum dynamics with measurement and feedback.

Repeated mid-circuit measurement and re-initialization steered an information-scrambling quantum Bernoulli map to a fixed point: about 5,000 entangling gates and 5,000 measurement-and-feedback operations, observing a dynamical phase transition between quantum chaos and classical order.

This is the formal publication of a 2025 preprint on an IBM superconducting processor, not quantum advantage or fault-tolerant computation. Latency and error accumulation in deeper circuits remain untested.

3. An AI graded cancer-treatment side effects from clinic-room audio.

VOICE-AE combined speech recognition, speaker separation and a language model to assign CTCAE grades across 39 visits by 31 prostate-cancer radiotherapy patients, matching expert consensus in 82.6% of cases.

The retrospective, single-institution evaluation needs care: 76.9% of labels were "no adverse event," so a trivial all-zero predictor already reaches 76.9%. Performance was weak at grade 2 and above; severe events were not validated. Prospective multi-site evaluation, consent and voice-data protection come first.

4. Turning wetlands into farmland adds little food and much flood risk.

Worldwide tracking from 2000 to 2022 found about half of converted wetland cropland yields less than existing farmland, contributing 0.1% of world crop production. More than half sits under severe flood risk, with exposure 23 times that of all farmland.

This is observational work from satellite data and global averages, not farm-level economics. Field validation of yields and income is still needed.

5. A human motor-neuron model of TDP-43 nuclear loss offered an RNA therapy foothold.

Human iPSC-derived motor neurons engineered to block TDP-43 nuclear import showed impaired neurite growth, reduced axon regeneration and hyperexcitability, plus mis-splicing of STMN2 and KCNQ2. A STMN2-targeted antisense oligonucleotide partially restored splicing and some functions.

TDP-43 nuclear loss appears in most ALS cases; the model links it to pre-symptomatic deficits in human cells.

It is a cultured-neuron study, not a trial. Recovery in a dish does not imply slowing disease in patients; animal work must validate effect, distribution and toxicity.

6. An atomic-scale Ni/NiMoO4 structure went into an alkaline water-splitting catalyst.

Oleylamine on NiMoO4 nanowires selectively reduced only Ni2+, building alternating domains thinner than 1 nm. The catalyst reached 10 mA/cm² at 14.4±2.9 mV overpotential; a separate anion-exchange-membrane electrolyzer delivered 2 A/cm² at 1.62 V and 80°C, with stability past 2,200 hours at 25°C.

High current and long life were not shown together under the same industrial conditions. Large-area electrodes, nickel usage and stop-start cycling still need testing.

7. Ignoring social vulnerability understates the urban heat-risk gap.

Across 1,029 cities from 2000 to 2019, heat risk grew about five times faster in developing cities of the Global South. Treating all residents as equally vulnerable understated the long-term gap by about 65% and within-region inequality by about 15%.

This is a risk-model analysis, not direct tracking of heat illness or deaths. City health data and cooling access are needed to verify it.

Across several of today's studies, the shift is not a record but what gets tested: the conditions that break performance in real settings. Heat at the interface, noise in measurement, imbalance in data, vulnerability in exposure. The record holds only where the setup holds.

Kaveri Seed Company was incorporated in 1976. It does research, production, processing and marketing of hybrid seeds. Founder, Chairman and Managing Director G.V. Bhaskar Rao started it with what the company's own disclosure calls a vision to transform Indian agriculture through science-driven seed development. Fifty years on, the seed reaches 12 agro-climatic zones, which are areas grouped by soil and weather. Those zones cover 18 states, so a dozen weather systems have to be pleased at once.

In January 2024 the board approved a ₹325 crore buyback, which is a purchase of its own shares. The letter of offer covered 44,82,758 of those shares. The adjusted share count stood at 5.59 crore in the year to March 2023. It stood at 5.14 crore a year later and has stayed there since.

In May 2025 the company agreed to buy the remaining 30% of Aditya Agritech for ₹23.6 crore. Aditya became a fully owned subsidiary on 11 November 2025.

Then came the tax file. A demand of ₹56.21 crore arrived in March 2024, and another of ₹69.58 crore in March 2025. The company's notice said the second one came mainly from disallowing the agriculture-income exemption it had claimed. By April 2026 the appeals had been allowed and the demands set aside. One order set aside ₹73.25 crore on 30 March. A second set aside ₹56.21 crore on 7 April. A third set aside ₹69.6 crore on 8 April. Three orders inside ten days is a brisk pace for an appellate calendar.

The consolidated group holds five subsidiaries alongside the Kaveri Employee Trust. Four of them are Aditya Agri Tech, Kaveri Microteck, Genome Agritech and Genomix Agri Genetics. The Bangladesh entity is the fifth.

text:
Sons of Liberty: The Immortal War

Sons of Liberty imagines an Enlightenment civilization among the stars, where immortal Founders return and the betrayal of liberty opens reality to eldritch horrors. This is its Second Declaration of Independence.

The Second Declaration of Independence

When the servants of a free people shall have assumed dominion over their masters, and the government instituted to secure their rights shall have become the principal instrument of their subjection, the restoration of that people to their original authority requires that the trust thus violated be resumed. A decent respect for the opinions of mankind demands that they should declare the causes which compel them to withdraw their obedience, and the principles upon which they propose to establish anew the securities of their liberty.

We hold these truths to be self-evident: that men are born possessed of rights which no government has conferred, and which none may rightfully take away; that among these are life, liberty, property, the freedom of conscience, and the pursuit of happiness; that governments are instituted for their preservation, deriving their just powers from the consent of the governed; and that whenever those entrusted with such powers shall employ them against the ends of their institution, the people may resume the authority delegated, abolish the offending establishment, and provide other guards for their future security.

The peoples of these States did not constitute themselves the property of a general government. They formed, each within its own political society, a judgment upon the compact proposed; and by their several voluntary acts established a common authority for certain enumerated purposes. The assent which bound one State could neither supply the assent of another nor extinguish the sovereignty from which either proceeded. Their Union was the consequence of their freedom, and could acquire no right to destroy the freedom which brought it into existence.

To say that a people may consent, but may never withdraw a consent abused; that they may appoint a servant, but may never dismiss one become their oppressor; that they may establish government, but must thereafter endure whatever government shall choose to inflict, is to confess that their liberty expires at the moment of its exercise. Such reasoning makes the first act of a free society the last which it shall ever be permitted to perform. It substitutes possession for allegiance, force for compact, and perpetual servitude for the government of men by their own consent.

Prudence will indeed dictate that institutions long established should not be changed for light and transient causes. The imperfections of men must be borne with while correction remains possible, and the peace of society ought not to be disturbed by every disappointment of its members. But when a succession of abuses, pursued through changes of officers and professions of amendment, discovers the same design of reducing a people beneath arbitrary power, patience ceases to be a virtue useful to their preservation. It becomes their right, and their duty to themselves and their posterity, to cast off the authority which has betrayed them.

Such has been the patient sufferance of these States; and such is now the necessity which constrains them to restore their former condition. The history of the government from the consolidation enforced under Lincoln to its surrender beneath the Final Compact is a history of powers assumed without grant, restraints continued without consent, and injuries defended by the necessities which those same injuries have produced. To prove this, let its acts be submitted to a candid world.

It has asserted that the Union may rightfully be preserved by the destruction of the consent upon which it was founded. It has carried war against constituent peoples, denied their capacity to judge the obligations of their own association, and made the sword the final interpreter of a compact whose authority proceeded from voluntary assent. Having obtained obedience by force, it has afterward cited that obedience as proof that force was unnecessary.

It has suspended the ordinary securities of personal liberty, detained citizens upon executive accusation, and obstructed the inquiry by which unlawful confinement might be exposed. It has claimed that the danger apprehended by an officer is sufficient warrant to dispense with the restraints imposed upon his office. Thus the safeguards established against oppression have been made to depend upon the permission of the oppressor.

It has raised emergencies into sources of authority, and preserved the powers assumed in their name after their alleged occasions had passed away. Each extraordinary measure has furnished a precedent for another, until the accustomed government has become the exception and arbitrary necessity the standing rule. The people have been promised the return of their liberties when safety was restored, while their rulers reserved the sole judgment whether safety could ever be attained.

It has erected a multitude of offices, and sent among us officers empowered to prescribe our conduct, examine our affairs, adjudge our offenses, and exact the penalties of their own commands. It has united in these establishments powers which a free constitution distributes, that ambition in one department may be restrained by duty in another. Under the modest name of administration it has introduced authorities which exercise dominion without acknowledging the responsibilities of sovereignty.

It has extended its inquiries into the private correspondence, associations, movements, and opinions of the people. It has required no particular offense as the ground of suspicion, nor any end to the suspicion when examination disclosed none. The innocent have been watched because they might become dangerous, and the power to watch has been enlarged because its own exercise taught them to distrust it.

It has concealed the purposes and proceedings of its officers while demanding an unlimited confidence in their integrity. It has withheld the evidence by which its conduct might be judged, punished those who disclosed its abuses, and treated the exposure of public wrongdoing as a greater injury than the wrongdoing exposed. Responsibility has thus been exacted from the governed and refused by their governors.

It has obstructed the communication of facts and opinions necessary to the judgment of a free people. It has procured through dependent instruments the suppression which it dared not openly avow, and represented opposition to its measures as enmity toward the country. It has sought to leave the citizen at liberty to decide, provided that he should hear only the arguments prepared to determine his decision.

It has made labor and property tributary to offices whose claims increase with the means employed to satisfy them. It has multiplied permissions for the ordinary occupations of life, imposed conditions upon the lawful use of possessions, and treated the industry of the citizen as a fund belonging to administration. The right to acquire and enjoy has been reduced to a favor renewed upon payment and withdrawn upon displeasure.

It has subjected commerce to instruments through which every exchange may be observed and every means of subsistence restrained. It has claimed authority to interrupt the use of a man’s earnings without a lawful judgment disposing of his rights. By commanding the medium through which necessities are obtained, it has sought command over the necessities themselves.

It has contracted obligations to be discharged from the labor of generations not yet born, and called the power to exact their payment a present possession of wealth. It has consumed the resources of posterity to purchase the acquiescence of the present. Those who could neither authorize its extravagance nor restrain it have been appointed its debtors.

It has invaded the powers reserved to the States, and obtained by threatened deprivation what it possessed no constitutional authority to command. It has made assistance the price of submission and employed the revenues of the people to purchase their surrender. Their local institutions have been retained that distant commands might appear to proceed from familiar hands.

It has pretended that an election releases its officers from the limits of their appointments. It has confounded the choice of a magistrate with the grant of whatever powers he might afterward desire, and the concurrence of a majority with a lawful title to the rights of others. By this doctrine, every successful party becomes for its term the sovereign proprietor of those who opposed it.

It has corrupted public deliberation by false accounts of measures, invented accusations, and assurances contradicted by facts known to those who uttered them. It has obtained assent by concealing the objects to which assent would be applied. Having deceived the people concerning its purposes, it has proclaimed their supposed approval as authority to accomplish them.

It has joined foreign establishments in undertakings beyond the powers entrusted to it, and offered the obedience of these States to councils which their peoples did not appoint. Through the World Economic Forum and the United Nations it has accepted the Final Compact as a rule superior to the constitutions from which its own lawful authority must proceed. It has presumed to alienate a sovereignty which it never possessed.

It has preserved the names of nations while depriving them of national judgment, the forms of representation while removing the matters upon which representatives might decide, and the ceremonies of consent while denying every effectual means of refusal. Under professions of equity, sustainability, and security, it has established a common administration of dependence. It has required mankind to receive dispossession as improvement and submission as the final condition of freedom.

In all these proceedings, the governed have been regarded less as the source of authority than as the materials upon which authority might operate. Their labor has been claimed, their property burdened, their speech supervised, and their allegiance demanded as an obligation incapable of termination. They have been told that government exists by their consent, and that they shall possess no power by which consent may be withheld. Whatever name may adorn this condition, its substance is slavery.

Nor has the injury ended with the subjection of men. The contradiction between liberty professed and servitude enforced has entered the foundations of our common existence. Oaths have become instruments of falsehood, declarations coverings for their own violation, and public virtue a title claimed by those who consume it. Through the dissonance thus nourished, the eldritch powers obtained their entrance, and Earth was brought near surrender by the authorities appointed for its defense.

The same rulers who prepared this calamity demanded an increase of power to arrest it. They prescribed deeper dependence as the remedy for dependence, greater secrecy for the consequences of concealment, and more compulsory unity for the ruin produced by force. Had their prescription prevailed, the destruction of mankind would have been completed under assurances that mankind was at last secured.

In every stage of these oppressions we have sought redress through the institutions established for that purpose. Petitions have been received without remedy, elections conducted without the removal of abuses, and promises of reform fulfilled by changes of language. The instruments employed by one administration have been preserved for the convenience of its successor. A government which thus secures its usurpations against the lawful correction of the people has dissolved the trust upon which obedience depended.

We do not resume our freedom that it may be delivered into other arbitrary hands. The return of those who assisted at the first foundation supplies counsel and service, but cannot supply the assent belonging to the living peoples of the States. Their conventions shall judge the Constitution proposed for restoration, and their voluntary acts shall determine the association into which they enter. No sword shall ratify for them, and no necessity alleged by another shall stand in the place of their own consent.

The government established by that association shall possess only the powers expressly delegated. The rights retained by individuals shall remain secure against the general government and against the authorities of their several States. Accession shall be voluntary, withdrawal lawful, and public office a trust whose obligations survive every convenience urged against their performance. The preservation of government shall never again be pleaded as a right to enslave the governed.

We, therefore, the representatives of the peoples of the several States, assembled by their authority, appealing to the judgment of mankind for the rectitude of our intentions, do solemnly publish and declare that the usurping government has forfeited its claim to our obedience; that its pretended dominion over these peoples is dissolved; and that its engagements under the Final Compact possess no authority to bind them without their own lawful assent.

The States resume their standing as free political societies, competent to provide for their defense, regulate their lawful affairs, establish commerce, and determine the associations conducive to their happiness. Those which ratify the restored Constitution shall unite as These United Planets of America, preserving in their common government the limited authority necessary to its appointed ends, and in their peoples the sovereignty from which that authority proceeds.

We claim no dominion over the lawful societies of other nations, and require no surrender of their institutions as the price of peace. We invite their peoples to judge whether the power which would command us has respected their own freedom, and whether a common danger does not require a faithful preservation of their distinct rights. Against the corruption which would dissolve all human meaning, we shall maintain the obligations openly undertaken and the truthful dealings by which free peoples may assist one another.

For the support of this Declaration, and for the faithful discharge of the duties it restores, we pledge to one another our lives, our fortunes, and our sacred honor. We accept the hazards of liberty because we have learned the price of its surrender. The government shall again be the servant of the people, and the people shall never again be held the possessions of their government. 

Thomas Jefferson July 4, 2028

text:
She couldn't march, so she built a weapon. Betye Saar was home with three young daughters when Dr. King was killed, and what she made instead of a picket sign was a mammy figurine with a rifle in her hand and a Black Power fist across her apron. Angela Davis said that little box started the Black women's movement.

The pencil came out first.

It was a short novelty pencil, the cheap kind, made to sit in a plastic hand. The hand belonged to a figurine about a foot tall.

Red dress with little flowers on it, a yellow polka dot scarf, a bandana knotted above the forehead, and a grin stretched so wide it had stopped being a grin. Her apron was a notepad, and that was her entire purpose.

She had been manufactured so a white woman could stand in her own kitchen and jot down what she needed from the store. Milk, bread, pancake mix.

In 1972 a Black woman in Los Angeles bought one of these things secondhand and pulled the pencil out of its hand.

Then she put a rifle in.

She left the broom alone, because the broom was half the message. Into the slot where the grocery list belonged she slid an old postcard of another mammy figure holding a light skinned baby, and over that she pasted a raised Black fist.

She wanted people to understand how those babies came to be.

She papered the back of the box with Aunt Jemima pancake labels, row after row of the same face, so there was nowhere for your eye to rest. She set the figure's feet in cotton, tucked a grenade in beside the rifle, and laid glass across the front like a museum case.

Eleven and three quarter inches tall, eight inches across, less than three inches deep.

She called it The Liberation of Aunt Jemima, and the woman who made it was named Betye Saar. She died in her sleep at home in Los Angeles on Sunday, July 26, ninety nine years old and four days short of her hundredth birthday.

To understand why a grown woman would arm a grocery list holder, you have to start with a man from Lake Charles, Louisiana.

Her grandparents came out of Louisiana around 1910, part of the same migration that carried millions of Black families out looking for a place where the rules were slightly less lethal. They landed in Los Angeles, and her grandmother settled in Watts when Watts was still half country, dirt lots and railroad tracks and chickens in the yard.

Her father, Jefferson Maze Brown, was born in Lake Charles. Her mother, Beatrice Lillian Parson, was mixed, mostly Irish on her side.

They met at UCLA in the 1920s, which is not a sentence you get to write about many Black couples of that generation. He taught Sunday school and she sewed.

Betye Irene Brown was born on July 30, 1926, the oldest of three children.

When she was five, her father got an infection. The white hospital near the house would not treat him because he was Black.

That is Saar's own account of it, told and retold in interviews across five decades, and it is the sentence sitting underneath everything else she ever made.

He died in 1931.

She was five years old, and her mother was suddenly a widow with three children and a sewing machine. Here is the part that stays with you.

Saar said that as a small child, before her father died, she had a kind of second sight, a sensitivity she called mother wit. After he died, she said, it faded.

She lost her daddy and something else went out of her at the same time. She spent the rest of her life going through other people's discarded belongings looking for objects that still had a spirit left in them.

Thirty eight years later she found an old wooden window frame and filled its panes with small scenes. In one of them, her parents are dancing.

In another one, her father is dying.

She called it Black Girl's Window, and the Museum of Modern Art bought it in 2019, fifty years after she made it.

After the funeral the family moved in with her paternal grandmother in Watts, then out to Pasadena to live with her great aunt Hattie. But Betye kept going back to Watts, summer after summer, because of what was going up over the rooftops there.

An Italian immigrant named Simon Rodia was building towers in his own backyard by hand. He started in 1921 and did not finish until 1954.

He built them out of what the city threw away.

Saar used to walk with her grandmother along the railroad tracks toward the market, and she would look up at those spires and stare. She described him decades later on the radio, said he drove a big car, and when he passed a pile of rubble he would stop and go through it.

Steel structures, wet cement, and pressed into the cement whatever he had found that week. Broken plates, tile, bottle glass, seashells.

She said she had seen corn cobs in there, and she had seen tools. That, she said, was the beginning of her becoming a recycler.

Understand what a little girl learned standing at the base of those towers.

Nothing is too broken, too cheap, or too ruined to be turned into something the whole world will line up to look at.

Pasadena taught her the second lesson. The public pool was closed to her and the streetcars were not.

On Sundays she went to the mostly white Christian Science church with her mother and the mostly Black Episcopal church with her aunt, learning early how to walk into two rooms and be counted differently in each one. Her mother sewed for a living and gave gifts accordingly.

Her brother and sister got bicycles and roller skates and Betye got art supplies, and every so often she worked up the nerve to ask why she couldn't have a bike. Two blocks over lived the boy who threw their newspaper on the porch, and his name was Jackie Robinson.

She graduated from UCLA in 1949 with a degree in design, and then the world showed her exactly how big a room it had set aside for a Black woman with a degree in design. There were not many galleries in Los Angeles then, she said later, and there were certainly none for Black artists.

So she made greeting cards.

She designed jewelry and housewares, and she worked as a social worker. By 1968 she was sewing costumes at the Inner City Cultural Center, a theater founded in Los Angeles after everything that happened in the summer of 1965.

Because on August 11 of 1965 a traffic stop in Watts went wrong and the neighborhood where she was born went up. Six days, thirty four people dead, more than a thousand injured, close to four thousand arrested, forty million dollars in property gone.

That was her grandmother's Watts, the dirt lots and the railroad tracks and the towers still standing in the middle of it.

When the smoke cleared, two Black artists named Noah Purifoy and Judson Powell walked out onto 103rd Street, which people had started calling Charcoal Alley, and began picking up what was left. Melted neon that had cooled into strange glittering shapes, burnt wood, twisted steel.

They gathered it by the ton, pulled in six other artists, and built sixty six sculptures out of the wreckage in thirty days. They called the show 66 Signs of Neon and it traveled the country.

That was the air Betye Saar was breathing in Los Angeles.

Black artists on their knees in the ashes of their own neighborhood, turning what America had burned into something America would have to look at. The year after that she walked into the Pasadena Art Museum and saw an exhibition of Joseph Cornell, a man who made small boxes out of marbles and feathers and old letters.

She remembered every box being lit like a jewel in a case. That gave her the form.

April 4, 1968 gave her the reason.

Dr. King was killed in Memphis and something in Betye Saar turned over. Her marriage was ending that same year, she had three young daughters in the house, and she was forty one years old.

She said it as plainly as anybody ever has. She was a mother with young children and she could not walk in a protest.

But she did have a weapon, and the weapon was art.

Sit with that for a second, because plenty of us are living in that exact position right now. Too much at home to march, too much anger to sit still.

She had already started collecting the ugly things. It began in the sixties with a friend who collected derogatory postcards, and Saar looked at them and thought, this is nasty, this is mean, and then went out and started buying them herself.

Swap meets and garage sales, junk shops from Pasadena down to the water. Cookie jars, ashtrays, salt and pepper shakers, lawn jockeys.

Little Black Sambo drawings, a cigar box label, an advertisement for beans, and a tube of toothpaste called Darkie. Grinning faces manufactured by the thousands and sold cheap into American kitchens, and a lot of them, she noticed, had been made overseas in the forties by people who had never met a Black person in their lives.

Most Black families threw those things in the trash or never let them through the door in the first place.

Betye Saar was carrying them home on purpose and stacking them in her studio. Her reasoning was not nostalgia, it was closer to evidence gathering.

They abolished slavery, she said, and then found a way to keep you a slave by making you a salt shaker.

And she asked the question any Black parent recognizes immediately. If our children only ever see themselves reproduced like this, how are they supposed to reach for anything better?

If that is how the world sees you, she said, eventually you start seeing yourself that way too.

So she asked herself a different question, which was how do you make Aunt Jemima a hero.

In 1972 an open call went out from a place in Berkeley called the Rainbow Sign. It sat at the corner of Grove Street and Derby in a modest beige building that had been a mortuary before a concert promoter named Mary Ann Pollar turned it into a Black cultural center in 1971.

Nina Simone played there in March of 1972, and Berkeley's first Black mayor declared it Nina Simone Day. James Baldwin came by, Maya Angelou read on the sofa, and Shirley Chisholm campaigned there.

You could get soul food seven days a week, take a dance class, learn Swahili, and see new art on the walls. The call went out to Black artists for a show about Black heroes.

Most artists submitted a hero.

Saar decided to make a heroine instead, and she went to her shelf of ugly things. She was nervous about it, and admitted later that she had real hesitation about using images that powerful and that negative, because she knew what those pictures had already done to how Black people saw each other.

Putting one on a wall in front of her own people was a risk and she knew it. The nerves did not survive opening night.

People walked into that room in Berkeley and got it on sight, a woman built to serve standing there with a rifle and no apology on her face.

Then Betye Saar went home and waited thirty five years to find out what she had done.

In 2007, at a museum in Los Angeles, Angela Davis gave a talk and said out loud that the Black women's movement started with The Liberation of Aunt Jemima. Saar was eighty one years old when she heard it, and she called it a real thrill.

Thirty five years. Think about that gap the next time somebody tells you to be patient.

In between, she just kept working. When her great aunt Hattie died in 1974 and left behind a trunk of letters, photographs, jewelry and a broken hand mirror, Saar built the whole trunk into a piece and called it Record for Hattie.

That same year she helped organize a Los Angeles group show for Black women artists. Black folks came out to support it, the white women of the feminist art world stayed home, and she remembered that for the rest of her life.

She had a solo show at the Whitney in 1975, three years after Alma Thomas became the first Black woman to get one.

She won two National Endowment for the Arts fellowships, traveled to Nigeria, Senegal, Haiti and Brazil, and came home each time with her suitcase full of other people's cast off things.

Decades later she started building on old washboards, the ridged ones your great grandmother wore her knuckles down on, because laundry was one of the only jobs this country would hand a Black woman in 1900. She said the quiet part out loud about those boards, that somebody's hands scrubbed on them, and for all we know they were washing sheets for the Klan.

In 1997 she took a mammy crumb brush and gave it rifle bullets for arms.

She was respected and she was not treated as major, and a curator eventually admitted why. Being Black, being a woman, and working in Los Angeles instead of New York had counted against her in the art world for far too long.

She was in her eighties and nineties before the big museums came running. At ninety three she had solo exhibitions open at the same time in New York and California.

Then in June of 2020, after George Floyd was killed in Minneapolis and the whole world went into the streets, Quaker Oats announced it was retiring the Aunt Jemima name and image. That face had been on the boxes since 1889, and Saar had armed the figurine forty eight years earlier.

Her response was two words.

Oh, finally.

Then she said the rest of it, because she was never in the comfort business. Taking a face off a pancake box does not retire racism, she said, because racism is sitting in too much of the culture, and people are still out here killing each other.

On May 2 of this year the Hammer Museum in Los Angeles honored her at its annual gala, and she was ninety nine years old.

The whole room stood up.

She kept her remarks short and told them what she had been saying since 1972, that most people never realize how important art is or how deep it reaches into everything they do. Somebody asked her secret for a long life, and she offered a good diet, being out in nature, and being a California girl.

Then she went home to the house she had lived in since 1962, the one with kitchen shelves full of the very collectibles she had spent sixty years taking apart, including a foot tall Aunt Jemima syrup bottle she had covered in beads. She died there in her sleep in the early hours of Sunday morning.

She left three daughters, Lezley, Alison and Tracye, two of them artists in their own right. She left six grandchildren and a pet tortoise.

And she left a small glass fronted box in Berkeley, eleven and three quarter inches tall, still holding a rifle where a pencil used to be.

She would have turned a hundred on Thursday.

There is a child in your family right now who has never seen that face on a grocery store shelf and has no idea what it was for. That is a victory and it is also a danger.

Betye Saar spent sixty years making sure nobody could ever stand up and claim those objects were never in our kitchens, never on our shelves, never sold by the millions with our grandmothers' faces on them.

She refused to throw the evidence away.

She did not argue with it, or write a letter about it, or wait for anybody to apologize for it. She picked it up, took out what they put in its hand, and gave it something else to hold.

So mark Thursday however you mark things. And the next time this world hands you something built to keep you small, remember that a five year old girl from Watts grew up and found a third option.

You do not have to keep it, and you do not have to burn it.

You can take the pencil out.

Betye Saar spent a lifetime rescuing forgotten objects and turning them into stories America could not ignore. I research overlooked histories like hers because the people who shaped culture deserve to be remembered. If you would like to support this work and help preserve more lost histories:
https://t.co/Vm6JEQzdIW
Every coffee helps keep these stories alive.

text:
412 Football Classic: Three Nights of @wpial7 Football on the South Shore

Western Pennsylvania high school football is heading to the South Shore as the inaugural 412 Football Classic takes over F.N.B. Stadium from October 15-17. The three-night showcase will bring six WPIAL programs to the home of the Pittsburgh Riverhounds, giving players and fans a unique opportunity to experience high school football under the lights with the Pittsburgh skyline in the background.

With non-conference action kicking things off Thursday, a Class 5A conference matchup on Friday and a Class 3A battle closing out the weekend Saturday, there should be plenty of excitement throughout the event. Here is a look at each matchup and the players to watch.

Thursday, October 15 — @Nesh_Sports (6-1,4-0) vs. @NCtrojansFB (4-3, 4-0)

7 p.m. | Non-Conference Showcase

The 412 Football Classic opens Thursday night with an intriguing matchup between the Neshannock Lancers and North Catholic Trojans. Both teams will have an opportunity to make a statement on a unique stage, with the Lancers looking to showcase their offensive playmakers against a North Catholic team accustomed to challenging competition in the WPIAL.

Neshannock will look to @Colin_0817 and Antwon Bongivengo to help lead the offensive attack, while North Catholic will turn to @WillWaskiewicz as a key target in the passing game. With plenty of attention surrounding the opening night, the team that executes and takes advantage of its opportunities could come away with a memorable victory.

Friday, October 16 — @phqbclub (1-6, 0-2) vs. @Moon_Football (1-5, 1-1)

7 p.m. | Class 5A Northeast Conference

Friday night brings conference football to F.N.B. Stadium as the Penn Hills Indians take on the Moon Tigers in a Class 5A Northeast Conference showdown. With conference positioning and playoff implications in the picture, both teams will have plenty to play for under the lights.

Penn Hills will look to use its athleticism and ability to make explosive plays to put pressure on the Moon defense. The Tigers, meanwhile, will rely on a physical approach led by @jance_jr On the defensive side, @CMiller_2028 and veteran lineman Richie Defallo will be among the players looking to help Moon slow down the Indians.

This matchup could come down to which team controls the line of scrimmage, limits mistakes and makes the most of its scoring opportunities.

Saturday, October 17 — @HopewellVikesFB (6-1,3-0) vs. @OLSHFOOTBALLHS (1-6,1-1)

7 p.m. | Class 3A Western Hills Conference

The showcase wraps up Saturday night with a Western Hills Conference battle between the Hopewell Vikings and Our Lady of the Sacred Heart Chargers. With both teams competing in Class 3A, the matchup provides an opportunity to make a statement as the regular season moves toward its final stretch.

Much of the attention will be on Hopewell QB @Armstrong_Qb elite left-hander who has verbally committed to Penn State. James Armstrong gives the Vikings a major playmaker under center, with Avery Bokor serving as a key target in the passing game. Two-way contributors @MasonCumbie15 and Langston Gwinn will also be important pieces for Hopewell.

OLSH will look to counter with a disciplined, balanced effort and find ways to contain the Vikings’ passing attack. If the Chargers can make things difficult for Armstrong and force Hopewell to work for every yard, they could make Saturday’s finale a competitive finish to the three-night event.

A New Stage for Western Pennsylvania Football

The inaugural 412 Football Classic offers more than three games on the schedule. It brings six WPIAL programs to a professional venue, creates a unique atmosphere for players and fans, and gives Western Pennsylvania high school football a chance to shine against the backdrop of Pittsburgh. From Thursday’s non-conference opener to Friday’s Class 5A showdown and Saturday’s Class 3A finale, each night brings a different storyline and @TheWPIALEdition will be there.

SANDISK $SNDK HAS AT LEAST $93.9B OF CONTRACTS AND A STOCK 33% UNDER ITS HIGH:

Sandisk (SNDK) at $1,581.82, -$27.64 / -1.72% on Friday.

Six of the seven stocks on this board sit 14% to 33% under a high from the past year, and four of those six beat analysts' profit estimates last quarter. The Len5es are flagging prices that carry a worry the latest report did not show. That is a reading of the prices.

The Milpitas, California company makes the flash storage in phones, laptops and AI data centers. It is #8 of 30 on the Hypergrowth Len5, which hunts early, fast-growing companies whose growth keeps speeding up. June quarter:

- Sales: $8.97B vs $1.90B a year earlier, +372%. Profit: $6.90B, against a $23M loss.
- Growth from the quarter before: +97%, then +51%, then +15% to +20% forecast for September.

Two-thirds of the latest jump came from higher prices, and the stock fell on worry that they have peaked. Sandisk's answer: eight customers signed multi-year deals worth at least $93.9B at the lowest prices in them, covering about half of fiscal 2027's output.

The verdict: STRONG on growth, PARTIAL on speeding up, since its own forecast slows it. The number that decides it: analysts expect $46.06 a share for September, just above the top of Sandisk's $44-$46 range. What would knock Sandisk off the Hypergrowth Len5: September sales under the $10.3B bottom of its forecast. It reports Thursday, October 29, after the close, confirmed.

MOMENTUM LEN5:

AbCellera (ABCL) at $12.55, +$0.53 / +4.37% on Friday. The Vancouver drugmaker is #3 of 30 on the Momentum Len5, which hunts stocks climbing for months on company news. The news: on August 10, a trial of its menopause drug cut hot flashes 83% after one injection, against 33% on a placebo. The stock is +81% since the close before, even after a $200M stock sale at $9.75. The verdict: the news earned the climb, and nothing else holds it up, since June-quarter sales were $4.1M. What would knock it off the Momentum Len5: first data on a second drug, due by year-end, disappointing. It reports Monday, November 9, after the close, confirmed.

QUALITY-VALUE LEN5:

Ingredion (INGR) at $95.09, -$0.02 / -0.02% on Friday, after touching a one-year low. The Illinois company makes food starches and sweeteners. This Len5 hunts durable, high-quality businesses at a discount: the stock costs about 9 times the $10.30-$10.90 of adjusted profit per share, which leaves out one-time items, that it reaffirmed for 2026. The worry is a purchase: in June it agreed to buy Tate & Lyle (TATYY) at $29.85, +$0.00 / +0.00% on Friday, a UK ingredients maker, for about $3.5B in cash, more than half its own market value. The verdict: the discount is real, and durability depends on absorbing the deal. What would knock it off the Quality-Value Len5: a cut to that $10.30. It reports tentatively Tuesday, November 3.

DEEP-VALUE & SPECIAL-SITUATIONS LEN5:

Broadridge (BR) at $165.45, +$0.24 / +0.15% on Friday. The New York company runs shareholder voting and mailings for companies. This Len5 hunts a strong business priced below a cautious value by trouble that can pass. The stock is 30% under its October 2025 high, at about 17 times the $9.60 of adjusted profit per share it earned in fiscal 2026. The worry: tokenized shares, ownership recorded as digital tokens, and paperless shareholder mail could wear down a steady business, though its contract-based sales grew 8%. The verdict: the business is not shrinking, and the price is paying for it to start. What would knock it off the Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5: contract-based sales growth under the 6% bottom of its fiscal 2027 forecast. It reports tentatively Tuesday, November 3.

GROWTH LEN5:

Penske Automotive Group (PAG) at $196.16, -$1.89 / -0.95% on Friday. The Michigan company runs car and truck dealerships and is #6 of 30 on the Growth Len5, which hunts profit growth at a fair price: about 14 times earnings, a profit in each of the last five years. The twist: on July 22 the private Penske Corporation and Mitsui & Co. (MITSY) at $608.00, +$3.05 / +0.50% on Friday, which own 72.6%, offered $210 a share in cash for the rest, with no decision date set. PAG closed $195.19 before the offer, $214.57 after, $196.16 Friday. The verdict: the price has given back the offer's jump, and June-quarter adjusted profit per share was $3.62 vs $3.78 a year earlier. What would knock it off the Growth Len5: a September quarter under last year's $3.23. It reports tentatively Wednesday, October 28.

HYPERGROWTH LEN5:

BridgeBio Pharma (BBIO) at $65.35, +$0.31 / +0.48% on Friday. The California drugmaker sells Attruby, a pill for a heart disease caused by protein build-up, and is #3 of 30 on the Hypergrowth Len5, which hunts early, fast-growing companies whose growth keeps speeding up. June quarter: sales $243.7M vs $110.6M a year earlier, Attruby +23% from March. The verdict: the growth is fast, and the quarter still lost $152.2M. What would knock it off the Hypergrowth Len5: Attruby growth from June to September under 23%. It reports tentatively Wednesday, October 28, after the close; the FDA's decision date for a second drug is November 27.

INCOME LEN5:

Global Ship Lease (GSL) at $44.58, -$0.90 / -1.98% on Friday. The Athens company rents 71 container ships to shipping lines at fixed daily rates. It is #1 of 30 on the Income Len5, which hunts cash returned to owners that the business covers. The dividend is $2.50 a year, 5.6% at Friday's price. June-quarter profit was $2.48 a share, so one quarter's $0.625 took 25% of it. Charters cover 100% of 2026 ship days and 90% of 2027. The verdict: covered about four times over and mostly contracted. What would knock it off the Income Len5: profit per share sliding toward the dividend as charters renew at lower rates. It reports tentatively Monday, November 9.

Four reports beat estimates, and the prices still sit well under a high. October 28 and 29 bring the first answers.

The main uncertainty is Tien’s own recent sequence. His Shanghai victory followed defeats in Beijing and at the US Open, so this is a favourable matchup assessment with limited room for a larger stake.

Ekaterina Alexandrova vs Leylah Fernandez — a familiar puzzle

Preview · WTA 1000 Wuhan · First round · Monday 12 October 2026

Only two ranking places separate Ekaterina Alexandrova and Leylah Fernandez, which makes this an evenly balanced first-round match on paper. The history between them, and what each did in Beijing, offer some separation, but not much.

THE MATCHUP

Alexandrova is ranked 28th, a year on from reaching her career-high of 10 in October 2025. At 31 and 1.75 m, she has five career titles, although her record of 17-22 this season has been uneven. Fernandez is ranked 26th, with a career-high of 13 from August 2022. The 24-year-old Canadian left-hander stands 1.68 m, holds six career titles and has a 22-23 record this season.

They have met four times, all on hard courts, and Alexandrova leads 3-1. Fernandez won the first of those meetings, 6-3 6-4 in the round of 32 in Adelaide in 2022. Alexandrova then won 6-4 7-5 in Cincinnati later that year, 7-6(4) 5-7 6-4 at the 2023 US Open and, most recently, 6-4 3-6 6-2 in the round of 32 in Adelaide in 2025. Most of those meetings were close, and Alexandrova has more often found a way to finish the job.

Fernandez's left-handed game changes the angles Alexandrova usually sees, which makes the head-to-head record all the more relevant.

FORM & CONTEXT

Alexandrova arrives off a strong week. In Beijing she beat Aliaksandra Sasnovich 6-1 6-4, Diana Shnaider 3-6 6-4 6-3 and Linda Noskova 6-2 6-2, before losing a tight quarter-final to Mirra Andreeva 6-7(4) 6-7(3).

Fernandez has had a high and a low in quick succession. She won the WTA 500 title in Singapore, beating Mirra Andreeva 6-2 7-5 in the quarter-finals, Maja Chwalinska 1-6 6-4 6-2 in the semi-finals and Talia Gibson 7-5 6-0 in the final. In her next tournament, though, she lost her opening match in Beijing, 2-6 6-4 3-6 to Kamilla Rakhimova.

This is the first match in Wuhan for both, on the same outdoor hard surface they used in Beijing.

THE DECIDING FACTOR

Alexandrova's Beijing campaign is the fresher evidence: a quarter-final on this surface, ending in two tie-breaks against Mirra Andreeva. Fernandez's Singapore title shows how dangerous she can be, but her early exit in Beijing interrupted that momentum. With the head-to-head also in Alexandrova's favour, the balance tilts slightly her way, though her uneven season keeps that lean a modest one.

THE CALL

The rankings are too close to separate them, but the 3-1 record and Alexandrova's stronger week in Beijing give her a slender edge in what should still be a close contest.

Ekaterina Alexandrova to win, low confidence.

text:
Jiri Lehecka vs Rafael Jodar — the Tokyo finalist meets his Montreal conqueror

Preview · ATP 1000 Shanghai · Third round · Monday 12 October 2026

Jiri Lehecka comes into this third-round meeting on the strength of a run to the Tokyo final last week. Rafael Jodar, ranked three places higher, holds the only head-to-head win between them. Two players who opened in Shanghai with three-set wins on Saturday now meet for a place in the last 16.

THE MATCHUP

The rankings barely separate them: Jodar is 13, Lehecka 16. Jodar, 20 and 191 cm, has a 38-16 record at tour level this season and won his first title in 2026. Lehecka, 24 and 185 cm, is 34-18 at tour level this season and has two career titles.

Their only meeting came earlier this season at the Masters 1000 event in Montreal, on an outdoor hard court, where Jodar won their last-16 match 6-3 6-3. That is a clear result on a similar surface and the strongest argument in Jodar's favour.

FORM & CONTEXT

Since then, the two have headed in different directions. Lehecka reached the Tokyo final, beating Zizou Bergs 6-3 6-7(3) 6-3, Ugo Humbert 5-7 6-4 6-4, Adolfo Daniel Vallejo 6-1 6-1 and Valentin Vacherot 6-4 6-2, before Carlos Alcaraz beat him 7-6(4) 6-4 in the final. At the Davis Cup he beat Ben Shelton 6-4 6-4 and Learner Tien 6-3 7-5.

Jodar's last few weeks have been patchier. He beat Alexander Bublik 6-2 6-3 at the Laver Cup and Cristian Garin 6-0 6-2 at the Davis Cup, but in Tokyo he lost his opening match 1-6 3-6 to the same Vallejo whom Lehecka later beat 6-1 6-1 in the quarter-finals. At the US Open he lost in the first round to Yunchaokete Bu 2-6 1-6 1-6.

Shanghai has offered little to choose between them. On Saturday Lehecka beat Nuno Borges 6-3 3-6 6-3 in 1:58:30, while Jodar came from a set down to beat Thiago Agustin Tirante 4-6 6-2 6-3 in 2:02:48. Both dropped a set, the durations were within a few minutes of each other, and both had Sunday off, so neither carries a physical edge into Monday.

THE DECIDING FACTOR

Recent level against the head-to-head. Jodar's 6-3 6-3 in Montreal shows he knows how to hurt Lehecka on a hard court, but Lehecka has since put together the more convincing stretch of the two, with a run to the Tokyo final and Davis Cup wins over Shelton and Tien. Jodar's defeats to Vallejo and Bu show a level that has dipped since the summer, and that is where Lehecka can turn round the Montreal result.

THE CALL

This is a genuinely open match. The ranking gap is negligible, the head-to-head belongs to Jodar, and their first matches in Shanghai were almost identical. The difference is in the weeks between Montreal and now, where Lehecka's results have been clearly stronger, and that is enough for a narrow lean towards the Czech.

Jiri Lehecka to win, low confidence.

Jeremiah 5-6 & 2 Timothy 4 | October 12th | 2026 Global Bible Journey

Experience the Word of God in a new, immersive way.

It’s About Growth, Not a Checklist

As we continue through October 2026, remember that this journey is about genuine spiritual growth, not just "checking a box" for the day. Our goal is to let these scriptures transform our perspective and our priorities. If you missed a few days or are just joining us for the first time—don’t worry! Just jump right in with us today. The path to growth is always open, and there is no "behind" in this study.

Today’s Reading

In Jeremiah 5–6, the prophet searches the streets of Jerusalem for even one person who does justice and seeks truth, revealing a deeply entrenched rebellion from the least to the greatest. The Lord sounds the trumpet of warning against impending siege from the north, exposing false prophets who heal wounds superficially by saying "Peace, peace," when there is no peace, while urging the people to ask for the ancient paths where the good way is and walk in it to find rest for their souls. Turning to the New Testament, 2 Timothy 4 brings Paul’s final letter to a stirring conclusion. Paul solemnly charges Timothy before God and Christ Jesus to preach the word in season and out of season, reproving, rebuking, and exhorting with complete patience and teaching. Anticipating his departure, Paul offers his triumphant testimony: "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith," resting in the assurance of the crown of righteousness awarded by the righteous Judge. text:
The law was written to be permissive: HB 904 allows licensed tracks to offer fixed-odds wagering, but never requires them to do so. Coverage at the time of passage stated explicitly that the bill doesn’t require Kentucky tracks to offer it.  The state authorizes a product and creates the licensing and tax framework, and each business decides whether to participate or not. 

Even if the rules were finalized tomorrow, Keeneland would still need an operator, a risk-management setup, and wagering systems in place within a few weeks. A spring 2027 launch, perhaps at the Keeneland Spring Meet, looks far more realistic than having it be implemented at the Breeders' Cup.  CDI flat out said "no" to having it at their tracks because their pari-mutual and ADW business are already highly-profitable.

text:
😂🤣 Boss, I understand your point, and you have raised a fair observation. But let’s not confuse a coastal highway with a beachfront driveway! 😂 A coastal road does not necessarily have to hug the Atlantic Ocean from beginning to end to retain its identity.

Even in the United States, we have several examples worth considering:

🇺🇸 Pacific Coast Highway (California): Portions of the coastal highway system run inland, passing through towns, hills, and developed communities rather than following the oceanfront continuously.

🇺🇸 U.S. Route 1 (Florida): This major coastal corridor passes through cities and inland sections while continuing to serve the Atlantic coastal region.

🇺🇸 U.S. Route 17 (East Coast): Known as the Coastal Highway in some areas, it travels significantly inland through states such as Virginia, North Carolina, and South Carolina.

🇺🇸 U.S. Route 101 (Oregon and Washington): Although widely associated with the Pacific Coast, portions run inland to accommodate geography, settlements, and transportation needs.

My brother, if these established coastal highways can have inland sections while retaining their coastal identity, surely we can acknowledge that a coastal highway does not need to offer an uninterrupted ocean view throughout its entire journey! 😂🤣

Of course, your observation about the proposed diversion of almost 300 km is worth examining. That is a substantial distance, and understanding the engineering justification, approved alignment, and implications for the communities involved is important.

Road construction involves several considerations, including terrain, environmental impact, construction feasibility, existing infrastructure, safety, and economic connectivity.

Ultimately, a coastal highway can be identified by the broader transportation corridor it serves, even when portions of its alignment move inland. The important question is whether the revised route continues to fulfill the project’s intended purpose.

And knowing that we both want meaningful infrastructure development and progress for Nigeria, I believe these are the kinds of constructive discussions worth having.

After all, my brother, a coastal highway shouldn’t have to swim inside the Atlantic Ocean before we agree to call it coastal! 😂🤣🎯

text:
@RBReich, how can an economist be this wrong about the economy?

You walked into my classroom with a six-minute video and a claim that the billionaire class is going all-in for Trump and the GOP so they can avoid paying their "fair share." Pull up a chair. I've got a red pen, a planning period, and a list of reasons this argument has more holes than a screen door on a submarine.

First the video. Jeff Bezos says you could double the taxes he pays and it still wouldn't help that teacher in Queens. You and Zucman treat it like a gotcha. It's not. Bezos can structure things so he reports little or no taxable income in a given year—no salary, no dividends, no realized gains. That's legal under the rules Congress wrote. Doubling zero is still zero. The fix isn't a new tax on paper stock he hasn't sold. It's closing the holes the people in Washington keep leaving open. Trying to reason with this framing is like trying to baptize a cat.

Then the big number: the richest 0.00001% of Americans—19 households—hold the equivalent of 14% of U.S. GDP in wealth, roughly $4 trillion.

Professor, I teach this exact mistake to fifteen-year-olds in the first week of physics. GDP is a rate. Dollars per year. Wealth is a stock. Dollars sitting there. Comparing the two is like saying your car has driven 150,000 miles and calling that 2,500 times the speed limit. It sounds scary. It means nothing. All the homes in America are worth more than one year of GDP. All the retirement accounts are too. That doesn't make Grandma's 401(k) a crisis. Your units are scrambled like a breakfast buffet at a cheap hotel. If one of my freshmen turned that in, I'd circle the units in red, write "SEE ME," and give him a chance to fix it. An economist who mixes a stock with a flow is more confused than a chameleon in a bag of Skittles.

You also say billionaires went from 1% of campaign spending in 2000 to 19% in 2024, and that's why the tax code is rigged. The top income-tax payers already pay the large majority of the federal income tax. The people who write the code sit in Congress. They draw the line one inch above their own heads every time, then act shocked when the people below it notice. In 1913 the income tax was a tiny levy on a handful of rich men. They swore it would never touch the working man. Go look at your paycheck stub and tell me how small it stayed. You speak an infinite deal of nothing on this one.

Zucman's proposal is a 2% minimum tax on net worth above $100 million. If someone is already paying the equivalent of 2% of their wealth in taxes, they owe nothing more. Only the ones "not paying their fair share" get hit.

"Fair share" is doing a lot of work there. France, Sweden, and Germany tried wealth taxes. They exempted the big shareholdings or valued them at a fraction of reality, then watched the money leave and the revenue disappoint. They backed out. Your video says the new version fixes that by having no exemptions. Europe already tried versions of that. The capital still left, or the valuation fights ate the revenue, or both. California is watching the same movie with Prop 40—people and assets already moving before the vote. You can't tax a moving truck. You can only wave at it. This plan is about as useful as a solar-powered night light. Or a screen door on a spaceship. Or training wheels on a tank.

And the political claim. Some billionaires are backing Trump and the GOP. Elon Musk put real money behind it in 2024. Others put real money behind Democrats—Bloomberg, Moskovitz, Hoffman, and the rest of the usual list. Both sides get checks. The difference is which set of policies those donors think will leave them with more capital and more room to build. That's not a conspiracy. That's incentives. When the tax, the regulation, and the energy policy make the next factory or the next headquarters more expensive in one place than another, the headquarters move. Texas and Florida noticed. San Francisco noticed too. You're all hat and no cattle on the "billionaires only support Republicans" line.

Here's the part that still bothers me as a veteran. Washington can find the will for a 2% tax on paper wealth "so the rich pay their fair share," but it still hasn't found the $10 billion over ten years for the Major Richard Star Act so combat-wounded, medically retired soldiers stop having their retirement docked dollar-for-dollar against their disability pay. That's about a billion a year. Pocket lint next to the numbers in your video. I'm one of those medically retired soldiers. The government that broke us still takes it back every month. If the fight is about greed, start with the greed coming out of a wounded vet's check.

My standing offer still holds. I keep hearing people with nine-figure households and book royalties yell "tax the rich" while they know every loophole and use the ones they wrote. File with the standard deduction. No itemizing. Pay double what the IRS says you owe and post the return. Then I'll sit still for the sermon on fairness. Until then you're the human version of a buffering wheel that never finishes.

Quinn's Law #1: liberal policies always do the opposite of what they promise. You want more revenue for schools, healthcare, and infrastructure, so you write a tax that chases the people who create the jobs and the taxable income to other states. The money doesn't stay. The companies don't either. The brain is an amazing organ. It starts working in the womb and doesn’t stop until you get elected to Congress—or apparently until you become a former Labor Secretary selling this.

But what do I know? I'm only a science teacher in a high-need district in Northeast Ohio, a retired Army combat medic, and a father of four who noticed that an economist who can't tell a stock from a flow is about as useful as a waterproof sponge in a rainstorm.

@TPUSA #MAGA #Veterans #Trump

text:
🇺🇲 🇺🇦 🇷🇺 FT: US officials are phoning Kyiv and European capitals to threaten the PURL weapons channel and intelligence sharing over Ukraine's refinery strikes

The United States is threatening to halt the main channel through which Europe buys American weapons for Ukraine, in order to pressure Kyiv to stop striking Russian oil refineries, the Financial Times reported on Sunday. Citing European officials who received calls or were briefed on them, the paper said US officials phoned Kyiv and European capitals on Oct. 10 and 11 and warned they could cut off intelligence sharing and PURL, the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List. "They are calling everyone," one official was quoted as saying. The FT named Pavlo Palisa, a deputy head of Zelensky's office, as one person contacted. The White House declined to confirm or comment on the calls, the FT said.

PURL is the NATO mechanism under which allies pay for US-made equipment and ammunition for Ukraine. Militarnyi, a Ukrainian outlet, put the total funded through it at more than $6 billion as of June. The threat would hit European budgets as much as Kyiv. Earlier Axios reporting said a Ukrainian source claimed a threat to intelligence sharing was made in Miami, while a US official denied that Trump's representatives had explicitly threatened a cutoff. Oleksandr Merezhko, head of Ukraine's foreign affairs committee, told the Guardian a cutoff of US intelligence would "blind" Ukraine's air defences, and that Ukraine would keep hitting refineries regardless.

The pressure runs alongside incentives for Moscow. The New York Times has reported that US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner offered Russia three inducements for a limited energy or maritime ceasefire: unlocking up to $100 billion in frozen Russian sovereign assets, approval of a Lukoil foreign-asset sale to Middle Eastern investors, some of whom have business ties to the envoys, and sanctions relief to let Belarus export potash. According to the Kyiv Post, Ukraine asked for safeguards including matching releases from the frozen assets and guaranteed military aid if Russia breaks a truce. These are anonymous-source accounts. No official has confirmed the terms.

The thread running through the weekend is fuel prices before the Nov. 3 midterms. Reuters reported that Trump blames Ukraine's refinery strikes for prices that threaten his party, and Ukraine says it has put out of action more than 45 percent of Russian refining capacity, a Ukrainian military claim. Trump announced an energy ceasefire on Sunday that Zelensky said he learned about from the news. If the FT account holds, the sequence is carrots for Moscow and a possible weapons squeeze on Kyiv, with the White House saying nothing on the record about either.

 Video peeps at Castro's family life

By Nancy San Martin. nsanmartin@herald.com. Posted on Mon, Nov. 11, 2002 in The Miami Herald

Snippets of a home video capturing private moments of Fidel Castro and his family will begin airing tonight on news programs on Miami's Spanish-language Univisión -- the first of a 10-part series that aims to uncover the much-guarded secret life of the Cuban leader.

The video obtained by WLTV-23 was taken out of the island by a friend of a former girlfriend of one of Castro's sons who recently fled Cuba.

Dashiell Torralba, 27, who had a two-year relationship with Antonio Castro Soto del Valle, Castro's son, tells reporter Mario Vallejo that she decided to release the video to seek revenge against the Cuban leader's longtime wife, Dalia Soto del Valle, with whom she had a tumultuous relationship.

''I wanted to get Dalia for all the damage she did to me,'' Torralba says in the television interview taped within the last month at an undisclosed Latin American country.

''What this segment does is demystifies the image of Castro as an imposing figure,'' Vallejo said. "For the first time, the world will be able to see the house of Fidel Castro -- the most secret place in Cuba -- the faces of his children and grandchildren and how they live.''

Antonio is one of five sons between Castro and Soto del Valle. He is known to have at least four others, including his first-born ''Fidelito'' and daughter Alina Fernández, who defected several years ago and is a vocal critic of Castro.

The segment, The Secret Life of Fidel Castro, offers a rare glimpse of the personal life of Castro, who has managed to maintain a high level of privacy throughout his 43-year rule. The state-run media in Cuba has never identified his immediate family and none of his offspring hold publicly visible jobs.

He has consistently declined to answer personal questions from international media, saying that national leaders should never mix their public and private lives. Castro also has said that his privacy was necessary because of security concerns given the hundreds of assassination attempts he says the CIA and exiles from Miami have mounted against him since 1959.

WLTV said it uses the 40-minute video it purchased from Torralba as a springboard to expose other secrets, such as Castro's private residential compound west of Havana known as Punto Cero, or Point Zero, and alleged ''illicit undertakings'' involving Castro's sons. The station declined to reveal how much it paid for the tape.

Tonight, viewers will see various family moments including Castro dressed casually at a dinner table set with elaborate dinnerware; grandchildren interacting with relatives; and Antonio zooming through the patio on a scooter.

Antonio Castro, an orthopedic surgeon, met Torralba in Havana after he divorced his first wife. Torralba blames their breakup on Soto del Valle. The friction apparently stems from the fact that Torralba is the niece of former Transport Minister Diocles Torralba, who was imprisoned on corruption charges as part of the high-profile 1989 drug-trafficking case that involved a number of high-ranking government and military officials, some of whom were executed.

''The important thing with this video is that people will see the other face of Castro,'' said Vallejo, a former television reporter in Cuba who left the island in 1997. "He preaches equality but that's just for everyone else, not him.''

The segment will air weekdays over the next two weeks on the 6 p.m. and 11 p.m. broadcasts of Noticias 23, WLTV's news hours.

text:
I had many odd jobs before graduating (building labourer, industrial cleaner, picker & packer, nightshift factory worker, retail), but my first degree-related one was in a summer in a water authority.

Most of the people in my team were just waiting for retirement. They’d talk about how much they despised the organisation they worked decades for while embodying the toxic culture that bred that resentment.

I recall them taking calls from developers waiting months for approvals, who’d explain to them the impacts on the builders, subcontractors and homeowners waiting downstream of their inaction. And I recall them hanging up the phone angry that somebody had the gall to follow them up. One time I even heard the team leader say “bottom of the pile for you” because the person on the other end of the line dare question his work ethic.

But I was eager to put my engineering to good use. I didn’t specialise in software, but understood systems and thought that the software, hardware and processes that governed the way the team interfaced internally and externally was archaic, inefficient and plainly ineffective.

I took the initiative to get in touch with the ‘innovation’ team and worked for weeks with them on an entirely new system that didn’t rely on the legacy technology in place, reduced interface steps and slashed administration. One day my group manager told me not to pursue it because too many peoples’ jobs would be affected and I didn’t have the authority to implement change.

So I spent most of my time reading online articles – and ironically, trying to make the most of my very unproductive introduction to industry, came across Ayn Rand and absorbed myself in free market economics.

When I wasn’t asking for more tasks or filling the voids reading, I used the company cars to drive to sites to watch capital works construction. Sometimes I’d be told by my own colleagues not to visit their site (and I knew it was because they didn’t want anybody monitoring them).

Needless to say, it was a thoroughly disappointing and eye-opening experience.

I could see from those few months how organisations with poor leadership can expel the very people they need while incentivising the worst people to stay.

text:
🇺🇲 🇮🇷 Murphy says Democrats should refuse to fund the Iran war if they win in November, and Barrasso answers that Senate Democrats already blocked the defense bill

Sen. Chris Murphy gave Democrats a closing message on Sunday and it is about money. Asked on CBS's Face the Nation what the party offers beyond "we're not Trump," the Connecticut Democrat said: "We should promise that if we win this election, we are not going to fund this war. We're not going to approve money for the Department of Defense without a commitment from the Trump administration that this war ends." 

Host Margaret Brennan had just cited CBS polling in which 58 percent of registered voters call the Democratic Party weak. Murphy said the war has been a disaster for the economy and for America's reputation, and that a promise to end it, plus a fight against corruption, "could result in a landslide." The midterms are on Nov. 3, 23 days away.

Murphy had just returned from Saudi Arabia and Qatar, and he described a war "spiraling out of control." By his account, Iran is restarting nuclear research at its Pickaxe Mountain site, which he said comes from open source reporting, and 20 Americans are dead with $100 billion spent. He said the administration is running an "active cover-up" of base damage. 

Brennan said the Congressional Budget Office has been unable to estimate that damage because the Pentagon has not supplied the information. Murphy opposed US involvement in Yemen after Saturday's Riyadh airport attack and urged Washington to "unilaterally end American hostilities." Jewish Insider reported on Oct. 9 that he wants Democrats to withhold Pentagon appropriations and a defense authorization bill next year without specific requirements to end the war.

Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso, a Wyoming Republican, answered later in the same broadcast. "He says, 'well, we ought to not fund things,'" Barrasso said. He argued that Democrats voted against the National Defense Authorization Act, calling it the first time in 65 years the bill has not passed, and said "the Democrats are all voting no on supporting our troops." 

CBS reported on July 14 that the Senate rejected an initial procedural vote on the NDAA, 50 to 46, with Democrats such as Sen. Richard Blumenthal calling the bill "a referendum on the Iran war." Thune also voted no, which lets him bring the bill back. Barrasso separated the authorization bill from the spending bills Murphy was describing.

The two answers show the fight Democrats and Republicans will carry to Election Day. Congress holds the funding power, and Murphy is telling voters that a Democratic majority would use it on the war. Barrasso says the party that blocks the defense bill cannot claim to support troops, and that lawmakers will be back after the elections. A pledge to withhold money is a campaign promise, and any spending bill would still need both chambers and a presidential signature or a veto override. https://t.co/R6VEn0i0TM

text:
PEACE TALKS

BERTRAND’S FINAL BOX

At present, “peace talks” increasingly resemble an excuse for jet travel, photographs and posh lunches.

How do you convince an adversary of genuine intent when every diplomatic proposal arrives with another kinetic layer attached?

Washington speaks of restraint while enforcing a blockade with military force. 

Tehran offers negotiations while attaching seven conditions, mining maritime space and threatening regional infrastructure. 

The Houthis negotiate through repeated attacks on civilian aviation.

Then comes the most dangerous contradiction: the United States is preparing a $2.8 billion package for Israel containing 40,000 additional 2,000-pound aerial bombs, 20,000 Mk-84s and 20,000 BLU-117s.

This is not the removal of a kinetic layer.

It is the industrial reinforcement of one.

Nor is Israel currently a predictable partner pursuing a clearly bounded Levantine settlement. 

Its government continues to widen tactical freedom while resisting the political constraints required for strategic stability.

That does not absolve Iran, Hezbollah, Hamas or the Houthis. 

It explains why none will believe Western assurances that today’s negotiation limits tomorrow’s bombardment.

This is Bertrand’s Box in its purest form.

Washington believes it is selecting leverage for peace.

Tehran sees preparation for another war.

Israel sees strategic freedom.

The Levant receives another generation of instability.

Diplomacy cannot work when every party arrives carrying a menu in one hand and a bomb inventory in the other.

Peace requires credible restraint, not merely better lunches between airstrikes.

text:
🇺🇸 NANCY PELOSI SAID WHAT MILLIONS OF AMERICANS WERE THINKING. NOW WASHINGTON IS TURNING ON ITSELF.

There's an old saying: people united by a common enemy often turn on each other when that enemy disappears.

Look at Washington.

Trump against Pelosi. Pelosi against Trump. Republicans fighting Republicans. Democrats fighting Democrats. Everyone talking about justice, accountability, and the Constitution while the political establishment tears itself apart.

Back in 2019, Politico reported that Nancy Pelosi had told senior Democrats something remarkable about Donald Trump:

**“I don't want to see him impeached, I want to see him in prison.”**

She understood that impeachment was a political process. Criminal accountability was something else entirely.

Seven years later, Trump has survived two impeachments. He has returned to the White House. The Epstein files continue to raise questions about powerful people and their connections. And Washington is still fighting over who should be held accountable.

But there's another scandal that deserves far more attention.

**What happened to the Ukrainians America promised to protect?**

When Russia launched its full-scale invasion, American politicians stood in front of cameras waving Ukrainian flags. They promised solidarity, safety, and refuge.

Thousands of Ukrainians entered the United States through Uniting for Ukraine, humanitarian parole, and other immigration protections. Now some of those same people face detention, immigration uncertainty, and the possibility of deportation.

Think about that. America offered people fleeing Russian bombs a place to rebuild their lives. Now some are facing the American immigration detention system.

And that system has a business model.

GEO Group and CoreCivic are publicly traded corporations that operate detention facilities under government contracts. Immigration detention generates revenue. More detention capacity and occupied beds can mean more money flowing through those contracts.

**Human suffering has become part of a corporate revenue stream.**

That should disturb Americans regardless of whether they vote Republican or Democrat.

The politicians who once posed with Ukrainian flags should have to explain what happens to the families they welcomed when their immigration protections become uncertain.

Pelosi wanted Trump in prison. Trump wants his enemies investigated. Both parties accuse the other of corruption.

Meanwhile, ordinary people are trapped in a system where political promises can disappear overnight, but detention contracts remain profitable.

Washington doesn't need another theatrical confrontation. It needs accountability — for politicians, for immigration authorities, and for corporations profiting from detention.

America promised Ukrainians refuge from war. That promise should mean something.
