I.The Hidden Architecture of Living Causes and the Passage from Organic Matter to Supernatural Intelligence

There exists within Martyn Paine's monumental Institutes of Medicine an extraordinary investigation of the moment at which a physical impression becomes an organic operation, an organic operation becomes an intelligible correspondence, and the correspondence discloses questions of agency extending beyond the material instrument through which it is manifested. 

The author's examination of the solar spectrum, the selective excitability of the retina, the formative energy of the embryonic germ, and the propagation of nervous influence through distant organs establishes an unusually intricate philosophy of living causation. Its most penetrating inquiry concerns the origin and determination of powers whose effects are visible while their governing principles remain concealed within the constitution of living nature.

One of the most remarkable passages occurs in Paine's consideration of the chemical and physiological properties of light. 

Drawing upon the optical investigations of his colleague John William Draper, he enters a world of spectral individuality, photochemical transformation, vegetal organization, and the differential sensibility of living tissues. 

The common solar beam is resolved into rays possessing distinct illuminating, calorific, chemical, and phosphorogenic properties.

 Silver compounds undergo transformations under particular regions of the spectrum; chlorine exhibits selective reactions; vegetation responds through changes of growth and movement; and substances such as the diamond are discussed in connection with the production of phosphorescent luminosity. The sevenfold appearance of visible light consequently opens upon a much larger classification of radiant agencies, several of which escape ordinary vision while remaining capable of producing remarkable physical effects.[1]

Here the anatomical instrument becomes indispensable to the manifestation of the phenomenon. A ray that produces a chemical alteration in a mineral substance may excite a particular sensation in the retina or contribute to a physiological change in a plant. Paine proceeds from the peculiar properties of the ray to the corresponding susceptibility of the receiving structure. The significance resides in this double determination. An external agency possesses its own character, while the organized substance upon which it acts possesses a distinctive constitution through which the final phenomenon is expressed.

The implications are extensive. Light, heat, electricity, atmospheric constituents, and chemical substances become subjects of investigation through their varying relationships with living tissues. The peculiarities of the receiving organ assume an importance equal to the characteristics of the external agent. Paine's resulting doctrine of organic individuality extends into nutrition, secretion, generation, sensation, pathological alteration, and the physiological operation of remedies.

The same principle governs his treatment of the nervous system, where the intricacy of organic correspondence reaches an exceptional degree.

The cerebrospinal apparatus, ganglionic structures, sympathetic nervous system, and pneumogastric nerves become the principal instruments through which impressions are transmitted, modified, and manifested among distant parts of the animal economy.

 Paine investigates their operations through a succession of experiments concerning muscular activity, the circulation of blood, the movements of the alimentary canal, secretion, respiration, and the responses of capillary vessels.
His threefold classification of remote, contiguous, and continuous sympathy offers a remarkably elaborate scheme of organic relations. Remote sympathy concerns the transmission of impressions between separated structures. Contiguous sympathy brings local nervous arrangements into consideration, particularly ganglia and plexuses. Continuous sympathy concerns the propagation of physiological or pathological influence through adjoining portions of a tissue. These distinctions provide the means for investigating how an impression may affect the original structure, spread through its immediate anatomical neighborhood, or produce a response in a distant organ.[2]

One particularly striking example concerns the influence of sunlight upon sneezing. The original impression enters through the visual apparatus, yet its consequences are manifested through respiratory and nasal activity. Paine treats the occurrence as an intricate example of nervous transmission, involving successive operations through the sensory and reflex mechanisms. 

The phenomenon is especially significant because the initiating agent and the responding apparatus belong to different functional arrangements.

The retina receives the physical impression, the nervous apparatus transmits and modifies its consequences, and the respiratory structures perform the resulting action. Thus a solar influence, apparently confined to vision, becomes capable of occasioning a complex bodily event.

The same principle appears in his analysis of grief, fear, disgust, anger, anticipation, and voluntary determination. Grief may be accompanied by lacrimation, fear by changes in cardiac activity and secretion, disgust by disturbances of the alimentary apparatus, and mental excitement by alterations in muscular activity and organic responsiveness. 

These phenomena are examined through the physiological relationships between intellectual impressions and nervous influence. 

The passions acquire a distinct organological significance, each revealing how mental activity may be followed by particular changes in the bodily economy.
Paine carries the investigation into the experimental distinction between the nature of an influence and the mechanism through which it produces its effects.
A single muscular apparatus may respond to voluntary determination or involuntary stimulation. Respiration may proceed without deliberate attention while remaining susceptible to conscious modification. Vomiting may arise through gastric irritation, medicinal influence, pregnancy, or mental emotion. The visible operation may therefore be similar while its initiating circumstances differ profoundly.
These observations become part of a philosophical inquiry into the relationships between the will, nervous activity, reflex causation, and the independent faculties of mind.

The implications extend into the physiology of disease.

Paine's doctrine of the specific vital constitution of tissues concerns the individuality of organic structures and their unequal susceptibility to external agencies. The mucous, muscular, serous, and vascular components of an organ possess differing physiological properties. An impression capable of provoking extensive alteration in one structure may produce a comparatively limited effect in another. The same organ consequently contains a diversity of susceptibilities, each associated with its particular arrangement and function.
This doctrine permits Paine to examine pathological phenomena through the relationship between organic locality and general constitutional condition. Inflammation, venous congestion, fever, changes of secretion, and disturbances of circulation are investigated as manifestations of altered organic properties whose effects may extend beyond their immediate anatomical origin.

Particularly important is his conception of the mutability of vital properties. The physiological condition of a structure may be altered by age, disease, climate, previous exposure, habitual influences, and the actions of medicinal substances. An agent acting upon a healthy tissue may produce effects different from those occasioned when the same structure has undergone pathological modification. 

The history of the organism becomes an element in the determination of its present susceptibility.

From these principles emerges Paine's comprehensive doctrine of vital habit, a subject especially valuable for the historical study of constitutional physiology. Acquired conditions, reproductive maturation, previous illness, and the successive periods of life are understood through changes in the organism's powers of responsiveness. The alteration of the organic constitution becomes a connecting principle between development, disease, therapeutic intervention, and the capacity for recovery.[3]

The question of organic form introduces an even more remarkable order of investigation.
In the incubated egg, Paine encounters a developing organization whose original material constituents undergo an extensive and highly ordered transformation. From the germinal structure arise tissues, organs, vessels, and physiological arrangements that acquire their characteristic functions during development. He examines the relationship between the nutritive materials present in the egg and the formative operations through which those materials become incorporated into the growing organism.

The problem is one of extraordinary philosophical depth. The chemical composition of the original material, the successive appearance of anatomical structures, and the acquisition of differentiated physiological properties must all be considered. Paine's doctrine of vital affinity supplies part of his explanation for the organized transformations taking place within the developing germ.
The subject acquires additional significance when approached through the biblical language of generation.

Ecclesiastes 11:5 directs attention to the hidden way of the spirit and the formation of bones within the womb. Psalm 139:13–16 develops the imagery of bodily formation through the language of inward possession, intricate workmanship, and the divine knowledge of the organism before its completed appearance. These passages furnish a remarkable theological correspondence for the embryological problem that occupies Paine's investigations: the appearance of organized form through processes whose governing order exceeds what can be discovered from the individual material constituents alone.
The distinction between the materials of formation and the governing principle of formation becomes central to this inquiry.
Pausing over the developing embryo, one encounters a succession of increasingly specialized structures whose appearance is coordinated with the establishment of particular functions. The physiological problem concerns the properties through which these transformations occur. The theological question concerns the wisdom according to which the living form is constituted.

Proverbs 3:19–20 supplies a particularly significant anchor for this second question. Wisdom, understanding, and knowledge appear as the governing attributes through which the foundations of the earth, the establishment of the heavens, and the opening of the depths are described. The scriptural arrangement links intelligent causation with the ordered operations of nature, permitting the investigator to examine physiological formation within the larger philosophical problem of creative wisdom.

The same correspondence acquires exceptional force in Proverbs 8:22–31, where Wisdom is represented in relation to primordial creation, the appointment of boundaries, and the establishment of the foundations of the earth. 

The passages provide a rich framework for considering the relationship between intelligible order, natural structure, and the determination of form.

Paine's treatment of the vegetal kingdom extends these questions into the operations of atmospheric assimilation, fluid circulation, growth, and generation. The leaf becomes an instrument through which atmospheric substances are appropriated to the formation of organized material.

 The structure of vegetation, its dependence upon radiant energy, and the circulation of nutritive fluids are incorporated into his general philosophy of vital properties.

His discussion of the solar spectrum is particularly important at this point. The physical influence received from the surrounding world becomes associated with the formative activity of a living structure. Through the operations of the plant, materials derived from the atmosphere enter the constitution of organized matter, furnishing nourishment for other living beings.
Paine connects this physiological dependence of animals upon the vegetal kingdom with the order of creation recorded in Genesis. In his discussion of atmospheric nourishment, he expressly appeals to Moses and the principle of divine design in considering the appearance of vegetation before animal life.[4]

The connection between the vegetal and animal kingdoms consequently becomes a problem of organic dependence, creative sequence, and the ordering of natural causes.
The investigation of animal heat introduces another layer of complexity.

Paine devotes an extensive discussion to calorification and the relation of organic temperature to chemical action. He considers the production of heat within living structures, its variations under different physiological conditions, and the influence of the nervous apparatus upon its manifestation.

His arguments concerning heat become especially interesting when associated with observations of temperature differences between healthy and paralyzed structures. The body presents a distribution of thermal conditions dependent upon circulation, tissue activity, nervous influence, and the existing state of the organism.
In the broader context of nineteenth-century natural philosophy, the problem becomes inseparable from theories concerning chemical combustion and the correlation of physical forces.

The transformation and transmission of physical action occupy an important place in Paine's criticism of explanations that derive the distinctive powers of life from the ordinary properties of inorganic matter. His engagement with the correlation of forces is especially revealing. He examines the relationship between heat, electricity, chemical action, and organic functions while defending the individuality of vital powers.

The appendix concerning animal sugar furnishes a remarkable chemical counterpart.

The glycogenic function of the liver, the appearance of sugar within the animal economy, and the suggested substitution of foetal functions through the placenta become subjects of sustained examination. 

Paine follows contemporary experimental investigations into the production of physiological substances and the changing offices of organs during development.

This material creates a significant historical connection between chemical transformation and the succession of organic functions. 

The developing organism possesses arrangements and dependencies that change as maturation proceeds. 

The problem concerns the manner in which particular functions become established and the conditions permitting their performance.

The subject of blood fluidity introduces another example of the same philosophical difficulty. 

Paine examines theories concerning the chemical conditions preserving blood in its liquid state, including the proposed influence of ammonia. His inquiry extends into the relationship between the composition of the circulating fluid and the physiological circumstances under which it remains within the living vascular apparatus.

The circulating blood, the heat-producing organism, the formative embryo, and the assimilating plant consequently become different sites for investigating the relations between physical materials and organic powers.

A further distinction emerges in Paine's treatment of the primordial cell and the boundary between animals and plants. Here the anatomical simplicity of certain organisms becomes a challenge to the classification of their powers. The cellular structure of a living being, the presence or absence of nervous organization, and the manifestation of movement or sensitivity must be considered together.

His account of the sensitive movements of Mimosa offers a striking illustration of vegetal excitability. The plant responds through its own organic constitution despite possessing no animal nervous system. The comparison becomes an opportunity to investigate the powers common to living beings and those peculiar to animal organization.

At the opposite end of the developmental scale stands the elaborate transformation of animals undergoing metamorphosis. The appearance of new anatomical structures is accompanied by the manifestation of behaviors appropriate to the altered condition of the organism. 

Paine considers these relationships in his discussion of instinct, where bodily organization and the powers of action become inseparable problems of natural history.

The ancient language of forma, potentia, actus, and causa finalis provides a useful philosophical vocabulary for examining this sequence. Form determines the organization of the structure; capacity concerns what the structure is able to perform; activity manifests the operation of that capacity; and final causation examines the relation of the arrangement to its characteristic purpose.

These concepts become particularly fruitful when examined through the relationship between instinct and anatomical metamorphosis.

The operation of instinct raises the question of how an animal performs actions suited to its constitution and requirements. Paine examines the selection of nourishment, characteristic movement, behavioral adaptation, and the appearance of instinctive faculties during development. He considers these phenomena in relation to memory, perception, and the distinction between instinctive and intellectual activity.

The inquiry ultimately reaches the faculties of the human mind.

In the appendix devoted to the physiology of the soul and instinct, Paine proposes that the operations of perception, judgment, memory, and will furnish evidence concerning the existence of intellectual agency. He approaches this problem through the relationship between mental activity and the nervous structures participating in its bodily expression.

The phenomenon of voluntary motion becomes especially important. A mental determination is followed by activity in the nervous and muscular apparatus. The will appears in Paine's argument as an initiating principle whose effects are manifested through an organized bodily instrument.

The relationship between cause and instrument consequently becomes the central philosophical problem.

The visible muscular movement reveals the activity of a physiological apparatus. The intellectual determination through which the movement is initiated introduces a question concerning the agency exercising command over that apparatus.

Paine pursues the consequences through his account of the substantive existence and self-acting nature of the soul.
The scriptural correspondence reaches particular clarity in Genesis 2:7, where the formation of man from the dust of the ground is followed by the divine communication of the breath of life. 

The Hebrew nishmat chayyim, the breath of life, directs attention to the relationship between formed material organization and its animation. 

Job 33:4 expresses the same causal relationship through the agency of the Spirit of God and the life-giving breath of the Almighty.

These texts furnish the theological foundation for examining the relation of bodily structure, life, and the spiritual origin of man.

The terminology of nephesh, ruach, neshamah, psyche, and pneuma opens an additional linguistic avenue. 

Their differing scriptural applications concern life, breath, spirit, living being, and inward agency. 

A philological study of these terms alongside Paine's distinctions among vital principle, nervous power, instinct, and soul would offer substantial material for investigating the historical relationship between biblical anthropology and physiological philosophy.

The culmination of Paine's natural philosophy occurs in a remarkable passage of the Supplement, where his attention turns from the organization of living beings to the crystalline constitution of primordial rocks.

In examining the formation of granite, he considers the ordered arrangement of mineral constituents and their association within a common structure. 

The regularity of the crystalline arrangement becomes evidence in his broader philosophical investigation of creative causation.

On printed page 927, Paine describes these mineral relationships as furnishing testimony of;

 “supernatural dependence.” 

His argument extends the philosophical significance of design from the animal and vegetal kingdoms into the structure of the earth itself.[5]

The significance of this transition is considerable.

The crystalline arrangement of mineral matter and the differentiated organization of living structures belong to distinct classes of natural phenomena. Paine nevertheless approaches them through a common inquiry concerning the origin of ordered form and the sufficiency of the causes proposed to explain it.

The question of primordial organization consequently passes from physiology into cosmological and theological philosophy.

His discussion of geological theory also introduces the problem of original causation. If the existing laws of nature are invoked to explain the appearance of living organisms or the first formation of terrestrial structures, the investigator must determine what those laws establish concerning the actual origin of the arrangements under consideration.

Paine pursues this issue through arguments concerning spontaneous generation, the first appearance of organic beings, crystalline formation, and the operation of creative intelligence.

His treatment of the alleged spontaneous production of microscopic organisms, including the historical controversy concerning Acarus Crossii, is particularly illustrative. 

The question concerns how a complex living organization could arise from materials possessing none of its characteristic anatomical or physiological arrangements.

The accompanying investigation of ancient fossil forms is equally significant. Paine refers to the eyes of trilobites as part of his criticism of geological systems that attempt to explain organic organization through general physical causes.

text:
@OpenAI is private. Its revenue correction still shook public markets.

On Thursday the @FT reported that OpenAI’s annualised revenue run rate was close to $50 billion, against the $70 billion previously reported. @Oracle’s shares fell 5.5% that day.

OpenAI says its business was still growing rapidly. The correction exposed how much confidence rested on a number that could not be reconciled in public.

The financial connections run through contracts. @Nvidia guarantees parts of OpenAI’s infrastructure commitments. Oracle has signed long leases to supply computing. @Broadcom backs financing for chips leased to @AnthropicAI.

A laboratory’s spending, a cloud’s backlog and a chipmaker’s orders can all depend on the same final customer demand.

This week’s Sunday Signal follows those contracts and the borrowing behind them to explain who carries the risk if the expansion disappoints.

For Britain, there is an opportunity here.

AI can keep delivering useful work while investors lose money. Cheaper models could make it more economical to use the knowledge inside an engineering firm’s drawings, maintenance records and repair histories. The commercial value comes from turning that knowledge into better decisions and work customers will pay for.

That is the purpose of the Stocksbridge proposal. Start with a paid pilot. Prove the available power, the customers and the full cost of doing their work. Expand when the evidence supports it. If existing capacity offers better value, use it.

Plus the weekly Tech & AI Layoff Tracker, including what employers actually say about AI’s role.

Build small, build under British control, and build for the bust.

text:
ANOTHER BLACK TRIANGLE DURING THE RENDLESHAM UFO INCIDENTS?

A former U.S. Air Force fighter pilot and test pilot has described a remarkable close encounter with a silent triangular craft in England on December 26, 1980—the same period as the famous Rendlesham Forest incidents.

His name is Dan Isbell, and his aviation credentials are substantial.

Speaking with Ryan Graves on the Safe Aerospace Podcast, Isbell described driving home around 10 p.m. after nuclear-alert duty at RAF Upper Heyford.

Suddenly, unusual lights approached rapidly from behind his Corvette, stopped abruptly, and hovered above trees bordering a golf course.

He pulled over, got out, and approached.

What he described was extraordinary.

The object appeared approximately 50–60 feet long, roughly triangular, with a rounded front and angular rear. It was dark, completely silent, and surrounded along its lower perimeter by constantly changing colors—purple, red, yellow, and occasionally green.

These weren’t conventional aircraft lights.

Isbell described something resembling a shifting plasma field. Remarkably, the illumination did not noticeably light the surrounding trees or ground.

At an estimated distance of 150 feet, he watched the object begin descending as he approached.

Isbell was no inexperienced observer. An aerospace engineer, F-111 fighter pilot, and eventual USAF test pilot, he had extensive knowledge of military aircraft and their performance.

He couldn’t identify what he was seeing.

Concerned about his safety and the potential consequences for his flying career, he returned to his car and drove away. He kept the experience private for more than four decades.

But there’s another intriguing dimension.

Isbell subsequently learned of a separate account involving a triangular object reportedly observed near RAF Upper Heyford’s weapons storage area around 1:15 a.m. on December 27—just over three hours later.

That witness also described unusual illumination beneath the craft.

Were these related encounters? We don’t know. But the dates, location, and similarities warrant serious historical investigation.

Isbell also offered an intriguing technical hypothesis: Could the luminous field have been associated with an electromagnetic propulsion mechanism?

That’s his interpretation, not something he directly measured. Nevertheless, it’s worth considering given his aerospace background.

The larger question is whether the December 1980 UFO activity in Britain extended beyond Rendlesham Forest to other American military installations.

Isbell’s testimony deserves considerably more attention than it has received.

I encourage you to watch his interview with Ryan Graves and judge the account for yourself.

https://t.co/qUhIuJLsR0

We just finished Matthew 27 at Church. The trial and crucifixion of Christ. We learned something important from the Hebrew Bible. 

When was the last time you read Isaiah 53? Song, below. 👇

Isaiah 53 (ESV)
1 Who has believed what he has heard from us? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?
2 For he grew up before him like a young plant, and like a root out of dry ground; he had no form or majesty that we should look at him, and no beauty that we should desire him.
3 He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief; and as one from whom men hide their faces he was despised, and we esteemed him not.
4 Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows; yet we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted.
5 But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed.
6 All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned—every one—to his own way; and the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
7 He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth; like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth.
8 By oppression and judgment he was taken away; and as for his generation, who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living, stricken for the transgression of my people?
9 And they made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death, although he had done no violence, and there was no deceit in his mouth.
10 Yet it was the will of the Lord to crush him; he has put him to grief; when his soul makes an offering for guilt, he shall see his offspring; he shall prolong his days; the will of the Lord shall prosper in his hand.
11 Out of the anguish of his soul he shall see and be satisfied; by his knowledge shall the righteous one, my servant, make many to be accounted righteous, and he shall bear their iniquities.
12 Therefore I will divide him a portion with the many, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong, because he poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and makes intercession for the transgressors.

text:
🌍 GLOBAL MARKET RECAP — OCTOBER 12, 2026
Geopolitical Weekend Special | Updated around 08:55 CEST

1️⃣ GLOBAL EQUITIES — MARKETS ARE PRICING THE POSSIBILITY OF PEACE WHILE PREPARING FOR FURTHER WAR
Global equities begin the week cautiously after a weekend in which attacks on Saudi civilian infrastructure, military action in the Gulf of Oman and continued Russian strikes on Ukraine competed with unexpected diplomatic announcements. Asian markets are mixed, with South Korean equities falling roughly 2%, Taiwan modestly weaker and Chinese blue chips relatively stable, while U.S. stock-index futures are slightly positive. Friday's Wall Street recovery, which saw the S&P 500 gain 0.59%, the Dow 0.83% and the Nasdaq 0.64%, has therefore not evolved into a convincing global risk-on environment. Investors are confronting a fundamental contradiction: diplomatic headlines offer the possibility of lower energy prices, but events on the ground continue to demonstrate that the conflicts remain active. The beginning of the U.S. earnings season adds another layer of uncertainty, particularly for technology companies whose valuations increasingly depend on sustained AI investment and exceptionally strong profit growth.

2️⃣ U.S. MACRO — THE ECONOMY IS BECOMING MORE VULNERABLE TO ANOTHER INFLATION SHOCK
The latest American consumer data reveal a growing disconnect between financial markets and households. Preliminary October consumer sentiment declined to 46.3, while one-year inflation expectations increased to 4.7%, reflecting deteriorating confidence in purchasing power and the economic outlook. These figures follow September's weak employment report, which showed only 29,000 additional payroll jobs and unemployment at 4.2%. The combination matters because the Federal Reserve is confronting slowing labour demand without clear evidence that inflationary pressures have been contained. Wednesday's September CPI report is expected to show headline inflation around 3.7%, heavily influenced by energy, making it one of the most important macroeconomic releases of the month. A higher-than-expected reading could revive concerns about additional tightening, while softer inflation would support the argument that growth can stabilise without further substantial increases in borrowing costs. The market's next direction will depend less on geopolitical promises than on measurable economic consequences.

3️⃣ BONDS & FED — THE MOST IMPORTANT MARKET IS CLOSED WHEN GEOPOLITICAL RISK IS HIGHEST
The U.S. 10-year Treasury finished Friday near 5.24%, with the 2-year around 4.79%, following a volatile week in which strong auction demand provided temporary relief to long-duration bonds. Today, however, U.S. cash bond markets are closed for Columbus Day, while the NYSE and Nasdaq will operate normally. This distinction is particularly important after a weekend dominated by military escalation and conflicting diplomatic announcements. Treasury futures, currencies, commodities and equities can react to the latest news, but the full cash Treasury market will not provide its usual confirmation until Tuesday. The Federal Reserve is widely expected to leave rates unchanged in October, with traders assigning roughly an 80% probability to a pause, although additional tightening later in the year remains heavily priced. Persistent fiscal deficits, expensive energy, sovereign refinancing requirements and the financing demands of AI infrastructure continue to justify significant attention to long-term yields. Today's apparent stability should therefore be interpreted cautiously: reduced bond-market participation can conceal rather than eliminate underlying financial stress.

4️⃣ EUROPE & FX — FISCAL FRAGILITY MEETS A NEW ENERGY AND SECURITY CRISIS
European markets enter the week facing an unusually complicated combination of geopolitical exposure, inflation uncertainty and sovereign borrowing pressure. France remains a particular concern as political divisions and the difficulty of producing a credible 2027 budget continue to undermine confidence in its fiscal trajectory. The euro is trading near $1.12, while the Dollar Index remains around 102.2, close to recent highs despite a modest pullback this morning. European policymakers are also participating in the IMF–World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, where debt sustainability, global growth and the consequences of armed conflict will dominate discussions. The direct economic exposure is substantial: expensive imported energy raises industrial costs, geopolitical uncertainty discourages investment and higher sovereign yields restrict fiscal flexibility. A genuine reduction in hostilities around Ukraine and the Middle East would therefore offer Europe significant relief, but markets need evidence of implementation. Until then, European equities and currencies remain exposed to a combination of external shocks and domestic structural vulnerabilities.

5️⃣ ASIA — ENERGY SECURITY IS AGAIN REDRAWING THE REGIONAL ECONOMIC MAP
Asian markets are reacting unevenly to the weekend's developments. South Korean equities are under pressure, Taiwan has weakened modestly and Chinese shares remain comparatively stable, while Japan's markets are closed for a public holiday. The distinction between energy-importing economies and AI-linked exporters is becoming especially important. South Korea and Taiwan benefit from exceptional demand for advanced semiconductors and artificial-intelligence infrastructure, but their manufacturing systems still depend on reliable energy supplies, maritime trade and predictable financing conditions. India illustrates another side of the problem: the rupee has strengthened sharply after the Reserve Bank of India introduced measures to redirect oil-related dollar demand and increase the cost of certain foreign-exchange positions. Those interventions may reduce immediate currency pressure, but they do not eliminate the underlying cost of imported energy. Across Asia, the geopolitical crisis is therefore transmitting through several channels simultaneously: oil prices, shipping insurance, exchange rates, domestic inflation and the availability of investment capital.

6️⃣ OIL, GOLD & COMMODITIES — THE MARKET REVERSES AS TWO WARS PRODUCE OPPOSING ENERGY SIGNALS
Oil has delivered one of the most revealing market reactions of the morning. Brent initially climbed toward $105.5 as investors reacted to renewed Houthi attacks and incidents involving commercial shipping, before reversing toward $103.3–103.5 following President Trump's announcement of a proposed Russia–Ukraine energy ceasefire. WTI similarly retreated toward $90–91. This volatility reflects two opposing geopolitical forces: the Middle-East conflict threatens international energy supply, while the possibility of reduced attacks on Russian and Ukrainian energy infrastructure raises expectations of greater fuel availability. Neither development should be interpreted prematurely. The proposed ceasefire has not been confirmed by both combatants, and attacks on Gulf shipping remain a genuine operational risk. Gold has recovered toward $4,198 per ounce, supported by softer oil prices and a slightly weaker dollar, although elevated real yields continue to limit its attractiveness. The key issue is no longer simply how much crude is produced, but whether energy can be transported, refined, insured and delivered without further disruption.

7️⃣ GEOPOLITICS — THE WEEKEND CONFIRMED THAT THE CONFLICTS ARE EXPANDING, NOT ENDING
The most alarming escalation occurred in Saudi Arabia, where Saturday's attack on Riyadh's international airport killed 13 people and injured more than 300, according to the latest reported figures. Another attack on Sunday killed one person and wounded 11, while Saudi air defences reported intercepting additional missiles and drones. The Iran-aligned Houthis have demonstrated their ability to threaten strategically important civilian infrastructure well beyond Yemen, increasing pressure on Riyadh and its regional security partners. Turkey, Pakistan, Egypt and Saudi Arabia have collectively condemned the attacks, while the possibility of a broader military response remains an important escalation risk.

The maritime confrontation has also intensified. U.S. Central Command reported that American forces disabled a Panama-flagged commercial vessel attempting to breach the blockade against Iran in the Gulf of Oman. Separate attacks on tankers have increased fears surrounding the Strait of Hormuz, while the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb remain exposed to Houthi military operations. These incidents are not interchangeable, but together they demonstrate how naval warfare, commercial shipping and energy security are becoming increasingly interconnected.

Meanwhile, Washington unexpectedly announced an immediate energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine. Yet neither Kyiv nor Moscow had confirmed a bilateral agreement when the declaration emerged, and Ukrainian authorities reported continued Russian attacks on energy infrastructure, including a combined heat-and-power facility in Kharkiv. President Zelenskiy reiterated that Ukraine would suspend attacks on Russian energy installations if Moscow genuinely ceased its own strikes. Until a reciprocal and verifiable arrangement exists, the announcement remains a diplomatic proposal rather than an established cessation of hostilities.

Additional violence in Gaza and southern Lebanon underscores that the regional security environment extends beyond one conflict or one maritime corridor. The immediate financial implications are most visible in oil and transportation costs, but the wider consequences include humanitarian damage, disrupted investment, higher insurance premiums, military expenditure and increasing pressure on government budgets. In this environment, differentiating confirmed events from battlefield claims and political announcements is essential.

8️⃣ ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE — THE NEXT EARNINGS SEASON WILL TEST THE ECONOMICS OF THE BOOM
While geopolitical uncertainty dominates the headlines, artificial intelligence remains one of the most important structural forces supporting global investment. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company is expected to report its sixth consecutive quarter of record earnings, with analysts projecting approximately 65% year-on-year growth in third-quarter net profit to T$746.3 billion. Demand for advanced manufacturing processes and chip-packaging technologies remains exceptionally strong, reflecting continued infrastructure investment by Nvidia and other major technology companies. Nevertheless, the market has become less willing to value every AI-related project on the assumption that future profits are guaranteed. The cancellation of Firmus Technologies' planned IPO and mounting concern over the financing requirements of data centres illustrate this changing attitude. The question is whether exceptional spending on computing capacity, electricity and infrastructure can generate returns sufficient to justify the associated debt and equity valuations. Strong results from TSMC would support the demand narrative, but forward guidance on pricing, capacity, capital expenditure and profitability may matter even more than the headline earnings figure.

9️⃣ CRYPTO — BITCOIN RECOVERS, BUT GEOPOLITICAL RELIEF IS NOT A VERIFIED BREAKOUT
Bitcoin is trading around $83.7K, Ethereum near $2.53K and Solana around $112 in the latest Monday-morning readings, recovering modestly from the previous week's decline. The move coincides with lower oil prices and reduced immediate concerns about another inflation shock, although the wider structure remains fragile. Bitcoin continues to trade below the resistance region established around $85K–87.4K, while the $80K area remains the principal support zone to monitor. Ethereum and Solana show greater sensitivity to changes in speculative liquidity, as is typical of higher-beta digital assets during periods of macroeconomic uncertainty. The weekend has also highlighted the limitations of treating Bitcoin as an immediate geopolitical safe haven: its short-term performance remains influenced by leverage, market liquidity and expectations for monetary conditions. For long-term accumulation, BTC, ETH and SOL should continue to be assessed through disciplined DCA and portfolio allocation, separately from speculative trading exposure. A sustainable recovery requires improving market structure, not merely a favourable political headline.

🔟 MARKET STRUCTURE — FINANCIAL MARKETS ARE TRADING EXPECTATIONS THAT THE BATTLEFIELDS HAVE NOT CONFIRMED
The central lesson of the weekend is that markets can react positively to the possibility of de-escalation even while military activity continues. The proposed Russia–Ukraine energy ceasefire helped reverse an initial oil rally, but its implementation remains uncertain. The escalation in Saudi Arabia and the Gulf has increased the probability of further disruption to commercial aviation, maritime traffic and energy infrastructure. At the same time, investors are approaching a decisive period of U.S. inflation data and corporate earnings, particularly for banks and AI-linked technology companies.

The principal transmission mechanism remains Geopolitics → Energy & Shipping → Inflation → Central Banks → Sovereign Yields → Dollar → Equities → Crypto. Alongside it, another structural relationship is strengthening: AI Demand → Infrastructure Investment → Power Consumption → Corporate Financing → Earnings & Valuations.

This week, I am monitoring Brent around $100–105, the U.S. 10-year Treasury around 5.20% and 5.35% when cash trading resumes, and Bitcoin around $80K support and $85K–87.4K resistance. Wednesday's U.S. CPI release, TSMC's earnings and the first major-bank reports will be particularly important.

The constructive scenario requires verifiable progress toward de-escalation, lower energy prices, stable yields and corporate profits capable of supporting existing valuations. The negative scenario involves renewed attacks on critical infrastructure, a hotter inflation report or a reassessment of AI financing and earnings expectations.

Markets are not yet pricing an end to war. They are pricing the probability that the economic damage may become less severe. Those are two fundamentally different propositions, and confusing them is one of the greatest analytical risks in the current environment.

Per Barnea, the Forum asked ICC prosecutor Karim Khan to withdraw his warrant applications against Netanyahu and Gallant as part of the deal, with the Hamas applications dropped too. Netanyahu then told the Americans he lacked a majority. Barnea's line: Netanyahu did not obey them, he operated them.

4) Netanyahu let it all die by July 27. His reasons, per Barnea: a deal nine months in would look like the end of the war without "total victory," he would have to explain taking Hague immunity alongside Sinwar, and Biden had just dropped out and Trump had just reconciled with him, so he would not hand Harris a win.

5) The weak link is the Khan motive. Barnea's single Israeli source says Khan believed Israel or Mossad was behind the sexual misconduct complaint against him and that dropping the Israelis would make it vanish. That is one anonymous source describing Khan's state of mind.

6) In October 2025 Netanyahu accepted a deal no better than this one, with no leverage left in Washington. Sinwar, Deif and Haniyeh were dead by then. So were hostages who were alive in July 2024.

Netanyahu was offered the hostages, a pause his generals wanted, a Philadelphi fix he could sell, and a way out of The Hague, all in one package. He refused, and he manufactured the coalition crisis he blamed for refusing. The hostages spent another year in the tunnels so he could continue the carnage in Gaza.

Didn't Mohammed bin Salman openly declare in May 2017 that they would take the battle into Iran itself?

When the United States imposed sanctions on Iranian oil, didn't Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries offer to compensate for the loss of Iranian oil supplies, effectively helping Washington increase economic pressure on Iran?

Didn't these countries provide military bases to the United States? Why is the role of these bases in American military operations against Iran, and the security risks they created, rarely discussed?

Furthermore, starting in 2015, the Saudi-led coalition, with American military and logistical support, carried out years of airstrikes against Yemen. Thousands of civilians were killed, and millions suffered through one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.

And these are just a few examples.

Of course, Iranian military actions must also be examined under international law, particularly regarding the protection of civilians. But portraying Iran as the sole source of instability while ignoring decades of hostile policies and military interventions by other regional powers is a selective reading of history.

The real question is: Where was your outrage when these governments spent years supporting policies that threatened Iran's security? Why should the history of this conflict begin only when Iran responds?

AMERICA'S MILITARY POWER IS NO LONGER WHAT HOLLYWOOD WANTS YOU TO BELIEVE

The uncomfortable truth is that the United States no longer possesses the overwhelming military superiority it once enjoyed. For decades, Hollywood convinced the world that the American military was virtually invincible. Reality tells a different story.

The last convincing demonstration of overwhelming American superiority was Operation Desert Storm in 1991. Since then, the world has changed dramatically.

America can no longer expect to wage wars against poorly armed opponents without suffering serious consequences. Even the Houthis possess ballistic missiles and drones capable of challenging vastly more expensive military systems.

The era of effortless military victories is over.

And this brings us to Donald Trump.

Trump understands that American dominance is increasingly difficult to maintain through military power alone. So instead of defeating America's adversaries, he seeks to turn them against one another.

Russia against Europe. China against its neighbors. Iran against the Middle East. Allies against allies. Everyone against everyone.

A world consumed by conflict is a world too distracted and divided to challenge American dominance.

In my view, that is the logic behind Trump's foreign policy: confrontation, manipulation, broken promises, economic pressure, and calculated chaos.

Ukraine's survival is not his priority. Neither is Russia's prosperity or China's stability. What matters is keeping America's competitors occupied, weakened, and dependent.

But there is one enormous problem with this strategy.

Sitting in the Kremlin is another aging ruler who has placed an extraordinary bet on Trump.

Putin apparently believes that his relationship with Washington can help him achieve what his military has failed to accomplish.

That could become the greatest miscalculation of his political career.

Because Trump has no permanent friends. He has interests, ambitions, and an obsession with appearing victorious.

The moment he concludes that cooperation with Moscow has become politically costly, economically damaging, or strategically useless, he could reverse course overnight.

And the man Putin considers his greatest opportunity could suddenly become his greatest threat.

Trump might turn against Russia not out of sympathy for Ukraine, not out of respect for international law, and certainly not out of moral conviction.

He could do it simply because destroying yesterday's partner might offer greater political dividends than protecting him.

That is the danger of building your entire strategy around a man whose loyalty lasts only as long as the benefits.

Putin thinks he is using Trump.

Trump thinks he is using Putin.

And both may discover that their calculations were disastrously wrong.

Nothing personal.

Just business.

Make America Great Again — even if the rest of the world has to burn.

BUFFALO FARMING IN KENYA: A NEW AGRICULTURAL VENTURE? 

- President William Ruto has directed the importation of domesticated water buffaloes as an alternative source of meat and milk.

- The move follows milk shortages worsened by prolonged dry weather.

- Kenya officially recognised water buffaloes as food animals through Gazette Notice No. 977 of January 31, 2025.

- The approval allows farmers to rear domesticated water buffaloes under controlled arrangements.

- A two-year pilot programme involving KAGRC and approved farmers will establish production standards.

- Local veterinarians will oversee the animals using existing cattle-handling and treatment practices.

- Technical studies were conducted in Brazil and India, countries with established buffalo-farming industries.

Benefits of Buffalo Farming

- Buffalo meat is leaner and lower in fat and cholesterol than beef, mutton and goat meat.

- It offers an alternative source of animal protein for Kenyan consumers.

- Buffalo milk contains higher levels of fat and protein than cow's milk, making it suitable for cheese, yoghurt and butter production.

- Buffalo farming could help supplement Kenya's existing food supply.

- The venture has the potential to diversify livestock production and create new opportunities for Kenyan farmers.

- Buffalo meat could also become a more affordable alternative to other red meats.

🇰🇪 The big question is whether buffalo farming can become a commercially viable venture for Kenyan farmers while helping address the country's food security challenges.

text:
Due to this year's permanent appointment exercise, Sabah lost 244 medical officers (MOs) because 333 transferred out of the state, but only 89 from outside Sabah reported for duty in that state.

Sabah's deficit of 244 MOs comprised 219 in hospitals and 25 in public health (district health offices and Klinik Kesihatan).

Out of 269 MOs posted to Sabah from outside, only 89 reported for duty (33%), 171 no-shows (64%), and 9 deferrals (3%).

Overall, 331 out of 511 MOs offered permanent positions in Sabah reported for duty (65%), according to JKNS data as of Oct 7, 2026.

All 242 MOs already serving in Sabah, who received permanent appointment offers in the same state, had reported for duty, even as only a third of doctors from outside Sabah reported for duty in that state.

Twenty-two public hospitals in Sabah suffered net MO losses. Only Kuala Penyu Hospital saw no change, while Tambunan had a net gain of 1 MO. Top MO deficits:
- Sabah Women and Children: -36
- Queen Elizabeth: -33
- Duchess of Kent: -26
- Tawau: -23
- Lahad Datu: -19

Out of 138 MOs from outside Sabah who were offered permanent posts in hospitals in the state: 80 no-shows (58%), 52 reported for duty (38%), and 6 deferrals (4%).

Five hospitals had 100% no-shows among MOs posted from outside Sabah: Papar, Tenom, Sipitang, Beluran, and Kunak.

Other hospitals with high no-show rates among MOs posted from outside Sabah exceeding 50%:
- Ranau: 86%
- Beaufort: 86%
- Tawau: 80%
- Kota Belud: 80%
- Pitas: 80%
- Kinabatangan: 80%
- Lahad Datu: 67%
- Kuala Penyu: 67%

A dozen public hospitals in Sabah are understaffed, following the 2026 permanent appointment exercise, based on available JKNS data on manpower needs in those facilities.

Five are running at below 60% operational capacity:
- Ranau (45%)
- Beluran (50%)
- Kudat (56%)
- Sipitang (56%)
- Kinabatangan (57%)

Based on JKNS data, the number of medical officers in Sabah dropped by 44% from 3,908 in 2021 to 2,208 in October 2026.

This would not be the first time that a movement  begun in profound moral clarity, and that achieved greatness, waned  away into a parody of itself—not because it was wrong but because it was  successful. Today’s civil-rights leaders have missed the obvious: The  success of their forbearers in achieving social transformation denied to  them the heroism that was inescapable for a Martin Luther King Jr. or a  James Farmer or a Nelson Mandela. Jesse Jackson and Al Sharpton cannot  write a timeless letter to us from a Birmingham jail or walk, as John  Lewis did in 1965, across the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, Ala., into a  maelstrom of police dogs and billy clubs. That America is no longer  here (which is not to say that every trace of it is gone). The Revs.  Jackson and Sharpton have been consigned to a hard fate: They can never  be more than redundancies, echoes of the great men they emulate because  America has changed. Hard to be a King or Mandela today when your monstrous enemy is no more than the cherubic George Zimmerman. The  purpose of today’s civil-rights establishment is not to seek justice,  but to seek power for blacks in American life based on the presumption  that they are still, in a thousand subtle ways, victimized by white racism. This idea of victimization is an example of what I call a  « poetic truth. » Like poetic license, it bends the actual truth in  order to put forward a larger and more essential truth—one that, of  course, serves one’s cause. Poetic truths succeed by casting themselves  as perfectly obvious: « America is a racist nation »; « the immigration  debate is driven by racism »; « Zimmerman racially stereotyped  Trayvon. » And we say, « Yes, of course, » lest we seem to be racist.  Poetic truths work by moral intimidation, not reason. In the  Zimmerman/Martin case the civil-rights establishment is fighting for the  poetic truth that white animus toward blacks is still such that a black  teenager—Skittles and ice tea in hand—can be shot dead simply for  walking home. But actually this establishment is fighting to maintain  its authority to wield poetic truth—the authority to tell the larger  society how it must think about blacks, how it must respond to them,  what it owes them and, then, to brook no argument. One wants to scream  at all those outraged at the Zimmerman verdict: Where is your outrage  over the collapse of the black family? Today’s civil-rights leaders swat at mosquitoes like Zimmerman when they have gorillas on their back.  Seventy-three percent of all black children are born without fathers  married to their mothers. And you want to bring the nation to a  standstill over George Zimmerman?"      

Shelby Steele (2013)

text:
THE SICK BUFFALO VS. TERMINAL CANCER
Author's note: With this post, I am opening a short series on the hidden relationship patterns between Thai women in the industry and Asian clients—Koreans, Japanese, and Chinese. Why them? First, because my current work in the industry brings me face-to-face with these demographics daily. Second, beneath their polished facades lie entirely different cultural codes that are completely alien to the Western mind. Let’s start with the basic mechanics: how the street adapts its lies to the color of a passport.

A single bar girl can tell three entirely different stories to three different men in a single night. To the Englishman, she will tearfully describe a sick water buffalo and a leaking roof. To the Korean, she will talk about her mother's sudden cancer diagnosis. To the Japanese man, she will confess a missed period and a pregnancy. To the Chinese man, she won't tell any story at all.

This doesn't happen because she is a pathological liar. It happens because she is speaking the exact language each of them is programmed to understand. A scheme in Pattaya is rarely just a scam. It is a masterful translation of poverty into a dialect the client can decode, allowing him to part with his money without losing face.

The entire industry relies on adapting the narrative to three variables: the client's emotional involvement, his willingness to pay, and his domestic cultural context. The Western man flies in looking for the illusion of "true love"—he needs a drama where he plays the savior. The Korean is looking for cinematic romance—he needs a fatal tragedy that makes him the main character. The Japanese man seeks a long-term, structured bond—he needs a heavy responsibility he can carry for years. The Chinese man comes for a service—he doesn't want drama; he wants a clean transaction.

The Western Client: The Cascade of Disasters
The infamous "sick buffalo" is no longer just a lie; it is an established literary genre. Back in 2004, a translated letter from a Thai bar worker circulated on an expat forum, becoming the ultimate encyclopedia of this style. In a single paragraph, she brilliantly compressed the death of a buffalo, a father’s broken leg, a collapsed roof, a brother’s motorcycle crash, that same brother’s arrest, a mother’s severe illness, a guilt trip blaming the foreigner ("this is because I am with you"), and a final threat to go with other men if he didn't wire cash.

This scheme operates purely on a cascading effect. Every new disaster logically flows from the last, leaving the target no time to breathe. The foreigner cannot verify a single fact, but he doesn't need to. He sees the narrative he desperately wants to see. He wants to be needed. He wants to believe his Bank transfer is literally saving a life. The "sick buffalo" still drains the wallets of thousands of Western men every year, not because they are stupid, but because the scheme exploits their deepest vulnerability: the white savior complex.

The Korean Client: Cancer and Death
Koreans represent the new, aggressive money on the grid. They pay more and stay longer, but they don't read old English forums and know nothing about sick agricultural livestock. For them, the street had to invent a darker, heavier genre.

In December 2024, the story of Danny, a South Korean tourist, made headlines. He met a girl in a Pattaya bar in 2020 who complained she was exhausted from the nightlife. Playing the hero, he offered her a full allowance of 50,000 baht a month to quit. Then, the script accelerated according to the laws of a K-drama: first, money for a father's funeral, then a car accident, an investment in a fake coffee shop, a miscarriage, and covering a brother's gambling debts. The climax was cancer. Danny wired 1.6 million baht for a life-saving surgery. A few months later, the girl's "sister" messaged him to say she had passed away. When the shocked Korean flew to Thailand, he found no grave, no hospital records, and no crematorium. He lost over 10 million baht in total.

The Korean client wants to be the tragic hero. A sick buffalo is too petty and comedic for his tastes. He requires fatalism, self-sacrifice, and a devastating finale. The scheme simply adapted to the exact cinematic genre he consumes at home.

The Japanese Client: The Pregnancy
The Japanese are old money. They have been flying here for decades, they know all the buffalo jokes, and they are far too cynical to believe in sudden cancer. But they have their own Achilles' heel: the pregnancy scheme.

In 2026, Japanese media analyzed a classic case. A wealthy Japanese man with 50 million yen in the bank regularly visited the same bar, dropping 40,000 yen a night on drinks for one specific girl and the staff. On one trip, the mamasan sat him down with a grim face and informed him the girl was pregnant, and out of deep shame, had fled to her rural village to give birth in hiding. The man panicked, insisting, "I always used protection, it physically cannot be me!"

But the trap was already sprung. The pregnancy scheme doesn't run on love; it runs on guilt and hyper-responsibility. The Japanese man doesn't want to be a savior; he is terrified of losing face and disrupting social order. He will pay child support for another man's (or a completely fictional) baby simply because his culture dictates that he must fulfill his duty. The concept of duty is baked into his DNA.

The Chinese Client: Rent-a-Wife
With Chinese clients, none of this works. They are absolute pragmatists. They don't believe in buffalos, they don't care about cancer, and they will easily ignore a pregnancy claim. They only believe in numbers and agreements. Therefore, the scheme disappears, replaced entirely by a contract.

The "Rent-a-Wife" model is not a scam; it is a straightforward commercial service. A retired Chinese man pays a Thai woman a fixed monthly rate. For 8,000 baht, he gets a basic companion. For 20,000 to 25,000 baht, he gets a well-groomed woman with industry experience. She cooks his meals, gives him massages, does his laundry, and calls him "husband." He knows exactly what he is renting. She knows exactly that she is on the clock. There is no drama, no suddenly ill relatives, no tears. For a Chinese pensioner living on 10,000 RMB a month, it is an incredibly cheap way to buy care and status in his old age. Scams aren't needed here—they are bad for business.

The Thai Client: Outside the Game
The most fascinating dynamic occurs when the client is Thai. A Thai man will never walk into a neon-lit Go-Go on Walking Street to buy an illusion. He goes to a dusty karaoke joint on the outskirts of town, pays a third of the price, buys zero lady drinks, and leaves no tip.

He doesn't believe in transactional love because he is a native to the culture. Statistically, 95 percent of all sex work in Thailand consists of Thai clients with Thai workers. And in that massive, underwater portion of the iceberg—completely invisible to foreigners—there are no sick buffalos, no cancer, and no fake pregnancies. There is only sex, a price, and a transaction. All those multi-layered emotional traps are strictly an export product.

The Mirror
Ultimately, a scheme is never just about extracting cash. It is a flawless mirror a Thai woman holds up to a foreigner's face, reflecting exactly what he desperately wants to see. You want to be a noble savior? Here is a collapsed roof. You want cinematic suffering? Here is terminal cancer. You want the heavy burden of duty? Here is a pregnancy test. You want pragmatic comfort? Here is the monthly invoice.

The street doesn't adapt because these girls take psychology courses. They adapt because they exist in a ruthless ecosystem where their family's physical survival depends entirely on their ability to read human beings. They segment their clients by nationality with the same cold, calculating precision a Western marketing executive uses to segment demographics.

text:
Let the welfare of the people be the supreme law.
Part 1 of 2
“salus populi suprema lex esto” ---- Cicero, On the Laws, III.8.
.
By Peter Spear
Research and Editorial Assistance by GPT 6.0 Sol
In the style of Dr. Professor Daniel Patrick Moynihan,
US Senator
.
There are occasions when a government must borrow whatever it can responsibly obtain. A republic fighting for its existence, for example, cannot make the preservation of its credit rating the condition of preserving itself. There will be little satisfaction in leaving impeccable accounts to the conquering army. This is an argument for keeping public credit available for an emergency. It is a peculiar argument for exhausting it in the ordinary conduct of government.
.
The governing rule ought to be plain: pay for ordinary government, including its social obligations, from ordinary revenue. In prosperous times, collect enough to pay interest and retire a measured portion of the debt. Borrow when circumstances truly warrant borrowing, and provide a plan for the return to fiscal order. A government should have to explain an exception. It should not make the exception its constitution.
.
The Roman antecedent is Cicero’s “salus populi suprema lex esto:”  let the welfare of the people be the supreme law. The words occur in On the Laws, in his account of the duties of the consuls. The people, rather than the convenience of their governors, are the object of the injunction. In a constitutional republic, preserving the state must mean preserving the institutions through which a free people govern themselves, free of the billionaires. Public finance is one of the means of that preservation. (Cicero, On the Laws, III.8.)
.
Ludwig von Mises understood that war finance could require borrowing. In “Nation, State, and Economy,”  he explained how collecting an entire war’s financial cost through immediate taxation could force property owners into costly private loans or distressed sales. Government borrowing could distribute the financial burden more practicably. It could not manufacture the weapons, food, or labor that a war required: those real resources had to come from the living economy. Survival may justify extraordinary finance; it does not abolish scarcity. (Mises, Nation, State, and Economy, “Covering the State’s War Costs.”)
.
Against this distinction between emergency and ordinary obligation stands a familiar political doctrine: the Republic may require services, but taxation to pay for them will damage the economy. Senator Chuck Grassley supplied a concise statement in a February 2015 interview: “And you don’t get economic growth by increasing taxes, by taking capital out of the economy.” One might have expected a senator concerned with deficits to ask what borrowing takes out of it. (PBS, Washington Week, February 2015 interview with Senator Grassley.)
.
He had been more categorical in a Senate speech on April 13, 2011: “Only growing the economy is going to reduce the deficit.” Later came the assertion that “increasing taxes doesn’t bring more revenue into the federal Treasury.” This idea of his, and the Tea Party, and now the MAGA NAZI Party, Trump and his henchmen, promotes a claim about incentives and would turn it into a law of nature. It also gives Congress an astonishing exemption: its decisions about spending cease to matter to the arithmetic of governing, while its decisions about collecting revenue cannot improve it. (Grassley, Senate floor speech, April 13, 2011.)
.
A tax payment changes who commands purchasing power. From the consumer who pays the tax.  To the government which must pay a teacher, purchase equipment, support an elderly person, or redeem a bond. These uses have different economic consequences, and some will be better than others. But to describe the transaction simply as ‘taking capital out of the economy’ omits the use to which the revenue is put. A criticism of waste is an argument for examining expenditure. (Congressional Budget Office, infrastructure spending analysis, 2021.)
.
It is not an argument that expenditure can be financed without cost. This would be, as George HW Bush fairly described it, “what I call a voodoo economic policy,” at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, while competing against Ronald Reagan for the Republican presidential nomination. (UPI Archive, April 10, 1980)
.
The Reaganites responded with outrage to be cut so hard. It seems to me to be a moderate response to the imbecilic argument that tax cuts pay for themselves. But then perhaps the out rage came from a place of recognizing they were being publicly exposed. For example when he called for a “kinder, gentler America.”  This too was received by the Reaganites as a cutting criticism. But again, their vociferous objection betrayed a guilty conscious. Yes, it probably was directed at them. (August 18, 1988,while accepting the Republican presidential nomination at the party’s convention in New Orleans, LA Times.)
.
Just so, when Biden described the Republicans as “sort of Fascistic,” the hysterical MAGA NAZI reaction also betrayed just this kind of  guilty conscious. If the shoe fits.
.
The alternative to taxation is not necessarily always private enterprise as is constantly claimed. It may sometimes be public borrowing. My point is only that persistent deficits can reduce national saving and compete with private investment for financing, a process economists call crowding out. And which I prefer to describe as longer lines at the loan window, as the Treasury cuts into the front of the line.
.
In a review of the empirical literature, the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimated that an additional dollar of federal deficit reduces private domestic investment by between 15 and 50 cents in the long run, with a central estimate of 33 cents. There is uncertainty in the amount; there is ample reason to examine the mechanism. (CBO, Working Paper 2014-02.)
.
This bears particularly on the ambitions of young businesses, which do most of the new hiring. An established company has assets, a record, and access to financing that an unproved enterprise may lack. Census Bureau research finds that young firms have much higher rates of net job creation than mature firms, although mature firms employ most workers. The distinction is useful: youth and the capacity to expand matter, not merely the sentimental appeal of smallness. Fiscal policy that improves conditions for investment deserves the  attention from anyone professing devotion to enterprise. (U.S. Census Bureau, Business Dynamics Statistics, February 16, 2022.)
.
Here Mises supplies a criticism remarkably inconvenient for those who invoke the market while defending permanent public indebtedness. In “Human Action,” he described investors actually choosing government debt because they want to be “free from the law of the market.” They prefer their income to rest on the state’s ability to collect taxes rather than on their own success in satisfying consumers. The entrepreneur’s competitive obligation has been exchanged for a public claim. (Mises, Human Action, XII.5.)
.
A Treasury security is a financial claim, not a storehouse containing unspent dollars. The government has already used the proceeds of its borrowing. Retiring debt therefore creates no new factory by an act of bookkeeping. Its economic promise lies in reducing the government’s financing demands and altering the choices available to savers, forcing them back into the market. Some may buy private securities; others may hold cash or foreign assets. Productive investment can benefit, but no public accountant can command every repaid bondholder to finance a startup. (Mises, Human Action, XVIII.5; CBO, discretionary funding caps analysis, July 2023.)
.
That is the defensible meaning of liberating capital: give private enterprise more room to compete for financing, while reducing the tax-supported claims accumulated against future production.
.
The claim is substantial without the extravagance of promising that every dollar retired becomes a dollar of new domestic investment. CBO’s analysis also allows for changes in private saving and inflows of foreign capital. A serious argument should survive the qualifications that reality imposes on it. (CBO, Working Paper 2014-02.)
.
The more spectacular promise is that tax reductions will produce so much growth that the missing revenue will reappear. President Donald Trump offered the appropriate scale of enthusiasm at a Cabinet meeting on December 6, 2017: “I see no reason why we don’t go to 4, 5, and even 6 percent.” His subject was economic growth and the tax legislation then being negotiated. An unsupported statement of what the President saw as being offered in place of a real estimate of what the Treasury could collect. (White House, Cabinet meeting transcript, December 6, 2017.)
.
The administration furnished a paper as well as an aspiration. On December 11, 2017, Treasury announced an analysis showing $1.8 trillion in additional revenue over ten years from expected tax revenues on GDP growth. The underlying exercise assumed average real growth of approximately 2.9 percent instead of 2.2 percent.  It attributed the improvement to tax changes and a wider package of policies, including regulatory, infrastructure, and welfare proposals. This was a conditional calculation of receipts under a stronger-growth scenario, not independent proof that the tax bill would produce that scenario. The Treasury inspector general’s inquiry recorded the assumptions. (U.S. Treasury, December 11, 2017; Treasury Office of Inspector General, tax-analysis inquiry, 2018.)
.
The congressional estimate was less accommodating. The Joint Committee on Taxation projected that the final 2017 law would raise the average level of gross domestic product (GDP)—the economy’s total output—by about 0.7 percent over the ten-year budget window. That meant a higher level of output, not an extra 0.7 percentage points of growth every year. And certainly not Trump’s “4, 5, and even 6 percent.” It estimated $451 billion in revenue recovered through growth against a conventional budget loss of $1.456 trillion, with another $66 billion in interest costs arising from the economic feedback. Roughly $1.07 trillion of additional deficits remained. Growth might help. It did not settle the account. (Joint Committee on Taxation, JCX-69-17, December 22, 2017.)
.
For proof look at what actually happened:
2017 Trump first term 665.5
2018 Trump first term 779.1
2019 Trump first term 983.6
2020 Trump first term 3,132.5
Trump’s 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act was originally estimated to reduce federal revenues by about $1.65 trillion over fiscal years 2018–2027, compared with continuing previous law.
.
Biden, and his brain trust made no effort to reverse the Trump tax cuts.
.
And now again:
2025 Trump second term 1,775.4
2026 Trump second term 1,993.0 *
The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimated a $4.5 trillion reduction in federal revenues over fiscal years 2025–2034, compared with its January 2025 baseline. Signed into law by Trump: July 4, 2025
.
Trump and his MAGA NAZI Party seem intent on ruining the Republic by every means available. With the help of his MAGA NAZI collaborators in Congress.
.
These are deficits accumulating year after year not due to the “Great Recession,” Obama,  or the height of the COVID19 pandemic, Biden, but as a pattern of incompetent governance down to this very moment.
.
Subsequent research gives the tax cuts credit where credit is due. Gabriel Chodorow-Reich, Owen Zidar, and Eric Zwick’s 2024 review found relative to what would have happened without the business tax cuts:
.
Corporate investment in physical assets, such as machinery, equipment, and buildings, increased by roughly 11 percent. However, Federal corporate income tax revenues—the money the Treasury collects from those taxes—decreased by roughly 40 percent, because of the lower tax rate and more generous deductions like depreciation to avoid taxes. ( American Economic Association)
.
The tax cuts encouraged investment, but the resulting economic gains did not replace the lost corporate tax revenue contrary to the multi-decade insistence of the “supply-siders.”  Investment can rise while the public accounts deteriorate. (Chodorow-Reich, Zidar, and Zwick, Journal of Economic Perspectives, Summer 2024.)
.
The distinction was familiar even within the supply-side tradition associated with Jack Kemp. His former adviser Bruce Bartlett told the House Ways and Means Committee in 2011 that their argument had been that growth would recover some of the revenue lost to a tax cut. Partial recovery is an intelligible economic proposition. Complete recovery is a much more demanding claim. One cannot pass from the first to the second merely by speaking with greater conviction. (Bruce Bartlett, House Ways and Means testimony, July 26, 2011.)
.
End of Part 1 of 2
Continued at:
Let the welfare of the people be the supreme law.
Part 2 of 2
.
