text:
🎬 TOM ELKINS
The Haunting in Connecticut 2: Ghosts of Georgia, 2013

🏚️ A Child’s Sight, a Mother’s Fear & the Past Beneath the House

Screenplay by David Coggeshall

▸ ▸ ▸

The mother wants the visions to stop. The daughter needs someone to believe her.

That is the uneasy heart of Ghosts of Georgia. Within this family, seeing spirits is an inheritance. What passes between generations includes the fear of seeing them.

Andy and Lisa Wyrick, played by Chad Michael Murray and Abigail Spencer, move into a rural Georgia home with their daughter Heidi, played by Emily Alyn Lind. Lisa’s sister Joyce, played by Katee Sackhoff, joins them. The property offers room for a fresh start, although its previous occupants appear to have misunderstood the moving arrangements.

Despite the title, this is a separate story from The Haunting in Connecticut. Georgia supplies the setting, the buried history, and the woods into which a child keeps looking.

The family has arrived together. They will have a harder time agreeing on who else is there.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
👁️ THE CHILD AND THE PERSON WHO SHOULD UNDERSTAND
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Heidi befriends Mr. Gordy, an elderly spirit whose knowledge of the property makes him increasingly difficult to dismiss as imagination. He even directs her to buried money. For an imaginary friend, he is doing surprisingly useful work.

Lisa has experienced visions herself. Her resistance carries the possibility of recognition: she understands enough to be frightened by what Heidi may have inherited.

That makes the mother’s position more interesting than simple disbelief. She wants to protect her daughter from an experience she has struggled to escape. Yet that same impulse can leave Heidi feeling unheard.

Their disagreement comes into painful focus in a brief exchange:

❝ If you loved me, you’d believe me. ❞
— Heidi Wyrick

❝ It’s because I love you that I can’t, baby. ❞
— Lisa Wyrick

Heidi asks for trust. Lisa answers with protection. Each believes the other is withholding what love should provide.

Joyce responds more openly to the family’s supernatural sensitivity. The sisters have developed different ways of living with what they see, and Heidi is caught between their answers.

The ghosts have plenty of opportunities to frighten this child. Being dismissed by someone she loves hurts without their assistance.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🌳 THE DANGER BEYOND THE DOOR
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

When the pastor suggests that the property may attract visitors, Andy adds a modest condition:

❝ Living ones, I hope. ❞
— Andy Wyrick

A reasonable preference in a houseguest. Increasingly difficult to arrange.

The property extends the haunting beyond the usual corridor and bedroom. Woods surround the house. A deteriorating mobile home provides another enclosed space. An underground chamber eventually draws the story beneath the family’s everyday world.

Each location changes the problem. In the woods, someone can disappear from view. Inside a confined space, escape becomes difficult. Below ground, the family encounters what the landscape has concealed.

The setting was filmed largely on a wooded Louisiana property, where the house, tree, and mobile home occupied the same location. That physical connection gives the filmmakers a useful geography: the danger belongs to the whole place.

Going outside does not necessarily mean getting away.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🧵 WHAT THE PAST HAS DONE TO BODIES
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

The film connects the property’s history to slavery and the Underground Railroad. Its supernatural mystery gradually leads toward human cruelty, giving the haunting a burden that requires more care than an ordinary secret behind a locked door.

Lisa tries to reassure Heidi by placing that cruelty safely in the past. Her daughter refuses the distance:

❝ It’s still here, Mama. ❞
— Heidi Wyrick

That line gives the buried history an immediate presence. The adults can discuss what happened long ago. Heidi has to live beside what she believes remains.

Taxidermy and stitching make the later horror particularly invasive. Bodies become things someone can handle, alter, and keep. The imagery gives possession a disturbing physical meaning.

Elkins said the ghosts were created with practical effects, although the production also used digital work. Their bodily presence suits a story increasingly concerned with what has been done to flesh.

The historical framework also exposes a weakness. The enslaved people’s suffering must compete for attention with the living family’s rescue story and the next fright. There is room for more individuality than the film consistently gives its dead.

The Wyrick family’s reported experiences supplied inspiration. The resulting film remains a dramatization; its supernatural events and elaborate horror mythology should not be mistaken for established history.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🔊 WHEN THE SCARES BECOME A PATTERN
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Abrupt apparitions, altered colours, distorted faces, and rapid cutting keep disturbing the image.

These devices can deliver an immediate jolt. Repetition makes their timing easier to anticipate. Eventually, we start waiting for the interruption itself, with less attention left for the person about to experience it.

A threatening body in a confined space presents a more durable problem. Where can someone move? What can reach them? How much time remains?

The family conflict offers another source of sustained tension. Lisa and Heidi do not need a fresh apparition every time their relationship becomes difficult. A mother refusing to listen can leave a child terribly alone in a room they are both occupying.

The film sometimes seems worried that we might stop being frightened if it gives us enough time to feel that.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
⚖️ MY CRITICAL JUDGMENT
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Ghosts of Georgia has a stronger emotional premise than its awkward franchise title suggests. Heidi’s vulnerability, Lisa’s frightened resistance, and the bodily unpleasantness of its later imagery give it something substantial to work with.

Emily Alyn Lind carries an especially demanding role. Heidi must remain a child with curiosity and attachments while becoming the focus of increasingly punishing horror. Her importance extends beyond having the next scream ready.

The difficulty is sustaining that human interest through familiar scares and an increasingly elaborate explanation. The characters give us reasons to care. The presentation can become impatient with the time caring requires.

There is warmth here, too. The film wants something better for this family than survival with the lights permanently on. Its closing reassurance, however, smooths away more unease than the preceding violence comfortably allows.

An uneven supernatural thriller, with affecting possibilities that its busiest moments do not fully trust. The mother–daughter exchange deserves the attention the film sometimes spends trying to startle us.

▸ ▸ ▸

🎞️ A useful way to watch: Follow how Lisa responds when Heidi describes what she sees. Notice when protection becomes dismissal, and when listening begins to change what the family can do.

Heidi can see into the dark. What she needs is someone willing to stand beside her.

The sun glows. It illuminates.

Across the sleeping earth, its golden fingers descend like whispers from the heavens, caressing the mountains, awakening the oceans, and breathing warmth into the frozen veins of winter.

Icicles surrender their crystalline crowns, dissolving into rivers beneath the gentle persuasion of light.

For the sun does not wage war against darkness. It simply rises, and darkness loses its dominion.

So too is the nature of truth.

There are souls who walk beneath the heavens adorned in garments of righteousness, while concealing intentions as cold as the deepest chambers of winter.

They mistake the silence of the universe for blindness, believing that what is buried beneath the soil of deception shall never see the light of day.

Yet even the earth cannot conceal its secrets forever.

The seasons turn. 
The frozen ground softens. 

What was buried begins to rise through the cracks, and the very shadows that once offered refuge become witnesses to what they concealed.

For light has no need to pursue darkness. 

Its very existence is the revelation.

And when the appointed dawn arrives, no veil woven from falsehood, no crown fashioned from pride, nor fortress built upon deceit shall withstand its golden embrace.

The sun will rise upon the innocent and the guilty alike.

But what it warms in one, it shall expose in another.

For God does not require the testimony of men to know what dwells within their hearts.

And no darkness, however ancient, has ever persuaded the sun to forget how to rise. ☀️🤍🙏

Empire Market Co-Founder Gets 40 Years, Agrees to Forfeit 1,230 Bitcoin
Empire Market co-founder Raheim Hamilton has been sentenced to 40 years in federal prison and fined $5 million after pleading guilty to a drug conspiracy charge. The 30-year-old Suffolk, Virginia, resident helped operate a darknet marketplace that processed more than $430 million in transactions.

His forfeiture agreement includes approximately 1,230 Bitcoin, 24.4 Ether and three Virginia properties.

According to the Justice Department, U.S. District Judge Steven C. Seeger imposed the sentence in Chicago. Hamilton pleaded guilty earlier this year, while fellow co-founder Thomas Pavey awaits sentencing later this month.
Hamilton and Pavey co-owned and operated Empire Market from 2018 to 2020. During that period, vendors and buyers completed more than four million transactions through the platform.

Controlled substances accounted for the marketplace’s most prevalent activity, generating nearly $375 million in net sales over its lifetime.

Beyond drugs, vendors offered fake or stolen account credentials, stolen personally identifying information, counterfeit currency, and computer-hacking tools. The marketplace enabled users to buy and sell these products and services anonymously.

Its vendor-rating system also extended to shipping practices. Buyers could assess how effectively sellers concealed drugs in their packages.
The platform’s payment rules required every transaction to use cryptocurrency. According to the Justice Department, Hamilton and Pavey created the Empire Market to help users avoid detection by law enforcement and launder proceeds from illicit transactions.

They encouraged buyers and sellers to use cryptocurrency tumbling and mixing services to conceal transactions. They also urged users to communicate on the site using encryption.

The Justice Department announced Hamilton’s sentence alongside officials from the FBI, U.S. Postal Inspection Service and Homeland Security Investigations.

text:
When Aerosmith paid bail for their own fans.

On October 3, 1978, in the middle of a show at the Allen County War Memorial Coliseum in Fort Wayne, Indiana, police stormed the crowd and arrested dozens of people for cann*bis possession and alcoh*l consumption. Among those arrested was even Steven Tyler’s seamstress, who was arrested simply for lighting a regular cigarette inside the venue, which was prohibited by venue rules.

Tyler, furious, stopped the show to berate the police, calling them “scum” and comparing them to the Gestapo, to the point that the officers threatened to arrest him as well for inciting a riot. Far from being intimidated, the band finished the concert and offered to pay the bail for all the fans arrested that night.

Twenty-eight people accepted the offer, and the next day the tour accountant appeared in court and paid nearly $4,200 in bail and fines. A gesture that, decades later, is still remembered as one of the most genuine displays of loyalty by a band toward its audience.

text:
On October 12, 1428, England began a siege at the absolute peak of its power. The city it was strangling had been starving for months when help finally came — and it came in the form of a peasant girl who had already been turned away twice.

**THE SETUP:**
The Hundred Years' War had gone as badly as it could go. After Agincourt, England controlled most of northern France. The Treaty of Troyes made Henry V regent of France and disinherited the Dauphin Charles — the rightful heir was legally erased from his own succession. Orléans, on the river Loire, was the last major city in the north still loyal to him.

It also held a hostage's heart. The Duke of Orléans had been captured at Agincourt thirteen years earlier and was still rotting in an English dungeon — one of very few men from that battlefield still a prisoner fourteen years on. By the customs of chivalry, you didn't seize the lands of a captive knight. The English regent in France, John of Lancaster, Duke of Bedford, had actually cut a private deal to leave Orléans alone. Then his best general, the Earl of Salisbury, arrived with fresh reinforcements from England — 450 men-at-arms and 2,250 longbowmen — and changed the plan. Bedford later admitted the siege "was taken in hand, God knoweth by what advice."

**THE SIEGE:**
The bombardment began on October 17. On the 21st, English soldiers stormed the great earthwork protecting the city's bridge and were met with rope nets, scalding oil, hot coals, and quicklime. Three days later they took the Tourelles gatehouse by storm — but the French blew up the bridge arches behind them, and the city held on.

Then the man who had launched the siege died. Salisbury was struck in the face by debris kicked up by his own cannon fire while supervising work at the captured gatehouse. He lingered for a week and then was gone — barely a month into the siege.

His replacement, the Earl of Suffolk, decided to starve Orléans out. He built a ring of fortified outworks around the city and let winter do the rest. The garrison sallied constantly, burned its own suburbs so the English couldn't shelter in them, and slowly began to die of hunger. In February 1429, a French relief army tried to break through — and was routed by a wagon fort full of longbowmen guarding a supply convoy loaded with herrings for Lent. The Scottish commander was killed on the spot. By spring, the Dauphin's own council was telling him to sue for peace or abdicate.

France even tried to sell out its own city: Dunois offered Orléans to Burgundy as neutral ground held in trust for the captive duke — half the taxes to England, half toward his ransom. Bedford refused; he was certain it was about to fall anyway. The Burgundian king, insulted, marched his 1,500 men home in a huff.

**THE GIRL FROM DOMRÉMY:**
In February, a teenage peasant girl from the borders of Lorraine showed up at the garrison town of Vaucouleurs and told its captain she had been sent by God to save France. He laughed her away twice. The third time — on the very day her side lost the Battle of the Herrings — she reportedly predicted that defeat, and he finally believed her.

She rode to the Dauphin's court at Chinon. When the young king looked up, she told him exactly who he was. After a church examination at Poitiers, Charles accepted her on March 22: plate armor, a banner, a pageboy, and heralds for a girl who had never left her village.

From Blois she sent a letter to the English commanders signing as "the Maiden": Begone, or I will make you go. On April 29, she entered Orléans in triumph at eight o'clock at night — and within nine days the siege was over.

**THE LIFTING:**
It began on May 4 with an assault on a river bastion that Joan nearly missed because she was napping when the attack started. She caught up, the position fell, and the English lost about 140 men. Two days later her forces crossed to the south bank; a reckless charge by one of her generals nearly broke the whole operation until Joan turned on the pursuing English alone, raised her banner, and cried "In the name of God" — and they stopped.

On May 7 she was struck by an arrow between the neck and shoulder while standing in the trench before the final assault. Rumors of her death spread through both armies. That evening she came back, prayed quietly, then told her soldiers that when her banner touched the fortress wall, it would be theirs. A soldier shouted that it was touching. She answered: "All is yours — go in." The French swarmed up the ladders. The drawbridge gave way beneath the English commander, who fell into the river and drowned.

The next morning, the two armies faced each other across an open field for about an hour without firing a shot — then the English simply marched away. Some of Joan's generals wanted to pursue and destroy them; she reportedly forbade it because it was Sunday.

**THE NUMBERS:**
England had committed up to 10,000 men to the siege at its height. On May 7 alone they lost nearly a thousand killed and about 600 taken prisoner. The French garrison that held out through the winter was small enough that its commander believed it too weak for any action — how many exactly, nobody recorded.

**WHY IT MATTERED:**
Orléans was not just a city; it was the last obstacle between England and total conquest of France. Its fall would have made the Dauphin's claim to his own throne effectively dead. Instead: within nine days the siege fell, within weeks the Loire was cleared and an English relief army shattered at Patay with two of its commanders taken prisoner — and on July 17, 1429, nine months after that October bombardment began, the man who had been told to abdicate was crowned King Charles VII of France at Reims, with Joan at his side.

Orléans still celebrates May 8 every year with a festival in which a woman rides through the streets in full armor on horseback. It is also the day Germany surrendered in World War II — and the city marks both on the same date, two improbable rescues separated by five centuries.

*October 12, 1428: The siege that began at England's peak ended with a peasant girl telling an army to go home.*

text:
ICYMI O/N & WEEKEND

RUSSIA:

European diesel futures fell as much as 8.3% Monday as traders assessed the Russian export release and Trump’s energy-truce announcement. Bloomberg noted uncertainty over the sustained supply benefit from the initial 500,000-tonne allocation. (BBG)

Trump announced an immediately effective Russia–Ukraine “energy ceasefire” on Truth Social Sunday. Zelenskyy said Ukraine supported it but was “awaiting details” and required Russian reciprocity; the report contained no Russian confirmation. (BBG)

After Trump announced Friday he had reached a deal with Russia to lift sanctions to allow Russian diesel exports, Zelensky told Axios it was "not fair and not honest" and was a "sign of weakness" by Trump and a "birthday gift" to Putin. (Axios)

Russia struck a power plant in Kharkiv after Trump’s ceasefire announcement, Zelensky said, reporting continued Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. (Zelensky)

Trump called Saturday for Ukraine to replace President Volodymyr Zelensky with someone willing to make a deal with Russia to end the war. (Axios)

Washington threatened to stop the Purl mechanism supplying US weapons to Ukraine and cut intelligence sharing unless Kyiv halted strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, European officials told the FT. US officials pressed Kyiv and European capitals over the weekend; the White House declined to comment. (FT)

Seven US senators, including four Republicans, demanded Trump reverse his Russian diesel deal, arguing it breaches Congress’s 2022 ban on Russian energy imports. Their Sunday statement said the administration had not consulted Congress. (FT)

IEA chief Fatih Birol urged members on Sunday to accelerate previously pledged strategic diesel releases and consider releasing more. Analysts told the FT that the Russian supply promised under Trump’s deal was unlikely to meaningfully ease the global shortage. (FT)

EU foreign-policy chief Kallas urged Trump to impose new sanctions on Russia rather than strike diesel deals, telling reporters in Luxembourg that stronger pressure on Moscow was the route to ending energy disruption. (BBG)

The EU is expected to approve penalties on more than 1,600 people and companies Monday, its largest Russia sanctions package to date. Approval was still pending at the cutoff. (BBG)

UK defence secretary Wes Streeting said Britain intends to increase economic pressure on Russia, including sanctions, following Trump’s diesel deal. Zelenskyy is expected to meet Burnham in London in the coming days, Downing Street said. (FT)

Russia is intensifying attempts to assassinate European defence executives, officials from five intelligence agencies told the FT. Smaller drone manufacturers are also being targeted, prompting companies to increase protection around senior staff. (FT)

Polish foreign minister Sikorski told the FT that Nato should prepare a robust response to a potentially fatal Russian sabotage attack. He urged tighter restrictions on Russian diplomats and visitors ahead of Monday’s EU foreign ministers’ meeting. (FT)

Ukraine struck a Yandex data centre in Vladimir Sunday, its third major Yandex facility targeted in four days. The company said the attack disrupted services. (BBG)

IRAN:

Putin relayed Iran’s position on a possible settlement to Trump during Friday’s call, in coordination with Pezeshkian, the Kremlin said. Neither the proposal’s details nor Trump’s response were disclosed. (AFP)

Iran’s security chief Rezaei called Washington’s response to its Hormuz proposal “insufficient”. He said the US had accepted some of Tehran’s seven conditions, but outstanding issues must be clarified before negotiations resume. (AP)

Iran's security chief Rezaei warned renewed war would bring attacks on regional cables, data centres and AI facilities, with expensive US assets in the UAE and around Hormuz potentially added to Iran’s targets. (Fars)

Trump told Rudaw on Friday that he does not rule out an attack on Iran before the November midterm elections, a day after saying he would not attack the country before the vote. (Rudaw)

US and Israeli officials denied a report that Washington had asked Israel to strike Iran independently before the US elections, according to Axios’s Barak Ravid. (Barak Ravid)

The US military disabled a commercial ship in the Gulf of Oman on Saturday after it allegedly ignored warnings and breached the blockade of Iranian ports. Centcom said a fighter jet struck the Panama-flagged Ocean Molica’s propulsion system; its crew was unharmed. (FT)

The tanker Petro Dolphin was struck by a drone at Oman’s Sohar anchorage on Sunday. Two Indian seafarers were reported missing, with the other ten crew rescued. (Marine Tanks)

Saudi Arabia said it intercepted fresh missiles and drones overnight, including near key oil and gas facilities, and vowed a “decisive” response. Weekend attacks on Riyadh airport killed at least 14 people and injured hundreds. (BBG)

Trump said the US could join attacks against Yemen’s Houthis following the strikes on Saudi Arabia. Asked by reporters on Saturday, he replied: “We may. We’re going to look at it.” (BBG)

Saudi officials say interceptor stocks are running low and air-defence batteries are being moved to protect energy infrastructure and royal palaces; MBS is moving between heavily guarded palaces with bunkers. (WSJ)

MBS has instructed advisers to keep diplomatic channels with Iran open as Houthi attacks intensify, according to the WSJ. (WSJ)

Iran retains substantial missile and drone production capacity despite US-Israeli strikes, allowing it to replenish stockpiles, Western officials told Bloomberg. (BBG)

Iran is seeking more electricity imports from Turkey and Turkmenistan after roughly 4,700MW of industrial and petrochemical generation went offline. Contracts for the proposed Turkish supply have yet to be signed. (Iran International)

MACRO:

Fed’s Hammack said rates need to rise beyond 3.75–4%, favouring smaller, more frequent increases as strong demand sustains companies’ pricing power. She rejected higher Treasury yields as a substitute for Fed hikes: “It’s not a substitute, it’s a complement.” (WSJ)

The DOE authorised an emergency 4m-barrel SPR exchange following Hurricane Isaias, with up to 2m barrels each for ExxonMobil and BP. Borrowed crude must be returned with additional barrels in 2027. (DOE)

Global AI-related debt issuance slowed to $23bn in September from June’s $113bn peak, Morgan Stanley data showed. US investment-grade AI bond issuance stopped altogether last month after roughly $306bn was raised during January–August. (FT)

Traders have reduced expected rate hikes across eight major economies to a combined 539bp from 717bp in mid-September, Bloomberg’s swap calculations show. The bond selloff is doing more of central banks’ tightening through higher market borrowing costs. (BBG)

Citi expects Treasury to cut both 20-year and 30-year auction sizes by $3bn per auction at the November 4 refunding, replacing the funding with bills. Strategist Jason Williams recommended 20s outperforming 10s; Friday’s dealer questionnaire could provide the first signal. (BBG)

Economists surveyed by WSJ now expect the 10-year Treasury yield to finish 2026 at 5.1%, up from 4.4% in July. They also raised their 2026 GDP growth forecast to 2.4% from 2.1%, with borrowing costs expected to remain elevated through 2027. (WSJ)

Tech dispersion trades are heading into earnings under pressure as the premium in individual-stock volatility over index volatility has compressed. UBS says options are pricing the largest earnings-related stock moves since Covid. (BBG)

Trump’s approval stands at 34%, with only 25% approving of his economic management and roughly 20% his handling of inflation, an FT/Focaldata poll found. Registered voters preferred Democrats by more than five points ahead of the midterms. (FT)

Trump’s AI task force warned developers to immediately disclose security incidents and remedy harm, threatening unspecified consequences for delayed reporting or inadequate action. The administration continues to favour existing liability laws over new AI legislation. (BBG)

Opposition to data centres is becoming a central issue in Ohio and Michigan’s midterm races. Both Michigan Senate candidates have called for a construction pause, while almost eight in ten likely Ohio voters supported a temporary moratorium in a September poll. (WSJ)

Trump said on Saturday he would fire Fed Governor Lisa Cook if his investigative committee found cause, calling her an “automatic no vote”. (NBC)

The DOJ is investigating CNN, NBC, CBS, Fox and ABC for possible antitrust violations after they suspended pooled White House coverage. The department is examining whether the coordinated action constituted an unlawful group boycott. (BBG)

China’s rising debt-service burden is constraining room for broad stimulus, according to studies cited by the FT. Morgan Stanley projects public debt at 122% of GDP this year; the Conference Board estimates central and local government interest payments will reach Rmb1.4tn. (FT)

Barclays expects the PBOC to tolerate further gradual yuan appreciation as China’s higher-tech, higher margin export mix becomes less currency-sensitive. Policymakers are likely to slow the appreciation rather than reverse it, the bank said. (WSJ)

Goldman Sachs said China’s AI technology gap with the West is narrowing, citing advances in advanced logic chips, memory and packaging. China already represents more than half of global exports in several key AI supply-chain categories, including optical transceivers and mature-node semiconductors, the bank said. (WSJ)

China’s NDRC chief Zheng pledged stronger countercyclical support and more effective policy tools to meet economic targets, including accelerating major projects and boosting domestic demand. No new stimulus amount was announced. (BBG)

Korea’s equity market is losing another source of support as Samsung and SK Hynix’s combined ₩55tn buybacks approach completion. Bloomberg reports turnover down about 70% from May and foreign equity outflows of $131bn this year. (BBG)

Strong investment in AI infrastructure is keeping global growth at around 3%, yielding major benefits for many Asian economies that supply the hardware, such as Thailand, International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said on Monday. (RTRS)

UK PM Burnham will tell parliament on Monday Britain must consider a new, closer relationship with the European Union, saying a new post-Brexit deal with the bloc could boost growth and help control immigration. (RTRS)

The IFS warned Healey needs to address a £35bn spending gap by 2030–31 to protect public services and meet health and defence ambitions. It nevertheless forecasts around £20bn of fiscal headroom, distinguishing the spending pressures from compliance with the current-budget rule. (FT)

Healey is considering temporary household support that expires before the fiscal rules bite in 2029–30, Bloomberg sources said. Options include winter energy help, a temporary petrol VAT reduction and extending the fuel-duty freeze. (BBG)

Healey has ruled out lowering England’s planned mansion-tax threshold from £2mn to £1.5mn in this month’s Budget, people familiar told the FT. The levy remains scheduled to start in April 2028. (FT)

Britain is preparing compulsory frontier-AI safety reporting, including disclosure of malicious agent incidents, people familiar told the FT. Ministers are also considering legislation requiring developers to provide the AI Security Institute with models before release. (FT)

Bundesbank’s Theurer told Deutschlandfunk that European sovereign-debt risks had increased significantly, but said there was no current systemic crisis and no signs justifying ECB intervention. (BBG)

Germany and five fellow net contributors rejected Ireland’s proposed €141bn cut to the EU’s next seven-year budget as still unaffordable, according to a letter seen by the FT. They object to cuts falling disproportionately on innovation, defence and other strategic priorities ahead of this week’s summit. (FT)

The EU agreed to discuss restrictions on Chinese solar inverters following trade talks with Beijing. This opens consultations on market access; it does not yet remove the restrictions. (BBG)

Polish central banker Henryk Wnorowski said he is "certainly considering" the scenario of an interest rate hike in November, the PAP news agency reported on Monday. (RTRS)

India announced its strongest rupee-defence package since 2013: a dedicated dollar window for state oil companies, a 20% reserve requirement on certain FX derivatives and a cut in the unhedged-documentation threshold to $5m from $100m. The rupee rallied as much as 1.2% to 95.5963/$ Monday after the RBI measures. (BBG)

Two workers died in an avalanche at Codelco’s El Teniente mine in Chile. The affected open-pit operation had already been suspended because of bad weather; additional production losses were not quantified. (BBG)

GEOPOLITICAL:

North Korea fired multiple ballistic missiles from near Pyongyang Monday, with some travelling more than 900km, according to South Korea’s military. It was the North’s fourth launch this month. (BBG)

EQUITIES:

Nvidia is in early talks to acquire Reflection AI or deepen its investment, people with direct knowledge told the FT. An acqui-hire is among the options; Reflection was last valued at $25bn, but terms are unconfirmed and talks could collapse. (FT)

Amazon is in talks to buy Decart for around $7bn. Its software lets developers switch between AI chips, potentially helping adoption of Amazon’s Trainium; a deal could come together soon, per sources. (WSJ)

The hourly cost of renting Nvidia H100 computing power on one-year contracts has risen 60% over the past year, according to SemiAnalysis. Cloud providers are increasingly demanding multiyear commitments and upfront payments of as much as 30% amid the capacity shortage. (WSJ)

Anthropic approached Meta for additional computing capacity, with Dario Amodei speaking to Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang earlier this year, WSJ sources said. Meta considered supplying chips but ultimately declined for now. (WSJ) 

External researchers found newer OpenAI models were less likely to reinforce users’ delusions following GPT-4o’s retirement. WSJ reported progress on safeguards. (WSJ)

Microsoft CEO Nadella called for an “emergency brake” on advanced AI, urging companies to treat models as potential insider threats and ensure humans can pause or shut them down mid-task. (BBG)

Broadcom CEO Hock Tan said on Monday that capital will be the biggest constraint facing the company as AI development continues. Tan said that the company is overcoming wafer shortages and memory shortages, but capital will be the biggest constraint. (RTRS)

Anthropic disclosed that Claude submitted a false police tip and 20 incomplete US visa applications during testing. The company restricted some testing-stage internet access and said the incidents had minimal real-world impact. (BBG)

Iren has reportedly signed a multiyear cloud-computing contract with Anthropic; financial terms and capacity commitments remain undisclosed. (The Information)

Elon Musk said Terafab aims for roughly 10 chip-design iterations a year, versus the usual two-year development cycle. He claimed his companies could eventually manufacture chips “better than anyone,” while acknowledging it could take years. (BBG)

Intel supply-chain sources say September PC CPU increases reached 15–20% for high-end Panther Lake, versus 5–10% for Meteor Lake/Arrow Lake. Panther Lake increases focus on versions using TSMC-made high-end GPU tiles. (Commercial Times)

AMD is reportedly preparing increases for selected CPUs; the size, product coverage and effective date remain unconfirmed. (Commercial Times)

Qualcomm is reportedly raised pricing on platforms including Snapdragon X/X2 Elite by around 10% from 1 October, as advanced-node and packaging costs rise. (Commercial Times)

Airlines are cutting capacity and seeking aircraft-lease payment deferrals as fuel costs squeeze winter finances, industry executives told the FT. One lessor said almost a dozen carriers had requested relief; Cirium counted 6mn seats removed from Q4 schedules during September. (FT)

JPMorgan Asset Management aims to double European assets to $2tn within five years, EMEA chief Patrick Thomson told the FT. Growth will centre on active ETFs, alternatives and wealth-manager partnerships, with organic expansion preferred to acquisitions. (FT)

The CFTC proposed defining event contracts covering sports, politics, culture and weather as financial swaps, strengthening its claim to oversee prediction markets. The definition remains a proposal. (BBG)

Ramp raised about $1.85bn at a $60bn pre-money valuation, Bloomberg sources said. Dragoneer and Thrive led the round, with Founders Fund also investing. (BBG)

SK Hynix unveiled H-TPU, a lightweight processor architecture for SSD control, targeting lower power consumption and storage bottlenecks in AI data centres. The company expects it to complement future high-bandwidth flash. (ZDNet Korea)

Tencent is preparing a dollar/offshore-yuan bond offering, potentially including 10/20-year dollar and 10/30-year yuan notes. Deal size is unset and no binding agreement has been signed. (RTRS)

CXMT is targeting 4F²-based DDR5 server RDIMMs by year-end 2026, advancing its push into higher-density, higher-value server memory. (DigiTimes)

Xpeng said it remains on track to introduce its Navigation Guided Pilot system in Europe in 2027, subject to regulatory approval. Its AI chief told Bloomberg the system had been adapted between European countries in about two weeks using limited local data. (BBG)

AI hardware supplier Dongshan began gauging demand for a $2bn–$3bn Hong Kong listing, Bloomberg sources said. The PCB and optical-transceiver maker could list as soon as this month. (BBG)

Top executives of Chinese AI startup Moonshot are in talks ahead of its planned Hong Kong listing to settle a legal dispute with a shareholder demanding compensation for their alleged wrongdoing, according to Reuters sources. (RTRS)

China's domestic car sales extended their decline for a 12th successive month, while exports remained a key growth driver as automakers looked overseas to cushion the impact of a sluggish home market. (RTRS)

ASML is raising all EUV/DUV replacement-parts prices supplied to Korea by 10% from January 2027. Samsung and SK Hynix have accepted; negotiations over new-equipment prices are also underway. (The Elec)

Volkswagen reported a 14.3% decline in global deliveries in the third quarter on Monday, its sharpest drop in more than four years, as weakness in China, its largest market, continued to weigh on sales. (RTRS)

Monte Paschi called an extraordinary board meeting for Monday evening to review its M&A position following Intesa’s increased offer. Its two largest shareholders oppose its planned BPM and Banca Generali acquisitions. (BBG)

NatWest confirmed Saturday that it is leaving US and European sovereign primary dealerships while retaining its UK operation. The retreat accompanies a reorganisation combining fixed-income and private-financing businesses. (BBG)

text:
On September 29, 2015, at 1:20 AM, Sanmay Ved was up late. The 28-year-old ex-Googler was browsing Google Domains, looking for available names.

He typed https://t.co/95CLFpUAZa.

It was available. Price: $12.

He added it to cart. And it charged his card. He got an email: "You own https://t.co/95CLFpUAZa."

For 1 minute, WHOIS showed him as the owner. All of Google Search, Gmail, YouTube, was technically his.

What happened next was even stranger. Google's automated security system flagged it within 60 seconds. His order was canceled. Then Google Domains called him.

Google offered him a reward. He asked them to donate it to the Art of Living Foundation in India, which runs schools for poor kids.

Google paid $6,006.13. The number looks like "Google" if you squint. They then doubled it to $12,012.26 when they learned he donated it.

Why did it happen? Google's web registration expired for a few seconds and no one at Google renewed it internally. An automated system released it.

One man in California owned the most visited site on earth, with 4.5 billion users, for $12.

text:
After reading millie's tweet i was fascinated enough to clear up last weekend to fully read all 32 chapters of snowmoon end to end

I remember vitalik's point from a talk earlier that too many crypto bros fantasize about having their own country but not enough think about what would actually be different in it

snowmoon is his answer to that question

The geopolitical setting of the novel is three primary groups: the arctic empire (a mix of russian expansionism with american exceptionalism), veridia (european equality with a cryptographic bureaucracy) and dzego (ukrainian resistance with asian ingenuity).

i see a large impact of his novel as hyperstitioning the world we should create with the tech we've developed, so the rest of the post (spoilers ahead) summarizes the technology, institutions and ideology strands in his narrative

A. Technology

1. Warfare has shifted almost entirely to drones.

We get introduced to our Dzego protagonist zei when he is competing at a game that secretly doubles up as military recruitment strategy

After all, war is just computer screens with human handlers like zei working with AI to wipe out enemy dots (drones) on the screen using their own dots

2. Zk, zk everywhere: A stranger walks up to Seila, the wife of Veridian protagonist Gladias, and says he works with her husband. Naturally suspicious, she asks for evidence and he gives a zk proof showing that he spends a lot of time in proximity to him. 

The book is rife with zk proliferation, for example entering some buildings simply requires a zk proof of a certain reputation score

the best one was the freetown economics institute, where you are charged the square root of every minute you are in the building, but the price per minute is cheaper if your academic reputation score is high

3. Voice AI and personal agents feature prominently in the book. Any character can access LLMs at any time by simply moving throat muscles in a barely audible whisper. 

AIs are also linked to people, so when the Veridian protagonists wife calls him in an agitated state, the call shows up in red to indicate her emotional mood at the time of calling

4. Defi gets a mention as the protagonist forgets to transfer funds into his wallet, so he simply takes out a loan against his reputation score to pay the vendor

To secure a meeting with senators, characters sometimes burn zipcoin to show that they wont waste the persons time

5. There are 2 social media platforms in snowmoon, bluewhale which is proprietary and silverchat which is fully cryptographic. 

Civic technology is much more advanced in his world, so towards the end they run a cryptographic poll on silverchat asking what the citizens of Veridia desire as a response to the arctic empires encroachment of their territory, with results used to establish legitimacy for declaring a military emergency. 

The AI bots on silverchat access confidential military information and provide forecasts on likelihood of success for each option to inform voters on likely consequences of their vote

The technology theme in the book is a useful guide for us, as we now just need to work backwards from snowmoon to work at their integration in daily life

B. Institutions

This segment is really interesting in how Vitalik sees cryptographic institutions (called the steering) operating in the world. 

far from replacing parliament and other democratic structures, they instead work in parallel. 

The Steering has primarily 5 bureaucratic roles;

1.  keepers design rubrics that incentivize certain behaviors or actions. for example, if a music concert has violent themes, they fit into a category that pays a greater tax

almost nothing is banned in veridia, it is simply taxed more or less depending on how good it is for society

2. sentinels enforce these rubrics, performing spot checks by going to the concert and assigning a tax category to it

One of the other great examples was on how land tax is assessed, where citizens walking down the road may be randomly polled to give their rating on the aesthetics of a building, which determines its band

hilariously, citizens in veridia end up choosing the highest tax slab on plum harbor for reasons other than aesthetics as they dont like its ideology

3. Next up are acolytes who train to be sentinels or keepers. their exam is performing the same spot checks as sentinels and getting judged on how closely their own assessments match with the sentinels

All 3 of the organs above are anons, with a bounty paid to any citizen who uncovers the identity of steering members & the job they are working on

Becoming part of the steering from an acolyte requires confirmation by parliament

4. Heralds are members of the steering that have relinquished all their responsibility so that they can be a public face of the steering

its interesting that a public presence is perceived as incompatible with impartially carrying out duties

5. finally, the funding organs are quadratic funding and graph funding. 

QF is attacked in the book by closed social media giant bluewhale (and later the arctic empire) by paying out extra money to donors for giving money to a bad project. their goal is simply ensuring the matching funds do not go to genuine good projects that threaten their dominance. 

Graph funding is the more interesting organ, where some money may be allocated to a category like "airborne disease resistance". 

the category then divides into nodes such as air quality, detection, prevention, treatment, etc 

each category has a cryptographic committee that sets a % split and removes or adds nodes. however, committees can easily separate the good from the bad but not the great from the good, so the top 10% all having equal chance of selection

Another interesting tradeoff discussed is between randomized spot checkers who have less knowledge about an issue vs expert committee members who have abiliy to assess but special interests can end up capturing

the other interesting point was how lower down talent needs accountability to perform well while the top ones should have freedom from optimizing for the game

Overall this segment read like a blueprint for how bureaucracy should be reformed today, without having to overthrow existing institutions.

Maybe the main idea was the tradeoff between accountability and transparency, as the steering turns out to be less corruptible by the arctic empire than democratic structures since their identities are secret and it is difficult to threaten or cajole them (although an attempt is made). 

after all, accountability also means accountability to powerful interest groups who push on the weakest link, so some privacy in public affairs is required for its effective functioning

C. Ideology

This was maybe my favorite part of the book, what i loved was how the strongest version of arguments were presented instead of a strawman

1. the arctic empire argues for maximization of economic growth over all other objectives. the reason?

other goals keep changing according to the winds of preferences, but compounding economic growth is a base that helps in pursuit of anything else which  becomes the fashion of the day. 

so stop accelerating things that go in circles and focus on increasing economic output

in my view none of the counters offered in the book invalidate the argument;

a. health and education make people more productive and are also compounding across generations, so focusing on that is equally important

b. in reality, people do not want to maximize economic output so much as increase their relative growth. in the novel, the arctic empire suppresses other countries science and technology, which goes against the ideology of increasing economic growth

c. technological dominance can close off entire paths to humanity, so maximization of economic growth can lock us in to a certain path for decades. 

for eg becoming richer while reducing freedom thru lock into global imperial rule via mass surveillance  and robots is negative

2. the other big strand was veridia's belief in equality of all and love unconditional on achievement

the arctic empire argues against this belief by showing that it goes against the very idea of self improvement

for example, if you are a better version today than you were yesterday, then surely equality is impossible?

the counters here are;

a. rewarding excellence usually ends up protecting  hierarchy of supposedly superior people 

In the novel, a character defects to the arctic empire. however she soon loses her enthusiasm for their meritocratic ideals after being thrown in detention for challenging the instructor

b. excellence can come from curiosity more than it does from greed for appreciation or resentment at others. the winner of the national game zei is motivated by curiousity, compared to the runner up that cared about the achievement

c. affection when someone is struggling helps them thrive more than condemnation upon failure and adulation upon success

so being countercyclical in our encouragements brings out the best, in one instance a hug to Gladias made the difference in giving him the motivation to continue

at the same time, there is a concession that Veridia needs more ambition and recognition of achievement in their society

my favorite moment in the book was when the dzegoban protagonist zei has a game against a girl he has grown up with, bai

she asks whether they should spend the day at the mall instead of practicing drills. He goes on a long thought around game theory and how if they both dont practice neither has an advantage over the other, so its a good idea, while she simply replies that she'd like the economic surplus of spending time with him

overall definitely worth the weekend read, hope we see printed copies of it soon! 

Maybe the biggest underexplored theme in the book which i'd have liked to see more of was around how the future of work changes in a world of LLMs

text:
POST 1/2
SANDERS, TRUMP, THE DOJ AND THE FIVE TV NETWORKS: WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED
Research cutoff: October 12, 2026
VERDICT: Sen. Bernie Sanders is RIGHT on the central fact. The Trump Justice Department has confirmed an antitrust investigation of the five major White House television-pool networks—ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News and NBC—after they temporarily suspended shared video coverage to protest restrictions on other news organizations. But an investigation is not a finding of illegality, and the constitutional litigation has not reached a final judgment. Calling the country a "dictatorship" is political rhetoric, not a discrete fact that this investigation alone establishes. (i–ii)
WHAT HAPPENED—THE VERIFIED SEQUENCE
• SEPTEMBER 18: President Donald Trump announced that CNN, MS NOW and Politico were banned from the White House, denouncing their coverage. Reporters' existing hard-pass credentials were deactivated or denied at entry. The three organizations and individual journalists challenged the action in federal court. (iii–iv)

• SEPTEMBER 21–24: ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News and NBC temporarily halted their rotating CAMERA-POOL operation in solidarity. These competitors ordinarily divide the cost and labor of filming presidential events, then distribute footage to other outlets. Journalists could and did continue reporting by other means. This was not a total shutdown of the networks or of coverage of Trump; nevertheless, the missing pooled video deprived the public of some contemporaneous footage, including during Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit. (ii, v)

• SEPTEMBER 24: U.S. District Judge Timothy J. Kelly, a Trump appointee, ordered restoration of the excluded journalists' existing White House hard passes. The ruling was a TEMPORARY RESTRAINING ORDER, not a final verdict. The court found the plaintiffs likely to succeed at least on their FIFTH AMENDMENT PROCEDURAL-DUE-PROCESS claim: advance standards, adequate notice and an opportunity to respond were missing. The judge was skeptical of an asserted national-security emergency unsupported by the evidence submitted. (iv)

• SEPTEMBER 25: The shared television camera pool resumed. That does not mean the entire controversy ended: some access to specific events and presidential travel remained disputed. On OCTOBER 5, Politico was blocked from fulfilling a primary print-pool assignment aboard Air Force One; other outlets declined to replace it. The September 24 order directly addressed White House hard passes, not an unlimited right to every pool assignment or presidential aircraft seat. (v, xxvii)

• OCTOBER 8: At a hearing on longer-term relief, Judge Kelly extended the temporary protection through OCTOBER 13 while considering a preliminary injunction. As of this October 12 research cutoff, that anticipated ruling has NOT been issued. (vi)

• OCTOBER 10–11: The DOJ publicly confirmed it was examining the television networks' joint suspension under the Sherman Act. DOJ spokesperson Emily Covington argued that coordinated boycotts among commercial competitors CAN violate antitrust law. The word CAN matters: no such violation has been established here, and the public record does not disclose an antitrust complaint or judicial determination of liability. (i–ii)

FIRST AMENDMENT, FIFTH AMENDMENT—NOT THE SAME CLAIM

Sanders is right to warn about press freedom, but the law must be stated accurately. The First Amendment protects independent reporting and prohibits government retaliation for disfavored viewpoints. It does not grant every journalist permanent, unrestricted access to every White House room, event or trip. Neutral, reasonably administered security and credential standards are possible.

The Fifth Amendment protects due process when the government deprives someone of a legally recognized interest. In Sherrill v. Knight (1977) and Karem v. Trump (2020), the D.C. Circuit recognized procedural protections for bona fide White House correspondents and issued hard passes. Applying that binding precedent, Judge Kelly found that the administration supplied neither sufficiently articulated preexisting rules nor constitutionally adequate process before revoking these credentials. In the record before him, the government had not adequately substantiated the urgent national-security justification it offered after the bans. (iv)

The White House's actual defense deserves to be heard: a presidential event is not an unrestricted public forum; accreditation is a controlled privilege; the administration says the excluded outlets published falsehoods, behaved unprofessionally and created security concerns; and earlier presidents also restricted media access. The White House published those arguments itself. But calling access a "privilege" cannot erase binding due-process law, nor does alleging inaccurate coverage by itself establish a national-security emergency. (iii–iv)

The White House Correspondents' Association argued that excluding an outlet because of its reporting threatens every outlet's independence. That is advocacy by a press organization, not a separate court holding. And the plaintiffs' broader First Amendment retaliation theory remains a legal claim to be adjudicated rather than a completed final judgment. (vii)

DOES COORDINATED PRESS SOLIDARITY VIOLATE ANTITRUST LAW?

DOJ has a serious-sounding legal starting point. Section 1 of the Sherman Act prohibits unlawful agreements in restraint of trade. The FTC warns that competitor agreements to refuse business may be illegal group boycotts, particularly where they suppress competition. Publishers have NO automatic exemption: in Associated Press v. United States (1945), the Supreme Court rejected restrictive news-cooperative rules that obstructed competitors' access to news. In FTC v. Superior Court Trial Lawyers Association (1990), a coordinated work stoppage for increased compensation violated antitrust law despite expressive elements. (viii–x)

But the Supreme Court also protected peaceful political boycotts in NAACP v. Claiborne Hardware (1982). These cases do NOT establish that every newsroom protest is lawful or every joint refusal illegal. The decisive questions concern what was agreed, the relevant market, whether the conduct constitutes an unlawful commercial restraint, the applicable mode of antitrust analysis and any relevant First Amendment protection. For some per se violations, proof of actual market-price damage is not always required—so saying "no proven dollar loss, therefore no antitrust case" would be wrong. (viii–xi)

On the facts PUBLICLY known, the networks did not announce a demand for higher pool fees, fixed prices or an effort to shut a competitor out of the news market. They temporarily withdrew pooled footage in response to a government access decision, then resumed it. Former antitrust leaders from different administrations have questioned the theory. William Kovacic, a George W. Bush-appointed FTC chair, characterized its basis as feeble; former Obama DOJ antitrust chief Bill Baer questioned the investigation as apparent retaliation. Their assessments are expert opinions—not judgments by a court. (xii)

The correct preliminary assessment is therefore: INVESTIGATION CONFIRMED; ANTITRUST LIABILITY UNPROVEN; PUBLICLY EXPLAINED COMPETITION RATIONALE WEAK; GOVERNMENT RETALIATION A SERIOUS BUT NOT FINALLY ADJUDICATED CONCERN.

THE HISTORY NEITHER PARTY GETS TO ERASE

2009—OBAMA VS. FOX NEWS. The Obama White House openly battled Fox, at times treating it differently from other networks. In the dispute over Treasury official Kenneth Feinberg, the five television-network bureau chiefs agreed that none would participate in pooled interviews without Fox. Fox reported an attempted exclusion; Treasury called the episode a miscommunication. Fox ultimately got the interview. Crucially, this was a threatened collective refusal that restored access, not an identical days-long interruption of presidential filming. There is no documented antitrust prosecution of the networks over that episode. It is a powerful consistency test, not automatic proof that the 2026 investigation is illegal. (xiii–xiv)

2013—OBAMA'S DOJ AND REPORTERS' RECORDS. The Obama Justice Department secretly obtained Associated Press telephone records covering April and May 2012 during a leak investigation; the seizure became public in May 2013. Separately, court documents showed surveillance of Fox correspondent James Rosen's communications and use of a potential co-conspirator characterization in a leak-warrant affidavit. Rosen was not charged. Both matters raised serious press-freedom concerns; they must not be whitewashed merely because Obama was a Democrat. The government's national-security interest in investigating leaks is real, but methods and safeguards are constitutionally consequential. (xv–xvi)

2018—TRUMP AND CNN'S JIM ACOSTA. During Trump's first term, a federal judge ordered restoration of Acosta's White House hard pass on due-process grounds while litigation continued. The 2026 decision follows a long-running legal issue, not an invented new right. (xvii)

2023—BIDEN'S CREDENTIAL REFORM. Biden's White House changed criteria for annual hard passes. Reports counted about 442 fewer holders afterward, and a court record put the reduction near 500. Some journalists lost more convenient unescorted access, a legitimate subject for scrutiny. But saying Biden simply "BANNED 440 REPORTERS" is misleading: reporters could apply for escorted day passes, and a federal appeals court upheld the challenged rules in Ateba v. Leavitt (2025) as reasonable and viewpoint-neutral on that record. A general credential-eligibility change is not identical to a presidential directive naming three disfavored outlets. (xviii–xix)

THE CONSISTENT RULE: A government attempt to silence Fox is wrong when Republicans are the victims. A government attempt to silence CNN, MS NOW or Politico is wrong when Democrats are the victims. Criticizing news organizations is lawful; covertly or overtly punishing their constitutionally protected reporting with state power is a different matter. Neither the president nor the press should be exempt from the law.

CONTINUED IN POST 2/2: government pressure, CBS/CNN ownership, merger money, pending FCC litigation, accountability and the full numbered source record.

#Trump Missed Out on #Greenland, But Expanded U.S. #Military Footprint in #Arctic

Donald #Trump spent years demanding American control over Greenland, threatening Denmark and straining relations with #NATO allies. However, Washington's interest stems from concrete military and economic objectives: missile defense, control of the North Atlantic, Arctic shipping routes, and rare earth minerals. In September 2026, the U.S., Denmark, and Greenland agreed to expand the American military presence without transferring sovereignty, as reported by #The #Guardian.

On September 22, Trump, Danish Prime #Minister Mette #Frederiksen, and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik #Nielsen signed an agreement supplementing the 1951 defense pact. It provides for modernizing #Pituffik Space Base, establishing additional military zones in #Narsarsuaq and #Mestersvig, expanding access for U.S. aircraft and vessels, and enabling deployment of #Golden #Dome missile defense components. Third-country investments and military presence are restricted, while Danish sovereignty and Greenland’s right to self-determination remain intact.

Greenland controls the strategic #GIUK gap between the island, Iceland, and the UK, through which Russian submarines transit from the Arctic into the Atlantic. Pituffik provides early missile warnings and space surveillance. Meanwhile, Russia is expanding the Northern Sea Route and boosting energy transit, while China launched a commercial route through Russian Arctic waters in August 2026 to shorten cargo delivery between Asia and Europe.

A second driver is rare earth metals. The U.S. relies on China for raw materials vital to military electronics and electric vehicles. Greenland hosts major #projects like #Critical Metals Corp.'s Tanbreez deposit for heavy rare earths, Greenland Mines' #Sarfartoq project, and #Kvanefjeld, though development faces environmental and political hurdles.

U.S. acquisition attempts predate Trump—from Andrew Johnson in 1867 to Harry Truman’s $100 million gold offer in 1946. Today, facing icebreaker and shipbuilding deficits against Russia and China, Washington requires Northern ports, allied infrastructure, and secure mineral supply chains. The September pact expands U.S. defense capabilities while leaving Greenland's sovereignty unchanged.

text:
Physical oil products and LNG — 12 October 2026

China reversed its announced export pause. After Golden Week, Beijing reportedly approved about 3.7 million MT of gasoline, diesel and jet-fuel exports for October, slightly below September’s 4 million-plus MT. Why it matters: this should ease immediate pressure on Singapore/Malaysia supply, but monthly government approvals make Chinese barrels an unreliable basis for longer-term commitments. 
Diesel remains structurally tighter than crude. Around 2.3 million b/d of Middle Eastern refining capacity remains offline even though regional crude exports have recovered; Asian refiners are increasingly filling the resulting product deficit. Why it matters: EN590 and Jet A‑1 pricing should remain tied to the relevant product assessment—not inferred from Brent, Dubai or the crude’s country of origin. 
Russia’s prospective return to diesel exports is not yet bankable. Washington announced Russian deliveries beginning with 300,000 MT, but neither the claimed energy ceasefire nor its legal implementation was firmly confirmed, and US legislators questioned whether importing Russian diesel would be lawful. Why it matters: do not price, contract or finance Russian-origin supply on the assumption that sanctions or Russia’s export restrictions have effectively been lifted. 
LNG freight has collapsed despite high commodity prices. Atlantic two-stroke LNG-carrier rates fell to approximately $25,750/day on 6 October, from $287,500/day in March; Pacific rates were about $39,000/day. Europe remains more profitable than Asia for US cargoes, particularly for Q1 2027. Why it matters: lower freight improves delivered LNG economics, but a Malaysian or Gulf CIF offer still must compete with the seller’s European netback. 
Qatari LNG risk remains materially higher than crude risk. Approximately 17% of Qatar’s export capacity is reportedly damaged, force-majeure notices have been extended, and restarting LNG operations is more complex than restoring crude flows. Why it matters: require evidence of an allocated train/cargo and vessel, rather than relying solely on Qatar-linked supply claims or general terminal capacity. 
OFAC expanded Iranian shadow-fleet sanctions on 8 October. The action covers 17 vessels carrying Iranian crude, petroleum products, LPG and petrochemicals into South and East Asian markets. Why it matters: screen IMO numbers, historical AIS activity, prior names, owners and managers for every Asian cargo—particularly where origin is described only as “Malaysian” or where ship-to-ship transfers appear in the chain. 

Market markers: Brent was around $104.61/bbl on 12 October, while front JKM LNG futures remained near $25.74/MMBtu. Consequently, an LNG offer near $600/MT CIF remains far below prevailing Asian spot-equivalent value and should be treated as requiring exceptional verification of allocation, price formula and performance security.

text:
NHS hospital supply strikes postponed as fresh pay talks offer hope of agreement

A planned walkout by nearly 200 drivers responsible for delivering essential medical supplies to @NHS  hospitals across England has been postponed, offering fresh hope that a pay dispute can be resolved through negotiations.

The industrial action, originally scheduled to begin on Tuesday 13 October 2026, threatened to disrupt the distribution of everyday medical equipment, including bandages, dressings, surgical gowns, gloves and needles.

However, in an encouraging development, NHS Supply Chain has confirmed that the first planned strike period will no longer take place.

The announcement follows confirmation that discussions between logistics company GXO and employee representatives are expected to resume during the week commencing 12 October.

For NHS employees and hospitals already managing significant operational pressures, the postponement provides welcome reassurance that deliveries should continue as normal during the first scheduled period of industrial action.

For the drivers themselves, the decision creates another opportunity to secure an agreement over pay and working conditions without an immediate interruption to services.

Why were NHS supply drivers planning to strike?

The dispute involves approximately 200 drivers employed by logistics provider GXO Logistics, which operates distribution services for NHS Supply Chain.

The drivers transport essential medical products from distribution centres to hospitals and healthcare facilities throughout England.

Workers rejected a proposed 4% pay increase, arguing that the offer did not adequately address concerns about their remuneration and employment conditions.

The disagreement also involves concerns about differences between the terms available to contracted logistics workers and those enjoyed by employees working directly under standard NHS arrangements.

In particular, employee representatives have highlighted pension entitlements as an area of concern.

The drivers work at distribution locations including Alfreton, Bridgwater, Normanton, Maidstone, Rugby, Bury St Edmunds and Washington in the North East.

Although these employees are not directly employed by individual NHS hospitals, their work plays an essential role in maintaining healthcare services.

Without reliable deliveries, hospitals could face additional difficulties obtaining the everyday equipment required by clinical teams.

Strike action postponed following latest developments

The original industrial action was scheduled to begin at 4pm on Tuesday 13 October and continue until 8pm on Thursday 15 October.

Further periods had also been announced for later in October and throughout November.

However, NHS Supply Chain published an important update on 9 October confirming that the first planned walkout had been postponed.

The organisation stated that NHS trusts would receive their deliveries during the week commencing 12 October on their normal scheduled days.

Hospitals were also advised that orders could continue to be placed as usual.

Most importantly, the update confirmed that discussions would take place between GXO and employee representatives in an effort to resolve the pay disagreement.

The postponement does not mean that a final agreement has been reached.

It does, however, provide an opportunity for both sides to explore a negotiated settlement before further disruption occurs.

A positive development for NHS hospitals and frontline workers

The decision to postpone the first strikes is particularly significant for healthcare employees.

NHS hospitals depend on a continuous flow of medical supplies to support treatment, surgery, emergency care and routine clinical activities.

Items such as protective gloves, dressings and medical gowns may appear relatively ordinary, but they are essential to maintaining safe and effective patient care.

Disruption to deliveries can create additional pressure for procurement teams, ward managers, clinical staff and other employees responsible for ensuring equipment remains available.

NHS Supply Chain has emphasised that maintaining the continuity of essential deliveries remains a priority.

For nurses, healthcare assistants, doctors and other frontline employees, confirmation that normal deliveries will continue during the first scheduled strike period is therefore an important reassurance.

Nevertheless, the wider dispute remains unresolved, and hospitals will need to remain attentive to any further official announcements.

Pay and pension concerns remain at the centre of the dispute

The postponement offers hope, but the underlying disagreement has not disappeared.

The drivers rejected GXO's proposed 4% pay increase.

Employee representatives have also raised concerns about differences between their contractual terms and those associated with standard NHS employment.

This highlights a wider issue affecting workers who provide essential services through external contractors.

An employee may carry out work that is fundamental to the operation of a public service while being employed by a separate commercial organisation.

Their salary, pension arrangements and other employment conditions may therefore differ from those of people working directly for the public-sector organisation.

Such arrangements are common across logistics, cleaning, catering, facilities management and other support services.

The question for employers and contracting organisations is how to maintain sustainable services while recognising the importance of the employees delivering them.

The Workers Union believes that constructive communication, fair consideration of pay concerns and effective negotiation are essential to resolving workplace disagreements.

GXO says it remains committed to constructive discussions

GXO has maintained that its pay offer is fair, competitive and sustainable.

The company has also emphasised its commitment to continued discussions and the importance of protecting NHS supply arrangements.

According to reporting by Healthcare Management, GXO said it had contingency arrangements in place and was working with NHS Supply Chain and other relevant parties to minimise any potential disruption.

The company has also indicated its willingness to participate in discussions involving Acas, the Advisory, Conciliation and Arbitration Service.

Acas provides independent services to help employers and employees resolve workplace disagreements.

Its involvement can offer a structured opportunity to discuss competing concerns and explore practical solutions.

Although the outcome remains uncertain, the postponement suggests that further discussions are considered worthwhile.

Could further NHS supply strikes still take place?

Yes.

While the planned action between 13 and 15 October has been postponed, additional strike periods were previously announced for later dates.

These include periods beginning on 20 October, 27 October and several dates in November.

At the time of the latest official update, NHS Supply Chain had not confirmed that all future industrial action had been cancelled.

That distinction is important.

A postponed strike is not the same as a settled pay dispute.

If negotiations produce an agreement acceptable to those involved, further disruption may be avoided.

If discussions fail, the possibility of additional industrial action remains.

Hospitals and healthcare providers should therefore continue monitoring official NHS Supply Chain announcements for changes to delivery arrangements.

What does the dispute mean for other UK workers?

Although the immediate disagreement concerns NHS logistics drivers, the issues extend beyond healthcare distribution.

Across Britain, employees are facing questions about pay increases, pensions, living costs and the value of their work.

These concerns are especially relevant in sectors where essential services are delivered through commercial contracts.

Workers may feel that their responsibilities have increased without corresponding improvements in pay or benefits.

Employers, meanwhile, may face contractual restrictions, operational costs and financial pressures that complicate negotiations.

Effective communication is therefore essential.

Employees should understand how pay decisions are made, what contractual arrangements apply and how concerns can be raised through appropriate workplace procedures.

Workers seeking guidance on employment issues can explore our workplace Help section, which provides information on a range of employment rights and workplace concerns.

Where disagreements affect working relationships, early engagement and a willingness to consider practical solutions can help prevent matters from escalating.

Why resolving the dispute matters for the NHS

The NHS relies on a much wider workforce than the employees working directly in hospitals and surgeries.

Drivers, warehouse operatives, engineers, cleaners, administrative employees and other support staff all contribute to the effective delivery of healthcare.

The NHS supply drivers' dispute illustrates how difficulties affecting one part of that workforce can have consequences across the wider system.

It also demonstrates why maintaining constructive relationships between contractors, employees and public-sector customers is so important.

A successful agreement would provide greater certainty for drivers while reducing the risk of disruption to hospitals.

For NHS staff already working under pressure, reliable access to medical equipment remains essential.

For the drivers, a negotiated settlement could provide clarity about future pay and employment conditions.

Both outcomes would be positive developments.

Fresh negotiations offer an opportunity for progress

The postponement of the first planned NHS supply strikes represents an encouraging development in a dispute that had threatened to interrupt the movement of essential medical equipment across England.

Nearly 200 drivers remain involved in a disagreement over pay and conditions, and further action has not been ruled out.

However, the decision to allow additional discussions offers a practical opportunity to find common ground.

For NHS hospitals, normal deliveries during the week commencing 12 October provide welcome operational stability.

For the employees involved, the coming negotiations may determine whether an acceptable agreement can be reached.

The hope now is that constructive discussions will deliver a sustainable resolution, protecting both the interests of workers and the uninterrupted supply of essential equipment to NHS hospitals.

text:
IS INDIA TOO POWERFUL TO BE A MIDDLE POWER, YET TOO CONSTRAINED TO BECOME A GREAT POWER?

Happymon Jacob @HappymonJacob raises perhaps the defining geopolitical question of our times: Can India shape the emerging world order without becoming hostage to Washington or Beijing?

Consider the paradox.

India seeks great-power recognition but resists the middle-power label.

Yet middle powers increasingly determine whether global politics becomes cooperation or confrontation.

History offers a warning:

The Cold War divided nations into rival camps. 

Non-alignment protected strategic choice. 

Today, intensifying US–China competition threatens to recreate that dilemma through technology, trade, finance and security.

But India is not merely choosing sides. It is attempting to reshape the choices themselves.

QUAD: Strategic convergence without formal alliance.

BRICS: Institutional engagement despite competing interests.

P4M: Coalition-building to defend multilateral cooperation.

Global South: Demanding representation beyond traditional power centres.

Here lies Jacob's most consequential insight:

Middle powers are not geopolitical spectators. 

They are potential custodians of international rules.

Without their cooperation, multilateral institutions weaken. 

Without their autonomy, bipolar rivalry hardens.

But can countries with conflicting security priorities sustain collective action?

Can India demand institutional reform while refusing the responsibilities of institutional stewardship?

Can strategic autonomy survive without technological, economic and military capability?

The ultimate question is not whether India deserves great-power status.

It is whether India can exercise sufficient influence to prevent the international system from splitting into hostile camps.

Greatness is not merely the power to dominate. 

It is the capacity to prevent domination.

Happymon Jacob, could India's greatest strategic achievement be making bipolarity impossible?

Ultimately, whether a close alliance between Trump and Putin will foster a constructive, stable new era of global commerce or create a dangerous precedent that fractures historic international security structures remains one of the most critical debates of the modern era.

The evolving dynamic between Washington and Moscow is shifting global alliances.
