text:
On this day, October 12, 1870, General Robert E. Lee died in Lexington, Virginia, at the age of 63.

One of the most famous military figures in American history, Lee’s life stretched from the early republic through the Civil War and into Reconstruction.

Robert Edward Lee was born in Virginia in 1807, the son of Revolutionary War hero Henry “Light-Horse Harry” Lee. He graduated second in his class from West Point in 1829 without receiving a single demerit and began a long career as an officer in the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers.

Lee distinguished himself during the Mexican-American War, particularly during Winfield Scott’s campaign from Veracruz to Mexico City. Scott came to regard Lee as one of the Army’s most capable officers.

In 1861, when the Civil War broke out, Lee opposed secession, but when Virginia left the Union, he declined an offer to command Union forces, resigned his U.S. Army commission, and chose to fight for his home state of Virginia.

In June 1862, Lee assumed command of what became the Army of Northern Virginia. Over the next three years, he built his reputation through campaigns that included the Seven Days Battles, Second Manassas, Fredericksburg, Chancellorsville, Gettysburg, the Overland Campaign, and the long defense of Petersburg.

Working with commanders such as Stonewall Jackson, James Longstreet, J.E.B. Stuart, and others, Lee repeatedly confronted larger Union armies. His aggressive style produced some remarkable Confederate victories, particularly at Second Manassas, Fredericksburg, and Chancellorsville.  His invasions of the North ended at Antietam in 1862 and Gettysburg in 1863.

In 1865, Lee was named General-in-Chief of the Confederate armies.  On April 9, 1865, Lee surrendered the Army of Northern Virginia at Appomattox Court House. 

After the war, Lee became president of Washington College in Lexington, Virginia—today Washington and Lee University. He spent his remaining years largely outside politics and encouraged former Confederates to accept the outcome of the war and rebuild their lives.

After suffering a stroke in September 1870, his health rapidly declined. Robert E. Lee died on October 12, 1870.

Lee’s legacy is that of one of the greatest military commanders in American History and a true gentleman. He was highly respected by both the North and the South. 

Robert E. Lee
January 19, 1807 – October 12, 1870

Kremlin spokesman Peskov has now publicly rejected Zelensky’s 60-day ceasefire proposal tied to holding Ukrainian elections, offering nothing in return.

▸ THE KREMLIN’S ANSWER

The proposal was simple: pause the fighting for two months, hold elections, and prove that Moscow’s endless demand for “legitimate leadership” in Kyiv was ever about anything but stalling. Russia said no.

Peskov offered nothing in response. Not a framework.

Not a timeline. Not even a pretense of negotiation.

The demand for elections was never about democracy. The object served as a weapon.

Zelensky called the bluff, and the Kremlin folded its hand without showing cards.

▸ THE ENERGY TRUCE SILENCE

When asked about Trump’s energy ceasefire, the Kremlin had nothing to say. Not confirmation.

Not denial. Just silence.

Trump announced a ceasefire as if it were settled. Kyiv learned about it from reporters.

Russian forces violated that one within days the last time it was declared.

Moscow cannot even be bothered to pretend it takes American initiatives seriously. The pattern is consistent: Washington proposes, the Kremlin shrugs, and the war continues.

▸ THE PATTERN

Russia has now rejected every ceasefire proposal put forward. The 60-day pause.

The energy truce. The Black Sea framework.

Each one met with silence or mockery.

The Kremlin treats Trump as a useful intermediary who applies pressure only on Ukraine while asking nothing of Russia.

Every American initiative becomes another opportunity for Moscow to demonstrate that only force will stop it.

Peskov's rejection states his intent.

Russia wants the war to continue since it holds the regime together.

🇺🇸US economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics for their work on the "microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation". 

The laureates were recognised for developing theoretical frameworks that bridge individual economic decisions with large-scale economic stability, providing central banks and governments with vital tools to manage shocks.

Robert E. Hall, Stanford University, researches the demand side of the economy, looking closely at consumer behavior and demand fluctuations to construct his stabilisation models.

Michael Woodford, Columbia University, examines the supply side, specifically investigating how companies set prices. Woodford is widely known as an architect of modern forward guidance, demonstrating how central banks can steer the economy by shaping public expectations about future inflation and monetary policy. 

According to the Nobel Committee, their combined work offers a stable foundation that allows policymakers to better smooth out the economy's peaks and troughs, particularly during energy crises or sudden shifts in consumer habits.

It depends on the state you live in, and if you live within city limits or not. It is generally unlawful to shoot a gun within city limits, unless you are a certain distance away from roads, and buildings. If a bullet winds up going off your property, that is also a problem. If a stray bullet hits someone or something, you are in very big trouble. There are also noise laws you might violate. 

Once you leave city limits, rules about roads and buildings generally go away. People who live outside city limits also have more land so it's harder for bullets to leave the property. 

I used to live in a state that was very unfriendly to firearms. I owned 612 tsubo of land. If had shot in my back yard there, the police would have shown up, and I'd have been arrested.

Now I live in a free state, and outside of city limits. I shoot in my back yard whenever I want because I own 36,000 tsubo of land. If the sheriff ever shows up at my house while I'm shooting, I'll offer to let him take a turn.

text:
Somebody just reached into the mouth of the most poisonous fish on the beach.

With a pair of tweezers.

And the fish did not fight back. Not once.

That is the part that should scare you.

Because this is a pufferfish. A body that can carry enough toxin to kill a room full of grown adults. A creature with no antidote waiting for you at any hospital on earth. A fish that Japanese chefs spend years learning to cut, and that some people have died just for eating wrong.

And a stranger knelt in the shallows, in flip-flops, and did something nobody in their right mind would try.

Watch the video first. Then come back here and read what you just saw.

Because I promise you, you did not see even half of it.

THE FISH THAT NOBODY WANTS TO TOUCH

Let's start with the obvious question.

Why is a pufferfish scarier than a shark?

A shark is loud about it. Fin, teeth, blood, panic. You know exactly what you are dealing with.

A pufferfish is quiet. It looks like a cartoon. It has the face of a confused grandfather. It has big round eyes, tiny fins, and a mouth that looks like it is permanently about to say "oh."

And inside that harmless face is a chemical called tetrodotoxin.

Here is what that name means in plain English: a nerve poison that switches off the signals between your brain and your muscles. First your lips tingle. Then your tongue. Then your arms go heavy. Then you cannot walk. Then you cannot speak.

And the cruelest detail of all: through most of it, you stay fully awake.

Your mind is clear. Your body is gone.

It is often described as around 1,200 times deadlier than cyanide, gram for gram. There is no widely available antidote. Doctors keep the patient breathing with a machine and wait for the body to clear the poison on its own.

That is the animal in this video.

Hold that thought. We are just getting started.

THE TRAP CALLED LOW TIDE

Now forget the poison for a second.

Think about the ocean the way the ocean actually works.

Twice a day the sea walks away. It pulls back across the flats and leaves behind thousands of small, shallow pools, warm as bathwater and getting warmer by the minute.

For crabs, that is just Tuesday.

For a fish, it is a countdown.

A tide pool in full sun is a brutal place. The water heats up fast. The oxygen drops. The salt gets thicker as the water evaporates. A pool that felt like a safe nursery at sunrise can turn into a slow trap by noon.

Fish get caught in these places every single day, all over the world. Most of them are never seen. Most of them never get a second chance.

The ones that do survive usually survive for one reason only: luck.

Wrong place. Wrong hour. Right person.

I keep coming back to those three words, because that is the whole story of this video.

The ocean did not bring this fish to safety. The ocean left it there.

Somebody else had to decide that it mattered.

A DEFENSE SYSTEM THAT IS ALSO A PROBLEM

You probably know the famous trick.

Threaten a pufferfish and it swallows water, fast, and swells into a hard, spiny ball several times its normal size. A predator that was about to eat a snack suddenly finds itself staring at something that looks like a mistake.

It is one of the best defenses in the animal kingdom.

But here is what most people never think about.

Inflating is expensive. It burns energy. It makes the fish clumsy. A puffed pufferfish is basically a floating balloon with fins that cannot steer it. In open water it can drift helplessly, and it cannot swim away from anything.

Its whole survival strategy is built around one assumption: that the danger is outside.

Make yourself big. Make yourself spiky. Make yourself impossible to swallow.

It is a perfect answer to an enemy that wants to eat you.

It is a terrible answer to a problem that is already inside.

Think about that for a second.

What happens to a creature whose only weapon is to get bigger, when the thing hurting it cannot be scared away?

You already know the answer. The answer is the video.

THE MOUTH

Let me tell you about the part of a pufferfish that scientists respect and sailors fear.

The mouth.

A pufferfish does not have teeth like yours. It has a beak. Four hard plates fused together into a cutting tool strong enough to crack open shells, snap off coral, and chew through crab armor like it is wet paper.

And it never stops growing.

That beak keeps getting longer for the entire life of the animal. In the wild, a diet of hard shells wears it down at exactly the right speed. In aquariums, keepers have to trim it by hand, or the teeth grow so long that the fish can no longer eat.

Now look at it from the other side.

This is a mouth that can break bone-hard shell. It sits on a body that is full of nerve poison. It belongs to an animal that, in a state of panic, will do anything to defend itself.

And somebody decided to work inside it.

I have been online for a long time. I have watched people do reckless, brilliant, stupid, beautiful things for views.

This was none of those.

There was no performance in it. No music. No dramatic cut. No one looking at the camera and saying "smash that like button." Just steady hands, and a fish that seemed to understand, at some level, that this was the only thing that could save it.

Which brings me to the question that kept me awake.

Why didn't it bite?

THE SCIENCE OF WHY IT STAYED STILL

I went looking for the answer, and I found three possibilities.

None of them are comfortable.

The first possibility: exhaustion. A fish stranded in shallow water has been fighting for hours. Heat, stress, low oxygen. Its body may simply have had nothing left to give.

The second possibility: fear so deep that the animal freezes instead of fighting. Biologists call it tonic immobility. You see it in sharks, in rabbits, in birds. The body decides that the safest move is to stop moving entirely.

The third possibility is the one that gave me goosebumps, and I will say it carefully, because science does not like to say it out loud.

Maybe it knew.

Animals understand pain far better than we used to admit. Fish have nerve endings that detect harm. They learn. They remember. They avoid places where they were hurt. Some species recognize individual faces.

If something inside your mouth has been causing you agony for hours or days, and a hand finally arrives that does not hurt you, how long does it take for the body to decide that this hand is different?

I do not know the answer.

But I know what I saw on that screen.

And I know I watched it three times in a row without blinking.

THE STRANGEST SECRET OF THE POISON

Here is something that will rearrange your brain.

A pufferfish does not actually make its own poison.

For a long time, scientists assumed it did. It made sense. The animal is the poisonous one, so the animal must be the factory.

But the evidence points somewhere stranger.

The toxin appears to come from bacteria, living in the food chain. Tiny organisms in the sea produce it. Small creatures eat those organisms. Pufferfish eat the small creatures. The poison builds up in the fish, in the liver, in the ovaries, in the skin.

The fish is not the maker. The fish is the collector.

And the proof is almost funny.

Pufferfish raised in farms, on controlled diets with no exposure to the wild source, end up with almost no toxin at all. Entire fish farms in Japan now raise safe, harmless fugu, and the animals look exactly the same as their dangerous cousins.

Same face. Same swagger. Same round eyes.

No poison.

So the thing that makes this animal so terrifying, the thing that has haunted kitchens and written itself into legend for centuries, is not part of its soul.

It is something it picked up along the way.

I want you to hold that sentence in your mind for the rest of this post.

Something it picked up along the way.

THE CHEFS WHO BET THEIR LIVES

In Japan, a pufferfish dish is called fugu.

It is a delicacy. It is also one of the only foods in the world where the person serving it needs a government license.

To earn that license, a chef trains for years, often two or three, under a master. They learn exactly which organs hold the toxin and exactly how to remove them without a single nick or leak. Then they sit an exam that includes preparing the fish and, in some regions, eating their own work.

The standard is simple: if you are wrong, someone dies.

Out of respect for the danger, restaurants have a culture around it. The cut is thin enough to see the pattern of the plate through the flesh. The taste is subtle, almost shy. The thrill is not in the flavor.

The thrill is in the risk.

There is a famous story from 1975. A celebrated Japanese kabuki actor, a man so revered that he was designated a living national treasure, sat down in a Kyoto restaurant and ordered several portions of fugu liver.

It is the most toxic part of the fish. The chef knew it was forbidden. He served it anyway, because the actor insisted, and because nobody says no to a legend.

The actor died that night.

He was a master of his craft. And he was killed by the thing he thought he could control.

Keep that in mind, because it brings us back to the shallows.

THE ARTIST NOBODY COULD IDENTIFY

Now let me show you the other side of this animal.

Because the pufferfish is not just a weapon with fins. It is also, quite possibly, the most underrated artist in the ocean.

Off the coast of Japan, a diver once began noticing something on the sandy seabed. Huge, perfect, symmetrical circles. Ridges and grooves, radiating from the center like a mandala. Around two meters wide, built into the sand, with a precision that looked almost designed by a machine.

For years, nobody knew who made them.

People guessed aliens. People guessed currents. People guessed pranks.

The truth was far more beautiful.

It was a tiny male pufferfish, only about twelve centimeters long.

Using nothing but its fins and its body, it spends days carving that structure into the seabed, working nonstop, tireless, obsessive, shaping every ridge. Then it decorates the center with shell fragments.

And then it waits.

Because the entire masterpiece is a message addressed to one person: a female. If she likes what she sees, she lays her eggs in the middle of it, and the currents of the design carry oxygen to them.

Think about that.

The same species that carries enough poison to bring down a stadium also carries enough patience to build a cathedral out of sand.

This is not a simple animal.

This is not a creature that deserves to be left in a puddle to die.

WHY YOUR THUMB STOPPED SCROLLING

I want to talk about you for a minute.

Because the internet is a loud, fast, tired place. You have seen ten thousand videos this week. Dances, arguments, ads, outrage, jokes, tragedies that last six seconds before the next thing arrives.

And yet, there is a very specific kind of video that makes people stop.

Not the flashy ones.

The quiet ones.

A person helping an animal, with no audience, with no script, with nothing to gain. There is something almost sacred in it. In a world that taught us to assume everyone is performing, we suddenly see someone who is simply doing the right thing.

It reminds us that kindness is not an idea.

It is a physical act. It has hands. It has patience. It takes time.

I have noticed something about the videos that spread furthest. They are rarely the most beautiful. They are rarely the most shocking. They are the ones that make a stranger feel, for forty seconds, that the world might be a slightly better place than they thought.

This video does that.

And it does it in the worst possible environment for kindness: a hot, shallow pool on a rocky shore, with a dangerous animal, a clock running down, and absolutely no guarantee that it would work.

That is the part that got me.

No guarantee.

THE ODDS THE FISH WAS FACING

Let me put numbers on the situation, so you understand how thin the margin really was.

A pufferfish, like most fish, cannot survive long out of water. Gills collapse. Oxygen stops moving. A fish stranded in a shrinking pool is running out of two things at the same time: water and options.

Inflate a pufferfish with air instead of water, and you create a deadly problem. Air trapped inside the body is extremely hard for the fish to release. It floats, it cannot dive, and its soft belly is exposed to the sun and to every bird in the sky.

Add to that anything lodged in the mouth, anything that interferes with how the fish eats, breathes, or closes its beak, and the clock stops being theoretical.

It becomes a few hours.

Maybe less.

Most animals in that situation never meet anyone.

This one did.

And here is the detail I cannot stop thinking about: when the moment finally came, when the hand moved, when the tool slid in, it did not look like panic.

It looked like trust.

I know. I know how that sounds.

Watch it, and tell me I am wrong.

TEN FACTS THAT WILL MAKE YOU LOOK AT PUFFERFISH DIFFERENTLY

Because you are going to be thinking about this animal for the rest of the day, here is some ammunition for your next dinner conversation.

One. Pufferfish have no ribs and no pelvic fins. Their bodies are built to stretch like rubber.

Two. Some species can swell to nearly three times their normal size within seconds.

Three. Their skin is covered in spines that lie flat when relaxed and stand straight up when inflated.

Four. Their eyes move independently. They can look in two directions at once.

Five. They are among the most poisonous vertebrates on the planet.

Six. They are also among the slowest swimmers, which is part of why they evolved a defense that does not need speed.

Seven. Their genomes are famously compact. Scientists use one species as a reference, because it carries unusually little genetic clutter.

Eight. Many keepers report that pufferfish recognize the person who feeds them, and will swim to the glass to greet them.

Nine. Their beak keeps growing for life, so in the wild the diet has to keep wearing it down.

Ten. Despite all of it, the poison, the spines, the beak, the bluff, they are slow, soft-bodied, and surprisingly easy to catch.

Which is exactly why this one needed somebody.

THE SENTENCE I TOLD YOU TO REMEMBER

Scroll back up for a second. Find the line about the poison.

Something it picked up along the way.

That sentence is the key to this whole story.

The most dangerous thing about this fish, the thing that gives it a reputation, a mythology, a place in legends and menus and nightmares, is not who it is.

It is something that found its way into the animal from the outside.

And now ask yourself what else a creature like that might pick up along the way.

The ocean is a place of constant exchange. It gives and it takes. It feeds animals, and it also hands them things they were never meant to hold. Whatever the sea puts in front of a hungry, curious mouth, that mouth will try.

I am not going to tell you what came out of this fish.

You will want to see that with your own eyes. I cannot ruin it, and I would not if I could.

But I will tell you this.

When it finally appeared, I stopped breathing.

Not because it was disgusting.

Not because it was shocking.

Because in that second, I understood how close the whole thing had been to ending differently.

WHAT THIS TAUGHT ME ABOUT FEAR

We are trained from childhood to fear certain animals.

Snakes. Sharks. Spiders. Anything with a reputation.

But reputation is not the same as nature.

The pufferfish has the worst reputation in the sea, and yet if you spend a few quiet minutes watching one, what you find is a nervous, curious, slightly clumsy animal that is trying very hard to get through the day.

It is not hunting you.

It is not plotting.

It is trying to survive in a world that was not designed with it in mind.

The poison is not malice. It is armor.

The puffing is not aggression. It is fear.

The hardest part of being human may be remembering that the things that look the most dangerous are often the ones that are most afraid.

And that the right response to fear is rarely more force.

It is steadiness.

It is patience.

It is a hand that does not tremble.

I think that is why this video hit me so hard.

Because the person in it was not brave in the way movies teach us. There was no shouting. There was no music. There was no hero shot.

There was just calm.

And calm, I am beginning to believe, is the most powerful tool a living thing can offer another living thing in trouble.

THE QUESTION I CANNOT STOP ASKING

Let me turn this around.

I want you to be honest.

Picture yourself in that spot. Low tide. Hot sun. A stranded fish. A dangerous reputation. A decision to make, and nobody watching, nobody asking, nobody who would ever know if you walked away.

Would you have stopped?

Not in theory. Not on the internet, where it is easy to be a hero.

On the rocks, with your hands, with your own risk.

Most people say yes.

Most people are not sure.

And somewhere between those two answers is the real reason this kind of footage spreads. We do not just want to watch a rescue. We want to find out who we would have been.

I will tell you who I would have been, honestly.

I would have taken a photo. I would have said "poor thing." I would have walked on.

And I would have felt a little bit worse about myself all afternoon.

Then I watched a stranger do the thing I did not do.

And I felt something shift.

THE FORTY SECONDS

Here is what I know about forty seconds.

It is not long enough to tell a life story. It is not long enough to explain a species. It is barely long enough to finish a coffee.

But it is long enough for something to change.

In forty seconds, a fish that was stuck went from being a problem to being a living thing. In forty seconds, a stranger's hands became the only thing standing between an animal and the end of its afternoon. In forty seconds, the entire food chain of fear, myth, poison, and legend was set aside for something much simpler.

Help.

I have worked in this space a long time. I have studied what makes people stop, what makes them share, what makes them send a clip to a friend with no caption except "you have to see this."

The formula is not complicated.

Tension. Stakes. A turn you did not see coming.

This video has all three, and none of them were planned.

The tension is the animal.

The stakes are its life.

And the turn?

The turn is the moment the hand moves.

I will not say more.

WHAT HAPPENS TO A FISH LIKE THIS

I get asked this every time.

What happens after?

The honest answer is that nobody in the comments ever knows, and nobody in the video says. The camera stops. The screen goes dark. The sea keeps moving.

That is how real life works. It does not hand you a clean ending.

But I will tell you what experienced marine biologists say about animals in this exact position. They say that the difference between life and death is often a matter of minutes. That a stressed fish can recover astonishingly well once the cause of its trouble is removed. That water, shade, and calm can restore a creature that looked finished.

They also say something I have never forgotten.

They say the sea is full of animals in trouble, and almost nobody is there to see it.

Which means every rescue we witness is not just a story.

It is a rare event.

It is one of the few moments the ocean lets us look into.

And you are about to look into one.

ONE QUESTION BEFORE YOU WATCH

Here is a small experiment.

Before you watch, answer one question in your head. Only one.

What do you think a creature does when it has been in pain for so long that it stops expecting relief?

Does it thrash? Does it hide? Does it fight whatever comes near?

Now watch the video and see how close you were.

I would bet money that almost nobody guesses right. And I would bet that somewhere around the halfway point, you will go quiet, and the only thing you will want to do is send it to someone.

When footage is real, the stakes are real, and the ending is allowed to take its time, that is what happens.

That is not a reaction you get from a joke or a stunt.

Some videos are made to be consumed.

This one is made to be felt.

And the strange thing about feelings is that you cannot fake them, you cannot rush them, and you cannot explain them to anyone who has not seen what you saw.

I can describe the shoreline.

I can describe the fish.

I can list every fact I know about the most misunderstood animal in the sea.

But I cannot give you the moment.

Only the video can do that.

BEFORE YOU PRESS PLAY

Let me give you a few instructions, because this is not a video to rush.

Turn the sound on. Real sound, not background noise. Listen to the water. Listen to the quiet. Listen to how still everything gets.

Watch the fish, not the hands. Look at the eyes. Look at the mouth. Look at the way its body moves when something changes.

Notice the moment the tension breaks.

You will know it when you see it.

And when it ends, do not scroll immediately. Stay for one more breath. Let it land.

Then do one thing for me.

Tell me what you felt.

Not what you think. What you felt. In the first second. Before the thinking started.

I read every answer. I always do.

WHAT THE COMMENTS WILL LOOK LIKE

I already know how this goes.

Within an hour, the replies will split into camps.

The first camp will say it is fake. It is not. Fake rescues are polished, lit, and cut to music. This one has wind, wet rock, and hands that are not afraid to get dirty.

The second camp will say the fish was never in danger. Maybe. But ask any marine biologist whether a stranded animal with something wrong in its mouth is in a safe position, and watch their face.

The third camp will say the poison makes the whole thing reckless. That camp has a point, and it is exactly why the video grips you. Courage only counts when something is at stake.

And then there is the fourth camp.

The quiet one.

The people who write four words and nothing else.

"I watched it twice."

That is the camp I am writing this for.

Because if you are reading this far, you are already one of them. You did not come here for facts. You came because some part of you suspects that the next forty seconds might leave a mark.

You are right.

It will.

THE LAST THING

We live in a strange moment.

Billions of clips. Billions of faces. Endless noise. Most of it will be forgotten by tomorrow.

But now and then, something small and honest slips through. A stranger. A shoreline. A fish that should have been left behind.

And for a moment, the internet does what it was supposed to do all along.

It connects us to something real.

I do not know the name of the man in the video.

I do not know where the shore is, or what the tide was doing, or what the fish thought as the water settled around it.

I know only this.

Something small was in trouble.

Someone noticed.

And someone cared enough to kneel down and do the hard, quiet, frightening thing.

If that does not make you want to watch, nothing I write ever will.

So go.

Press play.

And when it is over, come back and tell me I was wrong.

I do not think you will.

If this made you feel something, send it to the one person you know who still believes the world is worth being kind to.

Repost it. Follow for more stories from the strange, wild, beautiful places where animals and humans meet.

And if you are ever standing at a tide pool and see something that needs a hand, you already know what to do.

Be the one who stops.

P.S. One more thing, because the best part of any story is the part nobody expected.

When I first saw this video, I thought it was about a fish.

By the end, I realized it was about the gap between what we assume and what is true. The poison was never the point. The reputation was never the point. The point was a living thing in a hard place, and one pair of steady hands.

Some stories do not need a villain. They do not need a twist engineered by an editor. They need a living creature, a moment of real danger, and someone willing to stay calm while everything inside them says to run.

That combination is rarer than you think.

You can scroll for a year and not find it again.

Now it is your turn.

Watch it. Then reply with the one word that describes how it made you feel.

I will start: relieved.

text:
Watching these increasingly desperate attempts to rescue a rather stupid slogan by pulling bits of international law out of context is becoming genuinely entertaining.

The trick is simple enough. Start with something nobody disputes: states can change, split, merge or disappear. Then quietly replace it with a rather different proposition: states have no legally protected right to continue existing.

And hope nobody notices the switch.

Unfortunately, international law, and the courts actually interpreting it, are rather less accommodating.

In 1996, the International Court of Justice explicitly recognized the "fundamental right of every State to survival" (Legality of the Threat or Use of Nuclear Weapons, para. 96), linking it to self-defence under Article 51 of the UN Charter.

An awkward little detail for someone insisting that "no state - none - has a right to exist".

UN Security Council Resolution 242 (1967) is even more inconvenient when it comes to Israel. It explicitly affirms the sovereignty, territorial integrity and political independence of every state in the region, along with their right to live in peace within secure and recognized boundaries.

Apparently, the Security Council forgot to consult your interpretation of international law.

The Supreme Court of Canada also seems to have missed the memo. In its 1998 Reference re Secession of Quebec, it explained that self-determination does not normally grant a unilateral right to secession, and that states satisfying the relevant conditions are entitled to protection of their territorial integrity under international law (paras. 130, 154).

Which brings us to your wonderfully chosen example of Scotland.

You might want to read the UK Supreme Court's judgment of 23 November 2022 ([2022] UKSC 31).

The Court ruled that the Scottish Parliament could not independently legislate for an independence referendum. And here's the particularly amusing part: in paragraphs 88-89, it specifically considered the argument based on international-law self-determination, referred to the Canadian judgment, and rejected its application to Scotland.

The 2014 referendum happened because Westminster agreed to transfer the necessary authority.

So your supposedly devastating Scottish example actually illustrates the distinction you're trying so hard to erase.

Nobody is arguing that states enjoy some supernatural guarantee of eternal existence, immutable borders and permanent governments. That's a condition you invented yourself, attributed to your opponents, and then proudly demolished.

Congratulations on defeating your own argument.

Your historical examples don't fare much better.

Apartheid South Africa? Apartheid ended. South Africa didn't.

Nazi Germany? The regime was destroyed. German statehood continued, something the German Federal Constitutional Court explicitly addressed in its 1973 judgment.

Czechoslovakia? Dissolved by political agreement in 1992. Since when does the ability to dissolve something voluntarily prove that it had no legal protections beforehand?

Regime change, constitutional transformation, consensual dissolution, state continuity - these are different legal concepts. Treating them as interchangeable might make for a convenient political slogan, but it makes for dreadful legal reasoning.

And now we come to the part you seem particularly determined to avoid.

On 4 October 2026, the Green Party adopted a policy calling for a single Palestinian state throughout historic Palestine. That raises a rather obvious question: what happens to Israel as a separate state?

And that, of course, was the political context of Nick Robinson's question to Zack Polanski.

He wasn't asking whether countries have a divine right to exist forever. Or whether borders can ever change. Or whether Scotland should be allowed to hold a referendum.

He was asking whether Israel should continue to exist as a state, or be replaced by another one.

Not a particularly mysterious question, is it?

Of course Israelis and Palestinians should have equal rights. That's a perfectly defensible position. But equal rights alone tell us nothing about whether the political arrangement should involve one state or two.

And repeating that people have rights doesn't magically answer a question about the future of a particular state.

You can criticize Israel's government, argue for constitutional changes, defend Palestinian self-determination, or even advocate a negotiated one-state solution. None of those positions requires pretending that international law offers states no protection against being forcibly eliminated.

But you cannot take the absence of a right to eternal and unaltered existence, quietly turn it into the absence of any legally protected right to survival, and then announce that everyone who spots the sleight of hand has undergone some sort of collective lobotomy.

Especially when the courts you apparently forgot to consult have already made the relevant distinctions.

Perhaps the BBC journalists aren't the ones having trouble with elementary logic.

Perhaps they've simply asked a perfectly straightforward question that you would much rather bury under a mountain of irrelevant legal trivia than actually answer.

text:
Israel has no right to exist. That’s the position in international law. It has nothing to do with hatred of Israel or antisemitism.

In fact, no state – none – has a “right” to exist, including states busy extolling their democratic credentials.

If the UK had a “right” to exist, for example, it would mean that Scotland could not be allowed to vote for independence. Why? Because such a vote would break up the UK. It would be a violation of the UK’s supposed “right” to exist as the UK.

Which is precisely why the UK has no “right” to exist.

Peoples have a right to exist. When that right is abused, it invariably involves very serious violations of international law – often through crimes such as apartheid, ethnic cleansing or genocide.

States, by contrast, don’t have a “right” to exist. They simply do exist as a matter of fact – until they suddenly don’t. Like apartheid South Africa. Like Rhodesia. Like Czechoslovakia. Like Yugoslavia. Like Nazi Germany.

This is so obvious it should not even need stating.

Were states to have a “right” to exist, completely arbitrary factors such as their borders, demographic make-up and political institutions would be sacrosanct. Inviolable. It would be impossible for minorities to secede, for territories to be transferred, for apartheid structures to be overturned . Any such change would be a transgression of the state’s “right to exist” as it is.

And yet every single journalist employed by an establishment media outlet is suddenly playing dumb on this most elementary of issues. They’ve all suddenly had a collective lobotomy. They insist Israel must be the exception to the rule that no state has a “right” to exist.

Watch, for example, the BBC’s Nick Robinson berating Green party leader Zack Polanski for refusing to affirm Israel’s “right to exist”. Polanksi correctly argues instead that Israelis and Palestinians have a right to live in equality.

Why all this incendiary stupidity from our supposedly brightest and best journalists?

Find the answer in my latest article No state has a ‘right’ to exist – least of all an apartheid, genocidal state like Israel. A link to the full article is in the reply post ⬇️

text:
Overcoming Fear and Negative Thoughts; A Journey Back to Inner Peace(Please repost)

Allow us to begin with this; you do not have to fight your fear or force yourself to think positively to become free of negative thoughts. 

The first and most important step is to learn to stop giving those thoughts control over your inner world; observe from a neutral stand point, as if they are not your own, for in truth they are not. 

Fear is a part of the old matrix program. It may arise from past experiences, uncertainty about the future, or the mind trying to protect you from something it perceives as a threat. The goal is to reach a place where fear no longer dictates how you live. And this begins by returning to the heart center; by making the journey from the mind to the heart.

Stop fighting your thoughts

When a negative thought appears, do not panic, do not judge yourself, or struggle to push it away. Fighting a thought often gives it more attention and makes it return more frequently.

Instead, acknowledge it;

"I notice this thought, but I do not have to believe it. A thought is not a fact, and it does not define who I am."

Let the thought come and go without following it into a long chain of worry.

You are the awareness observing the thought, not the thought itself.

Bring yourself back to the present moment, back to the heart

Fear often lives in imagined futures and scenarios, while regret lives in the past. Your point of consciousness is focused in the present.

When you feel overwhelmed;

Pause, close your eyes,

Inhale a deep slow breath in through your nose,

Exhale gently, through mouth..

Relax your shoulders, jaw, and hands.

Repeat for a few minutes. You are reminding your nervous system that you can return to the present instead of following every frightening possibility your mind creates.

Stop feeding the cycle of negativity

Pay attention to what you repeatedly expose yourself to. Constantly consuming alarming news, arguments, hostile discussions, or frightening predictions can keep your mind in a state of tension.

You do not have to ignore what is happening in the world. You can remain aware without absorbing those energies.

Choose carefully what you watch, read, listen to, and discuss. Give yourself time for nature, music, silence, exercise, and meaningful conversations.

You can embody peace without avoiding reality. It is your choice as to how much of your attention you give to outer events.

Question the story behind the fear

When a negative thought appears, ask yourself;

Is this something I know to be true, or something I am afraid might happen?

Am I responding to what is happening now, or imagining the worst possible outcome?

Is there anything constructive I can do about this?

What would I think about this situation if I were feeling calm?

If there is a real problem, take one practical step. If it is an imagined possibility you cannot resolve right now, practice letting it remain uncertain without repeatedly trying to solve it. Always remember that you are doing well in the present. If you do not truly feel that way, shift your thoughts, shift your perspective.

Replace self criticism with self compassion

Sometimes the negativity you experience comes from the way you speak to yourselves.

Instead of saying, "Why am I like this? Why can I not stop thinking negatively?" Say;

"I am going through a difficult moment, and I can meet it with patience and greater awareness. I can take this one moment at a time. I am at the center, where it is peaceful."

Treat yourself with the same understanding you would offer someone you love.

Strengthen your inner connection

From a spiritual perspective, fear arises from identification with the temporary self. When a person believes they are only their body, personality, possessions, reputation, or earthly circumstances, the possibility of losing these things can become a source of anxiety, something that arises within your experience, rather than something that defines your deepest self.

Fear grows when trust in the Divine is lost. The mind tries to control the future because it cannot tolerate uncertainty. Inner trust allows a person to act without needing to know or control every outcome.

Fears and triggers can often reveal what still needs healing. Rather than condemning yourself for feeling afraid, you can look at the belief beneath the fear and bring it into awareness.

Love and fear represent different inner orientations. Love opens the heart, while fear tends to contract awareness around perceived threats, separation, and self protection.

Spend a few minutes each day in quiet meditation, prayer, or contemplation. Bring your attention to your heart and reflect on qualities such as love, gratitude, forgiveness, and trust.

You might repeat these words slowly;

I return to the present.

I release what I cannot control.

I allow my thoughts to pass without giving them power over me.

I choose love over fear, in every moment.

Take care of your physical body

Your mental and physical states influence each other. Lack of sleep, excessive caffeine, inactivity, and prolonged stress can make fearful thoughts more intense.

Try to maintain a regular sleep schedule, move your body daily, spend time outdoors, eat regularly, and make space for activities that bring you genuine enjoyment.

You do not need to solve every emotional difficulty through thinking. Sometimes your mind needs rest, your body needs movement, and your life needs a little more balance.

I hope this helps everyone that takes the time to read and understand this.

Much love to you all!(Please repost this so that it reaches others who may be looking for a bit of help and guidance.)

text:
September 14, 1913: A glimpse of the working undertaker

In McIntosh’s September 14, 1913 interview, Gheesling recalled handling a suicide victim whose body had stiffened in a cramped position. When he tried to straighten it, the torso unexpectedly rose into a sitting posture, startling him. The story illustrates practical familiarity with rigidity rather than precise time-of-death expertise (McIntosh, 5).

Bloomfield estimated 8,000 people had viewed Mary’s body at his establishment, an unverified attendance estimate. McIntosh also interviewed G. H. Brandon of Barclay & Brandon, who became Gheesling’s father-in-law less than two years later (McIntosh, 5) (Atlanta Journal, 20).

February 23, 1914: Gheesling at Jim Conley’s trial

On Monday, February 23, 1914, Gheesling testified during Conley’s trial as an accessory after the fact. His appearance concerned the hair Barrett had found on a lathe in the second-floor metal room. Dr. H. F. Harris had compared factory specimens under a microscope with hair taken from Mary’s remains after exhumation and questioned whether they came from the same person (Atlanta Journal, 17).

The dispute concerned whether the hair connected Mary with the proposed second-floor assault site. Gheesling was called to explain his treatment of her hair after removing the body (Atlanta Journal, 17).

He said he washed Mary’s long, thick hair with pine tar soap, removing dirt and oil and making its color lighter. He placed burial approximately fifty-six hours after washing. This offered a possible explanation for changed comparison samples, without identifying the lathe strands (Atlanta Journal, 17).

Hair growth after death: A separate error

Gheesling also suggested hair sometimes continued growing after death. Ordinary hair growth requires living follicle cells. Postmortem tissue changes can make existing hair appear longer, but do not establish continued biological growth. His claim was incorrect and must be separated from his firsthand account of washing Mary’s hair (Atlanta Journal, 17) (UAMS Health, 25).

May 1, 1914: His sworn affidavit in the appeal record

Dorsey introduced Gheesling’s affidavit in the state’s response to Frank’s extraordinary motion for a new trial, as reported Friday, May 1, 1914. It appears under Ground 1 of the counter-showing in the Georgia Supreme Court papers and identifies him as W. A. Gheesling (Atlanta Journal, 18) (Gheesling, 19).

He reported eighteen years in undertaking and repeated his account of pine tar soap, the hair’s altered appearance, and his mistaken belief about postmortem growth. His preparation of the hair thus entered the sworn appeal evidence (Gheesling, 19).

Mary’s stepfather, J. W. Coleman, separately stated hair shown by Detective Black resembled Mary’s. Coleman offered visual recognition, while Gheesling described treatment of her hair. Neither conclusively identified the lathe strands, but both addressed challenges to the state’s evidence (Gheesling, 19).

June 1915: Marriage and Frank’s clemency proceedings

June 7–10, 1915: Gertrude Brandon and municipal employment

On Monday evening, June 7, 1915, Gheesling married Gertrude H. Brandon at her father’s residence, 6 Park Street, in Atlanta’s West End. G. H. Brandon’s association with Barclay & Brandon linked the marriage to William’s former employer and early professional circle (Atlanta Journal, 20).

The June 10 item reported a honeymoon in Highland Park, North Carolina, a home at the Cooper apartments, and Gheesling’s work as a city marshal’s clerk. He had entered municipal employment after his documented undertaking work in 1914. The timing and reason for the change, Gertrude’s later history, and any children remain unestablished (Atlanta Journal, 20).

June 16, 1915: Hair and blood in Howard’s argument

While Slaton considered commutation, Frank’s attorney William M. Howard challenged the state’s interpretation of the physical evidence. The Journal of Wednesday, June 16, 1915, reported discussion of Harris’s inability to identify the lathe hair positively as Mary’s. Slaton asked about the undertaker washing her hair and whether treatment could have altered its appearance or texture. Dorsey acknowledged the washing (Atlanta Journal, 21).

Howard argued the state had not established a conclusive hair match. Gheesling’s preparation of the remains was still under discussion more than two years later. His blood evidence also entered the argument over the proposed metal-room assault (Atlanta Journal, 21).

On Monday, June 21, 1915, Slaton commuted Frank’s death sentence to life imprisonment. The sentence changed without the verdict being overturned. No new sworn Gheesling examination is established in the clemency material cited here. His role was through earlier testimony and the arguments based on it (Atlanta Journal, 26).

Later life and remaining family questions

1916: Fifty-six Westwood Avenue

The 1916 directory lists William A. Gheesling in the city marshal’s department at 56 Westwood Avenue, with his father still at 75 Broyles Street. It does not establish how long William remained in municipal service or whether he returned to undertaking (Atlanta City Directory, 22).

The record leaves a gap between 1916 and 1954 concerning occupation, the move to Florida, and the couple’s later household. The absence of identified children does not establish a childless marriage (Duggan, 1) (Atlanta City Directory, 22).

November 8–10, 1954: Reported death and obituary lead

Duggan’s genealogy places Gheesling’s death in St. Augustine, Florida, on Monday, November 8, 1954. If the reported birth and death dates are correct, he was seventy. An obituary index identifies W. A. Gheesling in The Atlanta Constitution on Wednesday, November 10, 1954, two days later (Duggan, 1) (Atlanta Constitution, 23).

The complete obituary and original death certificate remain unverified. Burial, final address, surviving relatives, occupation, and length of residence in Florida are unresolved. The obituary index cannot establish its unseen contents (Atlanta Constitution, 23).

Photographs and the Georgia Archives family file

No authenticated portrait is identified in the present record. The Georgia Archives’ Family Surname File inventory, updated in July 2022, lists Gheesling on page 18. It confirms a family folder exists, but does not establish whether it contains photographs (Georgia Archives, 24).

Possible portrait leads include the obituary, family papers, funeral-business photographs, and municipal collections. Any likeness requires an identifying caption or comparable documentation beyond a shared surname (Georgia Archives, 24).

Gheesling’s place in the case against Leo Frank

Gheesling connected the early examination of Mary’s remains with the prosecution of Frank and later disputes over the physical evidence. His strongest testimony described conditions he personally observed. His time estimate, recollection of Frank’s conduct, and explanations of the hair were more limited (Brief of Evidence, 6) (Atlanta Journal, 7) (Gheesling, 19).

The newspaper discrepancies and his acknowledged uncertainty belong beside those observations. His evidence supported parts of the state’s reconstruction, but did not independently identify the murderer, fix an exact time of death, or establish whose hair lay on the lathe (Atlanta Constitution, 8) (Atlanta Journal, 17).

KCC is accepting applications now for 12-day CNA training courses in Battle Creek and Coldwater in November, including:

> Nov. 2-19 at KCC’s Grahl Center campus in Coldwater

> Nov. 16-Dec. 10 at KCC’s North Avenue campus in Battle Creek

KCC offers CNA training via the College’s NURS 105: Nursing Assistant Training Program course, which consists of classroom, laboratory and clinical instruction and is worth three college credits. The 80.5-hour course prepares students to take the Michigan Nursing Assistant Test to become Certified Nursing Assistants (CNAs).

NURS 105 is a prerequisite course for KCC’s Physical Therapist Assistant and Radiography programs and is a great starting point for future Nursing students. The program offers future health students an opportunity to work in a field related to their future profession while working on their degree.

Those interested in signing up for Nurse Aide Training at KCC should start by setting up an appointment to meet with an academic advisor by calling 269-965-4124 or emailing advising@kellogg.edu.

🔥 GEOPOLITICS FOR IDIOTS: HOW TO FINANCIALLY STRENGTHEN YOUR ADVERSARY AND THEN SELL POLAND PROTECTION AGAINST HIS MISSILES! 🤡

Warning: this might get complicated. You will need to connect a few facts, apply some basic logic, and spend five minutes without worshipping Donald Trump. For certain sections of the Polish right, that may be a challenge beyond the processing capacity of their political brains.

Russia sells oil and makes money. Russia cooperates with Iran. Iran is an adversary of the United States. Russia invaded Ukraine, continues to bomb its cities, and represents the most serious military threat to Poland's security.

Still following? Good. That was just the warm-up.

Because whenever Washington makes decisions that enable additional transactions involving Russian energy resources, a question arises that no responsible Polish politician should ignore:

IS AMERICAN POLICY INADVERTENTLY HELPING THE VERY COUNTRY THAT POLAND IS SPENDING BILLIONS TO DEFEND ITSELF AGAINST?

And no, this is not a conspiracy theory. It is a legitimate question about financial flows, sanctions enforcement, energy interests, and European security.

Now comes the part that matters most, especially to those who treat the orange messiah as an infallible geopolitical genius.

🇵🇱 POLAND, NOT FLORIDA, IS ON NATO'S EASTERN FLANK!

We live next to the Russian threat. Polish taxpayers are financing enormous investments in our armed forces, air defense systems, fighter aircraft, tanks, and critical security infrastructure. Our children will live with the consequences of decisions being made today in Washington, Moscow, and Brussels.

Yet part of the Polish political right continues to behave as though the primary duty of a Polish politician is to applaud Donald Trump.

POLAND IS NOT THE 51ST AMERICAN STATE! THE POLISH PRESIDENT IS NOT THE WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY! AND POLISH TAXPAYERS ARE NOT AN ATM FOR SOMEONE ELSE'S GEOPOLITICAL EXPERIMENTS!

Karol Nawrocki, Adam Bielan, and all the other political admirers of Donald Trump: perhaps instead of another round of enthusiastic praise, photographs, and declarations of eternal friendship, you could finally ask Washington some serious questions.

Why should Poland bear ever-increasing costs to deter Russia if decisions made by our most important ally may simultaneously increase Russian revenues? What concrete security guarantees do we receive in return for spending billions on American weapons? Are American commercial interests always aligned with Polish national security? And when they are not, who in Warsaw has the courage to say so openly?

CAN YOU PUT POLAND'S NATIONAL INTEREST ABOVE YOUR PERSONAL FASCINATION WITH DONALD TRUMP, EVEN ONCE?

Because Trump can change his mind tomorrow. The day after tomorrow, he can announce another historic victory. On Wednesday, he might praise Putin. On Thursday, threaten Iran. And on Friday, declare that he has ended yet another war with a single telephone call.

But Poland will still be exactly where it is.

On NATO's eastern flank. Next to Ukraine, fighting for its survival. Within reach of Russia's military machine.

AND NEITHER A RED MAGA HAT, NOR A WHITE HOUSE SELFIE, NOR ANOTHER EXCITED SOCIAL MEDIA POST FROM A POLISH RIGHT-WING POLITICIAN WILL DEFEND OUR COUNTRY.

What can defend Poland is a strong military, credible deterrence, a reliable NATO alliance, a united Europe, a capable domestic defense industry, and politicians who understand the difference between national interests and personal admiration for a foreign leader.

This is not about abandoning our alliance with the United States. Quite the opposite.

It is about making sure that alliance is a partnership between sovereign countries that respect one another, rather than a relationship between a client and his political idol.

And that brings us to another question.

🇸🇪 WHY SHOULDN'T POLAND SERIOUSLY EXAMINE THE SWEDISH SAAB JAS 39 GRIPEN AS AN ALTERNATIVE FOR FUTURE FIGHTER PURCHASES?

The F-35 offers advanced stealth capabilities, sophisticated sensors, and integration with NATO systems. Those advantages are real and should not be dismissed.

But the Gripen deserves serious consideration too. Its operating concept emphasizes dispersed operations, rapid turnaround, relatively modest infrastructure requirements, and European industrial cooperation.

A proper comparison should examine procurement costs, lifecycle expenses, delivery schedules, weapons integration, survivability, operational capabilities, technology transfer, and Polish industrial participation.

The Gripen is not automatically cheaper in every configuration, nor does being manufactured in Europe make it completely independent of American technology. Some Gripen variants use American engines and other US-origin components.

BUT SHOULD POLAND CONTINUE TO CONCENTRATE SO MUCH OF ITS DEFENSE PROCUREMENT IN ONE COUNTRY WITHOUT SERIOUSLY EXAMINING THE STRATEGIC COSTS OF THAT DEPENDENCE?

That is a question worth asking before signing the next multibillion-dollar contract.

⚠️ NOW AN IMPORTANT FACTUAL DISCLAIMER, BECAUSE UNLIKE PROPAGANDISTS, WE DO NOT NEED TO INVENT EVIDENCE.

Russia earns revenue from exporting energy resources, maintains political and military cooperation with Iran, and continues its war of aggression against Ukraine. These are documented facts.

However, that does not mean every purchase of Russian oil directly finances Iranian missiles. Nor is there sufficient evidence to claim that Donald Trump personally finances Iranian military operations against the United States merely because Russian energy transactions occur.

To establish a specific financial connection, we must determine who purchased the resources, from whom, when, at what price, under which legal arrangements, and whether the transaction actually increased Russian government revenue.

We must also distinguish between decisions made by the US administration and commercial transactions conducted by private companies.

AN INDIRECT ECONOMIC EFFECT IS NOT THE SAME AS DIRECTLY FINANCING A SPECIFIC MILITARY OPERATION.

And there is another essential distinction: Poland purchasing American military equipment does not automatically mean that the money reaches Russia. American defense contractors, the US government, and Russian energy exporters are separate economic actors. Any claim that Polish defense spending ultimately finances Putin requires evidence of actual financial connections.

That is precisely why we should demand facts, contracts, sanctions data, and financial transparency instead of political fairy tales.

My argument is political and economic:

EVERY WASHINGTON DECISION THAT ACTUALLY STRENGTHENS MOSCOW FINANCIALLY DESERVES CRITICAL SCRUTINY FROM THE PERSPECTIVE OF POLISH NATIONAL SECURITY.

We do not need anti-Americanism. We do not need blind devotion to Trump either.

We need a strong alliance with the United States, a stronger Europe, and the ability to think independently.

Now, a little homework for everyone who still struggles to understand the difference between an alliance and political submission.

IF A US POLICY DECISION WERE TO GENERATE AN ADDITIONAL BILLION DOLLARS FOR RUSSIA, WHILE FORCING POLAND TO SPEND ANOTHER BILLION ON DEFENSE, WHO WOULD PROFIT AND WHO WOULD PAY THE BILL?

This is a hypothetical example, not a claim about a verified transaction. But the strategic problem it illustrates is very real.

You do not need a doctorate in geopolitics to understand it.

You need to know how to count, understand your country's national interests, and stop applauding every word coming out of the White House.

🇵🇱 POLAND'S NATIONAL INTEREST DOES NOT HAVE AN AMERICAN PASSPORT. IT FLIES THE WHITE-AND-RED FLAG!

POLAND FIRST. NOT TRUMP. NOT PUTIN. NOT PARTY POLITICS. POLAND!

text:
Much like Munich in 1938, the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact is often treated more as a rhetorical device than as a significant historical event. The discussion typically centres on two main narratives, neither of which is particularly illuminating: one insists that Stalin more or less triggered World War II, while the other contends that Western appeasement left Moscow with no choice and that the pact simply delayed conflict. So, let’s look at what the document says (WARNING: It’s old material I used for RWN. I edited it slightly to reduce bibliography-heaviness, but it might still not be very engaging).

- What did the pact actually do?
Signed on 23 August 1939, its secret protocol carved Eastern Europe into spheres of interest. Finland, Estonia and Latvia went to Moscow; Lithuania, at first, to Germany. Poland was split roughly along the Narew, Vistula and San, leaving the survival of any Polish state open. Germany also acknowledged Soviet interest in Bessarabia.
As it turns out, in 1939 EVERYONE was hedging. Poland had signed a non-aggression declaration with Germany in 1934 and took Teschen when Czechoslovakia was carved up in 1938. Hitler hoped to make Poland a junior partner against the USSR (see Rolf-Dieter Müller, Enemy in the East). When Warsaw refused his terms on Danzig, he ordered planning for an attack. The date: 3 April 1939, months before the pact signing.
Soviet Union had spent most of the 1930s as one of the most vocal advocates of a common front against Hitler: League membership in 1934, mutual assistance pacts with France and Czechoslovakia in 1935 (the Czech one binding only if France acted first). Paris never gave its pact a military convention, and London, wary of communism and doubtful of the Red Army after the purges, kept its distance. The Red Army could reach Czechoslovakia only through Poland or Romania, and neither would let it through. Historians still argue whether Stalin was ever fully committed to collective security or kept a German option open. But Munich, settled without Prague and without Moscow, gave him good reason to doubt the West.
The 1939 negotiations between Britain, France and the Soviet Union stalled for similar reasons. Warsaw refused to let Soviet troops in, while Moscow sought a free hand against what it called “indirect aggression” in the Baltic. Paris was keener on a deal than London, which showed little urgency: the Anglo-French military mission travelled to Moscow by sea (Chamberlain had flown to Hitler three times the previous September), and its British head had no written authority to sign anything. In May, Molotov replaced Litvinov, the main champion of collective security.
Meanwhile Estonia and Latvia, both under authoritarian regimes, signed non-aggression treaties with Germany, helping Hitler keep Soviet and British influence out of the region before his invasion of Poland. Estonia’s military leaders had intelligence ties with Berlin and hoped for German support against the USSR. A German report by Georg Dertinger described a secret Baltic understanding to consult Berlin on defence against the Soviet Union, with German help envisaged where necessary.
At this stage Germany could offer the Soviet Union what the West couldn’t or wouldn’t: neutrality, a territorial buffer, and a (shaky) ringside seat while the capitalist powers fought each other. The Red Army was also fighting Japan at Khalkhin Gol/Nomonhan. Stalin could have tried staying neutral without the deal, but how safe that would have been is another question. So he took the German offer.

- What happened after the treaty was signed?
By 17 September, when the Red Army invaded, the Wehrmacht had already inflicted a severe defeat on the Polish forces, though Warsaw resisted until the 28th. Stalin feared Germany might occupy the entire country, and Moscow justified its move by claiming to protect Ukrainians and Belarusians, who had indeed faced discrimination under Polish rule. Britain and France did not declare war on the USSR. Formally, the Anglo-Polish agreement limited British obligations to Germany. In practice, they could hardly have fought Germany and the Soviet Union at once, and after Poland fell there was little fighting on land in the West until spring 1940.
The treaty of 28 September fixed the border, moved Lithuania into the Soviet sphere in exchange for more Polish territory for Germany, and committed both sides to suppress Polish agitation against the other. Then each occupier remade its half. On the German side, tens of thousands of Poles, above all the educated elite, were shot in the first months, hundreds of thousands were expelled, and Jews were stripped of their rights and forced into ghettos: the first stage of what became full-scale genocide. On the Soviet side, the NKVD arrested officers, police, officials, landowners and clergy, moved hundreds of thousands of people to the Soviet interior in 1940–41, and in spring 1940 shot some 22,000 Polish officers and officials at Katyn and other sites.
Trade agreements came alongside the pact, in August 1939 and February 1940. Soviet oil, grain and raw materials went west; German machinery and military technology went east; Soviet transit routes helped Germany get around the British blockade. Berlin found the deal far less comfortable than it looks: Soviet demands competed with German rearmament, and Hitler disliked depending on Soviet supplies. The urge to seize Soviet resources fed into Barbarossa, though it can’t explain it alone.

- Did the pact cause the war?
No. Hitler decided to attack Poland well before signing the pact. The pact removed the immediate Soviet risk and made his timing much easier. Whether he would have struck without it, we can’t know. What turned a German-Polish war into a European one in September 1939 was Britain and France’s decision to stick to their guarantee to Poland. And the pact didn’t create Nazi expansionism: as we argued in the Radio War Nerd Munich series, Hitler and much of his military leadership wanted war sooner or later. Nor did it make Soviet expansion inevitable.

-  Were the two regimes the same?
No. Both Germany and the Soviet Union were totalitarian states. But Stalin did not pursue the Nazis’ genocidal goals, and his ideology, however bloody and hostile to liberal democracy, was profoundly different from Nazism. By late 1939, about 1.5 million Jews, including refugees from German-occupied Poland, were under Soviet control. Many were killed after Germany invaded in 1941. But between 160,000 and 230,000 Polish Jews survived in the Soviet interior, having fled, been evacuated or been deported there. For some, Soviet action had the (sometimes unintended) effect of saving them from the Nazis. That doesn’t make the Soviet Union guiltless. The Winter War, mass deportations, Katyn and the annexation of the Baltic states all followed. In Stalin’s mind, security and expansion were never opposites.

- Did the pact buy the Soviet Union time?
Yes: nearly two years, and a frontier pushed west by 200–300 km in Poland and more in the Baltic. The new defences were unfinished, Soviet forces were packed too far forward, and they lost much of that depth within days in June 1941. Stalin had expected a long war in the West. France fell in six weeks, and he then read the German build-up as pressure ahead of negotiations, moving to full mobilisation way too late. But those gains still mattered.
The panzer spearheads reached the Dnieper within three weeks, but the infantry and horse-drawn supply columns needed to hold the ground had to cover the same distance on foot. That gap, German supply problems and ferocious Soviet resistance, above all around Smolensk, left Barbarossa badly behind schedule by the end of July.

- Was it a real alliance?
No. There was never a military alliance: no joint command, no common long-term strategy and, of course, no Soviet war on Britain or France. It was of course  more than neutrality: a joint call for peace in September 1939, substantial trade, even the handover by the Soviets of some German and Austrian communist refugees to the Gestapo.
The relationship was tense from the beginning. After the Soviet Union invaded Finland in November 1939, Finland grew closer to Germany within a year and fought alongside it in 1941. The annexation of Bessarabia, which was recognized as a Soviet interest in the protocol, and northern Bukovina, which was not explicitly mentioned, brought Romania nearer to Berlin. In November 1940, Molotov visited Berlin to discuss joining the Tripartite Pact. Moscow’s tough demands (about Finland, Bulgaria, and the Turkish Straits) went unanswered, while Hitler had already ordered preparations in the East to continue regardless of the talks' outcome. The Barbarossa directive was issued in December, ironically followed by a new trade deal in January 1941. By then, both sides were mainly buying time.

- The bottom line
Great powers had long bargained at the expense of smaller nations, and they still do. A year earlier, at Munich, Britain and France had agreed to hand over the Sudetenland without consulting Prague. What set 1939 apart was how explicitly Berlin and Moscow divided Eastern Europe, and what followed on each side of the line.
The pact was neither the root cause of the war nor simply a Soviet land grab. It was a strategic arrangement between two vastly different regimes that, for a while, shared short-term interests while remaining mortal enemies. Stalin sought territory, depth and time, hoping Germany would exhaust itself in the West. Hitler gained a free hand against Poland, Soviet resources and temporary security in the east. Both gained, and both misjudged: Stalin misjudged Hitler’s timing, but Hitler misjudged the Soviet Union’s durability, which ultimately proved fatal for him.

text:
A digitally colorized late-in-life portrait of the American abolitionist and activist Harriet Tubman (1822-1913) at her home in Auburn, New York in 1911, two years before her death... 
⁣
Born into slavery, she suffered a severe head injury around age 12-13 when an overseer threw a heavy metal weight that struck her,  leaving her with chronic pain and narcolepsy accompanied by vivid, prophetic visions. Tubman said the attack "broke my skull" and from that day on, experienced extremely painful headaches and seizures, which would knock her unconscious for short periods of time.⁣
⁣
In 1849, facing the threat of being sold after her enslaver died, she escaped alone to Philadelphia via the Underground Railroad, a secret network of safe houses and abolitionists. She later adopted the name Harriet Tubman. Refusing to stay behind while her loved ones remained in bondage, she returned to Maryland around 13 to 19 times, guiding roughly 70 to 300 enslaved family members and friends to freedom in the North and Canada. Her fearless leadership and record of never losing a "passenger" earned her the title "Moses of her people". After the 1850 Fugitive Slave Act allowed escaped slaves to be recaptured, she redirected her rescue routes to end in Canada, where slavery was illegal.

During the American Civil War (1861–1865), Tubman served the Union Army as a cook, nurse, laundress, scout, and spy. On June 2, 1863, she became the first woman in U.S. history to plan and lead an armed military assault. She guided Union gunboats during the Combahee River Raid in South Carolina, liberating more than 700 enslaved people.
⁣
After the war, she had made enough money to reinvest in the community and help out veterans and freed slaves. In the 1890s, she underwent brain surgery to have the piece of metal removed from her skull. She was offered anesthesia, but chose to bite a bullet instead, like she had seen so many Union soldiers do when their limbs were being amputated. In her own words, she said the doctor, "sawed open my skull, and raised it up, and now it feels more comfortable".⁣

Later in life, settling in Auburn, New York, she supported the women's suffrage movement alongside figures like Susan B. Anthony and established the Harriet Tubman Home for the Aged and Indigent Negroes. She died in 1913, surrounded by friends and family members. Her last words to those in the room were, "I go to prepare a place for you,"⁣⁣ and was buried with military honors.

text:
Lebanon’s Hezbollah Problem Is Generational, Not Governmental

Lebanon’s central political problem cannot be reduced to Nawaf Salam, Joseph Aoun or the composition of the present government. Governments change. Presidents leave office. Parliamentary majorities rise and fall. Hezbollah, however, is not merely an electoral party participating in this cycle. It is a long-established political, military, social and ideological structure capable of reproducing itself from one generation to another.

That distinction is fundamental.

The Mahdi Scouts offer one illustration. The organization itself has reported approximately 75,000 members and describes an institutional structure devoted to education, social activity and the formation of successive generations. This does not mean that every child involved will become a Hezbollah fighter, and it would be wrong to treat an entire community as such. But it demonstrates something politically important: Hezbollah thinks institutionally and generationally, not merely electorally.

A government lasts a few years. An ideological ecosystem can last decades.

This is why Lebanon cannot approach Hezbollah's weapons as another temporary dispute to be postponed until the next cabinet, dialogue table or regional settlement. The question is ultimately constitutional: Can one sovereign state permanently accommodate two separate authorities capable of deciding questions of war, peace and armed force?

The Lebanese government has now answered that question formally. On March 2, 2026, the Council of Ministers declared that decisions of war and peace belong exclusively to the state, prohibited Hezbollah's military and security activities outside legitimate institutions, and called for its weapons to be handed to the state.  Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has subsequently described the monopoly of arms by the state as an irreversible process.

Hezbollah presents a different argument. It maintains that its weapons remain necessary while Israeli forces occupy Lebanese territory and while Israeli attacks continue. That security concern cannot simply be dismissed; Lebanon also has the right to demand Israeli withdrawal, cessation of attacks and implementation of international commitments. But one violation of Lebanese sovereignty cannot justify institutionalizing another. A sovereign state cannot permanently subcontract national defence to a political organization.

The danger is therefore not that Hezbollah survives one government. It is that Lebanon normalizes an indefinite dual structure: one republic possessing a constitution, army and government, and another organized force possessing its own arms, command structure, institutions and strategic relationships.

Such an arrangement eventually changes the nature of the state itself.

Some will consequently raise partition as the ultimate alternative. But partition would carry immense human, territorial, economic and security risks and could produce new disputes rather than resolve the old ones. Lebanon's mixed geography and interconnected economy make clean separation largely theoretical.

The more rational alternative remains the reconstruction of a single state: one army, one foreign policy and one authority deciding war and peace.

That does not require eliminating Hezbollah as a political movement. It requires transforming its relationship with the republic. Hezbollah may remain a political party, compete in elections, represent constituents and defend its political vision. What cannot remain indefinitely compatible with sovereign statehood is an autonomous military structure operating alongside the state.

Lebanon therefore faces a question much larger than the survival of Nawaf Salam's government.

Who will command the Lebanon of twenty years from now: the republic, or competing structures inside the republic?

If the state does not answer that question today, demographics, institutions and the passage of time will eventually answer it for the state.

#WarsoftheRoses

OTD in 1459 - Lancastrian & Yorkist armies faced each other at Ludford Bridge. 

The Yorkists were attempting to prevent the Lancastrians from crossing the river to Richard, 3rd Duke of York’s stronghold of Ludlow. They had built defensive ditches on their chosen ground complete with a makeshift artillery barrage. Tactics which one of their commanders Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick (the Kingmaker) would repeat in subsequent battles. 

But this encounter would not be a repeat of Warwick’s father the Earl of Salisbury’s triumph at the Battle of Blore a few weeks earlier. Not only did the Lancastrian army outnumber the Yorkists by a ratio of two to one they also had a trump card more potent than Warwick’s cannons. King #HenryVI himself was present, attired in full armour & mounted beneath the royal standard, forcing those in the Yorkist ranks to confront the reality of fighting against the King himself rather than simply seeking to remove ‘evil counsellors’ as their leaders alleged. The King also offered pardons to all who submitted & chose not fight against him.

This prompted the overnight defection of Anthony Trollope & his contingent of 600 seasoned troops from the Calais garrison, who had accompanied Warwick to England. 

As dawn broke on 13 October it became clear that the Yorkist lords - Richard, 3rd Duke of York; Richard Neville, Earl of Salisbury; Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick; Edward, Earl of March (later #EdwardIV) & Edmund, Earl of Rutland -  had all fled into exile leaving Henry to enter Ludlow unopposed. More on that in tomorrow’s post.
