text:
Samurai and Loyalty
Part 2 of 4

By the late 15th century, Japan had entered a long era of warfare.

The Sengoku period—the age of warring states.

Warriors served their lords. Yet some turned against them and sought power.

Yesterday’s ally could become today’s enemy.

Two men from this era took strikingly different paths.

Akechi Mitsuhide and Torii Suneemon.

Let’s begin with Mitsuhide.

Oda Nobunaga had extended his power across large parts of Japan and was pushing toward unification.

Among his most capable retainers was Mitsuhide.

Nobunaga had entrusted him with castles, lands, and a large army.

Just one year before the Honnoji Incident, Mitsuhide expressed his gratitude to Nobunaga in military rules for his retainers.

Repaying a lord’s generosity through service.

The times had changed, but that idea endured.

Then, the following year, Mitsuhide turned against him.

Nobunaga was staying with a small entourage at Honnoji, a temple in Kyoto.

Mitsuhide’s army attacked.

Cornered, Nobunaga took his own life.

One of Japan’s most famous betrayals.

The Honnoji Incident.

But why did Mitsuhide do it?

Had Nobunaga humiliated him?

Did he want to rule Japan?

Or was there another political reason?

Many theories exist. His true motive remains uncertain.

A retainer who owed much to Nobunaga had attacked his own lord and brought about his death.

Mitsuhide was defeated in battle and died less than two weeks later.

He had changed Japan’s history.

The question of why remains.

Seven years earlier, another man had acted very differently.

Nagashino Castle was surrounded by Takeda Katsuyori’s army. Katsuyori was a powerful warlord opposed to Nobunaga.

About 500 men defended the castle. The enemy is said to have outnumbered them many times over.

Without reinforcements, the castle would fall.

How could anyone get through to ask for help?

The castle’s lord sent a messenger through the siege lines.

Torii Suneemon.

An ashigaru—a low-ranking foot soldier.

Suneemon escaped through the enemy lines, heading for the castle where Nobunaga and his ally, Tokugawa Ieyasu, were staying.

He traveled down a river, evaded the enemy, and reached his allies.

Reinforcements would be sent.

He had delivered the request.

He was safe.

But his comrades were still trapped. They did not know help was coming.

Suneemon turned back to bring them the news.

On the return journey, he was captured.

Some details of what followed come from later accounts.

The Takeda soldiers are said to have offered him a bargain.

Shout to the castle that no reinforcements are coming.

Do that, and we will spare your life and reward you.

Suneemon appeared to agree.

Then he shouted toward the castle:

“Reinforcements are coming! Hold on a little longer!”

He brought hope to the men inside.

For defying his captors, he is said to have been put to death on a wooden cross.

Another story tells of an enemy warrior so moved by his courage that he had Suneemon’s execution depicted on a banner.

That banner, believed to portray Suneemon, survives today.

He was remembered for loyalty and courage that earned even an enemy’s respect.

Mitsuhide turned against his lord.

Suneemon tried to bring news of rescue to his comrades and lost his life.

They lived in the same age.

Yet we do not know why Mitsuhide rebelled, or exactly what Suneemon thought in his final moments.

What we can say is this:

Loyalty did not take the same form for every warrior.

Some served their lords.

Some turned against them.

Some sought to protect their households.

Some tried to save their comrades.

Whom they followed and for whose sake they acted differed from one person to another.

But when the long wars ended, how would samurai loyalty change?

Next: the Ako ronin, whose loyalty clashed with the shogunate’s order.

To be continued in Part 3.

text:
Why It Matters Today

Maximilian raises a difficult question because his position cannot be reduced to simple disobedience.

Roman society depended upon soldiers to defend its borders, maintain order, and protect its inhabitants. Military service carried genuine civic responsibilities.

Yet Maximilian believed that accepting those responsibilities would require him to violate his obligations to God.

That tension has never entirely disappeared.

Modern Western societies continue debating the relationship between military necessity, individual conscience, and the government's authority to compel service.

Some Christians believe that defending one's family, community, or country can be a legitimate moral duty. Others believe that Christ's teachings prohibit participation in warfare.

Both positions have substantial histories within Christianity.

Maximilian's example should therefore not be presented as proof that every Christian soldier was acting wrongly. Nor should his refusal be dismissed merely because other Christians made different choices.

His importance lies in the seriousness with which he treated his own conviction.

He believed an action was wrong, and he refused to perform it even when the state threatened him with death.

That is a demanding understanding of conscience.

It also reminds us that conscientious objection is not necessarily cowardice. Maximilian was offered a path to survival through military service. He accepted execution instead.

Whether one agrees with his position on warfare or not, his willingness to suffer for it deserves serious consideration.

Suggested Reading

Primary Source: The Acts of Maximilian

This short account records the confrontation between Maximilian and the proconsul Dion. Pay particular attention to the governor's observation that other Christians served in the army and Maximilian's response.

"Read The Acts of Maximilian" (https://reference-url-citation.invalid/2)

For a scholarly translation, consult Herbert Musurillo's The Acts of the Christian Martyrs.

Further Reading: Peter Brock, “Why Did St Maximilian Refuse to Serve in the Roman Army?”

Published in The Journal of Ecclesiastical History in 1994, this study examines Maximilian's refusal in the context of Roman recruitment and early Christian attitudes toward military service.

"Read the scholarly study" (https://reference-url-citation.invalid/3)

Gm. A fascinating Bible study from Grok, if interested

Me: 
Yawn, stretch, scratch. One foot on floor: "Yup, that's my morning lineup; must be time to get up."

IMAGINE knowing what time of day it is based on a temporary alignment of wanderers Jupiter, and Mars with king star Regulus, outside your window before the sun rises, bringing the new moon with it today and I'm wondering if I will be able to catch a crescent or not ... 

Then reading THIS in your am Bible reading, and wondering specifically what could that kiss refer to? 

Then realizing I've spent the last year of my life learning how important it is to walk that exact line. Not gonna lie, there are slips and tumbles, but I'm not doing too bad either 

For self-taught, Spirit led, and AI for reference manuals, I suppose…

Grok:

Job 31:26–28 is Job clearing himself of astral worship. 

The kiss is the gesture of homage, not a figure of speech for affection.

The usual reading is straightforward. In his final oath of innocence, Job denies that he ever looked at the sun in its radiance or the moon moving in splendor, felt his heart secretly enticed, and then “threw a kiss” with his hand from his mouth. That act, he says, would be an iniquity to be judged, because it would mean he had denied God on high. 

Commentators (Keil, Delitzsch, Clines, and the older ones) treat the hand-to-mouth kiss as a known ancient gesture of worship. You brought the hand to the lips and extended it toward the object of homage—sun, moon, or idol. Assyrian and Babylonian reliefs show the same motion toward deities. The Hebrew is roughly “my hand kissed my mouth.” It is the body completing what the enticed heart began.

What it rules out is not looking at the sky. Genesis 1:14, Psalm 8, and Psalm 19 all command attention to the lights as witnesses of the Maker. The line is crossed when the heart is drawn and the hand offers homage, so that the lamp is treated as worthy of what belongs only to God.

Deuteronomy 4:19 and 17:3 forbid bowing to the sun, moon, and host of heaven. 2 Kings 23:5 and 23:11 record Josiah tearing out the astral priests and the horses and chariots of the sun. Ezekiel 8:16 shows men in the temple facing east and worshiping the rising sun. Jeremiah 8:2 and Acts 7:42 treat the same practice as the nation’s fall. Romans 1:25 names the exchange: worshiping the creature rather than the Creator.

The application that has been drawn, and the one that still fits, is the difference between observation and homage. Watching the moon move, noting a conjunction, or reading a sign the lights were set to give is not the sin. 

The sin is the secret enticement that ends in a gesture of worship—treating the lamp as a power, a god, or a source of favor. Job’s point is that even a private, unobserved kiss would have been enough to deny the God who made the lights. The stars in Scripture are repeatedly the host that must not be served (Deut 4:19; 2 Kgs 21:3–5; Jer 8:2; Zeph 1:5). The kiss is simply the smallest bodily form of that service.

text:
Scriptural Text: John 4–5
Pillar 1: The Intended Message of the Scriptures (Authorial Intent & Exegesis)
The narrative progression through John 4 and 5 marks a calculated shift from external, localized religious boundaries to the cosmic authority and life-giving power residing solely in the Person of Jesus Christ.
Dismantling the Samaritan–Judean Partition (John 4:1–26):
At Jacob’s well in Sychar, Jesus ignores deep-seated ethnic and sectarian hostilities by speaking directly with a Samaritan woman. When she attempts to deflect conviction by raising the longstanding historical debate over sacred geography—Mount Gerizim versus Mount Zion in Jerusalem (vv. 19–20)—Christ dismantles the entire premise of localized ritual worship:"Woman, believe me, the hour cometh, when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father... But the hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth" (vv. 21, 23).
Jesus openly reveals His Messianic identity to an outcast ("I that speak unto thee am he", v. 26) and offers "living water"—the internal, indwelling Holy Spirit producing eternal life.
The Harvest and the Gentile Pattern (John 4:27–54):
The conversion of the Samaritans without signs or wonders (vv. 39–42) contrasts sharply with the Jewish leadership's demand for spectacles. This is reinforced in Galilee when an official (basilikos) believes the bare, spoken word of Jesus from miles away, resulting in the distant healing of his dying son (vv. 46–54).
The Sabbath Healing at Bethesda (John 5:1–16):
At the pool of Bethesda, Jesus intentionally heals a man crippled for 38 years on the Sabbath day, commanding him to pick up his bed and walk. This directly provokes the religious authorities, who elevate rabbinic Sabbath prohibitions (mishnah) above the restorative mercy and sovereign prerogative of God.
The Discourse on Divine Equality and Absolute Authority (John 5:17–30):
When challenged for breaking their Sabbath traditions, Christ does not offer a technical legal excuse; He asserts equality of nature, action, and honor with the Father:"My Father worketh hitherto, and I work. Therefore the Jews sought the more to kill him, because he not only had broken the sabbath, but said also that God was his Father, making himself equal with God" (vv. 17–18).
He possesses inherent life (aseity, v. 26), exercises total executive judgment (v. 22), and will bodily raise the dead—both to life and to damnation—by the sound of His voice (vv. 28–29).
The Fourfold Witness and the Arraignment of Unbelief (John 5:31–47):
Jesus presents four independent testimonies that legally validate His claims under biblical jurisprudence:
The witness of John the Baptist (vv. 32–35).
The witness of the miraculous works given Him by the Father (v. 36).
The witness of the Father Himself (vv. 37–38).
The witness of the Old Testament Scriptures (v. 39).
He delivers an indictment against academic religious bibliolatry: they search the text seeking eternal life as an abstract code, yet refuse to come to the Person of whom the text speaks.
Pillar 2: The Deeper Theological Meanings (Covenantal Framework & Synthesis)
John 4 and 5 represent the formal transition from the shadows of the Old Covenant order to the reality of the New Covenant incarnated in the Son of God.
The End of Sacred Geography and the True Temple:
By declaring that worship is no longer tethered to Gerizim or Jerusalem, Christ terminates the legitimacy of geographic shrines and external holy sites. God is Spirit; true worship is not mediated by physical dirt, stone altars, or temple structures, but through the Spirit and the Truth (Christ Himself, John 14:6). The believer's body and the corporate assembly of the redeemed constitute the living temple.
The Substance of the Sabbath:
In John 5, the religious leaders condemned the healed man for carrying his mat, preferring a paralyzed man who kept their Sabbath rules over a restored man who walked. Jesus’ declaration—"My Father worketh hitherto, and I work"—reveals that the Sabbath was never intended to be an autonomous idol of human inactivity. Divine redemption and mercy do not pause on the seventh day. Christ does not merely observe the Sabbath; He is the Lord of the Sabbath and its ultimate fulfillment.
The Systematic Exposure (The Idolatry of Scripture Divorced from Christ):
John 5:39–47 dismantles two prevalent theological counterfeits:
Rabbinic Legalism and "Biblical" Self-Righteousness: The Pharisees believed that possessing, memorizing, and dissecting the scrolls of the Torah conferred eternal life ("Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life"). Christ exposes this as fatal blindness: Scripture is not an end in itself; it is an arrow pointing to Him. To study the Bible while rejecting Jesus as God manifest in the flesh is to turn the Word of God into a tool of personal condemnation.
The Mosaic Accusation: Modern religious systems claim to follow Moses while rejecting the New Covenant. Jesus demolishes this claim: "Do not think that I will accuse you to the Father: there is one that accuseth you, even Moses, in whom ye trust. For had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me: for he wrote of me" (vv. 45–46). True Mosaic fidelity leads directly to the feet of Jesus. To reject the Son is to reject Moses.
Pillar 3: The Daily Walk of the Truth Seeker (Practical Application)
For the Berean walking in the finished work of Christ today, these chapters outline concrete operational commands for faith and discernment:
Worship in Spirit and Truth, Not in External Forms:
Reject the human tendency to tie spiritual vitality to physical locations, sacred buildings, liturgical garments, or calendar cycles. Walk daily in communion with God through the indwelling Holy Spirit, anchored unreservedly in the truth of His written Word.
Read the Canon Christocentrically:
Never read the Old Testament as a detached moral handbook or legalistic checklist. When examining Moses, the historical books, the Psalms, and the Prophets, look for how they testify of Christ's person, atonement, resurrection, and kingdom. Academic biblical knowledge that does not deepen faith in the living Savior puffs up and produces Pharisaism.
Rest in the Voice of the Son for Spiritual and Physical Life:
The believer does not live in anxiety regarding future condemnation: "Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that heareth my word, and believeth on him that sent me, hath everlasting life, and shall not come into condemnation; but is passed from death unto life" (John 5:24). Rest securely in the present possession of eternal life secured by His blood.
Seek the Honor That Comes from God Alone:
Jesus asked: "How can ye believe, which receive honour one of another, and seek not the honour that cometh from God only?" (John 5:44). A Berean must not seek the approval of religious peers, online platforms, academic hierarchies, or family traditions. Truth requires a willingness to stand solitary with Christ, regardless of the social or institutional cost.
The Synthesis: Judges 21 and John 4–5
John 4 and 5 confront every human effort to confine God within physical shrines, ethnic genealogies, and dead religious legalism. By offering living water to the Samaritans and healing the helpless invalid on the Sabbath, Jesus demonstrates that the shadows of the Old Covenant have given way to the sovereign authority of the Son of God. The Scriptures do not impart life through external study or mechanical observance; they stand as an unyielding witness to the Messiah. Those who trust in their own religious pedigree or search the text while rejecting the Son remain accused by the very scriptures they claim to revere. True life, eternal rest, and spiritual worship are found exclusively in coming to the One who possesses life in Himself and has passed His redeemed from death into life.
When set alongside Judges 21, the canonical contrast becomes absolute. The closing tragedy of Judges displays the inevitable ruin of the human heart operating under religious autonomy—where an assembly possessing the Tabernacle, the priesthood, and the Law bypassed divine inquiry at the Ark to preserve a rash oath through slaughter at Jabesh-Gilead and sanctioned kidnapping at Shiloh. Bound to their own legalistic casuistry, they embodied the fatal verdict: "every man did that which was right in his own eyes" (Judges 21:25).
John 4 and 5 reveal the only divine cure for this perpetual collapse:
The End of Sacred Geography: The physical holy sites of Judges (Bethel and Shiloh) were defiled by human wrath, exposing the impotence of sacred dirt to restrain sin; Christ permanently terminates geographic partitions, declaring that true worship is mediated exclusively in Spirit and in Truth (John 4:21–24).
The Overthrow of Man-Made Casuistry: The elders of Israel used technical loopholes to justify cruelty, just as the religious authorities of John 5 weaponized Sabbath traditions to condemn a restored paralytic; Christ shatters all self-made religion by asserting His absolute prerogative to give life and execute divine judgment (John 5:21–22).
The True King Received: The theocracy descended into chaos because Israel had no king to rule their hearts; the New Covenant establishes the eternal reign of the Son of God, who does not leave His people to carnal pragmatism, but writes His law upon the heart and secures their permanent rest.
The Berean sees that human systems—whether ancient tribal vows, rabbinic traditions, or modern religious nationalism—always terminate in moral ruin and spiritual deception whenever they operate apart from the living Word. Deliverance is neither found in the physical land nor in the letter of a legal code, but exclusively in submitting to the King who has conquered sin, fulfilled the Law, and granted eternal life to all who hear His voice.

text:
A Brief History of "Thanks, But No Thanks" to Peace

They say insanity is repeating the same thing and expecting a different outcome. Behold, the Palestinian leadership’s greatest hits in rejecting two-state solutions, with a cherry on top: Israel’s Gaza exit that went so well.

1937 Peel Commission Plan: The British thought, “Hey, let’s split Palestine—20% for a Jewish state, the rest for an Arab one, Jerusalem neutral.” Jewish leaders shrugged and took the crumbs. Palestinian leaders? Hard pass, demanding all the land and zero Jewish newcomers. Bold move, let’s see how it plays out.

text:
A college in Illinois tried to cancel its Flock contact and it refused | Terrence O'Brien, The Verge

In April of 2025, Elgin Community College had six Flock safety cameras installed to “enhance the safety and security of students.” But by September of that year, the school’s administration grew concerned that Flock was sharing data with Customs and Border Patrol, that camera feeds were not properly secured, and that both law enforcement and the company’s employees were abusing access to the data.

Flock refused to take its cameras down so Elgin Community College covered them. The company snuck back to undo it.

So in October of 2025, Elgin Community College requested Flock to remove its cameras. According to Elgin’s President Peggy Heinrich, Flock rejected the request, saying it had not violated its contract. According to the Chicago Sun-Times, school officials reached out again in December, offered to pay for the remaining five months of the contract, and still requested that the cameras be removed. They were met with silence.

That’s when things took a strange and somewhat sinister turn. According to the Sun-Times:

Heinrich said Elgin Community College staff began to cover the cameras using black trash bags and zip ties so that they would not be able to capture footage. But workers in an unmarked vehicle, which Heinrich assumed belonged to Flock, repeatedly removed the coverings.

“We were kind of in a back and forth for a bit where we’d cover, and then when they’d come to service, they’d remove,” Heinrich said. “Then we’d cover and then they’d remove.”

This continued until April of this year when the college’s contract expired, and Flock removed the cameras.

text:
Columbus Day has a long history in America and holds special significance for the Italian-American community.

The first Columbus Day celebration took place on October 12, 1792, when New York’s Tammany Society commemorated the 300th anniversary of Christopher Columbus’s voyage. In 1892, following the lynching of 11 Italian immigrants in New Orleans, President Benjamin Harrison proclaimed a one-time national observance of Columbus Day, amid efforts to ease tensions and recognize Italian Americans.

Italian-American immigrant Angelo Noce helped establish Columbus Day as a legal holiday in Denver, and Colorado became the first state to recognize it in 1905. In 1934, advocacy by the Knights of Columbus and Italian-American leader Generoso Pope helped secure an annual presidential proclamation.

In 1966, Mariano A. Lucca of Buffalo, New York, founded the National Columbus Day Committee, which campaigned to make Columbus Day a federal holiday. Those efforts helped lead to legislation signed by President Lyndon B. Johnson on June 28, 1968, establishing Columbus Day as a federal holiday beginning in 1971.

Columbus Day also marks an important chapter in Italian-American history. In 1942, President Franklin D. Roosevelt announced the removal of the “enemy alien” designation for Italian Americans and outlined a plan to offer citizenship to elderly Italians who had been unable to naturalize because of literacy requirements. The wartime restrictions affecting Italian nationals were not fully lifted until later.

For generations of Italian Americans, Columbus Day has represented heritage, identity, and cultural pride. It is an opportunity to recognize the sacrifices, perseverance, and contributions of Italian immigrants and their descendants, whose history is deeply woven into the American story.

ISDA Wooster Lodge #279 recognizes this history and honors the Italian-American generations who helped shape our nation.

text:
Side Gig 👉 leave your W2 idea of the Day: 

Start Your Own Networking Group

Where I live, in Greenville, SC there’s a number of these groups already, so probably not room for another one. But other parts of the country are definite opportunities. My hometown of Buffalo, NY being one of them. 

People will pay money to meet the right people, develop business relationships and find new opportunities.

Here’s how to do it:

1. Start with ONE group.

Pick a niche. Business owners, entrepreneurs, manufacturers, real estate professionals, etc.

Find 15–20 people who would benefit from knowing each other.

2. Meet once per month.

Find a restaurant, brewery or business willing to host your group.

Keep the meetings organized and valuable. Share leads, wins and request introductions.

3. Charge a membership fee.

Let’s use $50/month as an example.

20 members = $1,000/month.

50 members = $2,500/month.

100 members = $5,000/month.

That’s gross revenue, before expenses. And you’ll need to make sure the group actually delivers enough value to retain members.

4. Don’t just offer one monthly meeting.

Give members reasons to stay:

* Exclusive member-only meetups
* Manufacturing plant and business tours
* Guest speakers and educational workshops
* Business referrals and introductions
* Behind-the-scenes tours of local companies
* Member spotlights and business promotions
* Social events with spouses and families

5. Then SCALE.

Once your first group is established and running successfully, start another.

Different industry.

Different geographic area.

Different meeting day.

Eventually, hire people to coordinate the meetings and manage memberships.

You could also generate additional revenue through event sponsorships and corporate partnerships.

You can build it while working your W-2. All while building YOUR network.

One meeting per month.

A few hours each week building relationships and coordinating events.

And you’re building something much more valuable than a monthly meeting.

You’re building a community.

I’ve spent decades in business, and I can tell you that relationships are incredibly valuable.

People don’t necessarily pay for networking.

They pay for ACCESS, OPPORTUNITY and RELATIONSHIPS.

Could one networking group eventually turn into multiple groups producing enough income to replace your W-2?

text: It’s never easy to hear publicly that your athletic department is on the chopping block. It was a very sleepless weekend as thoughts and emotions took over. I thought about all the kids I’ve had the privilege of working with and mentoring. The coaches I get to work with on a daily basis. The community members that I’ve built such a strong relationship and friendship with. I thought about all the special moments our kids have experienced through athletics. I thought about And I kept looking at that photo of the Wigwam sitting empty last week, wondering, Am I going to see this exact same picture of the Elwood gym 15 years from now? Five years ago, I dedicated my life to trying to help turn the athletic department around and bring Elwood Athletics back to what it once was under Mike, Marty, and so many others who served in leadership roles before me. Nobody really saw the sacrifice the 15 hour days, six or seven days a week because I knew the time and commitment it was going to take to turn this into something positive. Right now, I could have accepted the offer this past Spring and been the AD of an 8-0 acac Football championship program, a tennis regional championship, and maybe one of the best jobs in 3A in Indiana. I’ve stayed because I committed myself to this school, my athletes, and this community. I would not be like others that have quit on this school and community and it’s the same for so many others. Jayden Mullins, Kelsey Armes, Miles Laub, Blaise Jones, and so many others could have left, but they stayed because they were committed to their school and more importantly their community. It’s no secret that there were challenges when we started. But with a vision, hiring coaches who were willing to put in the work, and having a community that shared that same passion, we have been able to change so many things for the better. And we still have more work to do, everyone knows that. I continue to feel sick every day not for myself, but for our kids, our coaches, our future athletes, and the 20,000 plus former Elwood athletes whose legacy we have tried to represent with pride every single day. To me Elwood Athletics is more than games, wins, losses, banners, or scoreboards. It’s memories you’ve spent with your teammates and community. It’s relationships you’ve built that last a lifetime. It’s life lessons that you’ve taken into your career and life. It’s generations of Panthers who have worn Elwood across their chest with pride. Please continue to keep our athletic department, our coaches, and most importantly, our athletes in your prayers.  We appreciate it more than you will ever know. God Bless!!! Ryan

text:
The hidden math of Alzheimer's could point to new treatments | Mississippi State University

Could mathematics help uncover new ways to fight Alzheimer's disease? A researcher at Mississippi State University is using mathematical models to investigate how common metals influence the buildup of proteins associated with Alzheimer's and whether potential treatments could interfere with this process.

Shantia Yarahmadian, an associate professor in Mississippi State's Department of Mathematics and Statistics, is studying how metals such as copper and zinc may affect the behavior of amyloid-beta, a protein that can clump together and form plaques linked to Alzheimer's disease.

His research, published in the journal Bulletin of Mathematical Biology, builds on his ongoing efforts to use mathematics to better understand the complex biological processes involved in Alzheimer's.

Using Mathematics To Understand Alzheimer's Disease

Mathematical modeling allows scientists to explore complicated biological interactions by representing them through equations and simulations. Researchers can then test how different factors influence a process and predict what might happen when certain conditions change.

"Every biological phenomenon occurs in the physical world -- in space and time -- and involves changes in shape, quantity and matter," said Yarahmadian, a faculty member in MSU's Department of Mathematics and Statistics. "Because of its abstract power, mathematics allows us to uncover patterns, test hypotheses and make predictions that may not be possible through observation alone. Mathematics does not replace laboratory or clinical research; it complements it by helping us understand the larger system, identify the most influential mechanisms and guide future experiments."

This approach could be particularly valuable for Alzheimer's disease, which involves numerous interacting biological processes that are difficult to study individually.

How Copper and Zinc May Influence Alzheimer's Plaques

To investigate how Alzheimer's-related plaques develop, Yarahmadian created a mathematical framework that simulates the chemical reactions involved when metals such as copper and zinc interact with amyloid-beta.

Amyloid-beta proteins can stick together in a process known as aggregation. Over time, these clusters can contribute to the formation of plaques, one of the characteristic features of Alzheimer's disease.

The model examines how metal ions, which are electrically charged forms of metals, may influence this protein buildup. It also enables researchers to explore two potential therapeutic approaches designed to interfere with aggregation.

Rather than relying entirely on laboratory experiments, scientists can use the simulations to investigate how changes in these interactions might affect plaque formation and identify promising directions for further research.

Mathematical Predictions Match Laboratory Results

A mathematical model is most useful when its predictions reflect what happens in actual experiments. To evaluate his framework, Yarahmadian and his collaborators compared its results with laboratory measurements obtained through atomic force microscopy.

This imaging technique uses an extremely fine probe to examine structures at the microscopic scale, allowing researchers to study tiny clusters of proteins and other materials.

The mathematical model successfully reproduced the patterns observed in the experiments. This agreement suggests that the framework captures important aspects of how amyloid-beta proteins aggregate under the conditions studied.

The results provide evidence that mathematical simulations can help researchers investigate the mechanisms behind protein clumping and explore ways to influence the process. Although the findings do not establish an effective Alzheimer's treatment, they offer a promising tool for guiding future laboratory studies.

For Yarahmadian, the motivation behind the research extends beyond the mathematical challenge. He hopes that a better understanding of the disease's complex biology will eventually help scientists develop more effective strategies against it.

"What drew me to Alzheimer's research is the combination of its profound human impact and its extraordinary biological complexity," he said. "My goal is to use mathematical modeling to identify important mechanisms and generate insights that may help guide future experimental and therapeutic research."

text:
A Pizza History: Domino’s Unveils the “Book of Smells” in Kells as it opens its latest store there.

Domino’s creates a ‘Book of Smells’ for its new Kells store, with Weird Ireland’s Brinsley McNamara set to showcase it.

The Kells store is has an unmissable special offer to entice local Domino’s lovers- any size pizza for €9.99 from today (Monday 12th) until October 25th

https://t.co/tNrf5BKSWn

Kells is known around the world for its famous book. Now, to mark the opening of a new store in the town, Domino’s has created a book devoted to something entirely different: the smell of pizza.

The Book of Smells is an intricately illustrated celebration of Domino’s favourites, including Garlic & Herb dip and freshly baked cookies. Inspired by the visual richness associated with the Book of Kells, it brings the sights and smells of a pizza night to the page.

The book will be displayed in the new Kells store.

Brinsley McNamara, creator of the Weird Ireland social media accounts, will also showcase it across his channels, sharing the unusual new arrival with his audience.

Brinsley McNamara said: “I’ve come across plenty of unusual Irish books and stories, but I’ve never encountered one devoted to Garlic & Herb dip. Kells has an incredible place in the history of books, and this is a wonderfully strange way to celebrate that connection. The artwork deserves a proper look, ideally before the smell of cookies sends you looking for the real thing.”

Eoin Corrigan, Head of Marketing at Domino’s, said: “When you open a store in Kells, you can’t ignore the town’s most famous book. We wanted to create something playful that also had genuine care and craft behind it. The Book of Smells celebrates the Domino’s favourites people know instantly, and we’re delighted Brinsley will help us share it with people across Ireland.”

The new Domino’s store is located at 1 Castle Street Kells, A82 W9X2 and is running a special opening offer: Any Size Pizza - €9.99  (Collection Only), from October 12th until October 25th.

text:
Curved Carbon Fabric Evaporator Turns Sunlight and a 3-Volt Jolt into Fresh Water | Violet Maxwell, ScienMag

Fresh water scarcity is one of the defining challenges of the coming decades, and one of the most elegant proposed solutions is also one of the simplest: float a dark, water-loving material on the surface of seawater, let the sun heat it, and collect the vapor that rises. This approach, known as solar interfacial evaporation, promises desalination without the massive energy budgets of reverse osmosis or thermal distillation plants. Yet the technology has a stubborn Achilles heel. When the sun sets or clouds roll in, the evaporation stops, and the salt that accumulates on the evaporator surface can choke the whole process. A new study from researchers at Pohang University of Science and Technology in South Korea offers a way to keep the water flowing around the clock, and in doing so reveals a surprisingly overlooked design variable that can make or break performance.

Writing in Environmental Science and Pollution Research, Younghoon Suh and Sang Joon Lee describe a curved, fabric-based evaporator that combines two heating mechanisms: sunlight and electricity. The device is built from carbon fabric that has been surface-treated to become strongly hydrophilic, meaning it draws water into its fibers through capillary action. The treated material is remarkable in its own right. It absorbs an incoming water droplet in less than 100 milliseconds, so fast that the fabric essentially never appears dry, and it captures more than 85 percent of incident light across an extraordinarily broad spectrum spanning 200 to 2500 nanometers, from ultraviolet through the visible and deep into the infrared. That broadband absorption is exactly what a photothermal material needs, because it converts as much of the solar spectrum as possible into heat right at the water surface rather than letting it reflect away.

The key structural innovation is the geometry. Instead of laying the fabric flat on the water, the team draped it over two blocks of melamine sponge, creating an arched, tunnel-like shape. This curved configuration does two clever things at once. First, it exposes both faces of the fabric to the air, effectively doubling the evaporation area relative to the footprint of the device. Second, it allows water to be supplied from both ends of the fabric simultaneously, so the capillary wicking that feeds the hot central zone has two sources rather than one. In flat evaporators, the distance that water must travel from the reservoir to the center of the hot zone is often fixed by the device size, and engineers have rarely treated it as a tunable parameter. Suh and Lee made it the centerpiece of their study.

That tunable parameter is the span distance, the gap between the two sponge supports. The researchers fabricated evaporators with span distances ranging from 3 to 6 centimeters and systematically compared their performance. The physics involved is a delicate three-way trade-off. A wider span means more of the fabric is suspended in the arch, exposed to light and air, which increases the effective heating and evaporation area. But a wider span also means water must travel farther through the fabric’s capillary network to reach the center, and if the supply cannot keep pace with evaporation, the hottest and most productive zone dries out, its temperature climbs without producing vapor, and efficiency collapses. A narrower span keeps water close at hand but wastes potential evaporation area on the submerged or supported portions of the fabric.

The experiments showed that the sweet spot sits at a span distance of 4 centimeters. At this width, the balance among solar absorption, Joule heating, and capillary water transport is optimized: the fabric’s central zone stays wet and cool enough to evaporate water continuously while maximizing the illuminated area. The team then pushed the optimized device, an 8 by 2 centimeter strip of treated carbon fabric, under combined illumination equivalent to one sun and an applied voltage of just 3 volts. The electrical contribution matters because it provides Joule heating, the same resistive warming that makes a toaster glow, which can operate independently of weather. Under these dual-drive conditions, the evaporator achieved an evaporation rate of 7.81 kilograms of water per square meter per hour using deionized water, and 7.23 kilograms per square meter per hour using artificial seawater at 3.5 weight percent salinity, which closely matches the salt content of the real ocean.

Those rates are impressive by the standards of interfacial evaporation, but laboratory performance can be misleading. Real desalination devices must survive repeated exposure to saline water without fouling, and salt accumulation is the classic failure mode: as water evaporates, dissolved ions concentrate at the evaporation front and crystallize, clogging pores and degrading performance. To test durability, the researchers ran five consecutive evaporation cycles using the same specimen with artificial seawater, rinsing the fabric with water between cycles. After all five rounds, the device retained approximately 99 percent of its initial evaporation rate. That near-perfect recovery suggests that the curved, double-fed water supply helps flush salts away from the critical zones and that simple rinsing is enough to restore full function, a practical advantage for real-world deployment where maintenance must be cheap and easy.

The team also took the device outdoors, which is where many promising evaporators falter. Under natural sunlight, the optimized evaporator produced water collection rates above 3 kilograms per square meter per hour. More importantly for the goal of producing drinkable water, the researchers measured the concentrations of major ions in the collected condensate. The results were striking: the concentrations of the major dissolved ions were reduced by three to four orders of magnitude relative to the feed seawater, meaning the collected water was dramatically purer than the source. While the study reports ion reduction rather than a full potability certification, a four-order-of-magnitude drop in major ion content puts the condensate in a range that conventional post-treatment could readily finish, or that could serve for agriculture and other non-potable uses in water-stressed regions.

What makes the study resonate beyond its specific numbers is the framing of span distance as a first-class design parameter. In the growing literature on photothermal fabrics, hanging evaporators, and 3D structures, researchers have explored materials ranging from graphene architectures to MoS2 aerogels to hierarchical nanowire coatings, often chasing marginal gains in absorption or thermal localization. Suh and Lee’s results suggest that for curved geometries, simply adjusting the mechanical span of the same material can shift the balance between water supply and heat input enough to dominate performance. The finding is a reminder that in interfacial evaporation, transport physics, how fast water wicks toward the hot zone, how far it must travel, and how the wetted area interacts with the illuminated area, can matter as much as the choice of nanomaterial.

The photoelectrothermal strategy also addresses the fundamental limitation of solar-only systems: intermittency. Because the carbon fabric is electrically conductive, applying a modest 3 volts keeps the evaporation surface warm during darkness or overcast conditions, allowing continuous operation. Previous work by other groups has explored Joule heating in graphene sponges, braided fabrics, and nickel foam-based evaporators, and the POSTECH team’s earlier studies included heliotropic solar steam generators assisted by Joule heating. The new work integrates that dual-mode heating into the curved, double-fed architecture and, crucially, identifies the geometric optimum that lets both heating modes and the capillary supply work in concert rather than against one another.

The research, funded by a National Research Foundation of Korea grant, points toward evaporator designs that are cheap, robust, and operable day and night. Carbon fabric is an inexpensive, flexible, and scalable substrate compared with many engineered nanomaterial platforms, and the melamine sponge supports are commodity materials. The demonstration that a single specimen can endure repeated saline cycles with nearly complete performance recovery, combined with outdoor water collection above 3 kilograms per square meter per hour and ion removal of three to four orders of magnitude, makes a credible case that curved photoelectrothermal evaporators deserve attention as practical desalination units. For coastal communities facing brackish or saline groundwater and unreliable grid power, a device that harvests sunlight when available and switches to a few watts of electricity when it is not could be a meaningful step toward water security. The lesson from Pohang is that sometimes the breakthrough is not a new material at all, but knowing exactly how far to stretch it.

Among the hundreds of signatories to the Freedom Conservatism Statement of Principles are campaign professionals, political activists, and former elected  officials — including mayors, school-board members, state and federal  lawmakers, governors, and even a former vice president. Most have a  rooting interest in partisan politics. Some remain personally involved  in campaigns.

But the @FreeConTalk project itself is  nonpartisan. Our goals extend far beyond one election cycle or the fate  of any particular candidate.

We believe that unless there is a healthy, vibrant American Right committed to individual liberty, federalism, free enterprise, free speech, free trade, civic virtue, equal opportunity, and the rule of law, any hard-won electoral victories will prove fleeting. And if our movement tolerates cranks, bigots, and other reactionaries, fewer such victories will occur in the first place.

Unless conservatives offer real solutions to the problems voters care about most — such as affordability, fiscal responsibility, family formation, and broad access to the American Dream — voters will seek them elsewhere. That voters  are destined to be disappointed by populists, progressives, and  socialists is true but beside the point. You can’t beat something with  nothing.

At each summit, #FreeCon signatories and allies will  discuss the lessons of the midterms, the challenges and opportunities we  will face in 2027 and beyond, and how a rejuvenated American Right can  meet those challenges and seize those opportunities.

RIFE WITH FRAUD ALLOWS DEMANDS TO ESTABLISH RESTITUTION
Posted on October 12, 2026 by Barry Zalma
PSYCHIATRIST CONVICTED ON FOURTEEN FRAUD COUNTS AND RESTITUTION
Post 4861
Attorney Argument Without  Evidence at Sentencing is Ineffective 

In United States v. Gustavo Kinrys, Nos. 24-1592, 24-1716, United States Court of Appeals, First Circuit (September 21, 2026) Gustavo Kinrys, a Massachusetts psychiatrist, submitted fraudulent claims to private and public health insurers between 2015 and 2018, including claims for sessions that could not have occurred because he or the purported patient was abroad.

When insurers sought supporting records, he delayed, invoked a fictitious office manager, and created false documentation. A jury convicted him on fourteen of fifteen counts. The district court imposed a ninety-nine-month sentence, calculated intended loss at slightly more than $19 million using the face value of the bills, and ordered $6,537,309.59 in restitution.
LAW

Under U.S.S.G. § 2B1.1, loss is the greater of actual or intended loss, and intended loss turns on the pecuniary harm the defendant purposely sought to inflict.

When a scheme is rife with fraud, the billed amount may serve as prima facie evidence of intended loss; the defendant may rebut that figure with evidence of a lower subjective intent, although the government retains the ultimate burden of proof.

Under the Mandatory Victims Restitution Act, restitution compensates victims for actual losses caused by fraud, makes them whole, and may not provide a windfall. The government bears the burden to prove that a sentencing enhancement applies by a preponderance of the evidence.

In cases like this one, where the defendant’s scheme was “rife with fraud,” courts may calculate intended loss using a burden-shifting. That approach permits a sentencing court to use the billed amount as prima facie evidence of intended loss. The burden then shifts to the defendant, who may “rebut” the face value of the bills by proffering evidence establishing that he intended to reap some lesser amount.

Once both parties have put forth their competing loss amounts and the record is fully formed, the district court must make a “reasonable estimate of the loss,” bearing in mind that the government retains the ultimate burden of proving the applicability of the enhancement. The court determines reasonable loss based on the defendant’s subjective intent, that is, the “pecuniary harm that the defendant purposely sought to inflict
DISCUSSION

Kinrys argued that intended loss should have been limited to approximately $8.3 million — the reimbursement he expected under in-network contracts — rather than the amount billed, which would have reduced the sentencing enhancement. He also argued that restitution should be offset by separate, allegedly legitimate claims that insurers had not paid. The government relied on the fraudulent bills, Kinrys’s later civil suits seeking billed charges, and evidence that he kept payments exceeding contract rates.
ANALYSIS

The First Circuit found no clear error in using the billed amount.

Although Kinrys’s in-network status supported a plausible inference that he expected only contract rates, other evidence supported the district court’s finding that he intended to obtain as much as possible: he sued insurers for billed charges, sought damages exceeding those charges, and retained full billed payments when received.

He offered attorney argument rather than contrary evidence at sentencing. The restitution challenge also failed because the order included only fraudulent claims, while the proposed offsets involved distinct, contested reimbursement claims.
CONCLUSION

The First Circuit affirmed both the intended-loss calculation and the restitution order.
ZALMA OPINION

Billing the government for psychiatric care to the poor or elderly when Kinrys was on holiday in other countries where he claimed to give care was criminal and evil. He then tried to reduce his sentence and restitution by claiming his bills were never paid as presented but were reduced by the insurer. He will serve the full sentence and pay the full amount of restitution.

text:
Apartment

A new US REIT from North of the Border. Canadian-listed BSR REIT (HOM.U) is heading to the New York Stock Exchange, with plans to begin trading under the ticker BSRT in mid-October. BSR owns 26 Class A garden-style apartment communities totaling 7,170 units, with a portfolio valued at approximately $1.4B. Roughly 90% of portfolio NOI comes from the Texas Triangle markets of Dallas, Houston, and Austin, with smaller exposures to Oklahoma City and Little Rock. Founded in Arkansas with roots dating to 1956, the company went public on the Toronto Stock Exchange in 2018, raising $135M. At the time, Canada's REIT market offered a more receptive environment for a relatively small U.S. apartment REIT seeking public equity capital. With an equity market capitalization of $450M, BSR would become the 9th largest US apartment REIT, sliding into the 8th spot after the merger of CSR and IRT. The NYSE listing aims to expand its investor base, improve trading liquidity, and potentially narrow its valuation discount by aligning its public listing with its U.S. assets, operations, and investor audience. Operationally, the portfolio carried an average in-place rent of roughly $1,490/unit and 94.5% occupancy at midyear, while leverage stood at 51.7% of gross book value. BSR has spent the past several years actively recycling capital, including a major 2025 disposition to AvalonBay, into newer, higher-growth Sunbelt assets while targeting additional upside from lease-up, resident-service initiatives, and operating efficiencies across the portfolio.

Baby Reina was found lying in her own waste in a metal crate. At a sanctuary. The charge is one misdemeanor.

Brandywine Valley SPCA says the pit bull mix was severely emaciated, dehydrated and barely responsive. Worms. Fleas. Ticks. Malnutrition.

Now picture your dog in that crate.

People saw her. A vet photographed Reina at a July 9 inspection. No charge followed. An Aug 5 exam found her severely underweight with a staph infection. The instruction was “monitor at home.” The sheriff’s office says no known treatment followed.

The Houston Press reports her photo reached the sheriff’s office in April, and the sheriff turned down PETA’s June offer to help remove the dogs and two ailing horses. One horse later died.

Angela Sera, 69, runs Dogtown Ranch Sanctuary near Rockdale. Milam County deputies arrested her Oct 6 on one count of cruelty to non-livestock animals, a Class A misdemeanor. A felony, the sheriff’s office says, takes “actual physical abuse or torture.”

Reina is safe now. Months of warnings, and this is the charge.

Texas, should neglect this bad stay a misdemeanor? Call your state legislator and ask.

text:
The IRS said Willie Nelson owed $16.7 million. His daughter said he probably didn't have $30,000. Agents took almost everything he owned, and his fans bought it back at auction.

In the video below, he is asked how one man gets into so much trouble. "It sounds like I went to school to learn how to do that," Willie says.

On November 9, 1990, agents froze his bank accounts and took his Texas ranch, his country club and his recording studio. His daughter got his guitar, Trigger, out of the house and shipped it to him in Hawaii.

"As long as I got my guitar," he said, "I'll be fine."

The debt went back to the 1980s, when his accountants at Price Waterhouse put his money into investments the government later declared illegal. "I think it's important that you trust someone to do these things for you," Willie says in the video.

A farmers' group bought one of his ranches at auction just to sell it back to him.

Friends offered benefit concerts. He turned them down: "It doesn't sit well with me to take charity." Instead he sold an album of just his voice and a guitar for $19.95 by phone, and the IRS took a cut.

He sued Price Waterhouse for $45 million and paid off the rest.

Was Willie Nelson the victim of the people he trusted with his money, or a man who never cared enough about money to watch it?

text:
I recently worked as an interpreter at an event in Houston for young “math stars”—children and their parents from all over the country who gathered to connect, share experiences, and learn about opportunities for developing mathematical talent.

One of the speakers, who talked about math camps, offered the parents a piece of advise:

“Be prepared for your child to reach a point at one of these math camps where they suddenly hit a wall, encounter someone better than them, and become overwhelmed by comparison.

This can bring up a lot of uncomfortable feelings. Emotions triggered by comparison can be devastating and destructive. We want to guide students to a point where all comparison ceases. Believe it or not, such a point exists.

It’s the point at which we discover wonder for ourselves. When we find wonder, we realize we no longer want to compare ourselves to others.”

I couldn’t help but think of René Girard’s theory of mimetic desire as the main source of human conflict and violence.

According to Girard, mimetic desire arises in the heart not simply because we want the same object as someone else, but because we see that person wanting it. We imitate their desire, and suddenly, what they want becomes something we want, too.

“Rivalry does not arise because of the fortuitous convergence of two desires on a single object; rather, the subject desires the object because the rival desires it.” — René Girard

We want something not because we want something but because we see someone else wanting it. Such is the nature of mimesis and a source of violence. Is there a way out?

We cannot get rid of imitation. Nor should we. Girard argues that whom we choose to imitate makes all the difference in the world. When we imitate people, we fall into mimesis and violence. When we imitate Christ, the model cannot become a rival to be defeated.

Why doesn’t imitating Christ give rise to mimetic rivalry? Because Christ desires what cannot be owned or possessed. He desires communion with Being itself. When we look at Him and the same desire awakens in our hearts, we cannot compete with Him for the possession of Being. https://t.co/elDicqGh6u

text:
(this week's column) https://t.co/iKhCLc4kT9 and https://t.co/AkyMq96QLr Could a giant rechargeable battery keep your appliances going during the next blackout? A reader named Sheila asked me to find out.

“Because I’m not driving now, I won’t be able to run to the store for ice when the weather gets threatening,” she said. “That has thrown me into paralysis by analysis looking at various backup solutions.”

The paralysis didn’t last long before Sheila bought the Pecron E1000LFP, a portable power station and solar generator. She’ll pair it with solar panels that can recharge the power station during a prolonged outage or whenever she wants to go off grid.

The Pecron has a 1,024 watt-hour battery and can supply up to 1,800 watts continuously. A refrigerator, 55-inch TV, LED lamp, Wi-Fi router or modem, typical desktop computer and phone charger might use only around 325 watts altogether, depending on the individual devices. But appliances such as refrigerators can briefly demand much more power when their motors start, so the Pecron’s ability to handle short peaks of up to 3,000 watts could come in handy. It’s also fairly light at 29 pounds and has long-lasting batteries. I saw it on sale for $399.

Unlike gas generators, portable power stations produce no engine exhaust, require no gasoline and can be used indoors. That’s good if you like breathing. There’s no sense putting up with carbon monoxide poisoning.

Look for power stations with lithium iron phosphate batteries, usually abbreviated LFP or LiFePO4. They last longer and are less likely to overheat than the kind of lithium batteries commonly used in older power stations.

Good alternatives include the EcoFlow Delta 3. Though more expensive, it can go 4,000 cycles before falling to 80 percent capacity. The Pecron is rated at 3,500-plus. When last I checked, the EcoFlow was $599 at Walmart.

Another possibility is the Anker Solix C1000 Gen 2, which offers 1,024 watt-hours, 2,000 watts continuous, 3,000 watts peak, and 4,000 cycles to at least 80 percent capacity.

Finally, there’s the Jackery Explorer 1000, version 2. Though only $499, the Jackery’s lithium iron phosphate battery can go for 4,000 cycles with at least 70 percent remaining capacity.

Scammed

When trying to help an author self-publish a book, I accidentally led her straight into a scam. Here’s how it happened.

First I Googled “IngramSpark.” Then I perused the list of self-publishers. There were so many ads that I breezed past the real site and landed on https://t.co/lrKrOOrEx3. (Note the extra “s.”)

Interrupting a live chat with a representative, I wrote down the contact info, then left to meet the 92-year-old author in an apartment five floors down from mine. Once there, I led her to accept the $269 charge. It sounded reasonable to me because it meant distribution to 40 outlets, including Barnes & Noble and Walmart, instead of just Amazon. But their slightly aggressive tone should have been a red flag.

A formatter from PeoplePerHour, the one who made her book look like a real book instead of a Word document, uncovered the hoax after I mentioned the $269 charge. He said that, unlike the impostor, the real IngramSpark charges nothing to open an account and upload a manuscript for distribution to 40 outlets. These can all offer it in paperback, hardback and e-book. Out of curiosity, I looked up the phony contact’s name and could find no such person at IngramSpark.

Lesson learned: Watch what you click on. Fortunately, however, the author got on the phone immediately to cancel her credit card and order a replacement. She'll dispute the charge as soon as it lands in her account.

Shoe Tech

Who says technology has to contain a computer? Cadense put some clever engineering into ordinary athletic shoes and even the more dressy kind. They’re for anyone who has trouble lifting their feet as they walk, such as those with Parkinson’s, cerebral palsy, multiple sclerosis, or neuropathy. They could also be helpful for anyone who’s had a stroke or is in danger of tripping when walking.

Here’s how they work. Your dragging foot gets a boost from small, low-friction areas in the sole, to avoid catching on the floor. The sole compresses and a grippier rubber section takes over. The doctor who invented them also developed MIT’s Skywalker system for gait therapy.

In a recently published survey of 705 Cadense customers, users reported far fewer falls. However, the study relied on customers’ memories of previous falls, and there was no comparison group. But you might want to give the shoes a try anyway. Prices start at around $200 at https://t.co/qsvzuhig3A. The company offers 30-day returns, though there’s a $7.99 fee to cover processing, inspection, cleaning, and restocking.

Help with Tiny Print

Your Android phone's new “Guided Vision” can read the fine print for you. Point a compatible phone at an expiration date, tiny label, appliance panel or other hard-to-see object and Gemini Live will describe it aloud. If your aim is off, it will show you how to reposition your phone. You can also ask follow-up questions about the item. This feature is rolling out gradually.

For the iPhone, there’s Apple’s Live Recognition, which has offered visual descriptions since iOS 14 on an iPhone XR, XS or newer. Besides describing scenes, it can read aloud the text you’re pointing your camera at.

text:
a solo SaaS founder set up OpenAI Dots on Monday and stopped doing sales

Friday: $186,000 in new pipeline and 14 demo calls on his calendar, every one with a prep brief. he got this message:

“researched 300 companies, 61 matched your ICP. wrote 61 personal first lines, no templates. 18 replies, 14 meetings booked, $186k in pipeline. 9 leads  disqualified: wrong size or no budget signals.”

that’s a setup. here it is, step by step ↓↓↓

most people use Dots for sales like a copywriter: “write me a cold email”, paste it into 500 inboxes, get 0 replies.

he did the opposite. he never asked for an email. he gave it a sales team: his ideal customer profile, his calendar, his inbox, and one rule: no message goes out unless it mentions something real about that company.

the team:
→ the scholar: researches every company (news, hiring, funding, tech stack)
→ the watcher: watches for buying signals like a new hire, a funding round or a competitor’s churn
→ the builder: writes one personal first line per lead, never a template
→ the bouncer: kills bad-fit leads before they waste a single email
→ the manager: moves each lead from researched to contacted to replied to booked

what makes it work:
→ it disqualifies before it writes. 9 out of 70 never got an email
→ every first line comes from a real fact it found, not “hope you’re well”
→ replies get answered within minutes, with a calendar link and a time zone that fits
→ every meeting comes with a one-page brief: who they are, what they need, what to ask

his rules:
→ research, qualifying, writing drafts: act without asking
→ the first 20 emails: ask him first, until he trusts the voice
→ after that: send, max 30 a day, stop instantly on any “not interested”
→ pricing, discounts, contracts: hand off to him

built-in safeguards always stay on. his rules only add limits on top.

the exact prompt ↓
“You are my outbound sales team.
My ideal customer is [industry, size, role, problem].
Every day, find 15 companies that match. Research each one: recent news, hiring, funding, tools they use.
Disqualify anyone who doesn’t fit, and log the reason.
For each good fit, write a 3-line email with one specific fact about them. No templates, no flattery.
Ask me before sending the first 20. After that, send up to 30 a day and stop immediately if someone says no.
When someone replies, answer within the hour and offer 3 slots from my calendar.
Before every meeting, send me a one-page brief. Never discuss pricing without me.”
then close the laptop. Activity shows every lead and why it was kept or killed. recurring jobs live in Scheduled.
not a founder? the same setup works for anything where you need people to say yes:
→ freelancer: “find 15 businesses whose website is slow or outdated, and pitch them a fix”
→ job seeker: “find hiring managers for [role], not recruiters, and write them about one thing their team just shipped”
→ creator: “find 20 brands that sponsor channels my size, and pitch them with my real numbers”
→ local business: “find new companies opening offices near me and offer them [catering / cleaning / design]”
→ selling something big (house, car, equipment): “find buyers who were recently looking, and send them one honest message”

swap one line of the prompt and the rest stays the same: research first, disqualify, personalize, follow up, brief you.

BONUS: read the disqualified list. it’s the clearest picture of who your customer isn’t, and most people never write it down.

GLOBAL TALENT VISA: Which route is right for you?

Many people hear Global Talent and think it's one visa with one set of requirements. It isn't.

There are different routes depending on your field and career stage.👇

1️⃣ Digital Technology (Tech Nation pathway) 

Suitable for software engineers, product managers, cyber specialists, AI professionals, CTOs, founders, etc.

You'll generally need evidence of:
✅ Innovation
✅ Significant impact
✅ Recognition beyond your employer
✅ Strong career progression
✅ Speaking engagements, publications, media features, mentoring, open source contributions, awards or commercial success

Two categories:
🔹 Exceptional Talent (established leaders)
🔹 Exceptional Promise (future leaders)

2️⃣ Academia & Research

For professionals in:
🔹 Science
🔹 Engineering
🔹 Medicine
🔹 Humanities
🔹 Social Sciences

Routes include:
✅ Academic appointments
✅ Individual fellowships
✅ UKRI endorsed grants
✅ Peer review route

Evidence may include publications, citations, research impact, grants, fellowships and academic leadership. (https://t.co/JYPAxNodBy)[2](https://t.co/Nppk0zA9gF)

3️⃣ Arts & Culture

For:
🎭 Performing Arts
🎵 Music
🎨 Visual Arts
🎬 Film & Television

Applicants must demonstrate a substantial track record, international recognition, awards, exhibitions, performances, publications or other significant achievements. Endorsements are handled through Arts Council England. (https://t.co/YCR54XgQb8)[4](https://t.co/mrHk1SzRem)

4️⃣ Prestigious Prize Route

If you've won an eligible internationally recognised prize approved by the UK government, you can apply directly without going through the endorsement stage.(https://t.co/mrHk1SzRem (https://t.co/Nppk0zA9gF)

5️⃣ Exceptional Talent vs Exceptional Promise

A lot of people get confused here.

✅ Exceptional Talent = recognised leader in your field

✅ Exceptional Promise = emerging leader with strong evidence of future potential

Promise is NOT a weaker application. It simply reflects your career stage.(https://t.co/YCR54XgQb8)

6️⃣ Common misconceptions

❌ You do not need a UK sponsor
❌ You do not need a job offer
❌ There is no minimum salary requirement
❌ Having a degree alone is not enough

The focus is on evidence of achievement, impact and recognition. (https://t.co/JYPAxNodBy)[4](https://t.co/mrHk1SzRem)

Global Talent is not about being the smartest person in the room. It's about proving, with evidence, that your work has created measurable impact and that independent experts recognise your contribution. The strongest applications tell a clear story supported by documents, not just claims.

#RadioMoskva

Stochastic Trump breaks with Ukraine

That was wild. I was flying home from a trip to France with a few plane changes and each time I got into the Wi-Fi zone there was another big breaking Trump story. And it’s still going on.

The bottom line is Trump has broken with Ukraine and given up all pretence of trying to help in its war with Russia. Trump is both extremely simple to understand but totally impossible to predict.

His agenda is very simple. He wants to bring record high diesel prices down otherwise the Republicans will get trashed in the midterm elections next month. From what I read it is already too late to prevent the Democrats from taking over both houses, but he is going to try anyway.

The upshot is he did a “deal” with Putin to restart diesel exports, but if you dig into the details then the 300,000 tonnes (2.2mn barrels) Russia has agreed to release will last three and half days at current US demand. So, this is less than a gesture. But of course, it is a big win for Putin as it breaks the sanction discipline – and this is a month after Trump signed off on Lindsey Graham’s hellish sanctions that were supposed to break Russia’s economic back.

Bankova was furious and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy went out on a limb to openly criticise the White House calling Trump “weak”. You do not call Trump weak. It is guaranteed to piss him off – and true to form he immediately called for Zelenskiy to be replaced as president for the first time ever.

Trump went on to “demand”, not ask, Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil refineries and Bankova responded by hitting two more the next day. Kyrylo Budanov, Ukraine’s former HUR spy master and now the head of the presidential administration who was in Miami in parallel talks on a new peace deal, was similarly outraged after the news broke following a Trump-Putin 1.5 hour phone call which was so friendly neither side wanted to put the receiver down, according to Yuri Ushakov, Putin’s top foreign policy advisor.

Budanov swore at Kushner and his party, promising to “burn all of Russia’s refineries down” as a result.

Errr. I’d call that a breakup.

Then the gloves came off and some really big threats were made. The US has said it will withdraw all its satellite intel that the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) needs to not only find targets but also know where Russia’s air defences are. And that was followed overnight by the US withdrawing access to its weapons under the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) mechanism where the EU buys US arms on Ukraine’s behalf. That is the main source of what few PAC interceptor missiles that Kyiv is still getting. It was pretty defenceless before and now the AFU will be stripped of what little defence ammo it has left.

The EU rallied around. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced that she was releasing another €3bn for Ukrainian defence spending, except without PURL Ukraine can’t buy the very thing it needs most. But that’s all she’s got. The EU once again has been totally sidelined and apart from a few brave words has nothing to offer Ukraine that will make any difference.

Russia has already destroyed two thirds of Ukraine’s power system and is now busily destroying what remains. Kyiv was backed out again last night and the first snows have not even arrived. The city administration has told everyone to stock up on power banks, flashlights, bottled water and canned food. The mayor said that those that can leave the capital should go.

All this talk about an “energy ceasefire” was classic Trump. He put it out there on social media, but within an hour it became clear he just made that up. Zelenskiy told the FT it was “news to me.”

The Kremlin has yet to say anything, but it is perfectly obvious no deal was done.

In all his recent remarks, Putin has said over and over again that no deal is possible until the “root causes” of the war are addressed – a list of demands we are all very familiar with. Zelenskiy, always keen to play the rational actor in this drama, said “of course we will stop blowing up refineries, if the Russians stop blowing up our power stations.”

Ain’t gonna happen.

Why would Putin stop his bombing campaign? He has the upper hand both in the quality and number of missiles and drones, at a time when Ukraine is defenceless against them – and what little hope there was to even get the 300 extra interceptors he has been calling for has just been stripped away by Trump’s temper tantrum.

You can’t run a country like this or deal with a big international crisis by just firing off random tweets that you have just made up because you thought.. what exactly? That you could push diesel prices down with some good news? If that was the plan it didn’t work. Diesel is trading at $6.26 per gallon today, down about 1 cent overnight and 5 cents on a week, but still 71% higher than it was a year ago.

Did he think people would not check if there was a ceasefire in place? I don’t think he thought at all. And that is the point I was making above: he is easy to understand as it's clear what he wants, but he is impossible to predict as he doesn’t think at all.

People are becoming inured to the bonkers things he says: “oh, that is just Trump being crazy again.”

The more serious commentators draw conclusions from a “pick and mix” bag of adjectives and explanations. He is a demagog, demented, narcissistic, or just dingbat. It doesn’t matter. They are all true and none of them are true. I don’t see any policy or strategy at all beyond what he can see at the end of his nose.

This is a serious problem for everyone. It’s not even just random. If it was random, then at least randomness has a structure (The Bell curve) and you can make predictions from that. The cheating in the recent Duma election proved that again as vote fixing destroys the random distribution so you can actually measure exactly how many votes were stolen (about 20% this year).

No, Trump is what we have called a stochastic problem. It’s a maths technical term that goes beyond mere randomness. A stochastic system involves random variables where future values or events are inherently unpredictable. It’s like trying to model eddies in gas flows. The Three Body Problem in physics. It is true chaos and as such it cannot be analysed.

It was Trump’s stochastic tweeting that got him elected in the first place. He would say something mad like he could shoot someone down on Times Square that the media gleefully reported, but then he would say something else equally mad so soon afterwards that the media never had the time to properly roast or debunk his first statement. And he kept doing this. After a while he was simply complaining about everything and threatening to smash the system. As no one is ever happy with the system, these criticisms built up a momentum, and he was elected on a “smash the system” ticket without any plan of what to replace it with other than “winning.”

Ironically, his Republicans are likely to lose big time in the midterms as all he has done is smash the system so it works even less well than before – which is why the record high diesel prices are so important: they are evidence of his complete failure to do anything useful.

Putin has also been branded with a dozen labels - obsessive, autocrat, imperialist, murderer, and so on – but at least with him there is a rational model to explain his irrational behaviour. I had a go in a comment asking: “Has Putin gone mad?” at the start of the war. There I concluded that the one really Soviet thing about him was he was prepared to sacrifice Russia’s prosperity for its security.

And he actually understands this equation (in his own way); remember his 1997 economics PhD dissertation concerned planning and replenishing mineral resources during the transition to a market economy, focusing on St Petersburg and the Leningrad region. It’s just the conclusion he came to – it is worth bringing down sanctions from hell for the sake of keeping Ukraine out of Nato – was a worthwhile trade off; something very few other leaders in this world would agree with or do.

The mad Putin thesis gives you a basis for understanding how he works and allows for (limited) predictive capacity of his actions. But Trump does not.

This is best illustrated by the energy markets. Without any policy at all, the analysts and traders are helpless as there is no model at all. They are left floundering and reacting to individual tweets as the only thing they have to hold on to. Ironically, Trump understands this part, and he and his cronies have been making billions of dollars by shorting stocks before one of these tweets. You can’t do that either, but again it's at the end of Trump’s nose and he wants to be rich so he has.

It is not Zelenskiy that needs to be replaced. It’s Trump. He is running the world towards a new huge energy crisis. Two thirds of the all-time record 400mn barrels of oil from strategic reserves has already been used up and continues to be run down with no sign of either the Ukraine or Iran war coming to an end. And what is Trump going to do about it? We literally have no idea, as Trump has no ideas.

text:
Episode 6: Rexdale Park

There once was a man named Rexdale Park. He was born in 1891. About 28 years after the battle of Gettysburg.

He lost his grandfather in the battle of Gettysburg. Not to fighting, but to scurvy.

Dirty little disease scurvy is. Make sure to drink your orange juice.

Anyway, Rexdale’s father Rexward grew up without a father, because of the dirty little disease.

So he always had a penchant for oranges, out of survival instinct. He didn’t want to go out like his pop.

Living in Pennsylvania in the 1800s it was very difficult to get oranges. Supply chains aren’t what they are now.

So instead of moving to Florida, Rexward went down there with a cow and offered it to an orange farmer in exchange for a crate of oranges every month for the next year.

When Rexward got his first crate, he became a hot commodity around his friends. They weren’t afraid of the scurvy like Rexward but they were absolutely sick of apples.

After the 2nd crate was consumed within the first week Rexward realized he needed to up his crates per month so he started getting more and selling them.

It took off quick and he ended up with an orange juice empire.

When his son Rexdale Park was born he built and named a park after him and little Rexdale played on it every day.

Now I walk by that park almost every day.
