🇵🇱🇺🇸🇷🇺🇮🇷 TIME TO WAKE UP! IF TRUMP FINANCIALLY BENEFITS PUTIN, AND WE FINANCE TRUMP'S AMERICA BY BUYING AMERICAN WEAPONS, ARE WE INDIRECTLY HELPING TO FINANCE PUTIN? ISN'T IT TIME TO CONSIDER SWITCHING TO SWEDISH GRIPEN FIGHTER JETS INSTEAD OF BUYING MORE F-35s? 🔥 GEOPOLITICS FOR IDIOTS: HOW TO FINANCIALLY STRENGTHEN YOUR ADVERSARY AND THEN SELL POLAND PROTECTION AGAINST HIS MISSILES! 🤡

Warning: this might get complicated. You will need to connect a few facts, apply some basic logic, and spend five minutes without worshipping Donald Trump. For certain sections of the Polish right, that may be a challenge beyond the processing capacity of their political brains. Russia sells oil and makes money. Russia cooperates with Iran. Iran is an adversary of the United States. Russia invaded Ukraine, continues to bomb its cities, and represents the most serious military threat to Poland's security. Still following? Good. That was just the warm-up. Because whenever Washington makes decisions that enable additional transactions involving Russian energy resources, a question arises that no responsible Polish politician should ignore: IS AMERICAN POLICY INADVERTENTLY HELPING THE VERY COUNTRY THAT POLAND IS SPENDING BILLIONS TO DEFEND ITSELF AGAINST? And no, this is not a conspiracy theory. It is a legitimate question about financial flows, sanctions enforcement, energy interests, and European security.

Now comes the part that matters most, especially to those who treat the orange messiah as an infallible geopolitical genius. 🇵🇱 POLAND, NOT FLORIDA, IS ON NATO'S EASTERN FLANK! We live next to the Russian threat. Polish taxpayers are financing enormous investments in our armed forces, air defense systems, fighter aircraft, tanks, and critical security infrastructure. Our children will live with the consequences of decisions being made today in Washington, Moscow, and Brussels. Yet part of the Polish political right continues to behave as though the primary duty of a Polish politician is to applaud Donald Trump. POLAND IS NOT THE 51ST AMERICAN STATE! THE POLISH PRESIDENT IS NOT THE WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY! AND POLISH TAXPAYERS ARE NOT AN ATM FOR SOMEONE ELSE'S GEOPOLITICAL EXPERIMENTS!

Karol Nawrocki, Adam Bielan, and all the other political admirers of Donald Trump: perhaps instead of another round of enthusiastic praise, photographs, and declarations of eternal friendship, you could finally ask Washington some serious questions. Why should Poland bear ever-increasing costs to deter Russia if decisions made by our most important ally may simultaneously increase Russian revenues? What concrete security guarantees do we receive in return for spending billions on American weapons? Are American commercial interests always aligned with Polish national security? And when they are not, who in Warsaw has the courage to say so openly? CAN YOU PUT POLAND'S NATIONAL INTEREST ABOVE YOUR PERSONAL FASCINATION WITH DONALD TRUMP, EVEN ONCE?

Because Trump can change his mind tomorrow. The day after tomorrow, he can announce another historic victory. On Wednesday, he might praise Putin. On Thursday, threaten Iran. And on Friday, declare that he has ended yet another war with a single telephone call. But Poland will still be exactly where it is. On NATO's eastern flank. Next to Ukraine, fighting for its survival. Within reach of Russia's military machine. AND NEITHER A RED MAGA HAT, NOR A WHITE HOUSE SELFIE, NOR ANOTHER EXCITED SOCIAL MEDIA POST FROM A POLISH RIGHT-WING POLITICIAN WILL DEFEND OUR COUNTRY. What can defend Poland is a strong military, credible deterrence, a reliable NATO alliance, a united Europe, a capable domestic defense industry, and politicians who understand the difference between national interests and personal admiration for a foreign leader. This is not about abandoning our alliance with the United States. Quite the opposite. It is about making sure that alliance is a partnership between sovereign countries that respect one another, rather than a relationship between a client and his political idol.

And that brings us to another question. 🇸🇪 WHY SHOULDN'T POLAND SERIOUSLY EXAMINE THE SWEDISH SAAB JAS 39 GRIPEN AS AN ALTERNATIVE FOR FUTURE FIGHTER PURCHASES? The F-35 offers advanced stealth capabilities, sophisticated sensors, and integration with NATO systems. Those advantages are real and should not be dismissed. But the Gripen deserves serious consideration too. Its operating concept emphasizes dispersed operations, rapid turnaround, relatively modest infrastructure requirements, and European industrial cooperation. A proper comparison should examine procurement costs, lifecycle expenses, delivery schedules, weapons integration, survivability, operational capabilities, technology transfer, and Polish industrial participation. The Gripen is not automatically cheaper in every configuration, nor does being manufactured in Europe make it completely independent of American technology. Some Gripen variants use American engines and other US-origin components. BUT SHOULD POLAND CONTINUE TO CONCENTRATE SO MUCH OF ITS DEFENSE PROCUREMENT IN ONE COUNTRY WITHOUT SERIOUSLY EXAMINING THE STRATEGIC COSTS OF THAT DEPENDENCE? That is a question worth asking before signing the next multibillion-dollar contract.

⚠️ NOW AN IMPORTANT FACTUAL DISCLAIMER, BECAUSE UNLIKE PROPAGANDISTS, WE DO NOT NEED TO INVENT EVIDENCE. Russia earns revenue from exporting energy resources, maintains political and military cooperation with Iran, and continues its war of aggression against Ukraine. These are documented facts. However, that does not mean every purchase of Russian oil directly finances Iranian missiles. Nor is there sufficient evidence to claim that Donald Trump personally finances Iranian military operations against the United States merely because Russian energy transactions occur. To establish a specific financial connection, we must determine who purchased the resources, from whom, when, at what price, under which legal arrangements, and whether the transaction actually increased Russian government revenue. We must also distinguish between decisions made by the US administration and commercial transactions conducted by private companies. AN INDIRECT ECONOMIC EFFECT IS NOT THE SAME AS DIRECTLY FINANCING A SPECIFIC MILITARY OPERATION. And there is another essential distinction: Poland purchasing American military equipment does not automatically mean that the money reaches Russia. American defense contractors, the US government, and Russian energy exporters are separate economic actors. Any claim that Polish defense spending ultimately finances Putin requires evidence of actual financial connections. That is precisely why we should demand facts, contracts, sanctions data, and financial transparency instead of political fairy tales.

My argument is political and economic: EVERY WASHINGTON DECISION THAT ACTUALLY STRENGTHENS MOSCOW FINANCIALLY DESERVES CRITICAL SCRUTINY FROM THE PERSPECTIVE OF POLISH NATIONAL SECURITY. We do not need anti-Americanism. We do not need blind devotion to Trump either. We need a strong alliance with the United States, a stronger Europe, and the ability to think independently. Now, a little homework for everyone who still struggles to understand the difference between an alliance and political submission. IF A US POLICY DECISION WERE TO GENERATE AN ADDITIONAL BILLION DOLLARS FOR RUSSIA, WHILE FORCING POLAND TO SPEND ANOTHER BILLION ON DEFENSE, WHO WOULD PROFIT AND WHO WOULD PAY THE BILL? This is a hypothetical example, not a claim about a verified transaction. But the strategic problem it illustrates is very real. You do not need a doctorate in geopolitics to understand it. You need to know how to count, understand your country's national interests, and stop applauding every word coming out of the White House.

🇵🇱 POLAND'S NATIONAL INTEREST DOES NOT HAVE AN AMERICAN PASSPORT. IT FLIES THE WHITE-AND-RED FLAG! POLAND FIRST. NOT TRUMP. NOT PUTIN. NOT PARTY POLITICS. POLAND! And one final question: SHOULD POLISH LEADERS PUBLICLY CHALLENGE WASHINGTON WHEN AMERICAN DECISIONS THREATEN POLISH SECURITY, OR SHOULD THEY CONTINUE PRETENDING THAT THE US PRESIDENT ALWAYS KNOWS BEST? AND BEFORE WE BUY THE NEXT AMERICAN FIGHTER JET, SHOULDN'T WE AT LEAST ASK WHETHER A EUROPEAN GRIPEN COULD BETTER SERVE SOME OF POLAND'S FUTURE DEFENSE NEEDS?

    WHO PICKS YOUR TOWN? Inside the Soros-Backed Push to Choose Where Migrants Settle

    A Washington think tank has drawn up a county-by-county migration shortlist—and wants private entities to sponsor arrivals directly.

    By: Natalie Winter, October 12, 2026:

        “enable local governments and private entities to sponsor immigrants directly”

    That is what the Niskanen Center, a Washington think tank whose immigration program receives Soros-foundation backing, wants policymakers to do. The instruction appears in its November 2025 immigration blueprint.

    Two weeks later, Niskanen published a county-by-county migration index, identifying hundreds of American communities as potential destinations for newcomers. Its proposed applications include planning where refugees and asylum seekers could settle.

    The complete published community list appears at the end of this article, organized by state. Check whether your county is on it.

    The agenda reaches straight into the question of who gets to shape your town: which places should receive newcomers, which private actors should help sponsor them, and how arrivals could be encouraged to stay.

    The Soros money behind the immigration program

    Niskanen’s own funding disclosure lists $300,000 from Open Society Foundation for immigration work, covering September 1, 2024, through February 27, 2026. That period includes the release of both proposals.

    George Soros founded Open Society. The same Niskanen disclosure lists another $400,000 from Carnegie Corporation of New York and $100,000 from Migration Policy Institute for immigration work, with grant terms also spanning the publications.

    Your county, scored for immigration

    The Migration Match Index report describes communities with:

        “aging, stagnant, or insufficient native labor supply”

    Its model screens unemployment, job openings, rental vacancies, affordability and age. Older residents and available apartments become indicators that a community could accommodate more migration.

The authors explicitly discuss using updated data to plan resettlement following:

    “an influx of asylum seekers at the border”

Niskanen also contemplates applications to a future refugee-admissions system. It acknowledges that local receptivity and migrants’ own choices matter.

Yet an economic score cannot answer the political question underneath it: who authorized someone else’s vision for the community?

An employer’s job offer—and a refugee’s destination

The separate immigration blueprint proposes state visa programs tailored to local labor needs, direct sponsorship by local governments and private entities, and:

    “incentivizing new arrivals to stay in specific states and regions.”

That would give regional economic interests more influence over where immigration takes place. The document also supports stronger employment verification and immigration enforcement; its local-sponsorship proposal sits alongside those measures.

STRATEGIC JUDGEMENT

The Houthis have achieved a strategic effect without destroying King Khalid International Airport: Riyadh’s air bridge is largely closed, international carriers are withdrawing and Saudi confidence in its air-defence architecture is under investigation.

Iran’s position is deliberately contradictory. 

Tehran offers to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis while rejecting the US response to its Hormuz proposal, threatening regional digital infrastructure and imposing its own contested rules on maritime passage.

The centre of gravity is now interconnected civilian infrastructure: airports, tankers, data systems and commercial confidence.

CONFIRMED DEVELOPMENTS

Sunday’s latest strike on King Khalid International Airport killed one person and injured 11. Combined with Saturday’s attack, the airport campaign has killed at least 14 and injured approximately 320.

Airport operations remain suspended. Approximately 99.7% of Sunday’s scheduled flights were cancelled.
Lufthansa and Air France-KLM are among carriers extending suspensions. 

US and European aviation authorities have warned operators about Saudi airspace.

Saudi Arabia is investigating why its warning and interception systems failed.

Turkey, Pakistan, Egypt and Saudi Arabia issued a joint statement supporting legitimate Saudi measures against the Houthis.

A UAE official has called for a coordinated Gulf response.

Assessment: The Houthis are no longer merely demonstrating reach. 

They are imposing partial aviation denial over the Saudi capital. The effect reaches investment, conferences, tourism, logistics and the credibility of Vision 2030.

CREDIBLE BUT PRELIMINARY
The Saudi investigation is reportedly examining whether UAS were used to complicate detection before cruise and ballistic missiles arrived. That sequence would indicate a planned saturation package rather than isolated launches. The findings remain preliminary. 

Yemen’s Houthis report overnight strikes on two districts of Sanaa and attribute them to Saudi Arabia. Saudi authorities have not confirmed responsibility. 

Houthi-run authorities report one killed and several wounded.

GULF OF OMAN–HORMUZ
Two separate tanker incidents on 11 October materially increased the maritime threat:
The Nicaragua-flagged MT Petro Dolphin was struck by a UAS near Sohar, Oman. 
Nine Indian sailors were rescued; two remain missing.

The Marshall Islands-flagged MT Valthera was struck by an unidentified projectile while transiting Hormuz, causing a fire.

India has formally condemned the attacks.

UKMTO has reclassified the Sohar incident as a confirmed attack but has not attributed responsibility.

Assessment: The operational boundary has expanded beyond the narrow Strait into Omani anchorage space. 

Ships cannot assume that reaching an anchorage or leaving the main channel ends their exposure.

Iran benefits from maritime fear even where attribution is incomplete. It also risks losing deniability because the IRGC has publicly threatened vessels using routes Tehran considers unauthorised.

IRAN AND DIPLOMACY
Tehran maintains that Washington’s response to its seven conditions for reopening Hormuz is insufficient.

Mohsen Rezaei has threatened regional cables, data centres and artificial-intelligence infrastructure if intense combat resumes.

Iran has simultaneously offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis.

Assessment: Iran is attempting to occupy three positions at once: mediator, threatened state and asymmetric enforcer. That may preserve tactical options, but it weakens the credibility of its diplomatic presentation.

🇺🇦 Zelensky challenges Trump's Russian diesel deal, questions its impact on global prices and proposes an agreement with Ukraine instead

President Volodymyr Zelensky challenged the economic rationale behind Donald Trump's agreement with Vladimir Putin to facilitate Russian diesel exports, arguing that the volumes under discussion are too small to meaningfully influence global fuel prices.

⚠️ Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday, Zelensky said Russia could currently export between 300,000 and 500,000 metric tons of diesel per month, compared with estimated global consumption of 120 million tons. On those figures, the proposed Russian volumes would represent approximately 0.25% to 0.42% of monthly consumption.

He questioned whether such limited additional supplies could justify the administration's decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel transactions, suggesting that other considerations may be influencing Washington's approach. The comparison, however, does not establish that the shipments would have no effect on prices: energy markets respond to marginal supply changes, inventories and expectations, particularly during periods of disruption.

⚠️ Zelensky then offered Washington a different proposition. If the United States wants an agreement affecting Russian diesel supplies, he argued, it should negotiate directly with Ukraine, whose long-range strikes have demonstrated an ability to disrupt Russian refining operations and threaten energy-export infrastructure.

Ukraine's proposed exchange would be straightforward: Kyiv would suspend retaliatory strikes against Russian oil infrastructure if Moscow stopped attacking Ukrainian electricity generation, transmission networks and other critical energy facilities, with credible guarantees that the arrangement would be respected.

Electricity, Zelensky emphasized, is Ukraine's overriding concern. Russian attacks have repeatedly damaged the country's power system, leaving civilians facing blackouts and emergency repairs. Protecting that infrastructure could also enable Ukraine to support neighboring European countries through its connections to the continental electricity grid.

⚠️ The Ukrainian president placed the dispute within the wider energy crisis, arguing that disruptions originating in the Middle East have played a much greater role in driving global fuel prices than Ukraine's campaign against Russian refineries.

He also warned that international attention to diesel was obscuring another potential crisis: Russia's interference with maritime trade and Ukrainian grain exports. Zelensky cautioned that prolonged disruption could threaten food supplies to importing countries in Africa, Asia and the Middle East.

The remarks sharpen the disagreement between Washington and Kyiv over the economic consequences of the war. Trump is seeking additional fuel supplies and lower prices for American consumers, while Zelensky argues that sanctions relief and restrictions on Ukrainian strikes should be considered alongside Russia's continued attacks on Ukrainian civilian infrastructure.

His counterproposal effectively asks Washington to recognize Ukraine's ability to disrupt Russian energy production as negotiating leverage, rather than treating it solely as an obstacle to stabilizing fuel markets.

Source: Zelensky's remarks at the Warsaw Security Forum, October 12, 2026.

text:
This Won't End Well... Seattle Becomes First City To Price-Fix Your Groceries | Tyler Durden, Zerohedge

This week the Seattle City Council passed Mayor Katie Wilson's "Fair Pricing and Transparency" ordinance in a 7-2 vote, a first-in-the-nation ban on so-called surveillance pricing.

The ordinance takes effect in 2027. The Washington Retail Association warned for months that the bill was rushed, would have significant and negative impact on prices, and that nearly all suggested fixes were ignored.

As approved, retailers must decide whether they can keep offering the tailored discounts and loyalty programs that Seattle families actually use or cancel all the programs and charge more for groceries.

Government should not be price-fixing consumer products.

Banning the use of loyalty cards and programs, fuel rewards, and targeted coupons hurts businesses and consumers alike.

Price controls do not make groceries cheaper. They flatten the tools stores use to compete for customers. When discounts vanish, the shelf price becomes the only price. That is how an "affordability" law raises a customer's grocery bill. A Greater Seattle Business Association and Seattle Latino Metropolitan Chamber guest column put it plainly: trying to control prices through experimental regulation has never worked, and this ordinance will make an already expensive city more unaffordable.

Jan Himebaugh of the Washington Retail Association offered a household example, nearly $1,000 in grocer loyalty savings this year for her family, the equivalent of more than 185 gallons of gas in a state where fuel is among the nation's most expensive. Those are not corporate talking points. They are the coupons that keep a cart full.

Thin-margin stores close. When they close, the result is the very "food deserts" Mayor Wilson has spent a campaign and a mayoralty promising to fight. Wilson has said Seattle will not accept food deserts as the cost of doing business, but the "Fair Pricing" policy creates a retail environment that does exactly the opposite.

A pricing ordinance that chases discounts out of the city works against that goal. You cannot subsidize corner markets on Sunday and make their discount model legally hazardous on Tuesday.

If Wilson wants more grocery access, the path is not to micromanage how a retailer prices a gallon of milk. It is to stop piling first-in-the-nation experiments onto businesses already carrying Seattle's tax and regulatory load.

Personalized discounts are not surveillance. They are how competitive stores keep prices down and stay open. Kill those discounts, and the desert grows.

text:
Madame Loomer discovers, with a pearl clutched to her throat, that Russia is not free. Putin, she informs us, murdered Navalny, poisoned him in his cell, and stages elections the way a conjuror stages a rabbit. Russian state media, she adds, dares to call Trump names. Ask anyone who lives there, she cries. Why should we accept a lie?

I have lived long enough to admire a woman who can weep for a Russian who died in Russia, and find not one tear for an American who died in Ukraine.

Navalny fell ill on a flight from Tomsk. The plane diverted. Berlin's physicians later spoke of a nerve agent kin to Novichok. The OPCW tasted the samples and nodded. Bellingcat named an FSB man and a hotel seam on a pair of underclothes, as though assassination had become a laundry service. The Grayzone muttered of Western laboratories and NATO purses. Maté himself allowed the allegation might prove true.

Now behold the masterpiece of professionalism. The man is already inside Russia. Stairs are plentiful. A heart may stop of its own accord. A motorcar may find him in the dark. A mugging may go wrong, as muggings so often do, and leave no laboratory embarrassed. A competent tyranny has a thousand ordinary deaths to choose from, each as quiet as a closed door. Instead our artists wait for a plane, sew Novichok into the seams of his underclothes like a tailor signing his work, and leave behind the moral equivalent of a bottle of vodka and a note that reads, in every capital, "we did it." What is this, Madame? Murder, or a press release with a pulse?

Professionalism would have finished the job in Omsk and spared us the opera. Instead the patient was packed west alive, returned, arrested, and at last found dead in Polar Wolf after a walk, with "sudden death syndrome" offered as the state's epitaph. A tyranny that cannot kill cleanly is still a tyranny. It is merely an incompetent one, and proud of its signature.

And yet. In the autumn of 2010 this same Navalny sat as a Yale World Fellow, sipping the air of New Haven while NED coin had once greased his youth movement. Komisar and The Grayzone insinuate a longer American hand. I will not swear to the CIA's fingerprint on his cuff. I will swear that a man known to four Russians in five, and trusted by almost none, makes a curious martyr for a country that never asked him to govern it. Levada's numbers are unsentimental: recognition high, approval a whisper. He was not Lyndon LaRouche. He was something rarer and less useful to us: a famous loser.

Meanwhile Gonzalo Lira, an American citizen, displeased Ukraine's security service with his opinions, and died of neglect in a dank Ukrainian prison in January 2024. The Grayzone has written of torture and of a body left to fail in the dark. Washington offered condolences and a shrug. Madame Loomer, who can smell a dictatorship three thousand miles off, has not, so far as the open record shows, spent a morning's pearl-clutching on an American left to rot in a jail funded by her own country's treasure. Where is her tweet for Lira? Or does an American corpse count only when the bars are Russian?

Ukraine is sold to us as the plucky democracy fighting on the side of light and the angels, paid for by the American taxpayer. Into that holy cause Madame pours her outrage for a Russian prisoner, and nothing for the American who did not survive the angels' custody. Hypocrisy so thick one might choke on it.

Last July she confessed she had been bamboozled by Russian propaganda and once imagined Ukraine free of Muslims, "so refreshing." Today she discovers Putin. The conversion is touching. The selectivity is not.

Mes amis, if Madame can smell a lie three thousand miles off, why does she need a passport to smell a jail?

text:
Warren Buffett's worst investment cost him about $200 billion. It started with a CEO shaving 12.5 cents off a promise.

In 1998 he told 350 University of Washington students about it, sitting next to Bill Gates. Gates was worth about $48 billion that spring. Buffett, about $36 billion. PBS filmed the whole hour.

A student asked about their best decisions. Gates brought up the worst one instead: buying the company Buffett's empire is named after. Buffett didn't argue.

The story behind it: in 1962 he started buying a dying textile mill called Berkshire Hathaway because it was cheap. In 1964 its CEO, Seabury Stanton, asked what price he'd sell his shares at. Buffett said $11.50. Stanton agreed. The written offer came in at $11.375.

"He chiseled me for an eighth," Buffett said later.

So he bought control of the company and fired him. Then he spent 20 years fighting a business that made no money. In 2010 he estimated that building on a mill instead of starting clean had cost about $200 billion.

What he told the students in that hour:

1. Cheap is not the same as good. A terrible business at a low price is a soggy cigar butt with one puff left.
2. Your biggest losses never show up on a statement. He said skipping deals he fully understood, like Fannie Mae, cost Berkshire many billions.
3. When a real opportunity shouts at you, swing big. That's no time to read about diversification.
4. Never do a deal with people who turn your stomach. He compared it to marrying for money: a bad idea for anyone, crazy if you're already rich.
5. Pick a partner who will tell you when your idea is dumb.

The most expensive decision of the century's best investor wasn't a bad bet. It was a grudge.

What's the most expensive grudge you've seen someone pay for?

text:
W. F. Anderson at the Mary Phagan Coroner's Inquest: The First Police Responder Under Oath

The Atlanta Policeman Who Described the Basement, Examined the Murder Evidence, and Questioned Newt Lee's Account of Discovering the Body

By M. Watts

Wednesday, April 30, 1913: Anderson Becomes the First Witness

On Wednesday morning, April 30, 1913, Atlanta Police Call Officer W. F. Anderson became the first witness examined when Coroner Paul Donehoo resumed the official inquest into the murder of thirteen-year-old Mary Phagan. Anderson had been among the first policemen summoned to the National Pencil Company during the early morning of Sunday, April 27, after night watchman Newt Lee telephoned police headquarters to report discovering a dead girl in the factory basement at 37–41 South Forsyth Street.

The six-member coroner's jury had originally assembled on Monday, April 28, and recessed. It reconvened on Wednesday at the undertaking establishment of P. J. Bloomfield on Pryor Street, where Mary's body had been held prior to her burial on Tuesday. Donehoo led the jurors to Atlanta police headquarters, where the witnesses were to be examined in the office of the Board of Police Commissioners.

The Atlanta Journal reported that the hearing began at approximately 9:10 a.m. The jurors were H. C. Ashford, L. Glenn Dewberry, J. C. Hood, C. A. Langford, John Miller, and C. Y. Sheats. Both Newt Lee and factory superintendent Leo M. Frank were being detained at police headquarters. Frank's defense attorney, Luther Z. Rosser, was also present during the proceedings (Atlanta Journal, 1).

Anderson's appearance was important because he had examined the basement during the first police response. His observations could help the jurors establish the body's position, the physical evidence around it, the possible entrances and exits, and the reliability of Lee's explanation of finding Mary.

The First Police Response: Sunday, April 27, 1913

Anderson began by describing the telephone call received at police headquarters shortly after 3 a.m. on Sunday.

The caller identified himself as Newt Lee, night watchman at the National Pencil Company, and reported discovering the body of a woman. Anderson asked whether the deceased was White or Black. Lee answered that she was White.

Anderson accompanied Sergeants L. S. Dobbs and R. J. Brown to the factory in an automobile driven by W. W. Rogers, commonly known as Boots Rogers. Newspaper reporter Britt Craig also accompanied the responding party.

When the officers reached the building, the street entrance was locked. They knocked until Lee descended from the second floor and admitted them. The watchman directed the party through a scuttle hole, an opening in the first floor containing a ladder descending into the basement.

Anderson described the interior as a poorly illuminated industrial cellar containing partitions, machinery, a boiler, rubbish, wood shavings, a toilet, and a rear exit. The officers moved toward the rear of the building, where Mary's body lay near the end of a partition on the left side.

Anderson told the inquest that the body was only a few inches from the partition and approximately six feet from an outside wall. Her head pointed toward the front of the factory, in the direction of Forsyth Street, and she was lying face downward.

His account in the April 30 Atlanta Georgian included the statement:

"I did not see the body until I reached it" (Atlanta Georgian, 2).

The remark demonstrates how difficult it was to see into the rear of the basement. Even officers who knew a body had been reported could not readily distinguish it from a distance.

Anderson Describes Mary's Injuries and Clothing

The coroner's jurors questioned Anderson about the physical condition of Mary's body.

He described a wound on the left side of her head near the temple and extending toward the back of the skull. Blood was visible on her head, and her eyes appeared bloodshot. Dirt and sawdust covered her face, mouth, eyes, and parts of her legs.

Her left shoe was missing from her foot, the left stocking was torn, and the skin below her left knee appeared scraped. Her clothing had been displaced upward, and the stocking supporters were unfastened.

Anderson identified wrapping cord and a strip of material torn from Mary's underclothing around her neck. The Atlanta Journal described the cord as approximately six or seven feet long. These objects were among the most important items examined because they were associated with the fatal strangulation (Atlanta Journal, 1).

Anderson also described how heavily soiled the girl's body had become. He said the dirt initially made it difficult to determine whether she was White, although Lee had already identified her race during the telephone call.

Other officers gave similar testimony. Sergeant Brown explained that the policemen examined an exposed area of skin beneath a stocking to establish the victim's race.

During a later portion of the hearing, Anderson was recalled to testify about the body's condition. The Journal reported that the legs were not completely stiff and that blood beneath the hair remained moist. The newspaper also attributed an observation about blood still flowing to Anderson.

These were observations made by a policeman, not a medical calculation of the time of death. The evidence did not establish precisely how many hours had passed since Mary was killed.

The Disagreement Over the Body's Position

One of the most consequential questions concerned whether Mary had been lying face upward or face downward when Newt Lee originally discovered her.

Anderson told the inquest that the body was face downward, with the head toward Forsyth Street. Lee, however, testified that he found her face upward, with her head directed toward the rear of the building.

The Atlanta Journal made this contradiction a central feature of its April 30 coverage.

If Lee had left the body untouched after discovering it and remained upstairs until the police arrived, the two descriptions could not both represent its unchanged position.

The disagreement raised questions concerning whether Lee had confused the direction of the body, whether the officers misunderstood his original account, or whether someone had moved it.

No explanation was established simply by identifying the conflict.

Anderson's account was supported by other responding officers, who described seeing Mary lying face downward. But Lee continued to maintain his own version during the inquest.

The contradiction was particularly important because the police were still investigating Lee as a suspect. Any inconsistency between what he claimed and what the responding officers witnessed attracted close attention.

Boots Rogers later complicated the issue by testifying that Lee originally told the police the body was lying on its face. That recollection differed from the face-up position Lee described at the inquest (Atlanta Journal, 1) (Atlanta Journal, 3).

The disagreement therefore remained a question of witness reliability and recollection rather than a settled demonstration that the body had been moved between the discovery and the police response.

The Hat, Missing Shoe, and Murder Notes

Anderson also described physical objects discovered around Mary's body.

He identified the yellow-paper murder note during the hearing and recalled seeing Sergeant Dobbs pick up one of the handwritten notes.

The notes appeared to implicate the night watchman and would become a central subject of the later murder trial.

Anderson also described the discovery of a pencil and writing tablet in the basement. The Atlanta Georgian quoted him:

"We also found a tablet and a pencil" (Atlanta Georgian, 2).

He could not say with certainty which of the four or five men present originally found those particular objects.

This was an important limitation. Anderson witnessed the initial evidence collection, but he did not personally discover or recover every item.

The newspapers also reported conflicting locations for Mary's missing shoe and hat.

The Georgian attributed to Anderson a location near the front and right side of the body. The Journal placed the missing slipper nearer the elevator, while Sergeant Dobbs subsequently described the hat and shoe together on a rubbish pile near the boiler.

These differences are significant because the original locations of Mary's belongings could help reconstruct how her body reached the basement and whether her personal effects had been moved separately.

The inquest reports do not establish one uncontested location for the objects.

The Bloody Handkerchief: A Reported Piece of Evidence

One unusual part of Anderson's testimony concerned a possible bloody handkerchief.

The April 30 Atlanta Georgian reported that Anderson was asked whether there were signs of a struggle near Mary's body. He answered that evidence of a disturbance existed behind the location where she lay and described a bloody handkerchief approximately seven or eight feet away.

This item deserves attention because it was absent from Anderson's condensed official trial testimony.

The subsequent courtroom proceedings provide an additional connection. On Wednesday, July 30, 1913, Solicitor Hugh M. Dorsey attempted to introduce several physical exhibits, including the cord, clothing, personal effects, and a bloody handkerchief.

The Atlanta Journal reported that the exhibits were admitted except for the handkerchief. Rosser objected because the item had not been sufficiently identified (Atlanta Journal, 4).

The two reports establish that a bloodstained handkerchief was discussed during the inquest and that a bloody handkerchief was subsequently offered during the trial.

They do not conclusively establish that the two accounts concern the same item or prove its ownership. Nor does the newspaper's description establish that the staining was scientifically confirmed as Mary's blood.

The handkerchief therefore remains an important but incompletely documented part of the early physical evidence.

The Rear Basement Door and the Pulled Staple

Anderson was questioned about the rear basement entrance.

He reported that a staple associated with the door fastening had been pulled loose. The Atlanta Georgian described the door as closed despite the disturbed hardware. The Atlanta Journal suggested that the fastening had been drawn and that the door had been opened.

These reports differ in an important detail.

The condition of the door could indicate possible access through the rear of the factory, but the damaged fastening did not establish whether an intruder had entered or escaped during the murder.

It also did not establish when the staple had been pulled loose.

Anderson's observation was nevertheless valuable because it documented the condition of an alternate entrance during the first police examination.

The rear door would receive additional attention during the trial and Governor Slaton's 1915 review, particularly when investigators and attorneys discussed whether James Conley or another person might have used it.

The Most Disputed Evidence: Could Newt Lee See Mary With His Lantern?

The longest-running controversy associated with Anderson's inquest testimony concerned the ability of Newt Lee to see the body from the basement toilet.

Lee explained that he had gone into the basement to use the toilet and left his lantern on the floor. When he emerged, he noticed something unusual near the partition.

Anderson examined Lee's lantern and described its glass as heavily smoked or darkened by soot.

He estimated that the distance from the toilet to Mary's body was approximately twenty-five to thirty feet.

Dr. J. W. Hurt questioned Anderson about the effective distance of the lantern's illumination.

The Atlanta Journal recorded the officer's answer:

"He couldn't have seen more than twelve or fifteen feet" (Atlanta Journal, 1).

The Atlanta Georgian reported an estimate of ten to twelve feet.

Anderson also believed the partition might obstruct the light, making recognition of a person from the toilet area particularly difficult.

The significance was apparent. If Lee could not see the body from where he claimed to be standing, the accuracy of his discovery account would be called into question.

Yet the issue required more care than simply comparing distances.

Lee said he initially noticed an unidentified object, thought it might be a prank, and approached it. Recognizing the outline of something unusual at twenty-five feet did not require identifying it immediately as a dead girl.

Lee had also spent time working in a dimly illuminated factory, and his eyes may have been more accustomed to darkness than those of officers entering from comparatively brighter surroundings. The actual extent of his dark adaptation cannot now be determined.

These possibilities did not invalidate Anderson's observations. They limited what could be concluded from them.

Anderson's Unsuccessful Telephone Calls to Leo Frank

Anderson testified that after examining the body and questioning Lee, he attempted to telephone Leo M. Frank, the superintendent of the National Pencil Company.

The telephone rang, but no one answered.

Anderson then contacted another person associated with the factory, identified in the April 30 Georgian as Mr. Haas. Sergeant Brown had instructed him to try to contact company officials.

The Atlanta Journal also reported Brown's corroboration of Anderson's unsuccessful attempts to reach Frank.

The police had a practical reason to contact the superintendent. A murdered employee had been discovered in the premises he managed, and the responding officers needed information about the factory and those who had access to it.

The unanswered calls later became part of the prosecution's circumstantial presentation concerning Frank's conduct.

However, Anderson's testimony established the attempted communications, not the reason Frank failed to answer. He could not determine whether Frank heard the telephone ringing or was asleep.

His evidence was therefore relevant to the early investigative chronology but did not independently prove that Frank knew about the murder.

Anderson Is Recalled to the Witness Stand

The April 30 hearing included another important moment when Anderson was recalled.

After the testimony of other officers, Mary's clothing was presented to the coroner's jury. The Atlanta Journal described her brother becoming visibly distressed when he saw the garments and leaving the room.

Anderson was questioned again about the clothing and the position of the body.

He reiterated that Mary was face downward, with her head toward the front of the building. He also described the condition of her legs and the moisture of blood beneath her hair.

The jurors were therefore comparing Anderson's observations with those of other officers and with Lee's account of discovering the body.

The clothing itself became part of the inquest's examination of the physical evidence.

Anderson's second appearance reinforced his role as a firsthand witness to the original basement scene.

What the Coroner's Inquest Established About the First Police Investigation

Anderson was also asked how thoroughly the responding officers had examined the factory.

He acknowledged that their first investigation did not include an examination of the second floor.

This is particularly important when considering the prosecution's later contention that Mary was murdered in the second-floor metal department and subsequently moved to the basement.

Anderson could testify about the condition of the basement. He could describe the body, its position, nearby objects, the rear doorway, and Newt Lee's statements.

He could not personally testify about the condition of Frank's office or the metal department during the first police response.

Later police investigations and other witnesses provided evidence about suspected blood spots, hair on the bench lathe, and the possible location of the original attack.

Anderson's testimony therefore established the starting point of the investigation rather than the complete reconstruction ultimately offered by the prosecution.

August 1–18, 1913: His Inquest Evidence Returns During the Murder Trial

Anderson testified for the prosecution at Leo Frank's murder trial on Friday, August 1, 1913.

The official Brief of Evidence preserved his sworn testimony on printed pages 39–40 (Fulton County Superior Court, 5).

During cross-examination, Luther Rosser questioned him about Lee's lantern and the original statements Anderson made at the inquest.

The following day's Atlanta Journal reported Anderson qualifying his original estimate. He acknowledged that someone could see the general shape of an object at a distance without recognizing exactly what it was.

A later nighttime experiment using a box covered with sacks demonstrated the possibility of seeing an indistinct object near Mary's original location (Atlanta Journal, 6).

On Monday, August 18, Rosser introduced part of Anderson's earlier coroner's inquest testimony.

That excerpt became Defendant's Exhibit 93.

It appears on printed page 307 of the Brief of Evidence prepared for the Georgia Supreme Court proceedings.

The document records Anderson's account of Lee emerging from the toilet, standing near his lantern, and observing something approximately twenty-five feet away.

Anderson stated:

"I could not see that far with the lantern that he had" (Fulton County Superior Court, 8).

He then estimated useful visibility at approximately ten or twelve feet.

Defendant's Exhibit 93 was an excerpt of Anderson's earlier inquest testimony introduced by Frank's defense during the original murder trial. It was not a separate statement taken by the Georgia Supreme Court.

It preserves a portion of his original inquest account in a formal legal document, making it particularly useful for comparing the contemporary newspaper reports with the evidence introduced at trial.

The complete original transcript of Anderson's April 30 examination has not yet been independently located.

Why Anderson's Inquest Testimony Was Important to the Case Against Frank

Anderson's evidence was important because it established what the first responding police officers encountered at the factory.

His description of the body's position, clothing, injuries, bindings, and surroundings helped create the original record of the crime scene. His account of the murder notes confirmed their presence during the first police examination.

His observations of the basement floor, partitions, rubbish, and rear exit were relevant to theories concerning how Mary's body reached the cellar and whether another entrance might have been used.

His unsuccessful telephone calls contributed to the prosecution's examination of Frank's activities after the discovery.

These observations could support aspects of the prosecution's reconstruction when considered alongside the testimony of other witnesses.

Yet Anderson did not witness the attack or personally identify the murderer. His testimony did not establish that Frank carried Mary's body into the basement, dictated the murder notes, or deliberately avoided the telephone.

Anderson's strongest contribution was his firsthand documentation of the original physical scene and his account of what Newt Lee said and did during the police response.

The lantern dispute was particularly important during the coroner's investigation because it raised early doubts about Lee, who was then being detained as a suspect. It subsequently became evidence that the defense used to examine the reliability of the first police reconstruction.

Both uses of his testimony are part of the historical record.

Conclusion: The First Witness and the First Official Reconstruction

W. F. Anderson's testimony on Wednesday, April 30, 1913, established an important foundation for the investigation into Mary Phagan's murder.

He was the first witness examined when the coroner's jury resumed its formal inquiry at police headquarters.

He described the original response, the condition and position of Mary's body, the evidence surrounding her, the rear basement door, the handwritten notes, and the difficulty of seeing through the poorly illuminated basement.

He also questioned Newt Lee's explanation of discovering the body and documented his attempts to contact Leo Frank.

The April 30 newspapers preserve details absent from Anderson's condensed trial testimony, including the reported bloody handkerchief, the original locations attributed to Mary's belongings, and the extent of the officers' first examination.

The subsequent introduction of Defendant's Exhibit 93 provides a rare surviving excerpt of his coroner's inquest testimony in the official trial evidence.

Together, these sources establish Anderson as an important early witness whose observations were revisited during the murder trial and preserved with the appellate record.

His testimony remains essential to understanding what Atlanta police observed during the first hours of the Mary Phagan investigation and how the original evidence was examined under oath.

text:
W. F. Anderson: Police Officer, Coroner's Inquest Witness, and State Witness in the Leo Frank Murder Trial of 1913

Identification and Background

W. F. Anderson was an Atlanta police officer who participated in the original investigation of Mary Phagan's murder on Sunday, April 27, 1913. He was among the first officers to enter the basement of the National Pencil Company after night watchman Newt Lee telephoned police headquarters to report discovering a young woman's body.

Anderson testified at the coroner's inquest on Wednesday, April 30, 1913, and for the prosecution at Leo M. Frank's murder trial on Friday, August 1, 1913. His testimony concerned the discovery of Mary's body, Newt Lee's account, basement lighting, physical evidence, and police attempts to contact Frank.

His trial testimony appears on pages 39–40 of the official Brief of Evidence. An excerpt from his original coroner's inquest testimony survives as Defendant's Exhibit 93, printed page 307.

His Full Name: Wyman F. Anderson

The 1913 Atlanta City Directory identifies Wyman F. Anderson, a policeman residing at 37 Hood Street with Mary Anderson, presumably his wife.

Earlier directories show that Anderson worked as a watchman for Traynham & Ray in 1901. By 1903, he was identified as a policeman. Directories from 1904 through 1916 continue to list him in police employment, although by 1916 his residence had changed to 24 Orange Street.

Anderson therefore had approximately ten years of documented police service when Mary Phagan was murdered in April 1913 (Atlanta City Directory, 18) (Atlanta City Directory, 19) (Atlanta City Directory, 20).

Was His Full Name Wyman Fleming Anderson?

A FamilySearch record identifies a Wyman Fleming Anderson as a son of William Edwin Anderson and Georgianna A. Jones, and a brother of Farris Furman Anderson (1883–1949).

The 1913 Atlanta directory places Wyman F. Anderson and William E. Anderson at 37 Hood Street. William E. was associated with a woman named Georgia, consistent with Georgianna.

The names and shared residence support the possibility that the officer's full name was Wyman Fleming Anderson. However, his middle name, parentage, birth date, and death date require confirmation through original census, marriage, death, or police personnel records.

The directory also identifies William F. Anderson, a Western Union cashier living at 233 Oglethorpe Avenue. He was a different individual and should not be confused with the police witness (Atlanta City Directory, 18) (FamilySearch, 21).

Sunday, April 27, 1913: The Discovery of Mary Phagan's Body

Newt Lee's Telephone Call

Shortly after 3 a.m., Newt Lee telephoned Atlanta police headquarters to report finding a young woman's body in the National Pencil Company basement on South Forsyth Street.

Anderson was on duty at headquarters. He testified that the officers reached the factory approximately five minutes after receiving Lee's call.

Lee admitted the officers and directed them through a trapdoor or scuttle opening into the basement, which they entered using a ladder.

Anderson described a dark basement, illuminated by police flashlights and Lee's lantern, whose glass had become smoke-darkened.

Mary's body lay near a partition, face downward, with her head pointing toward Forsyth Street. Anderson observed injuries, disarranged clothing, a torn stocking, and the material around her neck.

He also described blood in her hair as still moist and her legs as not stiff. These were the observations of a responding policeman rather than a medical determination of the time of death (Atlanta Journal, 1) (Atlanta Georgian, 2).

Anderson Attempts to Telephone Leo Frank

Anderson testified that he attempted to reach Frank at approximately 3:30 a.m. but received no answer. He continued trying for several minutes and made additional calls to people associated with the pencil company.

At approximately 4 a.m., he again attempted to reach Frank without success.

The accounts differ slightly concerning which members of the Haas and Montag households answered particular calls. These discrepancies should be preserved when reconstructing the exact chronology.

Anderson's evidence establishes unsuccessful attempts to contact Frank. It does not establish whether Frank heard the telephone or intentionally failed to answer it (Brief of Evidence, 3) (Atlanta Constitution, 4).

Wednesday, April 30, 1913: The Coroner's Inquest

Anderson Is the First Witness Examined

On Wednesday morning, April 30, the coroner's inquest resumed in the office of the Board of Police Commissioners at Atlanta police headquarters.

Coroner Paul Donehoo presided. According to the Atlanta Journal, proceedings began at approximately 9:10 a.m.

W. F. Anderson was the first witness examined.

He described the initial telephone report, the police response, conditions in the basement, Mary's body, physical evidence, and Newt Lee's explanation of how he discovered her.

Both the Atlanta Journal and Atlanta Georgian published detailed accounts of his testimony (Atlanta Journal, 1) (Atlanta Georgian, 2).

The Lantern and Newt Lee's Account

One of the most important subjects was whether Lee could have seen Mary's body from his claimed position using his smoky lantern.

Anderson estimated that the lantern would illuminate approximately 12 to 15 feet. When asked whether Lee could see 20 to 30 feet with it, he answered:

"He could not. He couldn't have seen more than twelve or fifteen feet."

The Atlanta Georgian reported an estimate of approximately 10 to 12 feet.

The distance from Lee's stated position to the body was roughly 25 feet. Anderson questioned whether the lantern could have illuminated the body sufficiently for Lee to recognize it.

These statements challenged Lee's account, although Anderson was estimating visibility rather than reporting measurements from a controlled experiment (Atlanta Journal, 1) (Atlanta Georgian, 2).

Mary's Position and the Physical Evidence

Anderson described Mary's body as lying face downward. Lee reportedly gave a different description of its position when he first discovered it.

The Atlanta Journal questioned this discrepancy, but the available testimony does not establish whether the body had been moved or who might have moved it.

Anderson also discussed a pencil, writing pad, handwritten note, apparently bloodstained handkerchief, and the rear basement door, where a staple had been pulled loose.

His statements concerning tracks and possible evidence of a struggle require particular care. At one point, he acknowledged that he had not personally observed where the body had allegedly been dragged. Other statements described physical marks and indications of a disturbance.

Observing marks on the basement floor did not, by itself, establish who made them, when they appeared, or whether they resulted from moving Mary's body (Atlanta Journal, 1) (Atlanta Georgian, 2).

May 1–8, 1913: Newspaper Reports and Corroborating Witnesses

On Thursday, May 1, the Atlanta Constitution reviewed Anderson's coroner testimony, including questions about the distance illuminated by Lee's lantern. Dr. J. W. Hurt was among those questioning him about the lighting conditions.

The Atlanta Georgian also identified Anderson as the officer who unsuccessfully attempted to contact Frank after Mary's body was discovered (Atlanta Constitution, 7) (Atlanta Georgian, 8).

On Thursday, May 8, W. W. "Boots" Rogers testified concerning the initial police response. Rogers described Anderson accompanying Lee upstairs into the factory office, keeping him under observation, and attempting to telephone Frank and other factory officials.

Rogers also discussed inconsistencies concerning Lee's descriptions of the body's position. His testimony provides an independent account of Anderson's actions during the first hours of the investigation (Atlanta Journal, 9) (Atlanta Georgian, 10).

July 30–31, 1913: Anderson Mentioned During the Murder Trial

Leo Frank's murder trial began Monday, July 28, 1913.

During the first week, Sergeant L. S. Dobbs and W. W. Rogers described the police response to Newt Lee's telephone call.

Dobbs identified Anderson among the officers who responded. Rogers described Anderson's activities with Lee in the factory office, including his attempts to contact Frank by telephone.

Reports in the Atlanta Constitution, Atlanta Journal, and Atlanta Georgian provide overlapping accounts of these events.

The July 31 Constitution report placed Anderson and Lee together in the office at approximately 3:45 a.m., while Anderson was attempting to contact people by telephone (Atlanta Constitution, 11) (Atlanta Journal, 12) (Atlanta Georgian, 13) (Atlanta Constitution, 14).

Friday, August 1, 1913: Anderson Sworn for the State

Nineteenth Prosecution Witness

Anderson testified for the prosecution on Friday, August 1, as the nineteenth state witness in the official recorded order.

Solicitor General Hugh M. Dorsey conducted the direct examination, and Luther Z. Rosser cross-examined him.

Anderson described Newt Lee's telephone call, the police response, the discovery of Mary's body, the unsuccessful telephone calls to Frank, and the basement conditions.

His testimony again addressed whether Lee could have identified the body using his lantern.

During cross-examination, Anderson acknowledged:

"You could see the bulk of anything that far, but you couldn't tell that far whether it was a person."

This statement qualifies his earlier testimony.

At the coroner's inquest, Anderson had questioned Lee's ability to see the body from approximately 25 feet. During the trial, he acknowledged that a large object might be visible at that distance without being recognizable as a person.

The difference between seeing an object and identifying it as a human body is important when evaluating whether his accounts were inconsistent.

Anderson also testified about tracks he observed near the left side of Mary's body, extending toward the shavings room. His observations did not independently establish when the tracks were made or who made them (Brief of Evidence, 3).

Saturday, August 2: The Newspapers Report His Testimony

The Atlanta Constitution published a dedicated article titled "Policeman W. F. Anderson Tells of Newt Lee's Telephone Call."

It covered his testimony concerning Lee's telephone call, the response to the factory, Frank's telephone, the lantern, and a nighttime reconstruction involving a box and sack positioned near where the body had been discovered.

The Atlanta Journal published an extensive account under the headline "Dr. Harris Collapses on Stand as He Gives Sensational Evidence."

Despite its headline, the article contains substantial questioning of Anderson about Lee's lantern, tracks in the basement, telephone calls, and his earlier inquest testimony (Atlanta Constitution, 4) (Atlanta Journal, 5).

Was Anderson's Coroner's Inquest Testimony Recorded?

During the August 1 cross-examination, Rosser questioned Anderson about whether his April 30 testimony had been recorded.

Anderson believed it had.

Rosser subsequently questioned stenographer H. L. Parry, who examined his records and said that he personally had not recorded Anderson's testimony.

Parry's statement does not establish that the testimony was never transcribed. In fact, another surviving trial exhibit confirms that a portion of Anderson's original inquest testimony was preserved (Atlanta Journal, 5).

Monday, August 18, 1913: The Defense Introduces Anderson's Earlier Testimony

On Monday, August 18, Luther Rosser read part of Anderson's April 30 coroner's inquest testimony into the trial record.

Solicitor Dorsey questioned whether Rosser intended to impeach Anderson.

Rosser answered:

"I take it for granted that he had just forgotten."

Judge Leonard S. Roan admitted the material.

The proceeding demonstrates that Anderson's earlier statements were available in written form during the trial and could be compared with his August 1 testimony (Atlanta Journal, 16) (Atlanta Georgian, 17).

Defendant's Exhibit 93: Anderson's Original Inquest Testimony Survives

Brief of Evidence, Printed Page 307

One of the most important surviving documents concerning Anderson is Defendant's Exhibit 93.

The exhibit reproduces a passage from his April 30 coroner's inquest testimony concerning Newt Lee's position, the lantern, and the distance to Mary's body.

Anderson stated:

"I could not see that far with the lantern that he had. With the lantern that he had I could see about ten or twelve feet, something like that."

This passage establishes that at least part of Anderson's inquest testimony survived and was incorporated into the murder trial record.

It allows researchers to compare the original inquest statement with his trial testimony and contemporary newspaper accounts.

The official citation is:

State of Georgia v. Leo M. Frank, Brief of Evidence, Defendant's Exhibit 93, printed page 307 (Brief of Evidence, 6).

The complete coroner's transcript has not been located in the material examined here. However, the existence of Exhibit 93 demonstrates that Anderson's original testimony did not disappear entirely.

Historical Significance of Anderson's Testimony

His Observations of the Crime Scene

Anderson was among the first police officers to enter the basement after Lee reported the body.

His descriptions of Mary's condition, position, clothing, nearby objects, and basement lighting are important evidence from the initial investigation.

However, the statements of other responding officers, particularly Dobbs and Rogers, must be considered when reconstructing the scene.

His Questions About Newt Lee's Lantern

Anderson challenged whether Lee could have recognized Mary's body from his claimed position.

His April 30 testimony estimated a useful lantern range of approximately 10 to 15 feet.

His August 1 testimony acknowledged that the bulk of a large object might be visible at a greater distance.

These statements are not necessarily contradictory. An object can be visible without being identifiable.

A reliable reconstruction should examine the exact lantern position, condition of the globe, distance to the body, obstacles, and whether the officers' later nighttime experiment reproduced the original conditions.

The Unanswered Calls to Leo Frank

Anderson described unsuccessful attempts to telephone Frank at approximately 3:30 and 4 a.m. on Sunday, April 27.

These calls are an established part of his testimony, although they do not explain why Frank failed to answer.

The exact chronology should be checked against the testimony of Rogers, Dobbs, and the individuals contacted at the Haas and Montag residences.

The Body's Position and Basement Tracks

Anderson described the body as face downward, while some reports attribute a different initial description to Lee.

He also described tracks near the body but could not establish who created them.

Both subjects are relevant to evaluating the early police investigation. Neither can be resolved from Anderson's statements alone.

The Importance of Defendant's Exhibit 93

Exhibit 93 establishes that the defense possessed and introduced a portion of Anderson's original inquest testimony.

This makes Anderson particularly important to efforts to reconstruct the lost or missing portions of the coroner's proceedings.

The original exhibit may also provide clues concerning how the inquest was recorded and where additional stenographic records were stored.

Newspaper Archive: Fifteen Identified Contemporary Articles

The following newspaper reports contain Anderson's testimony, describe his activities, or corroborate his involvement through other witnesses.

April 30, 1913

1. The Atlanta Journal: "Negro Watchman Tells Story of Finding Girl's Body and Questions Fail to Shake Him." Extensive account of Anderson's coroner's inquest testimony concerning the body, lantern, basement, and Newt Lee (reference 1).

2. The Atlanta Georgian: "Went Down Scuttle Hole on Ladder to Reach Body." Detailed account of the same testimony, printing Anderson's initials as W. T. rather than W. F. (reference 2).

May 1, 1913

3. The Atlanta Constitution: "Newt Lee Tells His Story During Morning Session." Reviews Anderson's testimony and the questions concerning visibility in the basement (reference 7).

4. The Atlanta Georgian: "State Enters Phagan Case; Frank and Lee Are Taken to Tower." Mentions Anderson's unsuccessful telephone calls to Frank (reference 8).

May 8, 1913

5. The Atlanta Journal: "Phagan Inquest in Session; Six Witnesses Are Examined Before Adjournment to 2:30." Rogers describes Anderson's activities with Lee (reference 9).

6. The Atlanta Georgian: "'Boots' Rogers Tells How Body Was Found." Additional testimony concerning Anderson, Lee, and the telephone calls (reference 10).

July 30, 1913

7. The Atlanta Constitution: "Officer Tells About Discovery of Body of Girl in Basement." Sergeant Dobbs identifies Anderson among the responding officers (reference 11).

8. The Atlanta Journal: "Defense to Claim Strands of Hair Found Were Not Mary Phagan's." Rogers discusses Anderson's actions in the factory office (reference 12).

9. The Atlanta Georgian: "Gantt Has Startling Evidence; Dorsey Promises New Testimony Against Frank." Contains Rogers's account of Anderson's telephone activity (reference 13).

July 31, 1913

10. The Atlanta Constitution: "Rogers on Stand Describes Visit of Frank to Undertakers." Places Anderson with Lee in the factory office at approximately 3:45 a.m. (reference 14).

August 2, 1913

11. The Atlanta Constitution: "Policeman W. F. Anderson Tells of Newt Lee's Telephone Call." Dedicated report of Anderson's trial testimony and cross-examination (reference 4).

12. The Atlanta Journal: "Dr. Harris Collapses on Stand as He Gives Sensational Evidence." Extensive Anderson examination and questions about the earlier inquest record (reference 5).

August 3, 1913

13. The Atlanta Journal: "State's Case Against Frank as It Stands After Week's Testimony Is Shown Here." Reviews Anderson's place among the prosecution witnesses (reference 15).

August 18, 1913

14. The Atlanta Journal: "Leo M. Frank Takes Stand, Tells His Story." Reports Rosser introducing Anderson's earlier inquest statements (reference 16).

15. The Atlanta Georgian: "Girls Testify for and Against Frank; 'I'd Die for Him!' Cries One." Discusses the defense's use of Anderson's testimony (reference 17).

These 15 reports constitute an identified newspaper collection, not a demonstrated complete inventory. Additional references may survive in unindexed editions or regional newspaper reprints.

Additional Research Needed

Confirm Anderson's Identity and Life Dates

The strongest identification is Wyman F. Anderson, the Atlanta policeman listed at 37 Hood Street in 1913.

The proposed middle name Fleming requires original documentary confirmation.

The most promising records include the 1900, 1910, and 1920 federal censuses, Georgia death certificates, Fulton County marriage records, cemetery records, Atlanta police personnel files, and city directories after 1916.

These records may establish his birth and death dates, parents, wife, children, career history, and burial location.

Locate the Complete Coroner's Transcript

Defendant's Exhibit 93 proves that a portion of Anderson's original inquest testimony entered the murder trial record.

A targeted archival search should examine Fulton County coroner's records, Superior Court case papers, original criminal exhibits, Georgia archival collections, and surviving stenographers' records.

The inquiry should specifically request Anderson's testimony from April 30, 1913, original notes, transcripts, and any surviving copy of Defendant's Exhibit 93.

The questioning of H. L. Parry raises the possibility that another stenographer recorded Anderson's appearance.

Compare the Lantern Testimony Word for Word

The April 30 newspaper accounts, August 1 testimony, August 2 reports, August 18 proceedings, and Exhibit 93 should be compared line by line.

Particular attention should be given to distances, the location of Lee's lantern, the condition of its globe, statements about visibility, and the difference between seeing an object and recognizing a body.

This comparison could establish whether Anderson materially changed his testimony or whether the apparent differences arose from abbreviated newspaper accounts.

Conclusion

W. F. Anderson, identified in Atlanta city directories as Wyman F. Anderson, was an experienced Atlanta police officer who participated in the earliest investigation of Mary Phagan's murder.

He responded to Newt Lee's telephone call shortly after 3 a.m. on Sunday, April 27, 1913, examined the basement and Mary's body, questioned Lee's account of the discovery, and unsuccessfully attempted to contact Leo Frank.

He testified at the coroner's inquest on Wednesday, April 30, and for the prosecution on Friday, August 1.

His observations were reported extensively in the contemporary Atlanta newspapers and preserved in the official trial record.

The most important surviving document is Defendant's Exhibit 93, printed page 307 of the Brief of Evidence, which reproduces part of Anderson's original coroner's inquest testimony.

The remaining historical questions concern the survival of his complete inquest examination, the precise meaning of his lantern testimony, and the confirmation of his full biographical identity.

text:
In the vast landfill of modern gaming where triple A spectacles bury themselves under layers of polish and predictability, Deponia from 2012 rises as a defiant mountain of refuse that somehow gleams brighter than any polished utopia. This is no ordinary point and click adventure. It is a cultural monument forged in the fires of German ingenuity at Daedalic Entertainment, a game that took the dying embers of a genre once ruled by LucasArts legends and reignited them with a blaze of absurdity, heart, and uncompromising character. You do not merely play Deponia. You inhabit its trash strewn world until its lessons about ambition, love, and the messy beauty of imperfect lives cling to you like the grime on its streets. It stands apart because it refuses the safe path of the noble hero and the pristine setting, instead delivering an unlikely protagonist and a love story that forces you to confront what it truly means to want something better while learning to value what you already have.

Picture the era of its arrival. The year 2012 saw the point and click form struggling for relevance amid the rise of cinematic narratives and open worlds. Studios had largely abandoned the hand drawn charm and inventory puzzles that once defined adventure gaming. Into this void stepped Deponia, a hand drawn steampunk cartoon masterpiece set on a planet literally named for landfill. Every structure is cobbled from discarded machinery, every character ekes out existence amid the refuse dumped from the floating city of Elysium above. This was not background flavor. It was the thesis. In a time when games chased photorealism and clean narratives, Deponia embraced the grime and the gags, proving that beauty could emerge from broken parts and that comedy could carry profound weight. Its visual style, refined yet chaotic, with characters whose expressions and animations burst with personality, made every click feel like an exploration of a living scrapyard. The fun of playing comes from that tactile joy of examining, combining, and failing spectacularly, all while the world reacts with the kind of dry wit that recalls the best of classic adventures yet feels wholly original in its German rooted absurdity.

At the center stands Rufus, the ultimate unlikely hero, a self absorbed inventor from the town of Kuvaq who dreams only of escaping his junk planet for the paradise of Elysium. He is lazy, egotistical, and endlessly scheming, the sort of figure most games would reject as a protagonist. Yet this is precisely why he becomes legendary. Through his repeated failed attempts to leave, and the chaos he leaves in his wake, the game teaches that heroism is not born of pure intention but of stubborn persistence even when the world sees you as a nuisance. Rufus is no Guybrush Threepwood clone despite the surface resemblance. He is more flawed, more abrasive, and therefore more human. The takeaway is clear. Your flaws do not disqualify you from growth. They are the raw material. When his latest scheme intersects with the arrival of Goal, an Elysian woman who falls into his world, the story shifts from mere escape to something deeper. You learn that true ambition requires looking beyond your own reflection. Rufus begins by projecting his fantasies onto her, seeing in this unconscious figure from above the ticket to a better life and the perfect companion. The lesson here is sharp. Idealization is a trap. Real connection demands seeing the person, not the symbol. As he helps her navigate the dangers of Deponia and the Organon forces that pursue her, his selfishness is tested. The moments where he must choose between his dream and her safety reveal that love, even the unlikely kind, transforms the dreamer into someone capable of selflessness. The general arc shows a man who starts as pure ego and, through the friction of care for another, begins to understand that saving a world or a person can matter more than saving yourself.

This love story is what elevates Deponia into masterpiece territory. It is not the conventional boy meets girl. Goal is from a world of order and technology while Rufus lives in chaos and scrap. Their dynamic forces a confrontation with class, with expectation, and with the reality that paradise may not be what it seems. The takeaway is that love does not erase differences. It forces you to bridge them. Playing through their interactions, you absorb that genuine affection emerges not from perfect circumstances but from shared struggle and the willingness to risk your own plans. Rufus’s journey with her teaches that the unlikely hero succeeds not by becoming someone else but by choosing, in key moments, to put another’s fate above his own desires. The planet itself, threatened by larger forces from above, becomes a metaphor for how personal growth can intersect with larger stakes. You leave understanding that dreams of escape are hollow if they abandon the people and places that shaped you.

The mechanics support this immersion perfectly. Point and click at its purest, with left clicks to interact and right clicks to examine, encourages constant curiosity. Inventory combinations reward lateral thinking, and the option to skip certain puzzles acknowledges that the story should never stall for the player who prefers narrative momentum. A tutorial eases you in, and the post completion Droggeljug mode that turns every description into nonsense is a cheeky reward for those who finish. This is fun because the puzzles serve the comedy and the character rather than existing in isolation. You feel clever not just for solving them but for living inside Rufus’s warped logic. In an era of hand holding, Deponia trusted its audience.

What makes it unique and a cultural icon is this refusal to sand down the edges. Critics noted its mixed reception, some calling the pacing glacial or the humor uneven, yet players embraced it. Sales reached hundreds of thousands quickly, with the first game alone becoming a high seller for Daedalic, and the series eventually moving millions of copies. It became a signature franchise because it captured the spirit of the underdog in both story and development. Hand drawn art in an age of 3D, a German original that found international voice through dedicated localization, an unlikable hero who earns affection through sheer chaotic charm. It stands out among other adventures of its field because so many chased nostalgia or safety. Deponia built a world from trash and made it feel alive, a love story that is absurd yet moving, an unlikely hero whose growth feels earned rather than mandated.

Behind the scenes, the vision came from Jan Müller-Michaelis, known as Poki, co founder of Daedalic. Originally conceived as a single game exploring the untidiness of life and distant goals, the trash planet idea provided the perfect playground for adventure design. Art direction refined Rufus from pure steampunk sketches into something weirder and more ownable, blending garbage collector aesthetics with eccentricity. The songs that bookend chapters, the detailed animations, the commitment to character over convention, all reflect a team that treated the medium with respect while having the freedom of the jester. Development learned from earlier Daedalic titles, streamlining controls and focusing the humor so that the heart could shine through the jokes. This craftsmanship is why it endures as a classic legend.

The must watch status is absolute because Deponia offers what few games manage. It is a complete emotional and intellectual experience disguised as a comedy of errors. You play to laugh at the scrapyard antics, but you finish having learned that the unlikely hero is often the one who changes most, that love is the force that redirects selfish dreams toward something greater, and that even a world of trash can produce beauty and meaning. It is a masterpiece not despite its rough edges but because of them. In an industry that often discards the imperfect, Deponia proves that the discarded can become the essential. Play it, inhabit its lessons, and you will understand why this 2012 gem remains a towering cultural icon of adventure gaming, a legend that refuses to be buried.

text:
I sincerely congratulate all military chaplains on their professional day!

The motto of the chaplaincy service is “to be there,” so chaplains are precisely the people who stand by service members during their most difficult moments.

They pray, listen, and offer support in the wake of loss; they help soldiers maintain their faith and inner strength in circumstances marked by daily losses, excruciating pain, and superhuman strain. Sometimes, a single conversation or simply being there means far more to a person than can be seen from the outside

I also want to highlight the work of the Jewish military chaplains—Yakov Sinyakov and David Milman. I know their work not just from stories—I’ve seen the dedication with which they serve people. They support Jewish service members, helping them preserve their traditions and connection with the Almighty even in the midst of war, yet they never turn away a person of another faith if that person needs help, prayer, or simply a kind word. This is exactly what true chaplaincy should be! 

Thank you to all chaplains of every faith who stand today alongside Ukraine’s defenders, the wounded, and the families of the fallen. May the Almighty grant you strength and wisdom and watch over you wherever you go! 

Thank you for the light you bring to those who need it most!
