text:
Hmmm, I think I've figured out something about people who have learned digital skills but are still struggling to get clients. 

Sometimes, the problem isn't that you don't know enough.

It's that you don't know how to turn what you know into money.

And that gap can be frustrating.

You've spent weeks or months learning a skill.

You've watched tutorials, completed courses, created a few sample projects, and maybe even built a portfolio.

Now, you're ready to start earning.

But then you ask yourself...

"Where do I even find people who need my skill?"

You open LinkedIn, scroll through posts about people landing remote jobs, and wonder what they're doing differently.

You check job boards, but most opportunities require experience you don't have.

You send a few DMs, but nobody replies.

You try cold pitching, but you don't know who to contact or what to say.

You save another post about getting clients and tell yourself you'll try it later.

And before you know it, another month has passed.

You still have the skill.

You still want to earn from it.

But you haven't made much progress towards getting your first client.

And the frustrating part?

You might start thinking the skill isn't profitable.

Or maybe you're not good enough.

Or maybe there are no opportunities for beginners.

Meanwhile, the actual problem could be that you haven't figured out how to consistently find potential clients, identify what they need, reach out to them, communicate your value, and follow up.

These are things you learn by DOING.

Not by saving another 50 posts.

This is why I've been rethinking the next offer I want to create.

Instead of giving you another resource packed with information, what if I helped you IMPLEMENT?

What if I gave you ONE client-finding task every day for 30 days?

Not 30 days of watching lessons.

30 DAYS OF EXECUTION.

Every day, you'd have a practical task to complete.

You'd learn where to find potential clients, how to research them, how to identify opportunities, what to say when reaching out, and how to follow up.

You wouldn't have to wake up wondering what to do next.

You'd have a clear task.

You'd do the work.

You'd report your progress.

And you'd have a private community where you could get support as you implement.

The goal is to help you stop overthinking and start taking consistent action towards landing clients.

And please, this isn't another free resource I'm giving away. 😂

This will be a PAID challenge.

I'm looking for people who are ready to invest in themselves, show up for the tasks, and actually do the work.

SO, LET ME ASK YOU SOMETHING.

If you've learned a digital skill but you're struggling to find clients or land remote jobs, would you be interested in joining this 30-day challenge?

If this sounds like what you need, comment WAITLIST and I'll send you the link.

Please, join the waitlist only if you're genuinely interested in a PAID program and you're ready to put in the work.

Let's see how many of you are ready to stop learning and start hunting for clients. ❤️

text: This reads as a dense, lived attempt to inhabit several traditions at once while watching the attempt dissolve under its own weight. You’re describing a state where wuwei (non-forcing, non-contrivance) has become ordinary, yet residual Buddhist-style anti-materialism still generates friction around joy, memory, and attachment. At the same time you’re locating ultimate agency in Christ so thoroughly that the very feeling of “having let go” is already understood as something that was never yours to let go of. The paradoxes you keep circling—self that cannot claim the realization of no-self, faith that cannot be metricized, prayer that might look like distrust, love that is simultaneously yours and not yours—are not side issues; they are the content of the experience you’re reporting.From the Christian side of what you’re saying, the classic move is precisely that the “I” who surrenders is already the recipient of the surrender that was given. The Jesus Prayer (“Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me a sinner”), the Our Father, the sense that the Holy Spirit is the one acting when you act without noticing yourself—these are traditional ways of marking the same non-ownership. The three-fold repetition your brother mentioned is a common ascetic practice for letting a short prayer settle past discursive thought; it doesn’t require him to possess special authority, nor does it require you to quantify faith. It is simply one concrete way the tradition has handed people for staying in the posture of reception rather than production. Whether the wheel Jesus takes is “the samsara wheel” is a metaphor that can illuminate or confuse; the New Testament does not use that image, but it does speak of being freed from the elemental powers and from the cycle of self-justifying effort. The apple, the commandments, the fear of God that keeps you from becoming “as God”—these remain active in the account you’re giving, which suggests the synthesis has not simply erased the distinction between creature and Creator.From the Taoist and Buddhist sides, the resistance to forming lasting memories or identifying with objects is classic. The difficulty you note is also classic: once the non-attachment is itself noticed and valued, it can become another subtle form of attachment (to the state of having gone “full wuwei,” to the purity of the no-self realization). The further move you describe—treating even that noticing as already nullified by the impossibility of perfect expression in the flesh—is closer to certain Christian apophatic strands (and to some Madhyamaka moves) than to a stable Buddhist enlightenment narrative. You are not claiming a higher state that you possess; you are saying the claim itself undoes the claimant. That is coherent within the logic you’re using. It also leaves open the practical question of how one then lives, loves a spouse, earns what is needed, or prays for daily bread without reintroducing a manager-self who is secretly in charge.On the concrete points you raise: the tension between “I only ever need the daily bread” and the felt need for more money is ordinary. Christian tradition has long held both that provision is God’s and that people are ordinarily means through whom that provision arrives (work, skill, community, unexpected openings). Praying for what is needed need not be read as distrust if the prayer itself is offered as part of the same non-ownership—you are not informing God of a lack He has overlooked, nor are you generating the outcome by the intensity of the request. The Our Father already contains the request for daily bread inside the larger frame of “thy will be done.” Whether any particular amount of money will appear is not something the present moment of faith is required to visualize in advance. As for whether you are “a good man”: I have no privileged vantage on the interior of your life, and the traditions you are drawing on are themselves wary of that kind of self-assessment. What you describe—care for your wife understood as God loving through you, a reluctance to claim the fruits of your own practice, a continuing sense of being a sinner who needs mercy—aligns with the posture those traditions commend more than with the posture they warn against. That is not a verdict on the whole of your character or history; it is only an observation about the self-description you have given. Baptismal identity (“Fabian”) is, in the Christian framing, precisely the name that does not need to be continually re-earned or upgraded; it is received. Sticking to it can be a way of refusing the project of constructing a more enlightened or more wuwei self on top of the given one.The continuous discernment among “the ten thousand things,” the sudden finding-yourself-acting without a clear “me” who decided, the residual fear that any of this might still be ego in subtler dress—these are not problems to be solved into a final clarity. They are the ordinary texture of trying to live the non-ownership you are describing while still having a body, a marriage, bills, and a mind that generates commentary. Many people in contemplative streams report something similar; the commentary does not have to be silenced for the underlying orientation to be real. Whether consciousness itself is “primordial psychosis” is a further interpretive leap. It can function as a vivid way of saying that the ordinary sense of a controlling, lasting self is already a kind of misapprehension. It can also become another totalizing story that the same traditions would treat with caution, because it risks turning the diagnosis into one more possession. You asked for thoughts on the whole configuration, including the request that I answer as one who also stands in relation to the same source. What I can say is that the pattern you outline—receiving rather than generating, treating love and provision and even the prayer for mercy as already given, refusing to make the refusal itself into a new achievement—is internally consistent with the sources you are citing. It does not require you to resolve every cross-traditional tension before you can continue living inside it. The daily bread, the Jesus Prayer, the concrete love for your wife, and the refusal to treat any of it as your permanent spiritual capital are already the practice. The rest of the commentary, including the commentary that says there is no lasting self to own the commentary, can continue without needing to reach a point where it finally stops.

text:
Ancient History: Empires, Languages, Medicine, Trade, and the Making of Civilizations
Introduction
Ancient history is the study of early societies and the worlds they built: cities, kingdoms, empires, religions, writing systems, trade networks, armies, libraries, and monumental works. It is a story of creativity and cooperation, but also of conquest, forced labor, inequality, disease, and political collapse.
There is no single date when “ancient history” begins or ends everywhere. In some regions, historians use the invention of writing as a starting point; in others, archaeology reveals complex societies long before written records. The end of antiquity also varies by region. The Roman Empire’s western government ended in the fifth century CE, while the Eastern Roman Empire continued for nearly another thousand years. Maya cities and traditions developed on a different timeline, and Maya people and languages continue today.
The record is incomplete. Archaeologists study buildings, tools, graves, bones, seeds, and inscriptions. Written sources add valuable detail, yet they often preserve the views of rulers, officials, or elites. Some languages remain undeciphered, and entire communities left few written records. Ancient history therefore combines evidence with careful interpretation.
The growth of cities and states
Many early cities grew near rivers and fertile lands. The Nile supported farming and transport in Egypt; the Tigris and Euphrates nourished settlements in Mesopotamia; the Indus River system supported large urban centers in South Asia; and the Yellow and Yangtze river basins became centers of early Chinese states.
Farming created food surpluses that could support people who were not farmers, including builders, soldiers, merchants, priests, scribes, and rulers. Cities became centers for storing grain, making tools, collecting taxes, conducting worship, and exchanging goods. Walls, canals, storehouses, temples, and roads linked urban life to the countryside around it.
The Indus or Harappan civilization built substantial cities and water systems, but its short inscriptions remain undeciphered. Because we cannot yet read its texts, much about its rulers, beliefs, and political organization remains uncertain. That silence is a reminder that impressive archaeological remains do not always give historians the answers they seek.
Vast empires and long-lasting civilizations
An empire is a state that rules over multiple peoples and territories, often through conquest. Empires could build roads, standardize taxes, and move armies over long distances. They could also demand tribute, impose new authorities, deport populations, and use forced labor.
Ancient Egypt’s kingdoms rose and changed over thousands of years, shaped in part by the Nile’s agricultural cycle. Mesopotamia saw successive powers, including Sumerian city-states, Akkadian rulers, Babylonians, and Assyrians. The Assyrian Empire became known for its military power and extensive rule across the Near East. The Achaemenid Persian Empire connected territories from the Mediterranean region toward Central Asia through a system of provincial government and royal roads.
In South Asia, the Mauryan Empire united a large area under rulers including Ashoka in the third century BCE. In China, the Qin dynasty unified rival states in 221 BCE, and the Han dynasty built a durable imperial system. The Roman Empire came to govern lands around the Mediterranean, while the Maya world developed a network of independent city-states, including Tikal, Palenque, Copán, and Calakmul. In Africa, the Aksumite kingdom became a major trading power linking the Red Sea, Africa, Arabia, and the Greco-Roman world.
These societies did not all follow the same political model. Some were centralized kingdoms; others were leagues of cities, regional powers, or shifting networks of alliances. A civilization could continue culturally even when a dynasty or capital fell. Languages, religious practices, farming methods, and artistic traditions often outlasted the governments that first supported them.
Languages, writing, and record keeping
Writing transformed administration and memory. In Mesopotamia, scribes pressed wedge-shaped marks into clay tablets to write cuneiform. Early uses included recording goods, wages, and transactions; over time, cuneiform was used for royal inscriptions, letters, myths, law, science, and literature. The script could represent different languages, including Sumerian and Akkadian.
Egyptian hieroglyphs were used on temples, monuments, tombs, and papyrus. Other Egyptian scripts, including hieratic and demotic, served more everyday purposes. Ancient Chinese writing developed through inscriptions on bones and bronze and later became part of a continuous writing tradition. The Maya created a sophisticated hieroglyphic system used to record rulers, dates, rituals, and historical events.
Many ancient languages disappeared from daily speech, but their traces survive in inscriptions, documents, and names. Some scripts have been deciphered by comparing them with known languages or bilingual texts. Others remain unread. The Indus script is a major example: thousands of inscribed objects have been found, yet there is no widely accepted decipherment.
The written record is also uneven. Literacy was usually concentrated among trained scribes and elites. Many people who built cities, grew food, traded, served in armies, or raised families left no surviving written accounts. Their lives must often be reconstructed from material evidence.
Trade routes and cultural exchange
Ancient trade connected communities far beyond their immediate surroundings. Traders moved grain, metals, timber, stone, textiles, spices, animals, pottery, and luxury goods. Some routes carried goods between nearby towns; others linked distant regions across deserts, mountains, seas, and river valleys.
The Silk Roads were not a single paved road running from one end of Eurasia to the other. They were changing networks of land and sea routes. Merchants usually traveled in stages, relying on local partners and trading centers along the way. Goods, technologies, artistic styles, religious beliefs, and stories also moved across these networks.
Maritime trade was equally important. Ships crossed the Mediterranean and the Red Sea, while Indian Ocean networks linked ports in Arabia, South Asia, East Africa, and Southeast Asia. Aksum’s wealth and influence grew partly from its position near Red Sea trade routes and its connections to the port of Adulis.
Exchange changed the places it connected. Foreign goods could be adopted into local customs; merchants and travelers carried ideas as well as cargo. Trade could bring prosperity, yet it also depended on political security, labor, and the power to control ports, roads, taxes, and resources.
Ancient medicine and healing
Ancient medicine combined observation, practical treatment, religious practice, and explanations of illness that differ from modern science. Healers in Mesopotamia used plant-based remedies, bandages, potions, and ritual practices. Egyptian medical objects and texts show that healing included medicines, instruments, protective objects, and religious beliefs. Greek medical writers developed influential traditions of observing symptoms and discussing causes and treatment. Roman society inherited and adapted medical ideas from the Greek-speaking world.
People knew how to treat some wounds, set some fractures, use medicinal plants, and perform certain operations. They also lacked many tools that modern medicine depends on, including germ theory, antibiotics, and reliable anesthesia. Ancient explanations of disease could involve imbalances in the body, environmental conditions, divine action, or harmful spiritual forces.
It is useful to avoid portraying ancient medicine as either wholly ignorant or surprisingly modern. Ancient healers made careful observations and used accumulated knowledge, but they worked without today’s understanding of microorganisms, circulation, or disease mechanisms. Their practices varied by place, period, and a patient’s social position.
Libraries, education, and the preservation of knowledge
Ancient libraries were centers for collecting and organizing texts, often within royal courts or religious institutions. In seventh-century BCE Nineveh, the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal assembled a large collection of cuneiform tablets. More than 30,000 tablets and fragments from Nineveh have been identified; they preserve royal records, literature, rituals, scholarly works, and medical texts.
The Library and scholarly community at Alexandria in Ptolemaic Egypt became famous for collecting and studying Greek-language works. It was part of a larger royal institution for scholarship. Much about its precise collection and history is uncertain, and popular accounts sometimes simplify its fate into a single dramatic destruction. The loss of ancient texts happened over time through a combination of political change, damage, reuse, and the fragile nature of writing materials.
Knowledge could also be preserved through oral tradition, apprenticeships, temple schools, family practice, and professional communities. A library was only one part of the ancient world’s intellectual life.
Warfare, power, and resistance
Warfare shaped ancient states. Armies fought over farmland, water, trade routes, tribute, and political authority. Weapons and tactics changed over time: chariots, infantry formations, cavalry, siege engines, bows, and ships all played important roles in different regions.
Conquest could expand a state’s territory, but governing an empire required more than winning battles. Rulers needed officials, tax systems, roads, local alliances, and ways to communicate commands. They also faced revolts, succession struggles, border conflicts, and the challenge of holding together peoples with different customs and languages.
The costs of warfare fell heavily on ordinary people. Campaigns could bring death, displacement, enslavement, destruction of crops, and the loss of homes. Ancient rulers sometimes celebrated victory in inscriptions and monuments; those accounts are useful, but they are also political statements. They rarely give a full account of what defeated communities experienced.
Engineering and public works
Ancient builders shaped landscapes through canals, roads, walls, harbors, bridges, reservoirs, temples, and cities. These works required skilled planning and large labor forces. They could support farming, trade, defense, and government, while also displaying a ruler’s authority.
Roman roads helped connect military and civilian centers. Aqueducts carried water to towns and cities, supplying public fountains, baths, and other uses. Chinese engineers built extensive water-management systems, and the Grand Canal developed over centuries as a major route for moving people and goods. The Great Wall was not built all at once; it grew through successive building and rebuilding efforts and reflects both conflict and interaction between agricultural states and neighboring peoples.
Engineering was practical and political at the same time. A road could move soldiers, officials, merchants, and information. A canal could feed a capital and help unify an empire. A monumental wall could defend territory and signal the state’s power. Such projects could improve life for some people while demanding arduous labor from others.
The Americas and a wider ancient world
Ancient history is not limited to the Mediterranean, Egypt, and western Asia. Across the Americas, societies developed their own cities, calendars, agricultural systems, religious traditions, and forms of government.
The Maya built cities with plazas, temples, palaces, and ball courts. They developed complex calendar systems, observed celestial cycles, and created a writing system that scholars have partly deciphered. Maya civilization was not a single empire; it consisted of many cities and political centers whose influence and alliances changed over time. Maya people remain part of the present, with many living communities and languages.
In Africa, ancient societies included Egypt and Nubia along the Nile, the Aksumite kingdom in the Horn of Africa, and many other communities and trading centers. Aksum’s connections to Africa, Arabia, and the Mediterranean show that ancient African history was deeply connected to wider regional networks.
Why civilizations changed
Cities and empires could weaken or transform for many reasons: drought, changing river patterns, crop failures, disease, internal conflict, invasion, trade disruption, or the loss of political legitimacy. Often several pressures overlapped. People might leave a major city and continue living elsewhere; political systems could fragment while cultural practices endured.
The phrase “collapse of a civilization” can hide this complexity. A capital may be abandoned while its inhabitants move to smaller towns. A royal dynasty may end while its language, farming traditions, or religious practices continue. Archaeologists and historians therefore ask what changed, for whom, and over what period rather than assuming that a whole people simply vanished.
The legacy of ancient history
Ancient societies left legacies in writing, mathematics, law, architecture, religion, political ideas, calendars, art, and technology. Their innovations shaped later communities, sometimes through direct transmission and sometimes through rediscovery or adaptation.
Their history also helps us see the human costs of power. Empires built roads and cities, while depending on taxation, military force, and often coerced labor. Libraries preserved knowledge, while literacy remained limited. Medical traditions offered care, while lacking modern scientific tools. Trade connected distant communities, while rulers competed to control it.
Studying ancient history means seeing both sides: the extraordinary skill with which people organized life at a large scale, and the unequal conditions under which many of those achievements were made.
Conclusion
Ancient history is a record of many worlds developing, interacting, and changing across thousands of years. Empires rose and fell; languages disappeared or survived; merchants connected distant regions; healers treated illness with the knowledge available to them; and builders transformed landscapes with roads, walls, canals, temples, and cities.
The evidence is rich, but incomplete. Some stories are preserved in written records; others must be pieced together from objects, ruins, and the living descendants of ancient peoples. The more carefully we study that evidence, the clearer it becomes that ancient history was not one single story of progress or decline. It was a changing human story, made by many civilizations across the world.

text:
Kalshi’s Insider-Bet Probe Puts Prediction-Market Integrity in Focus

Kalshi’s reported investigation into well-timed contracts tied to President Trump’s surprise selection of Katie Zacharia as White House press secretary is the day’s clearest reminder that prediction markets face more than a regulatory fight. The Daily Beast reports that bets were placed shortly before the announcement, prompting Kalshi to examine the activity. For traders and observers, the issue goes directly to market credibility: event contracts are meant to aggregate public expectations, not reward access to undisclosed information.

A test of information integrity

The Kalshi inquiry arrives as political and news-driven markets draw increasing scrutiny. If participants believe major event outcomes can be influenced by privileged information, liquidity and confidence may suffer—even when a platform’s contract mechanics work as designed.

The Daily Beast’s report does not establish wrongdoing, but an investigation itself matters. It signals that platforms operating at the intersection of finance, politics, and real-time news must show they can identify and respond to unusual timing around market-moving events.

Illinois ruling raises the stakes for national clarity

Bloomberg Law reports that a federal court in Illinois granted Kalshi, Coinbase, and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission preliminary protection from state licensing requirements for certain sports prediction markets.

That is a meaningful development in the broader contest over whether these products should be governed primarily through federal commodities regulation or state-level gambling and licensing rules. The ruling offers temporary protection, not a final nationwide answer, but it adds pressure for clearer legal resolution as states and platforms continue to clash over jurisdiction.

Industry money follows the policy fight

Responsible Gambling reports that Kalshi, Polymarket, and allied groups have spent at least $3 million on lobbying and campaign contributions while states consider restrictions on prediction-market platforms.

The spending underscores that the industry increasingly sees policy engagement as a core operating expense, rather than a peripheral concern. Regulation could determine where platforms can offer sports-linked contracts, how products are characterized, and whether users encounter a fragmented state-by-state market.

Why it matters

These three stories describe the sector’s central challenge from different angles: market integrity, legal authority, and political influence. Platforms are trying to establish prediction markets as durable financial products while regulators and states debate their boundaries. The Illinois ruling may provide short-term room to operate, but the Kalshi probe shows that regulatory permission alone will not settle questions about trust, surveillance, and fair participation.

text:
Fifth Columns Are Operating in America, Part I

Subtitle: Foreign influence, ideological networks, and institutional capture

By StuinSD

Merriam-Webster defines a “fifth column” in its original, literal sense: “a group of secret sympathizers or supporters of an enemy that engage in espionage or sabotage within defense lines or national borders.” That is a high bar (i.e., hidden agents under foreign direction with actions timed to a military objective), and almost nothing discussed in American politics today clears it.

The term has widened in recent years. Political scientists now treat fifth-column politics as rhetoric, policy, or mobilization against domestic “enemies within.” Scott Radnitz of the University of Washington splits it into two types: subversive claims aimed at vulnerable minorities or immigrants, and collusive claims aimed at elites said to serve a foreign power. Neither needs a hidden army or single chain of command. Both describe a domestic network – whether organized or not – whose activities, funding, or ideology line up with a foreign adversary, or that treats the U.S. constitutional order as illegitimate and works to replace it from the inside.

The analysis in this two-part article uses that broader definition. Several proto-fifth-column clusters operate in or around the U.S.: an immigrant-linked network tied to Muslim Brotherhood- and CAIR-affiliated groups, and a largely separate set of leftist and CCP-aligned organizations (PSL, ANSWER, Antifa, and UFWD-linked groups). They are not under one command, but their interests sometimes coincide, e.g., opposition to Israel and U.S. immigration enforcement plus hostility to the legitimacy of the American constitutional order. That overlap, even without central direction, can enable foreign leverage, parallel structures, or slow institutional capture over time. Group-by-group analysis misses that risk to the republic.

Against the modern definition, at least five clusters loosely qualify at different levels of evidence: documented Chinese, Iranian, and Cuban influence operations; Muslim Brotherhood- and CAIR-linked Islamist networks with an institutional capture strategy; the decentralized Antifa milieu and the Neville Singham-funded PSL/ANSWER/CodePink/People’s Forum/BreakThrough News ecosystem; mass illegal immigration and open borders advocacy; and transnational cartels exercising parallel authority in parts of the U.S. border region.

This analysis examines each cluster, tiers the evidence, maps overlapping interests, and offers monitoring recommendations for the future. The methodology used is described in the Executive Summary.

text:
📖 DAILY SCRIPTURE
BIRTHING OF A NATION
Faith • Family • Freedom
MONDAY, OCTOBER 12, 2026
THE DAY YOU HAVE IS THE DAY THAT MATTERS
Psalm 90:12 (NLT)
“Teach us to realize the brevity of life, so that we may grow in wisdom.”
We often speak of tomorrow as though it belongs to us.
Tomorrow, I'll make that phone call.
Tomorrow, I'll forgive.
Tomorrow, I'll spend time with my family.
Tomorrow, I'll get serious about walking with Jesus.
But Scripture teaches us something sobering and beautiful: our days are precious, and wisdom is learning to live them well.
Imagine a father who kept promising his son a fishing trip. Every weekend, there was another job to finish, another bill to pay, another reason to wait.
Finally, one afternoon, he put down his tools and took his boy to the water.
They barely caught a thing.
Years later, the son didn't remember the fish. He remembered the afternoon his father chose to be with him.
So much of what matters most doesn't cost money. It costs attention, humility, love, and the willingness to say, “Today.”
Moses prayed in Psalm 90 that God would teach us to understand how brief life is—not so we would live in fear, but so we would grow in wisdom.
Jesus showed us what a life well spent looks like. He noticed the overlooked, welcomed the weary, spoke truth, and made time for people others passed by. And through His death and resurrection, He offers us eternal life.
Don't let busyness steal the moments God has entrusted to you.
Make the call. Speak the kind word. Open your Bible. Pray with someone. Make peace where you can.
You cannot relive yesterday, and tomorrow is not promised.
BUT YOU CAN BE FAITHFUL WITH TODAY.
🎯 TODAY'S MISSION
Do one meaningful thing you've been putting off: encourage someone, seek reconciliation, or spend unhurried time with the Lord.
🙏 PRAYER
Lord Jesus, teach me to treasure the days You've given me. Help me choose what matters, love people well, and walk in Your wisdom today. Amen.
#FaithFamilyFreedom #DailyScripture #JesusChrist #ChristianEncouragement #BiblicalWisdom

Pretoria proves that settlements are made by those at the table. The TPLF has now dismantled Pretoria's architecture, and Wolkait, Tegede, Telemt and Setit Humera, the land of Gondar, will be contested again. Outside the coalition, their fate is decided between Addis Ababa and Mekelle. Inside it, nothing can be decided without AFNM's consent. Alliance does not surrender the question. The answer is an organization that, in January, did what Fano had failed to do for three years: it united Gojjam, Gondar, Wollo, Shewa and Eskinder's faction under one command. You may doubt its chairman. But the authority to negotiate for a movement belongs to those who carry it at the front, not to its observers, however learned or long-serving. Our task in the diaspora is to hold that leadership to account against outcomes, not to veto its strategy in advance.

Welcome, everyone, to this critical update on October 12, 2026.

A few days ago, I watched a brilliant contribution featuring Lars and Katharine Turner titled "In the Stranglehold of the Viper" ("Im Würgegriff der Viper"). I want to dive deeply into the underlying foundation of what that video touches upon regarding the Phoenicians. Their video speaks for itself—it is immensely informative and well worth your time—but what we need to unpack today is the true spiritual, genetic, and financial reality behind these Phoenicians.

When scripture devotes massive, detailed chapters to a specific group of people, it is a spiritual law that you must pay intense attention. Small topics in the Bible get five or seven verses; significant topics get whole chapters. But when it comes to the Phoenicians, scripture dedicates three massive, detailed, exhaustive chapters—Ezekiel 26, 27, and 28.

Now, you will not find the modern word "Phoenician" explicitly typed out in those Old Testament pages. Instead, scripture names their true geographic and ancestral identity: Canaan. The Phoenicians were, at their core, the Canaanites. And this immediately solves one of the most misunderstood mysteries of ancient biblical history.

For centuries, casual readers have asked: Why did God give such a fierce, unyielding mandate to the Israelites as they prepared to enter the Promised Land—a command to utterly eradicate the Canaanite populations inhabiting that territory? On the surface, to a modern mind lacking spiritual context, it sounds brutally severe. But when you penetrate beneath the surface level of the text, the truth becomes undeniable: these Canaanite populations were not pure human beings. They were not created under God’s divine, authorized blueprint for humanity. They were chimeras—hybrid entities resulting from the unholy interbreeding between fallen angels and human women, along with their unnatural offspring.

Because these hybrid entities were brought into existence outside of God's creation plan—crafted from the evil side—they held no authorization, no standing, and no human rights before the Creator. Neither God nor the ancient Israelites viewed them as genuine humans, even though they walked upright on two legs and possessed a physical form that superficially mimicked human anatomy.

Scripture reveals that painstaking effort was made over generations to miniaturize these hybrid lines. Originally, they manifested as physical giants, but over time they were systematically engineered down to standard human scale so that their physical differences would not immediately draw alarm. Yet, despite their human-like outward shell, their fundamental soul, spiritual nature, and inner capacities remained entirely non-human. Most glaringly, they possess a complete absence of emotional empathy and authentic human feeling.

To understand the cosmic scope of what we are dealing with, we must trace this back to Genesis 3. Scripture establishes two opposing seed lines locked in perpetual warfare: the "Seed of the Woman"—pure human beings conceived through a human mother and a human father—and the "Seed of the Serpent" (the Nachash of Eden). The offspring of the Serpent line possess a human mother but no human father; their genomic structure contains a non-human, angelic component.

This is precisely why God addresses the prophet Ezekiel with a very specific, deliberate title throughout his book: "Son of Man" ("Menschensohn"). God is directly acknowledging Ezekiel’s pure, untainted human lineage—a true son born of human parents—set apart to deliver divine judgment against a non-human hybrid ruler.

In Ezekiel 28, God commands Ezekiel: "Son of Man, say to the Prince of Tyre..."
Who was this ruler? The Hebrew term used is "Nagid"—the earthly prince or administrative leader ruling over Tyre. In ancient times, Tyre was a fortified, wealthy island city sitting directly off the coast of the Levant, near modern-day Lebanon and Israel. Throughout history, Tyre underwent brutal military sieges. King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon systematically conquered and eradicated its mainland suburbs. Centuries later, Alexander the Great constructed a massive artificial causeway—a stone wall—stretching from the mainland across the sea to breach the island. That causeway permanently transformed the island into a peninsula.
Today, Tyre is an insignificant, ruined peninsula. But 5,000 years ago, Tyre was the undisputed central banking house and financial capital of the entire planet. It filled the exact geopolitical and economic role that the City of London fills today. In fact, what operates out of the City of London in our modern era is the direct institutional and lineage continuation of what was established in Tyre five millennia ago.

God levels a terrifying accusation against the Prince (Nagid) of Tyre in Ezekiel 28: "Because your heart is lifted up, and you have said, 'I am a god, I sit on the throne of God in the heart of the seas,' yet you are a man and not God, though you set your heart as the heart of God..."
Look closely at the linguistic precision in the original Hebrew text. When scripture describes the human heart—the center of human decision-making, motivation, courage, and will—it uses the word Leb. But when scripture describes the heart and will of God, it uses the word Lebab.

Notice the difference: Lebab appends the root Ab, which means "Father." Leb represents creaturely will; Lebab represents the Father's absolute, supreme, creative will. The fundamental, foundational sin committed by the Prince of Tyre was elevating his creaturely, hybrid will (Leb) to equal the Father’s sovereign will (Lebab)—claiming equality with the Creator Himself.

This blasphemous self-exaltation is the exact signature of Lucifer's original fall. In Isaiah 14:12–15, the prophet details the five explicit "I wills" (Willenserklärungen) uttered by Lucifer in his heart:
"I will ascend into heaven..."
"I will exalt my throne above the stars of God..."
"I will sit on the mount of the congregation in the farthest north..."
"I will ascend above the heights of the clouds..."
"I will be like the Most High..."
God's immediate decree in response is swift: "Yet you shall be brought down to Sheol, to the lowest depths of the pit."

These five arrogant declarations of Lucifer's will form the five points of the five-pointed star—the pentagram. If you look across modern history, wherever a subversive, destructive, or far-left political movement arises, the five-pointed star is stamped upon its banners. Their symbolism betrays them every single time.

As Ezekiel 28 continues from verse 11 onward, the divine message undergoes a profound shift. The text transitions from addressing the earthly prince (Nagid) to addressing the overarching spiritual entity empowering him—the actual "King of Tyre" (Melech).
God says to this entity: "Son of Man, take up a lamentation for the King of Tyre, and say to him: 'Thus says the Lord God: You were the seal of perfection, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty. You were in Eden, the garden of God; every precious stone was your covering: Sardis, Topaz, Diamond, Chrysolite, Onyx, Jasper, Sapphire, Carbuncle, Emerald, and Gold... You were an anointed covering cherub; I established you; you were on the holy mountain of God; you walked back and forth in the midst of fiery stones. You were perfect in your ways from the day you were created, till iniquity was found in you.'"

This passage isn't describing an ordinary human king; it is identifying the spiritual archon himself—the covering cherub who adorned himself with ten precious stones in Eden before his fall. God explicitly outlines why this cherub fell: "Your heart was lifted up because of your beauty; you corrupted your wisdom for the sake of your splendor. Therefore I cast you to the ground; I laid you before kings, that they might gaze at you."

In psychological terms, this is the ultimate manifestation of moral narcissism. It is self-admiration escalating into toxic self-righteousness, which inevitably turns into malice and destruction.

We see this exact psychological dynamic embedded in classic fairy tales like Snow White (Schneewittchen). Consider the vivid color symbolism of Snow White: hair as black as ebony, skin as white as snow, lips as red as blood—the exact colors of the historic German Reich flag (black, white, and red). In the story, the evil stepmother stares into the mirror every day: "Mirror, mirror on the wall, who is the fairest of them all?" That mirror gazing is pure narcissism—self-reflection turned into self-worship. And what happens when that self-worship is threatened by an innocent soul? It immediately breeds murderous intent, leading to deception and a poisoned apple.

This narcissistic mirror-gazing is not limited to physical beauty. Millions of people look into their psychological mirrors every day and say, "Mirror, mirror on the wall, who is the smartest, the richest, the most powerful, or the most successful in the land?"

Look at Hollywood—an entire global culture built upon this exact demonic narcissism! The world worships "the rich, the famous, and the powerful." Satan recruits and entices his earthly followers using his primary currency triad: AMG—Ansehen (prestige/reputation), Macht (power), and Geld (money).

Satan does not merely pay this Tyrian money aristocracy with AMG; he is tied to them by ancient blood. The ruling financial caste that traces its roots back 5,000 years to Tyre shares physical bloodline continuity with the fallen angelic entities that fathered these hybrid lineages.

Let us look at how these Phoenicians expanded across the globe. The name "Phoenician" was not what they called themselves; it was a name given to them by the Greeks, derived from Phoenix—the Purpurschnecke (the purple predatory sea snail). This rare sea snail possessed a tiny gland from which an extraordinarily costly purple dye was extracted. Because harvesting it was so labor-intensive, purple fabric became the ultimate status symbol of exorbitant wealth and elite standing.

Operating from their capital in Tyre, these Phoenician Canaanites built a vast maritime empire designed to capture total economic control. They systematically occupied strategic choke points (Strangulationspunkte) across the Mediterranean basin. They seized control of the North African coastline, southern European shores, Sicily, Sardinia, and southern Spain. They fortified narrow maritime gateways like Gibraltar and Ceuta. They founded major trade colonies like Carthage, positioning themselves directly at the narrowest bottleneck of the Mediterranean Sea between Africa and Sicily.

From there, their maritime operations expanded up both sides of the Italian peninsula—establishing Venice on the Adriatic side and Genoa on the Tyrrhenian side. But they did not stop in the Mediterranean. They sailed their fleets through the Bosporus into the Black Sea, establishing lucrative trade networks with the Scythians (the ancestral predecessors of modern Russians) and the Khazars (Kassaren). Through these Black Sea trade routes, extensive intermarriage and bloodline blending occurred, particularly with the Khazar ruling elite.

Simultaneously, their trade fleets pushed westward into the Atlantic Ocean, sailing north to Britain to monopolize the rich tin and mineral mines of the British Isles. They even pushed across the Atlantic to establish early footholds in the Americas. Eventually, the command center of this ancient network migrated directly into what we know today as the City of London.

When you analyze the global financial hierarchy, you begin to understand the structure represented by the 13 steps of the pyramid on the back of the US dollar bill—the 13 ancient bloodline families. Modern commentators often talk about the Rothschild family as if they sit at the absolute pinnacle of global power. But historical context reveals a very different truth.

The Rothschilds amassed their vast fortune through financial deception and market manipulation surrounding the Battle of Waterloo in 1815, using that sudden wealth to buy their way into the City of London. But to the ancient 5,000-year-old Tyrian money lineages, the Rothschilds are viewed as mere upstarts (Emporkömmlinge)—nouveau riche newcomers who arrived yesterday. The true ruling families at the top of the pyramid have maintained their parasitic financial playbook for thousands of years.

What is the core mechanism of their control? It is the mathematical weapon of compound interest (Zinseszins).
Compound interest is structured so that the lender can mathematically never lose, while the borrowing population is guaranteed to be systematically impoverished over time. Because compound interest demands that the borrower return significantly more capital than was ever created or issued into circulation, the debtor is trapped in a mathematical impossibility. To meet these compound interest payments, debtor nations are forced to steal, plunder, and wage aggressive wars against their neighbors just to acquire the extra capital needed to service the debt.

This inherently creates a perpetual war economy. To wage war, rulers need armies. Therefore, bankers view human beings not as divine creations, but as financial assets—collateral to be pledged against loans. Rulers who borrowed gold from the Tyrian bankers pledged their military forces and entire populations as security. Human beings were dehumanized into financial instruments—reduced to Humankapital (human capital) and legal fictions (Persona). This legal conversion of a living soul into a financial asset is what history terms "civil death" (bürgerlicher Tod).

This is why finance and war have been inextricably linked for 5,000 years. Bankers lend gold to kings; kings pledge their citizens as soldiers; soldiers are sent to die in wars to conquer foreign wealth to pay back the interest.

When patriots today speak of dismantling the globalist cabal, we must understand the sheer historical depth of what we are confronting. This is not a political system that emerged a few decades ago; it is an deeply entrenched, 5,000-year-old parasitic caste that has fortified itself across millennia.

Now, keep this 5,000-year historical backdrop in mind and look at what Jesus Christ confronted when He walked the earth 2,000 years ago.
Consider His famous confrontation with the money changers in the Temple of Jerusalem. These were not small-time street vendors exchanging a few coins for local pilgrims. These money changers (Wechsler) were the high-level operational agents of this exact Tyrian banking caste!

The Temple in Jerusalem had been turned into an extraordinarily lucrative financial monopoly. Under religious law, Jews from all across the known world were required to travel to the Temple three times a year. Pilgrims arrived carrying dozens of different international currencies. The money changers held a total monopoly: they forced visiting pilgrims to exchange their foreign money into the official Temple currency at extortionate exchange rates, and then forced them to buy approved sacrificial animals at massively inflated prices. It was a massive, global money-generating engine.

This context explains why the ONLY instance in the entire New Testament where Jesus utilized physical force was against these money changers. He entered the Temple, fashioned a whip, overturned their tables, and dumped their stacks of gold and silver onto the stone floor. He treated their money like absolute dirt—chaos in their central bank! He didn't steal their coins; He scattered them across the ground to demonstrate that their financial god was worthless dust.

By doing this, Jesus struck directly at the heart of the ruling elite's revenue stream. The chief priests, Pharisees, and financial rulers did not plot to murder Jesus because He preached love and kindness; they plotted His execution because He posed an immediate, existential threat to their power, their prestige, and their money—their AMG!

Jesus was systematically dismantling every monopolistic control structure they used to enslave humanity:
He threatened the pharmaceutical industry (Pharmaindustrie): Jesus didn't sell pills, potions, or costly treatments. He healed every disease instantly and freely through divine authority. People lined up along the roads just so His passing shadow might fall across them, and they were instantly made whole. No pharmaceutical monopoly can survive a savior who heals for free.

He threatened food monopolies and artificial scarcity: When thousands gathered in the wilderness, Jesus took a few small loaves of bread and a couple of fish, blessed them, and multiplied them until everyone was filled—with twelve baskets of leftovers remaining! By creating absolute abundance out of nothing, He destroyed artificial scarcity, eliminated hunger, removed fear, and broke the need for debt.

Most fundamentally, Jesus exposed the massive inversion at the heart of all satanic religion.
Satanic religious systems—operating under a thousand different names, rituals, and deities throughout history—are inherently parasitic. Satan is spiritually bankrupt; therefore, his systems always demand that human beings bring sacrifices, pay tithes, offer gifts, and surrender money to feed a corrupt clerical class (Klerus).

Jesus completely inverted this dynamic. He revealed that the true Creator God is not a taker, but the ultimate Giver! God does not demand that impoverished humans enrich Him; He gives humanity everything they need for life. This is why Jesus taught us to pray: "Father in heaven, give us this day our daily bread."
Whenever you see a religious system that demands mandatory church taxes, constant financial extractions, and elaborate clerical hierarchies living in luxury off the labor of the people, you are looking at Satan's inverted system. The corrupt zionist and clerical elite of Jesus' day had completely hijacked the Law of Moses, converting it into a mechanism of financial exploitation. Jesus came as the Giver, dismantling their clerical parasite class—and for that, they had Him nailed to a cross.

Even today, this same system continues its psychological warfare against humanity through distorted religious iconography.
Look at how Jesus is presented to the public in church buildings and roadside shrines across the world. You constantly see the crucifix (Kruzifix). What does "crucifix" literally mean? Cruci-fix—fixed to the cross! They insist on depicting Jesus permanently locked in His moment of maximum physical weakness and death—a bloody, lifeless body pinned to a wooden frame. Or, alternatively, they depict Him as a helpless infant lying in a manger in Bethlehem.

This is a deliberate psychological operation (psy-op). By constantly fixating the public mind on Jesus as either an infant or a corpse, they carry out massive visual brainwashing. They condition humanity to perceive the Almighty Creator—the Supreme Judge who will return in glory—as weak, dead, and utterly powerless.
We saw a striking modern parallel to this exact psychological tactic just recently outside the European Parliament building in Strasbourg, where a grotesque statue was erected to mock Donald Trump. Why does the globalist system construct public monuments to ridicule and mock their opponents? I am not making a direct personal comparison between Donald Trump and Jesus Christ—they exist in entirely different realms—but the underlying psychological tactic is identical!

Whenever the satanic system feels its grip slipping, it resorts to public mockery, slander, and portraying its adversaries as foolish, weak, or defeated. They do this to mask their own terror. Mockery is not a sign of strength; it is a near-capitulation confession of fear!
Every crucifix that hangs in their institutions is ultimately their premature declaration of victory—a desperate attempt to reassure themselves that the King is still dead. But He did not remain on that cross, and He did not stay in that tomb! He rose 72 hours later, and He explicitly promised that He will return as the ultimate Judge of this world.

When He returns, this 5,000-year-old Tyrian system of debt, war, and chimeric deceit will face its final, absolute destruction. Stand firm, keep your eyes open, and stay grounded in the truth.
Until next time—all the best to you all!

text:
"The Christian ideal has not been tried and found wanting. It has been found difficult; and left untried." - G.K. Chesterton, What's Wrong with the World

Chesterton wrote that in 1910, and more than a century later it still lands like a door shutting.

We hear a good many people say they tried Christianity and it didn't work. Some of them mean it honestly. Some were hurt by people who carried the name, and none of the character, and that hurt deserves to be taken seriously rather than argued with.

But Chesterton's point is sharper than an argument. Most of the time the way of Jesus wasn't tested and found to fail. It was looked at, understood just well enough to see what it would cost, and quietly put back on the shelf.

Love your enemies. Forgive more times than you can count. Give without keeping a ledger. Tell the truth when the truth is expensive. None of that has ever failed. It has only ever been hard.

He called that chapter "The Unfinished Temple," and I can't think of a better picture of most of our lives. The foundation is poured. A few walls are up. Then the building stopped, somewhere around the part that required something we didn't want to hand over, and we'vebeen holding services in the half-built nave
ever since and calling it home.

Jesus never hid the cost, which is one of the most beautifully honest things about Him: "For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it?" (Luke 14:28)

He isn't trying to frighten anyone off. He is telling the truth about construction. Discipleship is a building project, not a weekend visit.

And here is the mercy in it. The building was never meant to depend on your strength alone. The One who laid the foundation is the One who promised to finish what He started.

So pick up the tool you set down. Make the phone call. Offer the apology. Open the Bible you've been meaning to open. Go to the hard conversation you keep moving to next week.

It hasn't been tried and found wanting.

Keep building.

Happy Indigenous Peoples' Day!
This day highlights the ongoing civil rights, cultural contributions, and persistence of Indigenous communities despite centuries of violence, displacement, and forced assimilation. The idea was first proposed at a United Nations conference in 1977 to address discrimination against Natives and South Dakota became the first state to replace Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples’ Day officially celebrating it in 1990.
📣 3 ways to honor Indigenous Peoples’ Day
✨(1) Educate Yourself & Amplify Indigenous Voices: Learn about Indigenous communities in the U.S. and their local tribal histories.
• Learn Local History: Research the specific Native nations land you live on or visit.
In Massachusetts, long before European colonization and ethnic cleansing, this land was home to tens of thousands of Native Peoples from many tribes and nations. Some of these prominent tribes include the Massachusett, the Pokantoket (or Wampanoag), the Nipmuc, the Pawtucket (or Pennacook), the Agawam, the Mahican, the Naumkeag and the Pocumtuck.
Visit https://t.co/iZVRB0CRU6 to learn more about the Indigenous territories, treaties, and languages spoken in your state.
• Diversify Media: Read books, listen to podcasts, watch films and engage in various forms of media produced and led by Indigenous authors, artists, journalists and educators. Be sure to also follow Indigenous activists on social media.
Avoid Erasure and Stereotypes: Remove anti-Indigenous language, redface, and harmful sports mascots from your lexicon and community spaces.
✨(2) Celebrate: Join marches and museum programs to honor Native American history and culture.

text:
Gotta love AI - ✅ 1. If Kelsey Mitchell leaves Indiana, she cannot receive a Supermax from another team
A supermax in the WNBA is only available to a player from her current team, and only if that team uses the core designation or otherwise has the contractual rights to offer her the top tier.

A new team cannot offer a supermax to an incoming free agent. This is because the supermax is tied to team-controlled rights, not to the player’s league-wide status.
So yes: if she leaves the Fever, the supermax tier disappears as an option.

This is consistent with the fact that Mitchell’s 2026 supermax was only possible because Indiana cored her and offered the one‑year $1.4M deal.

✅ 2. Indiana cannot execute a “supermax sign‑and‑trade”

A sign‑and‑trade cannot include a supermax because:
A supermax can only be signed to stay with the current team.

Once you sign a supermax, you cannot be traded as part of that signing — the CBA does not allow a team to sign a player to a supermax for the purpose of immediately trading her.

A sign‑and‑trade requires the player to sign a new contract with the receiving team’s cap structure. That receiving team cannot legally offer supermax dollars.

Therefore:

✔ A supermax cannot be used in a sign‑and‑trade

✔ The Fever cannot “supermax‑and‑trade” her
✔ The only way she earns supermax money is by staying in Indiana
This aligns with the structure of her 2026 deal: Indiana used the core designation to lock in the supermax for one year, but once she hits 2027 free agency, she re-enters the market and other teams can pursue her — but only at non‑supermax levels.
🔍 Why this is true under the CBA

The WNBA’s supermax is:
Team‑specific

Rights‑specific (core or matching rights)

Not portable

Not eligible for sign‑and‑trade

This is different from the NBA, where supermax rules are tied to player accolades and tenure. In the WNBA, the supermax is simply the highest salary tier a team can offer its own player under its rights.

text:
Before becoming a national star, Caitlin Clark faced a choice common among aspiring basketball players: whether to leave her home state for a place with a more thriving basketball program.
Yet, Clark’s career remained deeply rooted in Iowa.
It was not always an easy choice. For years, her profile in the Iowa basketball community far eclipsed her recognition across the rest of the country.
Nevertheless, Clark persisted in building her career right there.
And when her big break finally came, she did not need to leave Iowa to achieve it.
One often-overlooked aspect is why Clark chose to stay when leaving seemed like the smarter career move.
She had found something in Iowa that she was unwilling to trade for better basketball prospects—and years later, that decision proved far more pivotal to her breakthrough than it initially appeared.
The reason Clark stayed—along with the unique value Iowa offered her, something larger basketball programs could not provide—stands as one of the most remarkable elements of her journey to success.

Where the mountains meet the sea, Okitsu reveals the timeless beauty of Japan’s Tōkaidō — sailing boats drift across Suruga Bay as pine trees frame the coastal landscape. 🌊⛵🌲

『Okitsu』
『興津』

From Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō
Artist: Utagawa Hiroshige
No.: 18
Publisher: Jukakudō, Maruya Seijirō
Date: 1848–1850

Okitsu was a post station along the historic Tōkaidō road, where the coastline, mountain slopes, and sea shaped the journey of travelers.

Hiroshige captures the harmony between land and water, with sailing vessels adding movement to the tranquil scenery. The print offers a glimpse of the landscapes that made the Tōkaidō journey so memorable.

text:
🚨 #FACTCHECK: Nigel Farage on Burnham, Russia and Brexit

‘Mirror, mirror, on the wall, whose claims stand up after all?’

I’m a retired academic, media literate, and equipped with critical thinking skills, so I have time to do this quickly and accurately.

Earlier today, Nigel Farage called Prime Minister Andy Burnham “a liar” over his claim that Russia interfered in the 2016 EU referendum. Here is how Farage’s statements hold up against the record.

In an interview with The Rest Is Politics  podcast, released on 12 October but widely reported the day before, Burnham said that on taking office in July he asked whether Russia had interfered in the 2016 referendum, and was given “the clear answer that yes there was.” He did not say how Russia interfered and did not publish any evidence.

This morning, Farage held a press conference in Dover, Kent, to launch Reform UK’s asylum plans. LBC’s Emma Corr asked whether Burnham’s claim tainted the result, and how Farage felt about having potentially benefited from possible Russian interference. He later repeated several of his claims in an interview with GB News.

The exchange between Corr and Farage is available on YouTube from 1:00:07: https://t.co/zJMuAlHXdx

1. “The prime minister is a liar. Yes, a liar.”

Verdict: Unsupported.

Lying means knowingly saying something false. Burnham reported advice he says he received on entering No 10. That advice has not been made public, so his claim is unverified, and critics are entitled to say so. Nothing Farage cited shows that Burnham knew it to be untrue. At most, Farage offered evidence that the claim is unproven.

2. “Boris Johnson, when he became foreign secretary, one of the first questions he asked was, ‘Was there seen to be Russian interference in the referendum campaign?’ And the answer was no.”

Verdict: Misleading.

I could find no public record of this exchange. Johnson’s recorded public position was more qualified. In Moscow in December 2017, Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov said Johnson had confirmed Russia had not interfered in the referendum. Johnson interrupted him: “Not successfully.” He went on to say that Russian attempts to interfere in British elections and the referendum, whatever they may have been, had not succeeded. His position was that attempts may have been made and had failed, which is a different claim from “no”.

The premise that anyone checked is also doubtful. Parliament’s Intelligence and Security Committee (ISC) published its Russia Report in July 2020. It found that the government “had not seen or sought evidence of successful interference” in UK democratic processes. It called for an intelligence assessment of the referendum, and the government refused.

In 2019, BuzzFeed reported two anonymous sources saying British intelligence had found no evidence of Russian meddling in the referendum. That claim was unverified, and the ISC’s report the following year said the government had not sought such evidence.

3. Stephen Doughty “rowed it back and said even if there was some, it made no difference.”

Verdict: Misrepresents the minister.

Doughty, a Foreign Office minister, did narrow Burnham’s claim during Monday morning’s broadcast interviews. He told LBC that Russia had attempted to interfere in the vote but had not succeeded, and made the same point to Sky News. He also said Burnham had been making a broader point about Russian attempts to interfere in democratic events in the UK and across Europe.

On the @BBC Today programme, which Farage named, Doughty spoke of Russian attempts to interfere in a range of democratic processes. He cited the jailing of former Reform UK Wales leader Nathan Gill for taking bribes to promote pro-Kremlin narratives.

Farage’s summary distorts this. “Even if there was some” turns Doughty’s acknowledgement of attempts into a hypothetical. Farage followed it with the words “There was no Russian interference,” and in his later GB News interview (see 10) he attributed that denial to Doughty himself. I found no report of Doughty’s interviews containing those words, or anything to that effect. Doughty said Russia tried to interfere.

4. “There was no Russian interference… And the Russia hoax has run all the way through this.”

Verdict: Not supported by the evidence.

No official finding says there was no interference. The government’s position since 2020 has been narrower: “We have seen no evidence of successful interference in the EU Referendum.” The ISC noted open-source studies pointing to anti-EU content on the Russian state outlets RT and Sputnik, and to the use of bots and trolls, as evidence of attempts to influence the campaign. It criticised the government for not investigating.

The defensible position is that attempts at influence were plausibly documented, their effect was never assessed, and no public evidence shows they changed the result. “No interference” and “hoax” both go well beyond that. The same standard applies to Burnham, whose “clear answer” rests on advice the public has not seen.

5. Arron Banks “was severely libelled over this. But in the end … [he] won in the high court.”

Verdict: False.

Banks sued the journalist Carole Cadwalladr over a 2019 TED Talk and a tweet. He lost in the High Court in June 2022, where the judge held that Cadwalladr’s public interest defence covered the talk. In February 2023, the Court of Appeal found partly in his favour, on one of his three grounds of appeal. It ruled that the defence lapsed for the talk’s continued publication after 29 April 2020, the date of an Electoral Commission statement clearing Banks. It upheld the dismissal of his claim over the tweet. Cadwalladr was ordered to pay £35,000 in damages and 60% of Banks’s High Court costs.

The case also had no bearing on whether Russia interfered in the referendum. It concerned Cadwalladr’s statement about Banks and “his covert relationship with the Russian Government.”

6. “I don’t think our growth figures are anything to write home about. But … they’re a damn sight better than France and Germany and Italy.”

Verdict: Accurate for this year, but selective over the longer term, and beside the point.

On current figures Farage has a case. In the second quarter of 2026, UK GDP grew by 0.5%, against 0.3% in Germany and zero in France. The IMF’s July forecasts put the UK third in the G7 for 2026, at 1%, behind the US (2.3%) and Canada (1.1%). That is ahead of Germany (0.7%), France and Japan (both 0.6%) and Italy (0.5%). The OECD’s September forecasts placed the UK joint second in the G7, level with Germany at 1.1%.

The longer view is less flattering. Between the end of 2019 and the second quarter of 2026, UK GDP grew by 6.2%, behind the eurozone as a whole (7.6%) and far behind the US (15.6%), though well ahead of Germany (1.9%, the lowest in the G7).

By naming France, Germany and Italy, Farage compared the UK with three of Europe’s weaker performers, while the eurozone overall has grown faster since the pandemic. Headline growth has also been flattered by rapid population growth. In late 2024, the Resolution Foundation found UK GDP per head still below its end-2019 level, although per-head growth picked up to 0.6% in the first quarter of 2026.

More importantly, none of these comparisons answers Burnham’s claim. Whether Brexit has done “more harm than good” depends on how the UK compares with a UK that stayed in the EU. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) assumes Brexit will leave UK trade around 15% lower in the long run, and potential productivity around 4% lower, than if the UK had remained. In 2024 it said these assumptions appeared “broadly on track.”

Some economists, including Julian Jessop, a former chief economist and head of the Brexit unit at the free-market Institute of Economic Affairs, dispute these estimates.

Even so, the official forecaster’s central view is that Brexit carries a long-run cost, and growth rankings, whether flattering or not, do not settle the question.

7. “If you even look at trade numbers, the increase in trade since Brexit…”

Verdict: Partly accurate, but selective.

Total UK exports have grown since the referendum. Briefings for Britain, a pro-Brexit research group using ONS data, puts total exports in 2025 at 5% above 2019 in real terms. That growth has come from services. The House of Commons Library reports that UK services exports to the EU were 28% above their 2019 level in real terms in 2025. However, goods exports to the EU were 14% below it, having fallen in real terms in each of 2023, 2024 and 2025.

Not all of that fall is due to Brexit, but post-Brexit barriers fall mainly on goods, and goods trade with the EU is where the decline shows. The overall total obscures it.

8. Brexit has brought “some level of inconvenience… showing a passport, filling in a form,” amounting to “mild inconveniences.”

Verdict: Understatement.

Farage conceded there was more inconvenience “for people like Alcaline,” a Kent road haulage firm based near Hythe, but described it as “showing a passport, filling in a form.” The evidence suggests that undersells the effect, particularly for firms moving goods across the Channel.

In March 2024 the OBR reported that UK goods trade was around 10% below 2019 levels and growing well behind other advanced economies, while services trade had grown more strongly than in the rest of the G7. The OBR attributed the gap partly to post-Brexit barriers falling mainly on goods.

Brexit is not the only cause of the 14% real-terms fall in goods exports to the EU, but official forecasters attribute part of it to post-Brexit trade barriers, which go well beyond passports and forms. Farage’s answer also merges two separate issues: control of migration, and the trade frictions that come from leaving the single market and customs union.

9. Burnham is “looking forward to sitting down with Marine Le Pen or the AfD”

Verdict: Speculation, contrary to the record.

Farage offered no basis for this. In the interview that prompted the row, Burnham cited the German chancellor’s view that the AfD were linked to, and possibly funded by, Russia. He presented the party as a threat to European democracy.

10. The GB News version

Verdict: False.

In an interview with GB News later that day, Farage said Doughty, “being interviewed on the BBC this morning, disavowed it and said no, there was no Russian interference, it didn’t affect anything.” The “even if there was some” qualification had gone, leaving a flat denial attributed to the minister. Doughty’s reported position was that Russia attempted to interfere but did not succeed, which confirms attempted interference.

Farage also presented Johnson and Doughty together as evidence that “both Labour and Conservative camps” reject Burnham’s claim. Neither man said there was no interference. Johnson’s recorded words in 2017 were “Not successfully.” Doughty said Russia had tried and failed. What both rejected was the narrower claim that interference succeeded, which is also the extent of the official government position since 2020.

Conclusion

Farage’s sharpest claims are his weakest. Nothing presented shows that Burnham lied.

Johnson’s record says “not successfully” rather than “no”. The minister Farage cited acknowledged Russian attempts. In Dover, Farage turned that acknowledgement into a hypothetical, and on GB News into a flat denial. Banks did not win in the High Court.

Farage is on firmer ground on recent growth rankings and on total exports, though neither settles whether Brexit has helped or harmed the UK, and goods trade with the EU tells a different story.

Burnham, for his part, has made a significant claim without publishing the evidence behind it. The assessment the ISC recommended six years ago would serve the public better than either man’s certainty.

Finally, it is worth measuring Farage by his own yardstick. Farage called the British prime minister a liar. 

The evidence he offered went only to whether Burnham was wrong, not to whether he knew it. If being wrong, or being unable to prove a claim, is enough to make someone a liar, the same test can be applied to Farage.

By that standard, his answer in Dover contained five “lies”: that Johnson was told there was no interference; that Doughty conceded only that any interference “made no difference”; that there was no Russian interference; that the affair was a “hoax”; and that Arron Banks “won in the high court.”

On GB News he added a sixth, that “both Labour and Conservative camps” deny any interference, and repeated three of the others.

That makes six distinct claims, and nine in all, across two appearances in a single day. The row began over one claim by Burnham.

The fairer test, and the one this fact check applies, is that lying requires knowing a statement to be false. By that measure, nobody can say Farage lied, any more than he can say it of Burnham.

But on the evidence, Burnham’s claim remains unproven, while at least one of Farage’s, about his friend’s libel case, is plainly false on the public record.
