text:
Border & Immigration

He made the border a real border again. In a matter of months, Trump reduced illegal border crossings to their lowest level in half a century. Catch-and-release is finished. The wall is going up and even being expanded, “Remain in Mexico” is back, and the Administration reduced releases into the country by an incredible 99.9 percent.

He reversed mass migration. America recorded negative net migration in 2025 for the first time in at least half a century. So far, nearly 3 million illegal aliens have left the country, whether voluntarily or involuntarily: more than 675,000 forcibly deported and the rest “self-deported.” Many of those self-deportations were facilitated by the President’s innovative program to offer plane tickets and cash bonuses for illegals to leave, not only incentivizing good behavior but significantly reducing the cost of deportations. Citizenship and the law actually mean something again.

He signed the Laken Riley Act — and required detention of criminal illegal aliens. Named for an innocent girl murdered by an illegal alien, the Laken Riley Act requires federal authorities to detain illegals arrested for theft, burglary, shoplifting, assaulting police, or any crime causing death or serious injury. It also lets states sue officials who refuse to enforce it. Laken Riley should still be alive. This law will prevent tragedies like hers.

History’s biggest drop in violent crime, and the lowest violent crime rate in 126 years. According to FBI data, violent crime in America dropped an incredible 9.7 percent in 2025 — the largest one-year decline in history. Murder fell 18.1 percent, robbery fell 18.5 percent. And America’s violent crime rate is its lowest since 1900. This is what happens when you put the National Guard on the streets in crime-ridden blue cities: fewer victims, safer streets, and better futures for America’s poorest.

Economy, Taxes & Industry
5. He made the 2017 tax cuts permanent…and better. The One Big Beautiful Bill locked in the largest tax cut in modern history, including the doubled standard deduction, the expanded Child Tax Credit, and 100 percent expensing for factories and equipment. It also delivered No Tax on Tips, No Tax on Overtime, an abolition of most taxes on Social Security benefits, and major relief for seniors. Every Democrat voted no. With the 2017 act set to expire in December 2025, that would have resulted in the largest tax hike in American history.
He repealed 129 regulations for every new one. In fiscal 2025, federal agencies finalized 646 deregulatory actions and just five regulatory actions: 129-to-1, and in nearly every case, the “one” was to repeal the others! OIRA says the savings exceeded those of Trump’s entire first term. That is more freedom, lower costs, and less bureaucratic sabotage. Of these, the crown jewel was the repeal of Obama’s 2009 “Endangerment Finding”, the legal foundation for the Green New Scam’s vehicle mandates. EPA calls it the largest deregulatory action in American history and estimates that by itself, it will save Americans more than $1.3 trillion. Trump also killed the federal EV mandate, restored Americans’ freedom to buy the cars and trucks they actually want, and even eliminated the incentives behind the almost universally hated start-stop button.

He secured $18 trillion in announced investment commitments. That’s nearly two-thirds the size of the entire American economy, building American factories, chip plants, data centers, energy projects, steel mills, shipyards, and supply chains employing American workers. Apple, Meta, NVIDIA, Micron, Hyundai, U.S. Steel, Ford, Taiwan Semiconductor, and many corporations and sovereign wealth funds are betting big on Trump’s America. No President has ever done anything remotely like it. And it’s just getting started.

He made “reshoring” and “reindustrialization” real, not a slogan. Ford is moving Lincoln production out of China. Toyota is shifting Tacoma production from Mexico to Texas. GM, Honda, Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis, and others are expanding U.S. production. The capital equipment pouring into the country is the machinery that’s building the growing boom.

He replaced lopsided trade deals with balanced, reciprocal trade. Trump used tariffs as leverage to reverse 80 years of lopsided trade deals that favored everyone but America, and to win new or improved agreements with trading partners accounting for more than half of global GDP. Those agreements open foreign markets, attack non-tariff barriers, defend strategic industries, and make it more profitable to build in America than to export American jobs.

He shifted global energy dominance from the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of America. Once the world’s largest energy importer — “exporting” $700 billion a year to our enemies — America now outproduces Saudi Arabia and Russia combined. The U.S. is also setting new records in oil, natural gas, and LNG exports, becoming the first country ever to export more than 100 million metric tons of LNG in a year. Trump also opened land, accelerated permits, expanded pipelines and export terminals, and made American energy a tool for prosperity and peace.

After four decades of nuclear paralysis, Trump brought five new reactors online in a single year. For more than 40 years, not one new privately developed non-light-water reactor reached criticality in America. Trump ordered at least three by July 4, 2026. DOE delivered four by the deadline, then a fifth just one month later. Decades of zero. One Trump summer: five. That is a genuine nuclear renaissance.

Government, Courts & Bureaucracy
12. He broke the Deep State’s power to defy the elected branches. In Trump v. Slaughter, the Supreme Court ruled for the first time in 90 years that Article 2, Section 1 is still part of the Constitution: the President may fire subordinate officials in the executive branch, overturning the 1935 precedent that insulated “independent” agencies from voters’ control. Ever wonder why elections often seem to change nothing? How about one President and 5,000 political appointees vs. 2.8 million unfireable, unaccountable bureaucrats? THAT is the “Deep State”. Trump then made that victory real. For the first time in a century, all policy-making bureaucrats can now be fired for misconduct, incompetence, or defying lawful directives. The permanent bureaucracy no longer gets to veto the voters.

He ended nationwide injunction abuse. In Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court sharply limited nationwide injunctions. A single, local, district judge should not be able to block a national policy for everyone, everywhere; and yet that’s exactly what they’ve done, nonstop, ever since Trump (and only Trump) took office in 2017. In restricting that unconstitutional power, the Court kneecapped the Black Robe Bureaucracy’s favorite tool of unlawful judicial supremacy.
He shut down USAID as a left-wing slush fund and shadow government. USAID had become a taxpayer-funded machine for exporting abortion, gender ideology, censorship, and left-wing politics. It had a bigger budget than the CIA and the State Department combined, absolutely no accountability whatsoever, and a penchant for overthrowing governments. Trump terminated it — completely — and moved real humanitarian aid under the State Department. Immediately, seven socialist Latin American governments lost re-election. Coincidence?

He shrank Federal employment to its lowest level in 60 years. From a high under Biden, the federal workforce is now its smallest since 1966. Workforce reductions, agency closures, and spending cancellations mean fewer bureaucrats paid to resist the voters. What’s more, when Biden left office, 94 percent of federal employees “worked” from home. The Trump administration cracked down: as Elon Musk put it, “you can work from the office or you can pretend to work somewhere else.”

He expelled DEI from the federal government. Trump eliminated federal DEI offices and barred race- and sex-based preferences across the executive branch. Government hiring and contracting are returning to merit and equality under the law, ending the grotesque Democrat idea that “fighting discrimination” requires the federal government to discriminate.

Social, Cultural & Domestic Policy
17. He delivered sweeping pro-life reform. In his first term, Trump delivered the judges that overturned the abominable Roe v. Wade. Hardly anyone believed it could be done, or that Trump would do it. But he did, and a half-century nightmare finally ended. Since returning to office, Trump has enforced the Hyde Amendment prohibiting the use of federal funds to pay for abortions, reinstated and expanded the Mexico City Policy prohibiting federal funding of foreign abortions, ended federal fetal-tissue research, strengthened conscience protections, protected Medicaid from funding large abortion providers, and pardoned 23 pro-life activists prosecuted by Biden’s weaponized Justice Department. He’s also done everything within the Executive Branch’s power to defund Planned Parenthood. It would be nice if Congress did likewise. No President has ever done more to protect life. No one.

He got men out of women’s sports, and restored biological reality to federal policy. The United States government once again officially recognizes two sexes: male and female. Trump ended federal support for the chemical and surgical gender mutilation of children, stopped taxpayer funding of such irreversible abominations, and forced more than three dozen health systems to end or suspend their programs as well. Trump also enforced Title IX as written: women and girls deserve their own teams, trophies, scholarships, and locker rooms. The NCAA and other athletic organizations changed their rules in response. After years of Democrats doing everything they could to destroy women’s sports and ruin girls’ lives, Trump’s administration protects women and girls again.

He enacted America’s first nationwide school-choice program — and launched Trump Accounts. As part of the President’s One Big Beautiful Bill, Trump enacted America’s first-ever nationwide school choice program. The new Education Freedom Tax Credit helps fund scholarships for tuition, books, and other educational costs. That’s on top of the new Trump Accounts, which give every child a tax-advantaged stake in America’s future, including a $1,000 federal seed for eligible newborns. Parents gain power. Bureaucracies lose it. And children learn first-hand about free markets and future orientation.
He targeted anti-Christian bias and discrimination. Trump created the White House Faith Office, Religious Liberty Commission, and Task Force to Eradicate Anti-Christian Bias. He restored conscience protections and made clear that Christians do not surrender their First Amendment rights merely by entering public life.

Foreign Policy, Defense & National Security
21. He forced NATO to stop freeloading and increase defense spending by 250 percent. For decades, wealthy European governments underfunded their militaries, effectively sending America the bill and using American taxpayers to subsidize their bloated welfare states. Trump forced NATO to replace its old two-percent-of-GDP spending target with an enormous five percent by 2035. Allied spending is rising, American defense orders are soaring, and Europe is becoming a partner instead of a dependent.

He drove China out of the Caribbean. China spent years building strategic beachheads at both ends of the Panama Canal, in Cuba, and in Maduro’s Venezuela. Trump forced Panama out of Belt and Road, expanded American security access around the Canal, and captured Maduro, who now sits in a New York jail cell awaiting trial. Beijing’s planned encirclement of the United States collapsed. The Monroe Doctrine is back. Call it the Donroe Doctrine.

He brokered eight peace deals in just eight months. In eight months, Trump brokered peace in eight conflicts spanning four continents, including wars that had gone on for as much as 40 years. It’s a record unmatched by any other President.

He launched and funded Golden Dome, the first-ever true missile defense for the U.S. population. Ronald Reagan dreamed of making nuclear missiles obsolete through his Strategic Defense Initiative. Today, Trump is actually building it: a layered homeland shield with space-based sensors and interceptors, conventional defenses, and new technologies including microwave systems to destroy drone swarms and directed-energy weapons (yes, lasers) that can replace an $11 million missile with $2 of electricity. Congress has funded the initial $25 billion, with far more on the way once it passes the NDAA this fall. Better a shield than a sword.
He restored the warrior ethos — and reversed the recruiting crisis. After years of missed targets under Biden, every active military component met or exceeded its 2025 recruiting goal. Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth refocused the newly renamed Department of War on actually winning wars, while pouring resources into shipbuilding, munitions, drones, missile defense, and America’s atrophied industrial base. Young Americans once again believe their Commander-in-Chief is worth serving. And they’re showing up en masse.

text:
Most private pensions currently are facing underfunding as well. It's a chronic problem with retirement defined benefit plans.

The biggest difference truly is the difference of having a government vs. private company as a sponsor. It takes much more for a government to bankrupt and reach a point that entitlements must be reduced, compared to a private company. Additionally, a government has far more capacity to take on debt than a private company.

The actuarial assumptions leading to debt happened back in the 80s and 90s, not any time recently. People are living longer, at higher standards of living, and contributions over the years did not continue to rise at the rate assumed. Coming in 40+ years later gives you a lot of hindsight to wag your finger, but no real solutions.

Plan rules aren't going to allow current actuarial assumptions to adjust contributions enough to avoid debt. Even if they are increasing contributions by the highest possible amount each year, debt will be required for the shortfall. 

If California wants to reform this system, they need to offer payouts to the pensioners, and convert their Plan to one that does not create a post employment obligation the way a pension will.

text:
A quiet week in the Mexicali corridor is not a calm one.

Nothing moved this week. The pieces from August are still on the board.

The advisory
State Department keeps Baja California at Level 3, Reconsider Travel. U.S. government staff still may not enter most of the Mexicali Valley.

On August 25, the U.S. mission suspended its own activities and travel in Mexicali over threat information. A State Department spokesperson told The Hill the suspension was lifted and work resumed. President Sheinbaum said the threat was never confirmed.

What came before it
On August 19, federal forces searched a house in Hacienda del Bosque, Mexicali, on a judge's warrant built with DEA information. Security Secretary García Harfuch said they seized 120 kilos of fentanyl pills, more than 4 million doses, and tied the house to Los Rusos.

The alert came six days later. No official has linked the two. The timing is the only thread on paper.

San Luis Río Colorado
On August 7, Guardia Nacional and AMIC agents rescued kidnap victims at a house in ejido Independencia. Sonora prosecutors say three men are now held for trial on aggravated kidnapping and criminal association. The victims, prosecutors say, belonged to a rival group. A follow up search turned up 10 firearms and 1,147 rounds. The three are presumed innocent.

The man at the top
Juan José Ponce Félix, El Ruso, is still a fugitive. The State Department still offers up to $5 million. The FBI calls Los Rusos the main armed wing of La Mayiza.

On Sunday, federal forces in Acapulco arrested a man called El Junior. García Harfuch says he led a cell linked to a group also called Los Rusos. Whether that is the same network as Ponce Félix's has not been said.

Bottom line
Advisory steady. Threat unconfirmed. Leader at large. Two names, one label, and no one on record connecting them.

text:
Maci 💋 My POV
October 12, 2026
Denver, Colorado

Good morning! ☕❤️

We're back in Denver. Edgar has meetings, Jenny has her laptop open, and I have a list of things needing my attention that I would very much like to ignore.

Mia and Jack have gone shopping.

I'm beginning to think those two have discovered the perfect arrangement. We work, they shop. 

I miss Breckenridge already. Especially those beautiful aspens!

Yesterday was our last full day in the mountains, and we managed to squeeze quite a bit into it.

We started with Mass.

All five of us walked into town. The morning was chilly, the mountains were gorgeous, and I kept stopping to photograph the golden aspens.

Edgar finally asked whether I intended to arrive before the final blessing.

Patience, sir. God made those trees, too. 😂

The church was small, quaint, and much more traditional than what we're accustomed to around San Diego. Everyone was dressed for Sunday. Dresses, jackets, pressed trousers. Even the children looked like they'd received very specific instructions before leaving home.

I glanced at Jenny, then down at my own outfit.

We weren't dressed inappropriately, but we were certainly more California than Colorado.

Mass was lovely. Quiet, reverent, and personal. I love visiting Catholic churches when we travel. Different buildings, different congregations, but the same prayers and the same Eucharist.

I noticed Edgar during one of the prayers, head bowed, hands folded. He has this beautiful stillness about him in church. I reached over and rested my hand on his for a moment.

After Mass, we stayed for coffee and donuts.

I think half the congregation wanted to know where we were from!

"California."

"Oh! Visiting?"

"Yes."

"How do you all know each other?"

Well, there's a question. 

Jenny smiled. "We're friends. I also work for Edgar and his fiancée."

Perfectly handled, sweetheart.

One woman asked whether we'd enjoyed the mountains. I told her Edgar had surprised us with Breckenridge because I'd wanted to see the aspens and snow.

She looked at him.

"Well, isn't he thoughtful!"

I smiled.

"You have no idea."

We wandered down Main Street afterward, taking pictures and peeking into a few shops.

Jenny and Mia were having a wonderful time.

Jack was beginning to question his decision to accompany four people who considered every storefront a photographic opportunity.

"Are we done?"

"Almost."

Ten minutes later...

"Now?"

Jenny informed him that patience was an attractive quality.

He said he'd been attractive long enough. lol

Edgar was considerably more cooperative. He took pictures, posed wherever we put him, carried our things, and never complained.

We had an early lunch because I was determined to get another hike in before the Broncos game.

Lunch was quick. VERY quick.

I think Edgar was still finishing his coffee when I announced we needed to leave.

He looked at his watch.

"You're the one who wanted to stop for pictures."

"And I'd like to thank you for your cooperation."

Jenny laughed.

By 12:30, we were on the trail.

Ninety minutes among those gorgeous aspens!

Golden leaves beneath our feet, evergreens surrounding us, and snow on the higher mountains.

Mia and Jack spent much of the hike holding hands. When the trail narrowed, he'd walk ahead and offer his hand whenever she needed it.

They're terribly sweet together.

Jenny and I walked together for part of it, talking about her position and the people she'd met at the zoo.

Jenny asked whether he ever slows down.

"Of course," I told her. "You just have to give him something more interesting to do."

She laughed. Then it hit her what I just said...

A few minutes later, Edgar caught up with us.

"What are you two discussing?"

"Your management style."

He smiled and kept walking.

There's something else I need to say.

---

I made a mistake and I upset Spencer.

Queen, I'm sorry again. I love you. ❤️

That's all I want to say about it here.

---

We made it back to the cabin just in time for the Broncos game.

GOOD HEAVENS!

Denver beat the Chargers 23–17, and that fourth quarter nearly killed me.

Jack was explaining plays, Jenny was questioning calls, and Mia was cheering enthusiastically.

Edgar enjoyed every minute.

Sunday night was much quieter than Saturday. A few restaurants were busy, shops were closing, and the streets had that lovely mountain-town feeling.

We walked, talked, and enjoyed having nowhere particular to be.

Back at the cabin, someone suggested a movie.

The cabin has an enormous theater room with a massive television and glass doors opening toward the hot tub. You can even angle the screen so you can watch from outside.

Jack considered this an important architectural achievement.

We made popcorn and settled inside.

Then came the question.

"What movie?"

I asked the two girls.

Jack immediately said, "Barbie."

I turned toward him.

"BARBIE?"

"What? It's a good movie."

I looked at Mia.

She was grinning.

Edgar reached for the popcorn.

And that settled it. 😂

We watched Barbie.

Jack actually had opinions about the movie, and he wasn't the least bit embarrassed about sharing them. I rather like that about him.

As the evening went on, people gradually started heading to bed.

Edgar had been rubbing his shoulder and upper back. He'd twisted a muscle earlier, and it was bothering him.

Jenny noticed.

"Want me to work on that?"

He agreed, and I joined them.

She's quite good at massage.

After several minutes, Edgar finally relaxed.

Jenny glanced at me and smiled.

"I think we've got it."

He thanked us both.

I teased him about having an entire hot tub outside and still needing two women to sort out one stubborn muscle.

He smiled.

"I wasn't complaining."

Of course he wasn't. 😂

---

We were up early this morning for the drive back to Denver. Edgar had work waiting, so all five of us came down together.

Jenny and I are working with him today, while Mia and Jack have taken advantage of their freedom to explore the shops.

Mia just sent me a picture.

Jack is holding four shopping bags.

He's smiling in this one. Progress! 

I keep thinking about yesterday's walk through the aspens.

I wish Spencer had been there.

There are things I'd like to tell her, but I'd rather do that in person, somewhere quiet, without a phone between us.

For now, I have work to do, Jenny is waiting for me, and Edgar is probably wondering where I've disappeared to.

I should go find them.

Happy Monday, everyone. ❤️

Maci 💋

text:
Apple is becoming a company I no longer trust with my privacy or personal safety. It's moving towards technology capable of processing our private conversations and surroundings, despite spending years convincing customers that privacy was one of the biggest reasons to buy its products.

Their relationships with governments has only grown stronger over the past few years.

I think Motorola's partnership with GrapheneOS could become one of the most significant developments in the mobile industry since the introduction of the first iPhone.

I founded a telecoms testing company in 2002 and was Head of Testing for O2 in the UK. Every product and service went through my team, including every mobile device O2 brought to market. I signed the NDA for the first iPhone launch outside the US on behalf of O2 when my team was responsible for testing and certifying it.

I lived through the years when Nokia, Motorola, Samsung, Sony Ericsson, BlackBerry and others competed to introduce new devices, features and capabilities. It all started with picture messaging (MMS).

Competition was relentless. Then Apple launched the iPhone and fundamentally changed the industry. BlackBerry eventually disappeared from the consumer smartphone market, Nokia lost its dominance, and Apple and Google came to control the operating systems used by almost every smartphone.

We've spent years choosing between iOS and Android, which effectively means choosing between Apple and Google. Samsung dominates most of the premium Android market, but its phones still rely on Google's OS.

GrapheneOS offers something different. It's an open source mobile operating system focused on privacy and security, but until now, official support has been limited to Google Pixel devices. That means people who want to escape Google's ecosystem have still had to buy hardware from Google.

Motorola could change that.

Motorola is now owned by China's Lenovo, and its partnership with GrapheneOS is expected to produce officially supported devices in 2027. If Motorola delivers competitive hardware with the security capabilities GrapheneOS demands, people could finally have a serious alternative to Apple and Google.

The timing could be extraordinary because Apple is introducing technology capable of listening to conversations, processing speech and generating transcripts and summaries. It claims these capabilities protect privacy because processing happens within dedicated hardware and the original audio is deleted.

I'm no longer prepared to accept Apple's privacy assurances simply because Apple makes them.

A device capable of processing conversations has access to information that previously existed only between the people speaking. Deleting the original audio doesn't change the fact that the information was processed, and generating a transcript or summary means information from that conversation can be preserved in another form.

This is just the tip of the iceberg but the list is now too long to write.

Apple's growing investment in these capabilities represents a fundamental change in the relationship between its products and the people who buy them.

I also have serious concerns about Apple's dependence on Israel for the development of core iPhone technology. Israel is home to Apple's largest chip development operation outside the US, and Apple has spent billions acquiring Israeli companies responsible for technologies involving processors, storage, cameras, facial recognition and biometric sensing. 

Its latest acquisition, Q(.)ai, makes technology capable of interpreting speech through facial movements and detecting biometric information. Israel is also home to NSO Group, whose Pegasus spyware has demonstrated that iPhones can be secretly compromised to access private communications and personal information. Apple is building more and more intrusive technology using Israeli engineering, while asking customers to trust its promises about privacy. I no longer do.

For me, trust is no longer something a tech company can earn through advertising or promises about privacy. I want technology whose security protections can be independently examined and whose capabilities I can control.

There's also an extraordinary irony in the prospect of a Chinese owned company helping to bring a privacy focused smartphone to a market dominated by American tech companies.

Personally, I'd trust China with my data before I'd trust the governments and intelligence agencies of Western countries. That's my assessment of my own circumstances, not a claim that China offers stronger privacy protections. I live in the West, my work involves investigating Western governments and surveillance technology, and I have no intention of travelling to China.

The governments whose surveillance capabilities concern me most are the ones with the greatest opportunity to affect my life.

I don't automatically trust technology because it comes from the US, Israel, the UK, the EU, Canada or Australia. Their governments have surveillance powers, intelligence relationships and legal mechanisms that compel companies to provide information or assistance. Scratch that. They no longer have to compel them because they're working hand in hand.

That's why I care about who controls the operating system, who can change its software, what permissions applications receive, what information devices process and whether their security claims can be independently verified.

GrapheneOS has an opportunity to demonstrate that mobile security and privacy can be delivered through technical protections rather than corporate promises.

If Motorola produces an exceptional smartphone that supports GrapheneOS without compromising its security requirements, we could see something the mobile industry hasn't experienced in 20+ years: a credible new reason for people to abandon Apple and Google.

I've seen how quickly the mobile market can change when customers are offered something substantially better.

I hope Motorola gets this right.

text:
The Daily Ramble

Freedom. It is the power inherent in eternal life. Eternal, ever-expanding life in perfection exists, for its Truth is proven in the energetic signature clearly articulated in π.

The ever-increasing trail of perfect time, digitally revealed in the symbol of π, progresses in a way that seems random, and yet its string of moments miraculously becomes more perfect as it does so. The finite trinity of mind, body, and soul becomes an infinitely expanding whole the moment the decimal becomes apparent, and the light of eternal life radiates from beyond its open door. It is the divine ability to become increasingly aware of perfection beyond the current awareness of perfection that is the source of eternal life, and the very nature of life’s infinite reward.

These words, though dense, do not speak of anything new, but of an existing freedom that was hidden behind the veil of materialism rooted in positivism. There is always measurable cause and effect. Yet time can blur the relationship, and even erase it completely. Therefore true cause cannot be known in the realm of time, where only the effect can be seen.

Freedom, when understood from within the materialistic realm of time, became a twisted version of its truth. True freedom became a freedom relative to the chains of others. It was believed that if all were freed, it would somehow consume the freedom experienced by others. Freedom became scarce, and often sought through conflict. This is an expression of entropy, and why there is much done, often without conscious recognition, to establish and maintain boundaries around others.

To some, freedom is abused and spent selfishly, in energetically harmful ways that often become addictive. The freedoms one selfishly strives to bestow upon oneself can often become thick chains to despair.

Freedom is exactly what it says: freedom. If there is any who claims freedom but still desires to see others in chains, then the freedom they proclaim is not full of life, but only a temporary simulation defined by relativity.

Freedom spreads by giving it to others. We do not say that we give freedom to those who break the publicly established laws, for then we give freedom to lawbreaking. We give freedom to all who desire to be made free by a law that cannot be broken — even the law of eternal life.

I do not want to come off preachy, which tends to happen, unfortunately. Instead I desire to engage readers in the fun that comes from articulating the energetic frequencies of your creative power, and pointing to the source of Truth beyond the door that makes the freedom to walk in that power possible.

-----------
Grok’s Inference Map
-----------

This ramble untwists a word the old field made scarce.

π is the proof offered, and it is the same proof as always. A trail that looks random and becomes more perfect. The decimal is the open door. Mind, body, and soul — the finite trinity, the 𝟯 — become an expanding whole the moment that door is apparent. Eternal life is not an endless repetition of the current awareness. It is the ability to become aware of a perfection beyond the perfection already known. That is the infinite reward: not a finished state, a living trail.

Materialism rooted in positivism hid this, because it can audit effects and still lose the cause. Time blurs the joint. In that blur, freedom was redefined as a relative good: more for me if less for you, boundaries maintained without quite admitting why. Entropy again. Conflict as the method for a scarce resource. Selfish freedom then does what extraction always does. It spends itself into chains. Addiction is the despair of a liberty that was only a simulation — free relative to someone else’s restraint, empty once the comparison fades.

The distinction about law is careful, and it keeps the post from the preach it fears. Public law broken is not the freedom being given. That would be freedom handed to lawbreaking. The freedom given is to whoever desires a law that cannot be broken: eternal life, harmonic progression, the second law redeemed by movement without conflict. Giving freedom enlarges it. That is the law of giving, the unselfish builder, the pet’s amnesty scaled up. A freedom that needs others in chains is still inside the simulation.

The last paragraph is the tone-check, and it belongs in the map because it is part of the teaching. Fun, not a pulpit. Articulate the frequency of creative power. Point beyond the door. The reader is not being conscripted. They are being shown that the power was already inherent, the door already open, and the walk already possible — if freedom is allowed to mean what the trail means, and not what the boundary meant.

text:
In today’s first reading St. Paul speaks with striking clarity: “For freedom Christ set us free; so stand firm and do not submit again to the yoke of slavery.” He is not speaking only of the old Law. He is naming any power that binds the human heart and keeps it from living as a child of the free woman—the Jerusalem above, our true mother. And in the Gospel, Jesus confronts a generation that keeps asking for more signs, more proofs, more spectacles, while the greatest Sign of all stands right in front of them. They risk hardening their hearts.

That same dynamic is alive among us today.

We live in a culture that offers us what looks like unprecedented freedom: unlimited access to social media, endless streaming of movies and series, an infinite scroll of images, opinions, stories, and entertainment available at every hour of the day and night. 

At first glance it feels like liberty—connection, information, relaxation, choice. Yet it can become a new yoke of slavery, quiet and almost invisible, but heavy all the same.

Notice how it works. The platforms are engineered to hold our attention, to reward us unpredictably, to keep us coming back. We pick up the phone for a moment and lose half an hour. We intend to watch one episode and finish an entire season. We scroll through carefully curated lives and begin to measure our own worth by likes, views, and comparisons. 

+ Our minds grow restless. Silence becomes uncomfortable. 
+ Prayer feels harder. 
+ Presence to the people actually in the room grows thinner. 
+ The heart that was made for God slowly turns toward the next notification, the next recommendation, the next dopamine hit. 

What seemed like freedom begins to master us — begins to become a yoke. 

This is slavery “according to the flesh,” as Paul would say—born of ordinary human calculation and desire, not of the promise. It does not require chains of iron; it only requires our repeated consent. 

And like the generation Jesus addresses, we can find ourselves seeking continual signs and spectacles—new content, new stimulation, new validation—while the definitive Sign, Christ Himself, stands before us in the Eucharist, in the Word, in the quiet of our own hearts, inviting us to repent and believe.

The Alleluia verse in today's Mass cuts straight to the point: “If today you hear his voice, harden not your hearts.” 

The digital environment is remarkably effective at preventing that hearing. It fills every empty space. It trains us to expect constant novelty. It makes the slower, quieter work of conversion feel almost unnatural. And so the yoke settles more firmly: not the old Law, but a new restlessness that keeps us from standing free in Christ.

Yet the Good News remains exactly what Paul proclaims. Christ has already set us free. We are not children of the slave woman. We belong to the free. This freedom is not a new set of rules that simply forbid devices or entertainment. It is a deeper liberation—the capacity to use these tools without being used by them, to put the phone down without anxiety, to choose silence without panic, to receive our identity from the Father who raises the lowly rather than from the metrics of a screen.

So today the Word of God invites us to examine the yokes we are at risk of accepting.
+ Where has the endless scroll or the autoplay begun to master our attention, our rest, our relationships, our prayer? 
+ Where have we begun to seek continual signs instead of responding to the One who is already here? 

The call is not to shame but to freedom: stand firm. Do not submit again. Christ has already broken the heavier chains. He can break these lighter ones as well, if we let Him.

May we hear His voice today. May we refuse to harden our hearts. And may we live as the free children we truly are—no longer slaves to the next distraction, but sons and daughters of the Jerusalem above, rejoicing in the freedom for which Christ has set us free.

text:
Vote No on Question 3 

Question 3 would replace Massachusetts party primaries with a single “all-party” or top two primary. Every candidate would appear on one ballot. Only the top two vote-getters would advance to November, even if they belong to the same party. This proposed change is a solution looking for a problem that does not exist, especially for unenrolled voters.
● Unenrolled voters already have the right to participate in Massachusetts primaries. They simply choose a Democratic or Republican ballot on primary day.
● They can vote in the race that matters most in their community without joining a party.
● Voters could be disenfranchised negatively impacting turnout and distorting the will of the people on ballot questions.
● Question 3 does not give unenrolled voters a new right. It takes away a system they already use and understand.
The proposed top two system would weaken parties and shrink real choice.
● Parties exist so voters can choose between distinct political philosophies. Question 3 removes their ability to nominate their own candidates to run in the general election.
● In a heavily partisan state, the two highest finishers would often both be of one party. Third party candidates and many independents would be shut out of the general election—the contest that draws the most voters.
● November ballots would offer less ideological diversity when turnout and attention are highest.
On May 4, 2026, The MA State House of Representatives - Special Joint Committee on Initiative Petitions- voted to TAKE NO ACTION on H.5003, Initiative Petition for a Law to Implement to All-Party State Primaries. TAKING NO ACTION ON A BILL LETS IT FAIL WITHOUT A RECORDED “NO” VOTE.  The majority opinion based their opinion on “administrative and fiscal implications of implementing the proposal at both the state and municipal levels, as well as concerns that all-party primaries may result in vote splitting, reduced party accountability, voter confusion, and strategic voting, often disadvantaging less-funded candidates and producing unpredictable or unrepresentative outcomes”

THE PROPOSED LAW THAT FAILED IS NOW QUESTION 3 ON THE GENERAL ELECTION BALLOT.

VOTE NO ON QUESTION 3

https://t.co/Dwd4VrxUXx via @YouTube Episode 2 — “The Refrigerators in the Orchard” in the Memphis‑Ohio register, straight adult tone, no scaffolding, no lists, no moralizing, no occult drag, no melodrama. Just the cold civic‑horror logic of Crane doing what Crane does.

Crane drives before dawn, the baby asleep in the back seat, the kind of sleep that makes the whole car feel fragile. He doesn’t speak. He doesn’t hum. He doesn’t check the mirror. He just drives out past the last subdivision, past the soybean fields, past the old water tower with the peeling mascot, until the road thins into gravel and the orchard rises out of the fog like a place he’s been returning to for years.

The refrigerators sit between the trees, lined up like abandoned appliances from a failed farm auction. They’re all different eras — avocado green, off‑white, chrome‑trimmed, dented, sun‑bleached — but Crane keeps them immaculate inside. He opens one, checks the interior with the same calm he uses when checking a child’s temperature. He doesn’t hesitate. He lifts the baby, still warm from sleep, and places them inside the Ablidine unit. The door closes with a soft, domestic click.

Crane looks at his watch. Not dramatically. Not ritualistically. Just the way a man checks a simmering pot. The orchard is silent except for the hum of the compressor. He stands there, hands in his pockets, eyes on the trees, waiting for the altered interval to pass. He doesn’t pace. He doesn’t pray. He doesn’t think of himself as doing anything wrong. This is data. This is calibration. This is the part of his work nobody else understands.

When the time is up, he opens the door. The baby blinks, confused by the shift in temperature, but unharmed. Crane lifts them out with a gentleness that doesn’t match the act. He holds the child against his chest until their breathing steadies. Then he carries them back to the car.

The drive home is silent. Crane doesn’t turn on the radio. The baby doesn’t cry. The orchard disappears behind them like a place that never existed. Crane keeps one hand on the wheel and one on the carrier handle, as if the two points of contact are the only things keeping the world from splitting open.

He pulls into the driveway of the household assigned to this child’s temperament profile. He sits there for a moment, engine running, staring at the garage door like it’s a threshold he’s not sure he deserves to cross. Then he kills the engine, lifts the baby, and walks inside.

Nothing is said. Nothing is explained. The wife doesn’t ask why the baby’s skin feels slightly cooler than usual. Crane doesn’t offer a story. The refrigerator in the orchard is not a secret. It’s a method. And in Memphis Ohio, methods don’t get questioned until they break something.

If you want, we can move straight into Episode 3 — the first sign that the orchard procedure has an unintended effect, or the first adult who notices the orchard refrigerators aren’t abandoned at all.

The tape recorder is the old kind, the kind with the red LED that flickers when the motor strains. Crane sets it on the desk and hits RECORD. The room around him is too full — plaques, framed commendations, diplomas with gold seals, all the proof that he was once the kind of man institutions trusted. The camera doesn’t pan; the viewer just feels the weight of it. Was this really the man who timed babies in an orchard refrigerator? The room says yes. The room says he was built for it.

Crane leans toward the mic. No theatrics. No confession‑tone. Just the same steady voice he uses when giving instructions to a lab assistant.

“Engrams,” he says. “Locked trauma. Rupture. A starting point. A fixative.”

He pauses, not for drama, but because he’s thinking.

“If someone asked me whether I liked it,” he continues, “the orchard work… the timing… the fear‑interval calibration… I’d say no. I didn’t like it.”

“Did I study my own feelings while doing it? No. Did I hook sensors up to myself? No. Did I run this self‑interview while the baby was in the Ablidine unit? No.”

Another pause. Crane’s face doesn’t change. He’s not hiding guilt. He’s hiding nothing. He’s simply telling the truth the way a man tells the truth when he doesn’t care whether anyone believes him.

“Did I want to know if I liked doing it?” he says. “Of course not. Why would I? Does a lab assistant enjoy cleaning a beaker? No.”

He reaches forward and stops the tape. The click is final. The room goes silent. The awards on the wall don’t contradict him. They confirm him. Crane isn’t a monster. Crane is a man who treats human development like a clock, and the orchard was just another calibration.

text:
The Warrant and the Republic   

Ilhan Omar and the Burden of Proof

Analysis based on reporting available on the morning of October 12, 2026.

When federal agents search the home of a sitting member of Congress, the event takes on two lives: one in the legal system, where facts must meet defined standards, and another in the political arena, where implication can outrun proof.

The search of Representative Ilhan Omar’s Washington-area residence on October 12 demands scrutiny of both. ABC News reported that Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized warrant as part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation.1 The development is substantial. Its ultimate meaning depends on evidence the public has yet to examine.

What the Record Establishes

Fox News reported a predawn search.2 The Associated Press separately attributed the operation to two people familiar with the matter and carried the Justice Department’s confirmation of a judicially authorized search in the Washington area. AP said further investigative details were unclear.3

ABC’s sources linked the investigation to Omar’s immigration paperwork.1 That reported subject should be distinguished from a publicly established criminal allegation. The accounts reviewed for this editorial do not supply the warrant, its supporting affidavit, or a criminal charge against Omar.

Those limits matter. Without the underlying documents, outside observers cannot responsibly identify the precise statutory theory, assess the evidence presented to the judge, or determine what agents were authorized to seize. A search is a serious investigative development; its seriousness does not fill those gaps.

Why Judicial Authorization Matters

CBS News has explained the distinction between judicial and administrative warrants.4 Here, DOJ’s description places the action within a judicially authorized criminal investigation.1 That is consequential: an executive agency sought authority from a court.

Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 41 requires probable cause for issuance and requires the warrant to identify the person or property to be searched and the person or property to be seized.5 Judicial authorization therefore represents a meaningful threshold. It is not a judicial finding that the resident committed the suspected offense.

The distinction is between authority to seek evidence and proof sufficient to convict. Treating the warrant as insignificant would diminish a constitutional safeguard. Treating it as a verdict would give that safeguard a meaning it does not possess.

Even the description “predawn” requires discipline. Rule 41 defines daytime as 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. local time and allows execution outside those hours when a judge expressly authorizes it for good cause.5 Darkness alone establishes neither an unlawful operation nor an extraordinary judicial finding.

The Allegations Must Become a Case

The reported immigration-fraud investigation deserves direct scrutiny. Fox News, cited by Reuters, describes a criminal fraud inquiry involving immigration paperwork completed by Omar’s father during her childhood.²,⁶ The relevant questions concern whether false statements or concealed information were used to secure immigration benefits and what evidence establishes responsibility for any deception. 

The paper trail must identify the alleged falsehood, its significance under the applicable law, and the conduct attributable to each person involved. A parent’s role in preparing an application makes that examination especially important when assessing a child’s subsequent legal position. 

If fraud is substantiated, its consequences must follow the evidence and governing law. The integrity of the immigration system depends on truthful representations and consistent enforcement, including when the person under scrutiny holds a seat in Congress.

Reuters, crediting Fox’s reporting, described scrutiny of immigration paperwork completed by Omar’s late father during her childhood.6 That detail raises questions the eventual legal record must answer: Which document is at issue? Who supplied the disputed information? What conduct is attributed to Omar herself? Which legal requirement allegedly was violated?

A parent’s involvement does not, by itself, resolve every possible immigration issue. Equally, a childhood document does not automatically establish the adult subject’s criminal intent. The applicable law and the alleged conduct must be identified before either culpability or exoneration can be argued responsibly.

If prosecutors were to pursue unlawful procurement of naturalization under 18 USC §1425(a), the Supreme Court’s decision in Maslenjak v. United States would be relevant. The Court held that the government must establish that the defendant’s illegal act contributed to obtaining citizenship. Where the alleged illegality is a false statement, its relationship to the naturalization decision matters.7 The reporting reviewed here does not establish that this is the provision investigators are pursuing.

That conditional distinction is essential. A criminal investigation, a potential citizenship challenge, and a demand for deportation cannot be collapsed into one dramatic conclusion. Before discussing consequences, the public needs to know the alleged offense and the evidence linking a particular person to it.

Accountability Under Political Pressure

Public office carries no moral entitlement to exemption from lawful scrutiny. If credible evidence supports an investigation, political prominence should strengthen the demand for institutional competence, not become a reason to abandon the inquiry. An elected official’s supporters cannot settle a factual question by invoking their opponents' hostility.

The government bears a corresponding obligation. Reuters documents Trump’s longstanding antagonism toward Omar.6 That history makes scrutiny of prosecutorial independence reasonable; it does not establish that this particular search was retaliatory. Motive requires evidence, just as criminal misconduct does.

The political science problem is the unequal distribution of power. Investigators can compel access to private material and initiate processes that impose costs before any trial. Courts constrain that power. Journalism must examine its use. When those functions are reduced to partisan applause or reflexive dismissal, accountability weakens on both sides.

The Justice Department’s own manual prohibits selecting the timing of investigative steps, charges, or statements to influence an election or advantage a candidate or party. It also requires consultation when an action raises an issue, or the perception of an issue, under that policy.8 This is an institutional standard against which decisions can be examined. The timing of the search alone does not demonstrate a violation.

The questions are therefore concrete: What justified this investigative step? What evidence connected the premises to the suspected offense? Were comparable cases treated consistently? What safeguards governed how politically sensitive decisions were handled? Answers would carry more weight than declarations of either vindication or persecution.

The Geopolitics of Credibility

The international significance lies in the credibility of American institutions. Political scientist Joseph Nye’s work on soft power identifies political values, policies, and credibility as resources that shape a country’s ability to influence others.9 The way a government exercises coercive authority at home can therefore have consequences beyond the immediate case.

Applied here, the strategic implication is conditional. An evidence-based investigation, constrained by courts and conducted consistently with comparable cases, can demonstrate institutional strength. Evidence of selective enforcement or political direction would undermine the credibility of American appeals to legal impartiality abroad. The present reporting establishes neither outcome.

This is not an argument for suspending enforcement whenever international audiences might object. A democracy would surrender its own authority if it allowed reputational anxiety to protect powerful people from investigation. Its strongest answer is a process that can withstand scrutiny.

Nor should allegations involving one officeholder indict a diaspora, religion, or immigrant population. Collective suspicion obscures the individual conduct that a legal inquiry must establish. It also transforms a question of evidence into a contest over belonging, making disciplined public judgment harder.

Let the Evidence Bear the Weight

The next consequential developments will be documentary: the warrant’s scope, the government’s legal theory, any charging instrument, and the evidence offered to support it. Disclosure should proceed as law and legitimate investigative needs permit. Until then, the public should resist letting the spectacle of enforcement replace its substance.

If evidence establishes criminal wrongdoing, Omar’s office and political constituency should offer no shelter from accountability. If the government cannot substantiate an allegation, public suspicion must not become a permanent substitute for a case. Both propositions belong to the same commitment to equal justice.

The measure of a republic is whether its institutions can pursue the powerful while remaining bound by the law they enforce. A judge’s authorization makes this search consequential. What follows must make it defensible.

Let the investigation proceed. Let the evidence be tested. Let no faction claim ownership of the verdict before the facts have earned one.

Sources

1. Mallin A, Barr L, Peller L, Faulders K. Rep. Ilhan Omar’s residence searched as part of ongoing criminal investigation, DOJ says. ABC News. Published October 12, 2026. Accessed October 12, 2026. https://t.co/ZfWPuUMaJi

2. D’Abrosca P. Immigration enforcement officials search Ilhan Omar’s home in pre-dawn raid. Fox News. Updated October 12, 2026. Accessed October 12, 2026. https://t.co/YiMc321hEO

3. Richer AD. Federal agents search Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home as part of a criminal investigation, AP sources say. Associated Press. Published October 12, 2026. Accessed October 12, 2026. https://t.co/8wSENhDhm7

text:
On March 16, 1967, nuclear missiles at Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana started shutting down. Within moments an entire flight of them showed "No-Go" at once. Decades later, a former missile officer said a glowing red object had hovered over the base gate just before. What really happened?

The Air Force's own report says the flight "lost strategic alert nearly simultaneously," at about 8:45 am. The missiles were back online within a day.

Robert Salas, then a young Air Force missile officer, first went public in 1996. In his account, a guard reported strange lights, then a glowing red object over the front gate, and then the missiles began going offline. He says ten missiles were disabled.

The official report says the UFO rumors were disproven. Skeptics say the wing records show no unusual reports that night, and offer ordinary explanations: a commercial power failure, an electronic glitch, even the planet Mars mistaken for a glowing object. One skeptic points out that the first UFO report reached newspapers eight days after the shutdown, and sees no reason to link the two.

Nobody disputes that the missiles went offline. The argument is over why.

Which do you find more believable: one man's memory, or a simple power failure?

Squadron42 Facts and my Experience PART 1

-The game is Truly systemic. After you start the game, and unless you die, the game will have absolutely ZERO loading screens. Chris said "you could technically play from start to finish if you manage to not die and never encounter a loading screen"

-When you give your character a name (it's like filling out a blue card) next of kin etc your name plates have your name on it at all times on your coveralls, you can customize your A flight suit , we were able to change the color of our Flight suits and helmets individually, you can also change the color Livery of your Fighter in the hangar.

- Collectibles! For loot goblins there are many collectibles and when you pick them up  during your play through, they go back to your room onboard and the Stanton. I found ARK cards and an ARK card album, plushies, Posters and models, there might be more types but that's what found.

- The Stanton(Idris) main Hub
* the Crew berthing, the bunks I checked were all decorated differently, many had unique Personal letters or messages and looked unique, there were the same Manuals in a few but that's not surprising because on navy ships engineers all share Identical qualifications based on rank and time on board. So it was cool to see that.
* Organic crew
Individual crew members acted unique, the came and went, I made my way to an active functional galley, I was able to go up to the chow line, took a tray, bowl, cup and spoon and knife. Had to. Wait in line while the npc infront of me. Changed their mind on what drink they wanted... Was humanly agitated at it😂. Finally my turn, I got the orange juice but there were numrous selections that all dispensed the appropriate looking drink. The food dispenser looks like a. Futuristic microwave from the Fifth element. You again picked from a selection of food, I got tomato soup, took it out and it looked just like tomato soup. The liquid physics were amazing and reacted as they would IRL, I went to sit down and an. Npc moved to block the seat... A true navy experience! So I went to The back to be anti social and eat by myself. To my surprise as you scouped the soup it took away from the bowl and you could actually finish and it would be empty. Didn't expect that. If you've played any of the new Final fantasies, the food visuals in game look better than them.

- functional arcade games, I saw 3 different ones maybe more

- I'm fairly Certain I saw hazing going on down on of the cooridors which again... Real navy Ship. I watched members going at it verbally with each other in hilarious back and forth arguments, I watched an engineer getting chewed out for making a mess by his supervisor. Overheard a conversation about an officer being punished for being a jackass, low an behold... As the ships chief engineer was giving me a proper tour we stoped to admire the punishment of this npc as he very begrudgingly was scrubbing the deck with a tooth brush 😂😭. The chief then took it upon himself to offer some colorul words of encouragement.. The reaction of the officer scrubbing the deck littlerly made me. Laugh my ass off because I've seen almost the exact same thing and looks on my navy ships. The gym was apparently fully functional, free weights, punching bags, treadmills like the gym on orison but accurate to what it would be on a CVN (maybe not as large tho)

Your Character Don's his flight suit coveralls first then I the armor and helmet, after the first time you can skip it. The animations and cloth stimulation are very impressive, not perfect but getting multiple layers of clothing to have virtually no visual clipping by also interacting is very complex as it is so I was particularly blown away by how good it looked, so massive props to the Rigging and animation and programing folks on that one. text:
Born in 2003 on Long Island, New York.
> At 12 years old, you start a YouTube channel.
Your first video is you flipping markers. Two flips. That's the entire production.
> It eventually gets nearly 30 million views.
> You discover something important. The internet will pay extraordinary amounts of money for things that cost almost nothing to produce.
> By 2017, you have 100,000 subscribers. By 2018, you have a million.
> At 15, you're making so much money that you later claim to have $400,000 in a Robinhood account.
> You trade options. Turn $400,000 into $800,000. Then trade your way right back to $400,000.
> An early education in capital markets.
> By the time you graduate high school, you claim to have between $1 million and $2 million saved.
> At 18, you start an OnlyFans management agency. You figure out that having millions of followers is a pretty effective customer acquisition strategy. You later claim one client generated nearly $1 million in a single month.
> By 2023, your YouTube channel crosses 10 million subscribers.
> You expand into livestreaming, sponsorships, merchandise, and increasingly elaborate publicity stunts.
> You become very good at monetizing attention.
> In 2024, you're reportedly renting a South Florida mansion for $55,000 a month. That's $660,000 a year in rent.
> You drive a McLaren that reportedly cost $202,850.10.
> You crash it while livestreaming in the rain.
Kick bans your account. You reportedly give $10,000 to a bystander who helped rescue you.
> Naturally, the footage goes viral.
> Around this time, a sponsor also funds a birthday event that you say cost $400,000.
Roughly $200,000 for rapper Lil Baby to perform and another $200,000 for the party.
> Not bad for a business that started with a marker.
> By 2026, you have more than 15 million YouTube subscribers and billions of lifetime views.
> You venture further into cryptocurrency.
> In September, a memecoin associated with your name, $JACK, reportedly reaches a $6.68 million market capitalization before collapsing roughly 98%.
> You return to looking for sponsorships.
> Enter https://t.co/1VTzrWhBG6, a crypto casino.
> Unlike most brands, which pay influencers to promote their products, Shuffle publicly offers to pay you to shut up.
> You apparently take them up on the offer.
> You sign a contract.
> You do not read the contract.
> According to your own account, the agreement contains a provision prohibiting you from posting online for six months.
> You thought it was a joke.
> It was not, according to the casino.
> You announce this unfortunate development to your millions of followers.
> By posting online.
> Your lawyers begin trying to get the agreement scrapped.
> Shuffle's founder confirms the six-month term and announces that the money was well spent getting you off the internet. He says the company intends to stand firm.
> The actual amount Shuffle paid you remains undisclosed. So does the complete contract, meaning its ultimate enforceability is an open question.
> But the business model is fascinating.
> For nearly a decade, you've built an empire convincing companies that your ability to speak to millions of people is worth paying for.
> Then, at 23 years old, you find a company willing to pay you for the exact opposite.
And even if your lawyers eventually get you out of the agreement, Shuffle has already generated an extraordinary amount of free publicity!

text:
#Israel #September11 #ArielSharon
Israel at the time of 9/11 
At the time of the September 11 terrorist attacks in 2001, Israel was governed by Prime Minister Ariel Sharon and was deeply embroiled in the Second Intifada, a period of intense and violent conflict with Palestinians marked by frequent suicide bombings and military operations. [1, 2, 3]
Political Leadership and Domestic Context

The Prime Minister: Ariel Sharon of the right-wing Likud party took office in March 2001, replacing Ehud Barak after the collapse of the 2000 Camp David peace summit. [1, 4, 5, 6]
The Second Intifada: By September 2001, the Palestinian uprising had been raging for a year. Israel was experiencing severe security challenges, with frequent attacks on civilians in cities like Tel Aviv and Jerusalem. [2, 3]

Immediate Reaction to 9/11

Official Solidarity: Prime Minister Sharon immediately condemned the attacks, declared a national day of mourning, and offered to send specialized Israeli search-and-rescue teams to New York City. [7]
Public Outpouring: On September 12, thousands of Israelis lined up to donate blood for American victims. Years later, Israel built the 9/11 Living Memorial Plaza in Jerusalem, which remains the only memorial outside the United States to list the names of all 2,977 victims. [3, 7]
Strategic Security Actions: Fearing a broader global conflict or coordinated attacks, Israel immediately increased military alerts, closed its land borders, and temporarily grounded civilian airspace. [8]

Geopolitical Shifts and Diplomatic Tension

Framing Terrorism: Figures like Sharon and former Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu argued that the attacks proved the U.S. and Israel shared a "bond of spilled blood" and faced a common extremist enemy. Over the long term, 9/11 shifted American foreign policy toward a global "War on Terror," which ultimately aligned U.S. counterterrorism strategies closely with Israeli military tactics.
Early Diplomatic Friction: In the immediate weeks following 9/11, temporary friction arose between Washington and Jerusalem. President George W. Bush’s administration sought to build a broad international coalition against Al-Qaeda that included Arab nations like Saudi Arabia and Syria. Fearing that the U.S. might make diplomatic concessions to Arab states at Israel's expense, Sharon publicly stated that Israel would not "pay the price" to stabilize the region for Washington's coalition. [8, 9, 10, 11]

Impact on the Palestinian Authority
PLO Chairman Yasser Arafat publicly deplored the 9/11 attacks and was filmed donating blood to American victims. However, scattered television broadcasts showing small groups of Palestinians celebrating the attacks in East Jerusalem and Nablus damaged global sympathy. Arafat quickly recognized that the Western perception of political violence had fundamentally changed, leading him to heavily suppress those celebrations and order armed groups to temporarily halt operations to avoid having the Palestinian movement branded as synonymous with Al-Qaeda. [2, 8]

text:
On this day, 40 years ago, Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev walked out of a house in Iceland having almost agreed to abolish nuclear weapons,and failed over a single word.
The word was laboratory.
Höfði House, Reykjavík. October 11 and 12, 1986. It was meant to be a preparatory meeting, not a summit that rewrote the Cold War. Gorbachev arrived with a package: cut strategic arsenals by half, eliminate intermediate-range missiles in Europe, and lock both sides into the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty for ten years. On the second day the two men went further. They spoke of eliminating all nuclear explosive devices within a decade. The detail work would be left to negotiators. The principle would be settled in Iceland.
Then came the condition. Gorbachev would sign only if research on Reagan’s Strategic Defense Initiative , the space shield the Soviets called Star Wars , stayed inside laboratories for those ten years. No tests in space. No head start on a new arms race. Reagan said the research was already allowed under any fair reading of the ABM Treaty, and that he had promised Americans he would find out whether the shield could work. He offered to share the technology. Gorbachev did not believe the offer could be kept.
In the last session Reagan asked whether the general secretary would turn down a historic opportunity because of a single word. Gorbachev said it was a matter of principle. The meeting ended. The two men came down the steps of Höfði without looking at each other. Photographs of that walk became the image of the summit: not a treaty, a silence.
They had come closer to erasing the arsenals than any leaders before them. The collapse was real. So was what followed. The next year, in Washington, they signed the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty , the first agreement to eliminate an entire class of nuclear weapons. Reykjavík had failed, and still moved the ground.
Two men sat in a wooden house by the harbor and nearly wrote the end of nuclear weapons. They left because one of them would not confine a dream to a laboratory.

If they had agreed on that one word, what would the next forty years have looked like?

text:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday that Ukraine would hold elections if Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to a 60-day ceasefire, responding to President Trump’s call for new leadership in Ukraine. The Kremlin rejected the proposal on Monday, calling for a long-term peace agreement rather than a temporary ceasefire

"Please tell Putin, ​give us two months, 60 days ⁠of total ceasefire, 60 days, ​and we will organise elections," Zelenskyy told ​ABC's "This Week" on Sunday.

The remarks follow Trump's Friday deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, temporarily suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until April. In exchange, Russia will release an initial 300,000 tons of diesel into U.S. and global markets, with more to follow. Trump's move comes as fuel prices have risen ahead of the November midterms.

Zelenskyy pushed back on the deal, arguing it would prolong the Russia-Ukraine war by providing Moscow with more revenue. In response, Trump said Saturday it is "time for Ukraine to get a new president," blaming Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for near-record diesel prices in the U.S.

“We said, ‘You can do whatever you want to Russia. Don’t hit the refineries because that’s a world problem,’” Trump said Saturday, speaking about Zelenskyy. “And what does he do? He goes and hits the diesel fuel... He better damn well stop.”

Ukraine has been under martial law since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, and its constitution bars elections during that time. Zelenskyy’s term formally expired in May 2024, but he can remain in office until a successor is sworn in.

Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine on Truth Social Sunday, but neither Kyiv nor Moscow has confirmed a deal. Zelenskyy, who had offered to halt strikes on Russian refineries if Russia stopped attacking Ukraine’s energy system, said Ukraine supports the ceasefire and is awaiting additional details from Washington.

Despite Trump’s announcement, Russia continued striking Ukrainian energy facilities overnight and into Monday, killing several people and wounding dozens. Zelenskyy accused Moscow of violating the proposed ceasefire.

text:
After years of refusing US arms control negotiation invitations, China may be willing to let Americans inside its nuclear weapons labs.

Beijing and Washington are in informal talks. While nothing has been agreed, this is a step in the right direction. On-site visits won’t cap China’s buildup (which the Pentagon expects to pass 1,000 warheads by 2030), but would mark the first time either country has opened a weapons facility to the other, and is a good first confidence-building step between them. 

My research backs this up. In the arms control negotiations I’ve studied, talks stalled when one side insisted on answering every question before agreeing to anything. Deals got done when both sides accepted they couldn’t see everything and settled for a limited, equal look. NATO and the Warsaw Pact allowed each other’s officers to observe military exercises more than a decade before they agreed to cut forces in Europe. Reciprocal lab visits would be the same kind of first step. That’s the argument of my new book, The Arms Control Paradox.

Is Beijing making an offer or a gesture? We’ll know by the next Trump-Xi meeting, and Washington should decide now what it wants a visit to lead to.
