text:
U.S.–China Stability: Making Restraint Credible - The United States and China can reduce confrontation without resolving their underlying political differences, but durable stability requires enforceable procedures that make restraint observable and violations consequential.

The September 2026 summit produced identifiable mechanisms: trade and investment boards, recommendations concerning $30 billion of non-sensitive goods in each direction, and an emerging-technology dialogue with an incident communication channel. These are announced institutional arrangements, not evidence that strategic rivalry has been contained. The White House

Taiwan remains a decisive legal and political constraint: U.S. assistance must support sufficient self-defence, with requirements determined through American statutory processes. Taiwan Relations Act

The principal judgment is that selective, monitored restraint is more feasible than a comprehensive bilateral settlement. Its success depends on preserving deterrence, protecting third-party interests and separating commercial implementation from security concessions.

The decisive uncertainty is whether both governments will accept compliance assessments that can expose their own failures and survive a serious political dispute.

U.S.–China Stability Will Be Paid for in Industrial Capacity
The contradiction in U.S.–China relations is that diplomatic accommodation can change faster than the industrial and security dependencies it is supposed to contain. The September 27, 2026 procedures for the U.S.–China Board of Trade identify officials and a negotiating process, but they do not manufacture alternative supplies, guarantee market access or settle Taiwan’s security requirements. The governing choice is whether Washington, Beijing and European governments will use the breathing space created by selective cooperation to finance resilience and make commitments executable. If they treat administrative relief as evidence that exposure has disappeared, the next dispute will reach factories, infrastructure and defence procurement before governments can restore what they have conceded. Stability must therefore be judged by the capacity to sustain essential activity under pressure, rather than by the monetary value attached to summit announcements.

A smaller deficit does not buy independence
The U.S. Census Bureau figures show goods imports from China falling from $440.319 billion in 2024 to $308.652 billion in 2025, while exports fell from $143.272 billion to $105.978 billion. The deficit narrowed by 31.8%, calculated from the recorded values. During January–August 2026, imports were $183.524 billion, down 16.3% against the corresponding 2025 period, while exports were $73.903 billion, up 0.7%. These figures establish a contraction in direct trade. They do not establish how much Chinese production remains embedded in goods purchased elsewhere, or whether a replacement supplier can operate without the same upstream inputs.

Europe’s numbers expose a different constraint. Eurostat’s April 2026 publication records EU goods exports to China of €199.6 billion and imports of €559.4 billion for 2025, producing a €359.8 billion deficit in that statistical vintage. Machinery and mechanical-appliance imports accounted for €106.5 billion; electrical machinery and related equipment accounted for €164.9 billion. Those broad categories cannot identify the component whose absence stops production. The deficit measures the direction of expenditure; industrial dependence turns on substitution, qualification and the time needed to restore delivery.

The September 27 terms for the “30-for-30” framework value product lists using calendar-year 2024 bilateral trade and leave tariff reductions to domestic legal processes. Their approximately $30 billion valuation on each side is neither future trade guaranteed nor tariff savings delivered. Confusing the negotiated scope with its commercial result would turn an administrative proposal into an economic achievement before customs authorities or customers have acted.

Relief at the border can leave the factory exposed
The International Energy Agency’s July 2026 analysis reports a 9% decline in critical-mineral investment in 2025, alongside approximately $65 billion in public-finance commitments. The contrast matters: governments can announce support while private investment contracts, and commitments can remain undisbursed. An extraction project does not resolve a refining bottleneck; a refining facility does not establish that a manufacturer has accepted its output.

The European Commission’s October 9, 2026 selection of 46 additional strategic raw-material projects offers a concrete response, but its composition makes the execution problem visible. Eight projects concern extraction, 11 processing, 19 recycling and eight integrated activities. Among projects selected in 2025, the Commission reported 25 completed environmental impact assessments and 17 construction permits. Those categories may overlap. Neither is commercial production, and counting them as delivered capacity would conceal the remaining financing, construction and qualification burden.

The Critical Raw Materials Act sets non-binding 2030 benchmarks of at least 10% of annual EU consumption from EU extraction capacity, 40% from processing and 25% from recycling, with a 65% ceiling on dependence on a single third country. Meeting those benchmarks requires usable capacity across successive production stages. Procurement must support a qualified product and a reliable purchaser, rather than reward designation alone. Otherwise, public support can finance an asset without securing the industrial function it was intended to protect.

Conditional permission is not a settled market
The January 15, 2026 Bureau of Industry and Security rule makes certain advanced-computing exports eligible for case-by-case review, subject to technical and transaction conditions. The thresholds include total processing performance below 21,000 under the regulatory definition and total DRAM bandwidth below 6,500 gigabytes per second. Supply certifications, recipient safeguards and third-party testing remain part of the arrangement. This is bounded discretion, not unrestricted access.

NVIDIA’s August 26, 2026 release illustrates the distance between regulatory eligibility and commercial execution. The company reported $96.2 billion in revenue for the quarter ending July 26, 2026, including $89.0 billion from Data Center, while its following-quarter outlook assumed no Data Center compute revenue from China. That planning assumption does not prove that no licences were granted. It does show why governments cannot infer commercially significant access from a revised review policy.

China’s Announcement No. 70 of November 7, 2025 suspends six specified control measures through November 10, 2026; it does not remove every rare-earth restriction. Announcement No. 18 of April 4, 2025 separately covers specified items associated with seven elements, including dysprosium, terbium and yttrium. The relevant bargain must identify which instrument changes, which products remain controlled and which permissions firms can actually obtain. A promise about “minerals” is too broad to tell a purchasing manager whether an order can be delivered.

National interests prevent a single European bargain
Italy’s July 2026 exports to China increased 27.6% year on year in nominal terms, according to Istat. That one-month result gives Rome reason to pursue practical access, but no basis for assuming that supplier vulnerability has diminished. Italy’s commercial interest is to keep sales executable while protecting sensitive capabilities; the special-powers framework originating in Decree-Law No. 21 of 2012 supplies a separate protective baseline, whose contemporary application requires the applicable legal measures.

France has to distinguish overseas responsibilities from sectoral market access. Its 2026 foreign-trade report identifies Chinese demand as important for aeronautics, luxury goods, cosmetics, wines and spirits, pharmaceuticals and agri-food products. Investment scrutiny offers a means of preserving openness with conditions: the economy ministry reports that 49% of authorised investments in 2025 carried conditions. This is neither a China-specific rate nor proof that monitoring succeeds. It makes continued verification an administrative obligation, rather than a task completed at approval.

Germany’s eight projects in the Commission’s October 9, 2026 selection put diversification into a delivery framework. Battery recycling in Aachen and lithium extraction in Zinnwald address different stages; neither designation establishes operating output. Berlin’s problem is to connect finance, production and customer acceptance while accounting for the cost of alternatives. A longer project list does not protect a factory until a qualified input reaches it.

The United Kingdom’s July 2026 Joint Economic and Trade Commission record concentrates on services access, professional qualifications and data flows, while its National Security and Investment Act report records 1,324 notifications and nine final orders during April 2025–March 2026. These are different populations, not an approval ratio. London is simultaneously pursuing access and reviewing security exposure. Its AUKUS commitments add an industrial constraint: the Commons Defence Committee records a forecast requirement for 40,000 additional defence and civil nuclear workers by 2030. Services diplomacy cannot substitute for that workforce.

Security obligations cap the scope of accommodation
The Taiwan Relations Act prevents American defence assistance from becoming merely a commercial negotiating token. Section 3 assigns requirements to the President and Congress, informed by military review. Any adjustment must satisfy that process. The monetary value of trade concessions cannot establish that Taiwan’s defensive needs have fallen, and diplomatic reassurance cannot demonstrate the operational restraint needed to support such a judgment.

European military contributions face their own restoration costs. The German navy’s completed 2024 Indo-Pacific deployment lasted 208 days and covered approximately 45,000 nautical miles, while its official account retained the NATO northern flank as the core task. The experience demonstrates reach and sustainment; it does not establish permanent availability. NATO’s Article 4 provides consultation, while Articles 5–6 define collective-defence obligations and geographic scope. Governments must specify the contribution they can sustain rather than imply that alliance membership supplies an automatic response to an Indo-Pacific contingency.

The UK National Cyber Security Centre’s April 2026 advisory on covert networks makes the infrastructure boundary equally clear. An incident channel can support clarification, but routers, remote-access controls and monitoring still require protection. Suspending defensive work in anticipation of political reciprocity would exchange an existing safeguard for an outcome not yet demonstrated.

The next two years will expose the cost of administrative peace
Between October 2026 and October 2028, the consequential test will be whether selective accommodation becomes usable commercial access and qualified industrial output. November 10, 2026 is the stated expiry of China’s specified suspension, not a prediction of renewed controls. January 17, 2028 is the Commission’s published full-application date for the revised investment-screening framework. Both dates require governments to prepare implementing decisions and administrative capacity before claiming that the institutional transition has reduced exposure.

The Critical Raw Materials Act’s 2030 benchmarks leave manufacturers facing a timing problem during these next 12–24 months: industrial restoration may take longer than a licensing or political decision. Inaction would leave firms paying for inventory, delayed production and replacement sourcing, with public budgets exposed to pressure for emergency support. Unfunded qualification and continuity work would also weaken defence procurement when suppliers encounter the same bottlenecks.

The U.S.–China Board of Trade can create room for that investment, but it cannot deliver it. The cost of the choice already being pursued—selective, conditional relief—is the obligation to maintain protection and finance alternatives while cooperation is tested. Governments that omit that expenditure will preserve the appearance of stability by leaving manufacturers, infrastructure operators and procurement authorities to absorb the next interruption.  -https://t.co/CHQSQr18Ui via @https://debuglies.com

text:
On Saturday in Tuscaloosa, Keelon Russell waited for Holly Rowe to finish interviewing Gunner Stockton, then walked up and congratulated the quarterback who had just beaten him. The habit he was following is about 170 years old, and it started in English boarding schools. Thomas Hughes published Tom Brown’s School Days in 1857, and that same year the term “muscular Christianity” spread through a Saturday Review piece on a Charles Kingsley novel. Kingsley’s argument was that games “conduce, not merely to physical, but to moral health.” Team sports became a way to build character, and playing fair was the lesson.

By the 1880s, that idea had a flagship team. Nicholas Lane Jackson, an assistant secretary of the Football Association, founded Corinthian Football Club on Sept. 28, 1882. He started it after Scotland’s run of wins over England, with a roster of top amateurs. The club’s rules barred it from cup competitions, and it played mostly friendlies. The story told about the Corinthians is that when they conceded a penalty, their goalkeeper stepped aside and let the ball in, and when they won one, their captain chipped it over the bar. The amateur ideal behind that behavior also had a class edge. Working men had six-day work weeks and could not afford to play for free. In cricket, amateurs got separate dressing rooms and separate gates, and they were addressed as “Mr.” The Football Association legalized payments to players in 1885.

The penalty kick shows where the honor system ran out. William McCrum, an Irish linen manufacturer and amateur goalkeeper, proposed it in 1890 because he was tired of foul play. On Feb. 14, 1891, Notts County led Stoke City 1-0 in an FA Cup quarterfinal when a County defender deliberately handled a shot on the goal line. The rulebook offered only an indirect free kick, and County lined up a wall on the goal line and held on. Four months later, on June 2, 1891, the rules body approved the penalty kick in a Glasgow hotel. According to one account, some English public-school administrators resisted it because they did not believe gentlemen would cheat. Until then, the sport’s rules assumed nobody would foul on purpose.

The ideal went global anyway. Charles Miller, called the father of Brazilian football, played for the Corinthians in 1892, and Sport Club Corinthians Paulista in São Paulo took its name in tribute. At the 1908 London Olympics, Bishop Ethelbert Talbot of Pennsylvania preached at St. Paul’s Cathedral to the athletes. Pierre de Coubertin repeated the message soon afterward: “The importance of these Olympiads is not so much to win as to take part.” Georgia won 20-17 on Saturday, and Russell stood on the field long enough to shake Stockton’s hand.

text:
Handwritten Letter to Marcello Truzzi on CIA and the Paranormal - from someone who used to work for CIA 

transcript 👇

CONFIDENTIAL
Dear Marcello,

It looks as if I won’t have access to e-mail for a bit. But I promised to answer your question about my career with the U.S. government. The truth, strange as it may seem, is that I was an employee of the CIA for about a year in the mid 80s. I applied and was accepted while I was at Duke, then officially joined after a summer goofing around in Europe following graduation.

I was in a training program that would put me overseas in a technically-oriented assignment, assisting case officers with certain projects.* Because of that I was under cover, and had to tell friends that I worked as a civilian in a very boring-sounding job at the Pentagon. When I traveled abroad on business, it was with an official passport.

The job was interesting and challenging in some respects but within six months or so I decided it wasn’t how I wanted to spend my career. When you are undercover at the Agency you tend to develop an ‘us v. them’ attitude toward the rest of society - and the world - because you are constantly trying to protect your cover and all that goes with it. The satisfaction I got from the job, including the sense of accomplishment and contribution to the Cold War effort, wasn’t enough worth the psychological sacrifice. I considered and was even accepted into a much more sensitive, “sexy” training program for non-official-cover case officers, believing that I would be able to have much greater impact there. But at the last minute I decided not to join, and instead accepted an offer from a defense contractor in Virginia. (I was also moonlighting then as a member of a small startup company, working on avionics technology - we were all Agency engineers.)

I was not in the Directorate of Intelligence, as Wingfield has speculated.

CONFIDENTIAL
I left the Agency not just because I had good prospects elsewhere, and because of the psychological sacrifice just mentioned, but primarily because I’d become convinced that the people calling the shots were not the best and the brightest. More accurately, the “system” that ran things wasn’t as good as it could have been. You are probably aware of this already, but NOC officers masquerade as engineers, salesmen, etc., not diplomats, and when they are arrested, the US govt doesn’t even admit knowing them. I’d already seen one case where it appeared that one of our guys was exposed by sloppy practices at high levels. On a much less significant scale, I’d also been the victim of bureaucratic fuck-ups. It was the most difficult decision I’d ever made, but in the end I decided to leave the Agency and the prospect of a “James Bond life” behind. That was late 1986.

It turned out to be a good decision, despite the many pangs of regret I’ve felt over the years. Had I gone to a foreign country and spied under non-official-cover, I’d probably be dead or in jail now. The reason is that Aldrich Ames sold lists of undercover employees to the KGB, at a time when I would have been on one of those lists (because of my initial, low-grade cover assignment).

Although the Agency encouraged me to think about returning in the months after I left (they even deliberately delayed the transfer of my clearances to my new company), I never went back. My only contact with them has been to seek approval for a reversion to “overt” status - so I can legally admit I worked there. That was a couple of years ago.

CONFIDENTIAL
Naturally, I have not advertised the fact that I was once a CIA employee. I told Sandra Martin, when she was my agent, and she spread it around (thanks, Sandra!). That is how George Wingfield heard, and, I guess, how you heard, although when the story began to spread I told a few other people.

Let me be clear about this: When I was at the Agency I knew nothing about government interest in the paranormal, and I had no interest in that subject myself. When I began to work as a journalist, I had zero contact with anyone whom I’d known while at the Agency. In other words, it would be inaccurate to say that I’ve ever made use of my past Agency career in my journalistic work. As people like Hal Puthoff know, that is even particularly true for Remote Viewing: I was not even certain that the CIA had sponsored early RV work until I was well into the project. None of the characters in the book is a person I remember working with, and none of the current or former Agency employees I spoke to for the book was aware of my past employment there. Wingfield’s and Azadehdel’s rants notwithstanding, my interest in crop circles and UFOs was purely journalistic and personal.

But you can see how people might have got the wrong idea, had I made my association with the Agency known from the beginning of my interest in the paranormal. Now that interest is coming to an end—I hope!

Best wishes to you and your family for Christmas and the New Year.

text:
Let’s talk about why ultrasound is critical for those with Long Covid, and using the Mindray MX7 settings as a baseline. 

If you have Long Covid, then you are also fighting fibrosis. Plain and simple. Not controversial. You need to remove fibrosis to get healthy, and ultrasound is uniquely capable of doing that.

The Mindray MX7 has a fibrosis specific setting. Many versions of ultrasound can do what it can, but implemented differently. I️’m not familiar enough yet with the space to speak to other machines.

Mindray has a feature called Natural Touch Elastography (a form of strain elastography). Its main practical differences from many other systems are:

•Compression source: Many strain elastography modes require the operator to manually pump or rhythmically compress the probe. Natural Touch is designed so the patient’s own breathing and/or vascular pulsation can supply the compressive force.
•Operator dependence: This reduces variability between users and sessions because results are less sensitive to how hard or consistently the operator presses.
•Quantification: Strain-ratio measurement lets you compare a stiff region to nearby normal tissue with a number, not just color.
•Color map: Side-by-side B-mode + color stiffness map (commonly red = stiffer, blue = softer; always check the legend).

Elastography uses the normal imaging frequencies of the probes in use (commonly ~5–13 MHz on linear probes). There is no special “fibrosis frequency” or proprietary pulse sequence. 

Academic work on ultrasound and reprogramming ion channels spans a range of frequencies (~0.5–10 MHz); the Mindray can’t match that exactly, but the practical approach can be longer dwell and scrubbing times with ordinary diagnostic ultrasound energy to mimic the same effects of these research papers.

Practical advantage for stiffness mapping 
- It is great to have an ability to watch an area shift from red toward blue under continued scrubbing as visual feedback for local stiffness reduction and improved circulation.
- It does not emit special therapeutic frequencies or pulse rates unavailable on other diagnostic ultrasounds. 
- Other manufacturers also offer strain elastography (some also support physiological-motion compression with little or no manual pumping, but I don’t know which at this time). Natural Touch is simply an implementation that supports consistent stiffness mapping during longer, motion-based sessions. 
- The broader mechanical effects (possible micro-calcification breakdown, lymphatic clearance support, ion-channel modulation, etc.) come from the ultrasound energy and duration/motion themselves, not from a unique elastography frequency.

I️’m not selling anything here, I️’m just offering open-source research for those who are suffering and want to try and get healthy.

Remove fibrosis. Clean your lymphatic system and fascia. Wake up your cells. Get healthy.

Compare Nigeria’s numbers with those of other global oil producers. The United States produces over 10 million barrels per day for 330 million people, yet sells petroleum strictly at market-determined prices. Qatar holds some of the world's largest gas reserves for under 500,000 citizens, yet had to cut energy subsidies significantly to maintain long-term fiscal health.

As Minister Oyedele noted, comparing local crude allocation to local agricultural produce like garri or cassava—a misleading analogy popularised by media commentary—is a fundamental misrepresentation of global commodity markets and contractual energy economics. For Atiku to suggest that Nigeria can fund unlimited production subsidies without bankrupting the state is either financially reckless or fundamentally dishonest.

*Price Modulation vs Subsidy Restoration: Unpacking the 30-Day Strategy*

Atiku’s attempt to frame NNPC Retail’s decision to forgo its profit margin as a "return to the fuel subsidy" is a deliberate mischaracterisation designed to mislead the public and incite public dissatisfaction. First, NNPC had offered the discount to celebrate the 66th Independence anniversary. It merely offered to extend the discount by another 30 days.

The administration’s intervention is a market-smoothing price modulation framework, not a return to unbudgeted federal spending. When NNPC Retail agrees to sell fuel at landing cost for 30 days during an unprecedented global crude price spike, it is not writing checks to opaque import cartels. It is leveraging its corporate balance sheet to absorb short-term global volatility, backed directly by President Bola Ahmed Tinubu.

Furthermore, the Federal Government’s negotiation of an interim N1,350 per litre ceiling on ex-gantry costs is a structural shock absorber, not price control. Under this framework, refiners and importers absorb short-term cost spikes above the ceiling and recover those costs later when global crude prices cool or local exchange rates adjust. N1,400 today and N1,400 tomorrow provides far greater economic stability than N1,500 today and N1,300 tomorrow.

Rapid, erratic price swings trigger immediate, panic-driven hikes in commercial transport fares that rarely decrease even when fuel prices drop. The ceiling protects commuters from permanent hikes in transport prices. The ceiling is reviewed transparently every month based on published cost audits, preventing the hidden accumulation of opaque state liabilities.

*Structural Solutions: The Administration’s Multi-Pronged Economic Approach*

While critics offer cheap soundbites, the Tinubu administration has deployed concrete, structural policies across the entire energy and economic value chain by establishing a state-backed strategic energy reserve to release refined products whenever global supply disruptions or private hoarding threaten price stability—securing long-term supply without fixing market prices.

President Tinubu's administration is rapidly expanding Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) infrastructure in partnership with state governments. At 60-70% cheaper than premium motor spirit (PMS), CNG offers a permanent structural alternative for commercial transporters.

The government has secured domestic refining operations through naira-for-crude arrangements to insulate pump prices from foreign exchange volatility. It has introduced windfall taxes on energy operators that attempt to gouge consumers during crises, explicitly earmarking the revenue for transport vouchers and minimum-wage support.

President Tinubu's government is already enforcing the 2025 tax reform laws to dismantle illegal road levies and using NIPOST digital address codes to reduce freight and food

$IONQ  IonQ Takes Command of Quantum-Era Security: With Elisity, the World’s Governments and Businesses Now Have One Trusted Full-Stack Partner. Against China, Russia and the Q-Day Clock: How Elisity Makes IonQ the Global Leader in Quantum-Safe Security and Networking

Issued by Friends of IonQ

Please take the time to read this in full, because most observers are going to miss the importance of what IonQ announced today and the importance of what occurred directly lines up to everything the Friends of IonQ has been realizing was needed during our exhaustive research the past few months.  

@IonQ_Inc  agreement to acquire @ElisityInc  is one of the most consequential moves in the company’s history, and it is the move we had been hoping to see. With it, IonQ takes an unequivocal position of strength in a security market that is growing fast and becoming more alarming by the month, and no other quantum computing company can match it. For months our research on China, Russia and the countries now racing to protect themselves kept reaching the same conclusion. IonQ had assembled the strongest quantum-safe portfolio in the industry: quantum computing, quantum networking, quantum key distribution through ID Quantique, quantum random number generation and post-quantum cryptography. 

One layer was still missing, and it was the layer adversaries exploit first: control over who and what is allowed to reach what inside a network. We wanted IonQ to own that layer, and now it will. Elisity brings identity-based Zero Trust to every user, device, workload, AI agent and non-human identity. Its IdentityGraph enforces least-privilege policy through a software layer that does not depend on the network underneath. The deal is all-stock and worth up to $1.3 billion, including an earnout of up to $150 million, with closing expected in the fourth quarter. It gives IonQ the whole path: the key that encrypts the data, the link that carries it, and the identity that is allowed to use it. This is not a cybersecurity tuck-in. It is the step that completes IonQ’s full stack, and it arrives exactly when governments and banks are being told to act.

The timing matters because of the threat. Over several months, our reports on China and Russia have documented a quantum partnership between Russia and China that is deeper, better funded and more deliberate than most Western observers assumed. Our reports went far and wide due to the incredible accuracy contained. Both states are pursuing quantum computing, quantum communication and the human networks that move expertise between them. Meanwhile their cyber services are already inside critical networks today. Salt Typhoon reached deep into American telecommunications carriers. UNC3886 attacked Singapore’s critical infrastructure and then all four of its major telcos, which Singapore’s Cyber Security Agency called “a deliberate, targeted, and well-planned campaign.” Russian services have spent years probing European energy, government and diplomatic systems. Behind them come other dubious players: North Korea’s industrial-scale theft and its fake IT workers, and the commercial brokers who sell access to whoever pays. Super intelligence is now accelerating all of it. 

IonQ frames the challenge as two overlapping priorities: containing attacks that move at machine speed today, and protecting sensitive information against the quantum threat tomorrow. @ElisityInc  answers the first, and @IonQ_Inc  quantum-safe portfolio answers the second. All of this feeds harvest-now-decrypt-later, where adversaries copy encrypted traffic today and wait for a quantum computer to open it. As the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission has reported, China is among the adversaries already doing exactly that. Our own conclusion is blunt: encrypted data stolen today is a quantum loss already in progress. IonQ’s announcement quotes @NiccoloDeMasi: “Q-Day is coming much faster than predicted.” The adversaries do not need to break today’s encryption today. They only need to be inside the network and patient. Elisity is built to stop the first step, and IonQ’s quantum-safe products are built to make the patience worthless.

Our China research shows how far ahead of the official picture Beijing already is. In “China’s Quantum Push: What Beijing Is Assembling in Plain Sight,” we documented from China’s own procurement, standards and government records a state program that is further along than the assessments most U.S. and allied officials still cite. A China Telecom-controlled center in Beijing’s E-Town district is building a full-stack quantum ecosystem that, in Beijing’s own words, is benchmarked against IBM Qiskit and NVIDIA NVQLink. The research institute that leads Beijing’s quantum-AI consortium belongs to CETC, the state defense-electronics group, and is on the U.S. Entity List alongside three other consortium members. China’s state carriers run quantum-secured networks across some 40 cities and report 7.2 million quantum-communication users. Those carriers sit on the Pentagon’s list of Chinese military companies, and China’s mobilization law lets the state requisition their facilities. PLA universities co-draft China’s national standards for quantum computing and quantum key distribution, and hardware for the next generation of quantum satellites is already in procurement. When the Chinese Academy of Sciences released its 15th Five-Year Plan on September 28, we tested our findings against it. Of 49 findings, 39 were confirmed or partly confirmed and none was contradicted. China is not racing toward a single device. It is racing to own the whole stack, and Beijing has said so in writing.

The danger reaches beyond China’s borders. Origin Quantum’s Wukong cloud, run by a company on the U.S. Entity List, had logged more than 49 million remote visits from 192 countries and regions by June 2026. The United States, Russia and Japan were its top foreign users, and its operating system is now free to download. A state ordnance conglomerate led its latest funding round. China is writing its own standards for post-quantum encryption and quantum networks, and it aims to offer a global quantum communication service by 2027. Russia is a willing partner in that push. The Chinese Academy of Sciences and Rosatom signed a quantum and photonics memorandum during President Putin’s state visit in May, and our Hub and Spokes update traces sustained access by a Chinese state-funded trapped-ion program to members of a Russian national-program team. The strategic question for every allied government is now concrete: whose operators sit inside its keys, whose clouds hold its research, and whose code runs on its networks. Our answer is an in-alliance quantum-safe stack that allies operate themselves, and this acquisition takes IonQ a long step toward being the company that supplies it.

That is why we see this as a full-stack deal rather than a bolt-on. Our China validation report makes a point that the quantum industry rarely says aloud: key distribution does not protect compromised endpoints or insiders. Post-quantum cryptography and QKD protect data in transit, but they cannot stop a compromised device or a stolen identity from moving sideways once it is inside. 

Microsegmentation stops that lateral movement. Elisity’s roadmap goes further and adds cryptographic inventory and quantum-risk data to IdentityGraph. A bank or ministry could then see which assets still run vulnerable cryptography, who can reach them, and how to fence them off while migration proceeds. Every regulator we have studied asks institutions to do exactly this, in roughly this order: inventory the cryptography, contain the risk, then migrate.

The U.S. government shows how wide the gap is. A Government Accountability Office audit, released publicly this month, found that none of the 24 major federal agencies it reviewed had fully put in place the post-quantum preparation practices the White House requires. Twenty-three lacked documented processes to keep a cryptographic inventory, and 19 were not using automated tools to discover the cryptography running on their networks. The Office of Management and Budget estimates the migration of priority federal systems at roughly $7.1 billion. That missing inventory, with an automated map of what is running and who can reach it, is exactly what Elisity’s IdentityGraph roadmap is designed to supply. The deadlines are fixed:

* January 2027: the NSA’s CNSA 2.0 requires new national security system purchases to support quantum-resistant algorithms.
* End of 2030: Executive Order 14412 requires high-value federal systems to move key exchange to post-quantum algorithms.
* 2030 and 2035: NIST’s draft plan retires RSA and elliptic-curve encryption after 2030 and bans them after 2035.

With Elisity, IonQ can sell the whole sequence instead of only the last step. No other company can do that.

The commercial case is just as strong. Elisity has more than 100 deployments worldwide and a growing roster of Fortune 500 customers. Its revenue and customer count are doubling year over year, and it reports zero churn. It works in a microsegmentation market IonQ sizes at more than $10 billion. The opportunity is enormous precisely because the world is so far behind: Juniper Research projects that only 27 percent of businesses worldwide will have deployed post-quantum cryptography by 2035. Elisity brings what quantum vendors have always struggled to build: a trusted seat with the chief information security officer, and enterprise and government sales channels that reach buyers long before they have a quantum budget. IonQ reported 40 percent year-over-year multiproduct revenue growth in the second quarter of 2026. Elisity gives that growth a far wider funnel. A customer who starts with Zero Trust today becomes the natural buyer of PQC, QRNG, QKD and eventually quantum computing tomorrow, all from a vendor already inside the security perimeter. Keeping James Winebrenner as CEO of the business protects the team and the customer relationships that make it valuable.

Our Switzerland report shows why this matters to sovereign buyers. Switzerland is home to ID Quantique, the Swiss secure-network infrastructure and the Geneva Quantum Network. It also faces documented Russian and Chinese intelligence activity on its soil, from Geneva’s international organizations to its research and banking sectors. Switzerland’s National Cyber Security Centre has taken a deliberately post-quantum-first position: in its December 2025 brief, QKD is “explicitly not considered” a stand-alone solution. Elisity speaks directly to that view. IonQ can now offer Swiss authorities and banks a layered answer: PQC everywhere, QKD where fixed high-value links justify it, and identity-based segmentation across the entire estate. That is a better fit for the Swiss doctrine of sovereignty by design than any single technology, and it lets IonQ meet the regulator where it already stands rather than argue with it.

Italy shows the same pattern in a European Union and NATO setting. Our Italy report documents sustained Russian and Chinese pressure on Italian defense, space, ports, telecommunications and the networks that carry Mediterranean traffic. Italy’s response is gathering pace through its national post-quantum roadmap, its quantum strategy and the financial sector’s own preparation. The Bank of Italy’s Milano Hub is an immediate door, with a key date on November 5. Italian banks, energy operators and public administrations need cryptographic inventory, containment and migration all at once, delivered by a vendor that can respect Italian and European sovereignty requirements. Elisity turns IonQ’s Italian proposition from “quantum technology for the future” into “security your teams can deploy this quarter, on a path to quantum safety.”

In Asia the fit is just as direct. In Singapore, the Monetary Authority of Singapore has asked financial institutions since 2024 to build cryptographic inventories and crypto-agility, and in July 2026 it set formal supervisory expectations for quantum resilience by the end of the decade. IonQ, through ID Quantique, already supplies the quantum key distribution behind Singtel’s national quantum-safe network. MAS has tested both PQC and QKD with its leading banks, and the S$220 million FSTI 4.0 grant scheme gives those banks money to act. With Elisity, IonQ can walk into DBS, OCBC, UOB, HSBC and the payment operators with a supervisory-ready answer covering inventory, segmentation and quantum-safe transport. In South Korea the opportunity is written into law. The amended Quantum Technology Industry Act, passed by the Cabinet in May, makes quantum security compulsory across more than 600 public bodies from November 20, 2026. That covers ministries, local governments and public institutions such as KEPCO. The National Intelligence Service has set PQC milestones running from 2027 to 2029. ID Quantique’s QKD was the first to pass NIS verification and already protects a government network linking dozens of departments. IonQ also holds a Ministry of Science and ICT agreement and a growing KISTI partnership. Recent authentication failures at several major Korean banks are a reminder that identity, not only encryption, is where attackers walk in. Elisity closes that gap for a market that is now legally required to buy.

These four countries (and there are others) tell one story. Each faces the same Russian, Chinese and North Korean pressure. Each regulator is converging on the same playbook: inventory, contain, migrate and verify. And each wants a trusted vendor that can deliver the whole playbook without handing control of its networks to anyone else. China, meanwhile, is offering the world its own stack: its clouds, its standards, its quantum-secured links. Before this deal, IonQ could answer the migrate and verify parts better than almost anyone. After it, IonQ can answer all four, through a single relationship that begins with a product the customer needs today. As @NiccoloDeMasi put it, Elisity “will bring proven enterprise policy enforcement scale and deployment experience to our quantum security strategy and will give IonQ a strong growth platform to serve customers.” That is how a quantum company becomes a security platform with worldwide reach, and how quantum revenue stops depending on when a customer is ready to buy a quantum computer.

We believe the market has not yet priced this in. It is the same blind spot our China research exposed: the assessments most officials still rely on describe a Chinese quantum program that Beijing has already moved past. Markets tend to value what they can measure this quarter, and the security consequences of quantum computing build quietly until a mandate, a breach or a deadline makes them impossible to ignore. Those deadlines and many others are now on the calendar:

* Korea’s mandate in November;
* Italy’s financial hub this fall;
* Singapore’s supervisory expectations;
* the NSA’s January 2027 requirement;
* China’s own 2027 target for a global quantum communication service.

In our view, Elisity is the piece that lets IonQ turn its quantum leadership into sales across every one of those markets. We strongly believe from a commerical viewpoint that this acquisition lines up perfectly with that incredible commerical opportunities that @IonQ_Inc is lining up. "## The ₹800 Crore Scam: The Fall, Rise, and Legal Chess Match of Bureaucrat A. Mohan
In April 2016, the Andhra Pradesh Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB) unraveled one of the most high-profile corruption scandals in the state's history. At the center of the storm was Adimoolam Mohan (popularly known as A. Mohan), a powerful bureaucrat whose immense wealth shocked investigators and the public alike. Frequently misidentified in sensational media headlines as a senior "IAS officer," Mohan was actually a state-level Group-I officer who had risen through the ranks to become the Deputy Transport Commissioner and later the Joint Transport Commissioner of Andhra Pradesh.
The trajectory of his case—from a massive multi-state raid to his reinstatement, promotion, and a decade-long trial—offers a textbook study on the realities of India's systemic infrastructure.
------------------------------
## The Evidence and the Raids
The ACB did not act blindly; the raids were the culmination of months of intelligence gathering built on concrete evidence:

* Whistleblower & Operator Complaints: The primary catalyst was a wave of formal complaints filed by transport operators in the East Godavari district. Mohan had established a reputation where operators who refused to pay bribes faced sudden vehicle seizures, permit cancellations, or fabricated regulatory violations.
* The Kakinada Checkpoint Financial Trail: ACB intelligence tracked an organized extortion ring at the Kakinada Anchorage Port. Informants verified that Mohan’s ground staff were systematically collecting a mandated illicit fee of ₹1,000 per truck. By charting the daily flow of thousands of vehicles, the ACB calculated a multi-crore cash network feeding directly back to Mohan, estimated at roughly ₹3 crore every month.
* Paper Trails of Benami Companies: Prior to the raids, investigators uncovered eight shell companies registered under the name of his daughter, Tejasri. A cross-reference of these companies' bank records showed massive cash deposits and real estate transactions that were completely disproportionate to her known sources of income, providing the legal "prima facie" proof required to secure a search warrant.

On April 28, 2016, the ACB launched massive, simultaneous raids across nine strategic locations spanning Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, and Karnataka. While the official "book value" (the registered purchase price) of his properties was recorded at around ₹100 crore to ₹120 crore, the ACB officially estimated the actual real estate market value to exceed ₹800 crore.
During the multi-day operation, the ACB seized and documented a massive hoard of wealth, including:

* 2 kilograms of solid gold and 5 kilograms of silver ornaments.
* 14 luxury flats in Hyderabad, a massive five-storey building in the upscale Jubilee Hills neighborhood, and a commercial office building in Panjagutta.
* Over 50 acres of prime agricultural land spread across the Nellore, Prakasam, and Chittoor districts.
* Documents mapping out the eight shell companies used to launder illicit bribe money into legitimate assets.

------------------------------
## Arrest, Jail, and Current Legal Status
Immediately following the raids, the ACB registered a formal Disproportionate Assets (DA) case against him. Mohan was arrested, produced before the specialized Vijayawada ACB Court, and remanded to judicial custody. He was immediately suspended from service by the state government and sent to the Challapalli prison, where he spent his initial months behind bars.
Today, A. Mohan is no longer in jail. Under the Indian legal system, individuals accused of economic offenses and disproportionate assets are typically granted bail once the initial phase of interrogation is complete and the chargesheet has been filed, provided they are not deemed an immediate flight risk. Mohan secured his release on bail and has remained out of custody while his trial slowly progresses.
His case has turned into a protracted legal battle:

* The Slow-Moving Trial: Because the assets are spread across three different states and hidden behind complex corporate veils, verifying the exact valuation and ownership of every piece of property has taken years, dragging the trial out in the specialized anti-corruption judiciary.
* Aggressive Defense Strategy: Rather than waiting for a trial verdict, Mohan’s legal team has taken an aggressive approach. He remains a highly active petitioner in the Andhra Pradesh High Court, repeatedly filing criminal petitions (such as under Section 482 of the CrPC) attempting to quash the ACB’s proceedings entirely. His lawyers argue that the ACB’s ₹800 crore figure is a hyper-inflated estimate calculated using speculative market rates, asserting that his actual holdings are far closer to his documented income and the official book values.

------------------------------
## The Shocking Twist: Reinstatement and Promotion
Perhaps the most startling development in this saga is that A. Mohan returned to his government job and even managed to secure a promotion while his criminal trial remained active.

* Reinstatement: Following his 2016 arrest, he was placed under suspension. However, on September 25, 2018, the government of Andhra Pradesh officially revoked his suspension.
* Promotion: He returned to active duty and was subsequently promoted from Deputy Transport Commissioner to Joint Transport Commissioner. High Court records show him still fighting legal battles regarding administrative perks (such as unpaid annual grade increments dating back to his suspension period) while holding this high-level office.

------------------------------
## What This Case Says About the Indian System
The journey of A. Mohan's case exposes critical vulnerabilities and structural paradoxes across the four pillars of India's administrative and legal framework:
## 1. The Indian Judiciary: Protection of Rights vs. Systemic Delay
The judiciary is designed to uphold the principle of "innocent until proven guilty" and protect citizens from arbitrary state power. This ensures that an accused individual has every right to challenge evidence, file quash petitions, and secure bail. However, in practice, these procedural safeguards are heavily leveraged by wealthy defendants to create endless delays. The judiciary suffers from extreme vacancy backlogs and procedural bottlenecks, allowing high-profile corruption trials to drag on for decades. By the time a final verdict is reached, the public impact and deterrence of the justice system are severely diluted.
## 2. The Police and Investigating Agencies (ACB)
The initial phase highlights that Indian investigative bodies are fully capable of executing complex, highly coordinated, multi-state operations. They successfully mapped an intricate network of benami properties and shell companies. However, the police often lack the specialized forensic auditing resources required to fast-track economic offense trials through the courts. Furthermore, the fact that an official could openly amass such massive wealth for decades points to a breakdown in internal vigilance, where anti-corruption bodies frequently operate reactively rather than proactively dismantling systemic graft.
## 3. The Politicians and Political Will
Bureaucrats do not operate in a vacuum. A monthly extortion ring yielding crores requires political patronage or, at the very least, deliberate blind spots from those in power. The fact that Mohan’s suspension was revoked and he was promoted while his criminal trial for a ₹800 crore scam was active highlights a glaring paradox in political will. While politicians publicly campaign on "zero tolerance for corruption," administrative systems frequently allow tainted officials back into power due to shifting political alignments, legal technicalities, or influential lobbying.
## 4. The Indian Constitution and Civil Service Rules
The Indian Constitution provides unique, robust job security to government employees. Under Article 311, no civil servant can be dismissed or reduced in rank without a rigorous, formal departmental inquiry. This law was originally written into the Constitution to protect honest bureaucrats from being vindictively fired by corrupt politicians. Ironically, this exact constitutional shield is what allows corrupt officials to thrive. Because a suspension cannot legally be extended indefinitely without a concluded trial, governments are often forced by civil service rules to reinstate accused individuals. The A. Mohan case demonstrates how a constitutional protection designed to safeguard bureaucratic integrity can be systematically inverted to shield the corrupt from immediate accountability.
A decade after the initial raids, the state continues to pursue the case. Until the specialized court delivers its final judgment, A. Mohan remains a free, working, and promoted man on bail, using the higher judiciary to fight the very corruption case that was meant to end his career."

text:
Beyond the Laughs: John Candy's Secret Contract to Care for the Crew Hollywood Forgot

While filming Planes, Trains and Automobiles in 1987, the shoot was brutal: icy winds, deep snow, and long days in rural Illinois. Most stars hid in heated trailers between takes.
But John Candy stayed outside.
He chatted with crew members, offered encouragement, and handed out fresh, hot coffee he'd arranged himself, knowing the catering truck's brew was lukewarm.
Candy's compassion wasn't a one-time gesture. It was a condition of his success.
The Man Who Fed the Crew
During the making of Uncle Buck, Candy noticed that younger crew members were often left to survive on vending machine snacks because the budget only covered meals for lead talent.
Without notifying a single producer, Candy quietly hired a hot food truck at his own expense, ensuring the entire team had something warm and substantial to eat. He believed no one should work hard under tough conditions and go unfed.
Director Chris Columbus, who worked with him on Only the Lonely, recalled how Candy learned every single crew member’s name by the third day. Each morning began with a personal greeting, and each night ended with a handshake and a genuine "thank you."
When a birthday was overlooked by production, Candy quietly organized a surprise cake and music between scenes.
Beyond the Spotlight
His approach came from his early years at Toronto's Second City, where he hauled equipment and cleaned stages long before fame hit. That experience instilled a deep respect for every job on set.
On Splash, when a sudden downpour threatened to destroy cameras, Candy didn't run for cover. He stayed behind, joking with the tech crew while helping them haul and save thousands of dollars worth of gear.
On a freezing night shoot for The Great Outdoors, he noticed shivering crew members. He immediately ordered portable heaters and blankets from a local supplier, covering the cost himself.
He famously refused preferential treatment. Once, learning the crew was crammed into coach while stars sat in first class on a flight, Candy gave up his first-class seat to a weary camera assistant and sat in the back without telling anyone.
John Candy never sought recognition for these acts. He never mentioned them in interviews. Directors and co-stars only began sharing these stories after his passing.
To Candy, true success wasn't about the size of the trailer. It was about uplifting the people behind the scenes. In a business obsessed with stars, John Candy made it his mission to honor the people who made the magic happen. His legacy rests on the quiet warmth and humanity he showed to the people the industry often overlooks.

text:
A Colorado woman is taking legal action after being mistakenly accused of stealing a $25 package, raising serious questions about police surveillance technology and the protection of personal privacy.

Chrisanna Elser filed a federal lawsuit against Flock Safety, two Colorado towns, and police officials after receiving a criminal summons in September 2025. The accusation reportedly stemmed from license plate tracking cameras. According to the lawsuit, Sgt. Jamie Milliman connected Elser's Rivian truck to a package theft in Bow Mar. Elser denied involvement and offered evidence from her vehicle cameras and phone location records.

She later established that she was attending a gown fitting when the theft occurred. The criminal summons was voided on October 15, 2025, after she submitted evidence supporting her account.

The lawsuit alleges unlawful surveillance, invasion of privacy, and constitutional violations. Flock Safety maintains that its cameras accurately recorded the vehicle's location and that investigators are responsible for interpreting the information.

Elser says the experience demonstrates how easily someone could face accusations based on surveillance records. Should police be required to obtain additional evidence before using license plate tracking technology to pursue criminal charges?

text:
The Future of Egypt in Prophecy

From Tribulation Invasion and Divine Smiting to Millennial Healing and Worship

Introduction

Egypt is one of those nations that modern prophecy teachers either ignore completely or drag into the newspaper every time somebody sneezes near the Nile. One crowd treats Egypt as nothing more than a museum filled with pyramids, mummies, and vacation photographs; another crowd turns every cabinet change in Cairo into the opening trumpet of the Apocalypse. The Bible does neither. Egypt appears from Genesis to Revelation’s prophetic setting as a real country, inhabited by real people, occupying real territory, and standing in a long, complicated relationship with Israel and the God of Israel. It sheltered Abraham during famine, enslaved Abraham’s descendants, raised Moses in Pharaoh’s court, felt the plagues of Jehovah, watched its firstborn die, saw its army buried beneath the Red Sea, received Jeremiah after Jerusalem fell, sheltered the young Lord Jesus from Herod, and will appear again in the closing movements of Gentile history. You cannot dispose of that record by calling Egypt a symbol of “the world” whenever convenient. Egypt may illustrate the world spiritually in certain applications, but the prophetic passages speak of the geographical nation by name. When God says Egypt, Assyria, Israel, Jerusalem, the Nile, and the land, the safest procedure is to assume that the Author has not forgotten elementary geography.

The future of Egypt is remarkable because it refuses to fit the simplistic alternatives commonly offered by careless theology. Egypt is neither promised uninterrupted prosperity nor sentenced to national extinction. It will be invaded, humiliated, smitten, disciplined, and stripped of its old pretensions. Yet it will survive. It will cry unto the Lord, receive deliverance, know the Lord, offer sacrifice, make vows, and participate in the worship of the King during the Millennium. Isaiah calls Egypt “my people” without turning Egypt into Israel. Zechariah threatens Egypt with withheld rain without removing it from the kingdom. Daniel places Egypt in the path of the final northern conqueror without suggesting that its national identity disappears. Ezekiel announces Egypt’s humiliation as “the basest of the kingdoms,” yet also speaks of its restoration as a recognizable people. Judgment does not erase its identity, and blessing does not transfer Israel’s identity to it. The same God who can bless Egypt without making Egypt Israel can bless Gentile believers without making the Church Israel. That distinction ought to be simple enough for anyone who can tell two nations apart on a map, but theological fog has a peculiar ability to make educated men lose abilities possessed by schoolchildren.

This study will follow Egypt’s prophetic course through Isaiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, and Zechariah without forcing every verse into the same hour or pretending that every ancient judgment awaits a future fulfillment. Some prophecies had direct historical applications to Pharaohs, Egyptian dynasties, and the Babylonian invasion. Other passages explicitly reach into “the time of the end,” “that day,” the coming of the Lord, and the reign of the King over all the earth. Sound interpretation respects both horizons. We will distinguish historical judgment from prophetic pattern, Tribulation invasion from millennial discipline, national preservation from individual salvation, and divine blessing from national supremacy. The resulting picture is coherent and astonishing: the nation that once asked, “Who is the LORD?” will be forced to discover the answer. Egypt will pass through judgment without being annihilated, survive without retaining supremacy, be healed without being absorbed, worship without religious pluralism, and receive blessing beneath the government of Israel’s Messiah. Pharaoh once refused to let God’s people go; in the coming kingdom, Egypt’s people will travel

text:
**A FAILED PEACE MEETING IN SEPTEMBER 1776**

I’ve been reading David McCullough’s “John Adams”, and I just finished the section on the meeting that took place on Staten Island in September 1776 between Benjamin Franklin, John Adams, Edward Rutledge, and British Admiral Lord Richard Howe (one of the two Howe brothers serving as peace commissioners; his brother, General William Howe, was commanding the army).

It lasted nearly three hours. Howe did most of the talking. He was gracious, even melancholy, and clearly hoped something could still be worked out. But the reality was stark: the Howes had almost no real negotiating authority. Their commission basically authorized them to offer pardons—if the Americans would submit and abandon independence. That was it. As Franklin pointed out, that meant Howe really had nothing of substance to offer.

The Americans, representing Congress, were equally clear: independence was not on the table. They were not there to surrender or renounce the Declaration. Howe eventually said he was sorry the gentlemen had come so far for so little purpose, because if the colonies would not give up “independency,” further negotiation was impossible.

They met, they talked, they parted. One of Howe’s staff later wrote that nothing remained but to fight it out against “the most determined hypocrites and demagogues” compiled of “the refuse of the colonies.” Meanwhile, Adams learned years later that he had not even been on the British list of those eligible for pardon—he was to hang.

McCullough notes that the Declaration of Independence had passed a first real test. The war would go on.

It’s a striking reminder of how early and how completely the two sides were talking past each other. The British still saw the conflict as a rebellion that could be settled with pardons and restored loyalty. The Americans already saw themselves as an independent people with no intention of going back.

Your thoughts?

God bless
~Uncle Felix

text:
🌎 🪶 **HONORING INDIGENOUS PEOPLES’ DAY** 🪶 🌎

**Today, I choose to celebrate the people, cultures, and civilizations that existed throughout the Americas long before Christopher Columbus arrived in 1492.**

While some recognize this day as Columbus Day, I personally prefer to honor Indigenous Peoples’ Day. I believe it offers us an opportunity to appreciate a much broader and richer history of the Americas.

🌎 **THE AMERICAS WERE ALREADY HOME TO MILLIONS**

Historical research estimates that approximately **60 million Indigenous people** lived throughout North, Central, and South America before European arrival. Although estimates vary, one thing is certain: these lands were already home to established societies with rich traditions, languages, governments, and remarkable achievements.

**Indigenous peoples came in many beautiful shades, including dark-skinned populations whose ancestry in the Americas predates the transatlantic slave trade.**

It is important to recognize that not every dark-skinned person in the Americas has the same ancestral history. Indigenous ancestry, African ancestry, and the blending of these heritages all contribute to the diversity we see today.

🇲🇽 **THE REMARKABLE MAYA CIVILIZATION**

One of the greatest examples of pre-Columbian achievement is the Maya civilization, which flourished across present-day southern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize, and portions of Honduras and El Salvador.

Thousands of years before Columbus, the Maya had already accomplished extraordinary things:

✨ Developed advanced mathematical concepts, including the use of zero.

✨ Created sophisticated calendars and studied astronomy with remarkable precision.

✨ Constructed magnificent cities, pyramids, temples, and ceremonial centers.

✨ Developed an elaborate writing system to record their history and knowledge.

✨ Established agricultural techniques, trade networks, and complex systems of government.

The Maya were among many advanced Indigenous civilizations throughout the Americas, including the Olmec, Zapotec, Mixtec, Mexica (Aztecs), and Inca.

**Their descendants are still here today**, carrying forward languages, traditions, knowledge, and cultural identities that have endured for generations.

🌍 **RECOGNIZING THE DIVERSITY OF OUR ANCESTRY**

I also believe it is important to recognize that the history of dark-skinned people in the Americas cannot be explained through slavery alone.

Dark-skinned Indigenous peoples lived in the Americas long before the transatlantic slave trade. Over time, Indigenous and African communities also developed shared histories, families, and cultural traditions that remain an important part of the Americas today.

Our histories are diverse, interconnected, and worthy of understanding beyond the simplified narratives many of us learned growing up.

❤️ **A DAY OF RECOGNITION, RESPECT, AND REFLECTION**

For me, Indigenous Peoples’ Day is not about dismissing history. It is about recognizing more of it.

It is about honoring the original inhabitants of these lands, acknowledging their contributions, and appreciating the civilizations that helped shape the world long before European exploration.

It is also a reminder that Indigenous peoples are not simply figures from the past. They are living communities whose cultures, identities, and contributions continue to enrich our world.

**Today, I celebrate their resilience, their heritage, their accomplishments, and their lasting legacy.**

🌎 **HAPPY INDIGENOUS PEOPLES’ DAY!** 🪶

*History becomes more meaningful when we make room for everyone's story.*

text:
For years, Carine lived without most of her nose after cancer treatment.

Then doctors began rebuilding a new one in an unexpected place: her forearm.

Carine, a French woman in her 50s, had been treated for nasal cavity cancer in 2013. Radiotherapy and chemotherapy saved her life, but she lost a large part of her nose and the front of her palate.

Several attempts at reconstruction failed, and wearing a facial prosthesis proved difficult. Carine later said she became increasingly isolated and rarely wanted to leave home.

Doctors in Toulouse eventually offered her a completely different approach. 

Using 3D images taken before her cancer treatment, engineers created a custom synthetic structure shaped like her original nose.

Instead of placing it directly on her face, surgeons first implanted the structure beneath the skin of her forearm.

For two months, her own tissue and blood vessels gradually grew around it, transforming the 3D-printed framework into living, vascularized tissue.

In September 2022, surgeons were ready for the next stage.

They removed the reconstructed nose from her arm and transferred it to her face. Using microsurgery, they connected its blood vessels to vessels near her temple so the tissue could survive in its new position. 

Skin from her thigh was then used to repair the area of her arm where the reconstruction had developed.

The operation worked.

After ten days in hospital and several weeks of antibiotics, Carine was recovering well. She could breathe through her reconstructed nose and began noticing something she had missed for years.

Smells.

“I also find the smells of my garden,” she said after the surgery. “I can go out, I come back to life.” 

Further procedures were still needed to refine the shape of her nose and continue reconstructing her teeth and mouth, so the process wasn't finished with that single operation.

The breakthrough was significant for another reason.

Doctors in Toulouse said this type of reconstruction had never previously been performed in such a fragile and poorly vascularized area using this combination of a custom 3D-printed biomaterial and tissue grown on the patient's own arm.

A structure first created on a computer had spent two months becoming part of Carine's body before surgeons moved it to the place it had been designed for.

Nine years after cancer changed her face, she could once again breathe through a nose of her own.

“Hi,”says Daniel, stepping out of hiding and freezing the scavengers in mid-step.  “Welcome to the Waldorf Astoria.”

The scavenger leader’s eyes narrow, flit left and right suspiciously.  “Where are your people?”

“Oh, around,”says Daniel glancing about.  “Listen, I hate to be the bearer of bad news, but this ship’s core is about to go critical, so I would strongly suggest you reconsider your long-term plans here.”

“Do you now?”asks the leader.  A beat.  Then: “Kel!”

The merc to his left moves, the slightest of shift of his weapon and – POK! – a single shot to the chest.  He goes down.  Another merc reacts, swinging his weapon wide – POK! – single shot; he goes down too.  Then, a barrage of P-90 fire sends them all scattering for cover as Daniel ducks out of range.  The mercs respond, projectiles and energy beams glancing off the hull.

“When it rains, it pours,”notes Jack.

“With occasional intermittent hail!”adds Daniel as they return fire.

Minutes pass.  Jack tries contacting Rommie and McKay, but all he gets is static, the anomaly’s pulses interfering with comms.

The barrage continues, back and forth, eating into time they don’t have.  Jack and Daniel are pinned down.

A lull in the shooting.  Suddenly, Daniel perks up.  

“What’s that?”  He throws a look to Jack who strains to listen and hears –

A distant skittering of mechanical legs growing louder and closer.  Daniel’s eyes widen at the sight of –

Dozens of spider-like bots rounding the corridor behind them, skittering across the floor, walls, and ceiling.  Jack and Daniel barely have time to react, ducking to shield their faces.  But the bots scramble over and past, straight for the mercs who immediately turn tail and run, retreating into an aft section – that seals shut behind them.

Jack and Daniel poke their heads up.  WTF?  At which point Maia, Rommie, and McKay round the corner.  Maia says she’s bought them time.  Now they need to abandon ship.  Jack throws a look to Rommie who tells him: “She was telling the truth.”

Daniel jumps to his feet and goes to the utility room holding Rhea.  Jack raises his P-90 as Daniel opens the door.

The room is empty.

Not to belabor the point but WTF?!

Maia escorts the away team to the hangar and the waiting puddle jumper.  There, she tells them she will seal the bay to further delay the scavengers so the team can make good their escape.  She’s staying behind as her final duties will be in service to the ship, and Traugott Corporation.  What do you do?

A – Convince her to come along.  She’s proven herself.

B – Take advantage of her offer and get out of there.  No time to waste.

CHOOSE!

text:
First Mission: The Ghost Ship (Part 4) - "The Advance Team" #Amalgaverse

After calming a frightened Rhea and securing her in a utility room, Jack and Daniel prepare to head back and confront the service android.

Suddenly, McKay’s panicked voice comes over radio.  He tells them that the ship’s core will go critical in less than 40 minutes.  They have to abandon ship.  He’s headed to the bridge with Maia to pull Rommie.

Jack and Daniel exchange looks.  Jack keys his radio and raises Rommie directly, bringing her up to speed fast.

“It’s Maia’s turn to open up,”he tells Rommie.  “Find out who’s telling the truth.  If she refuses, put her down same as the big bot.”  A beat.  “Can you do that?”

Rommie can.

“Just once I’d love for one of these spooky ghost ship ops to go smooth,”says Jack as he and Daniel turn to head back to the jumper.

KA-CLUNK.  The bulkhead door dead ahead releases.  Jack and Daniel melt into the shadows as it grinds open.

Through it comes the scavenger advance team, a hard-looking pack of mercs and marauders – human, alien, and cyborg – mismatched weapons up and ready, moving with easy menace.  They start forward, straight toward Jack and Daniel’s position.

What do Jack and Daniel do?

A) Hit them now while they have the cover advantage.  But this puts the scavengers between you and the jumper.

B) Let them pass.  But this puts the scavengers between you and the rest of the away team.

C) Talk to them.  Warn them that the ship is about to go critical.  You lose the advantage of surprise but could defuse the situation without firing a shot.

CHOOSE!

text:
First Mission: The Ghost Ship (Part 4) - "Unexpected Company" #Amalgaverse 

Aboard the Enterprise-D, Pilot alerts Kirk from his neural graft cradle on the bridge: “Captain, I’m detecting an FTL window opening off the port bow.”

“On screen,”orders Kirk.

The viewscreen holds on the empty starfield, then a distant flash as a vessel drops into sub-light.  The image punches in.  Jury-rigged and battle-scarred, it is unmistakably a scavenger ship, no doubt drawn by the freighter’s emergency beacon, silenced too late.

The bridge tenses.  As Kirk and the others look on, a smaller shape launches from the scavenger ship – a shuttle, streaking straight for the Waldorf Astoria.  And the away team.

“We came to offer help,”observes G’Kar.  “They have come to help themselves.  Scavengers are nothing if not honest about their appetites.”

What does Kirk do?

A – Hail the scavengers.  Warn them off.  Tell them you have people on board rendering aid, then alert the away team to the company headed their way.

B – Hail the scavengers.  Order them to recall their shuttle and clear out.  Ready weapons.

C – Hold comms silent but go to ready posture, and get word to the away team at once.

CHOOSE!

*The Record Speaks: Concrete Dividends of the Tinubu Reforms Since 2023*

Atiku’s narrative asks Nigerians to forget the unsustainable fiscal precipice the nation faced before May 2023. The courageous removal of the toxic fuel subsidy and the unification of the distorted foreign exchange market were not choices of convenience; they were surgical interventions required to save the Nigerian economy from total collapse.

Despite global headwinds, these foundational reforms have delivered dividends across multiple sectors. The multi-trillion-naira drain that starved state governments of capital for education, healthcare, and infrastructure has permanently stopped.

Nigeria's wealth now goes directly to the 36 states and local governments. They now receive record federal allocations through FAAC, unlike in the past, when corrupt fuel-smuggling syndicates benefited.

Second, the government eliminated multi-day fuel queues. For decades, Nigerians spent days sleeping at filling stations due to artificial scarcity, hoarding, and unpaid subsidy claims. Today, despite global energy shocks, fuel queues have been eradicated nationwide because market forces drive supply.

The dangerous gap between the official and parallel exchange rates—which let well-connected political elites collect official dollars cheaply and sell them on the black market for instant billions—has been eliminated. The administration has curtailed currency round-tripping, restoring international confidence in Nigeria's financial systems.

Third, direct social safety nets and wage support. Rather than subsidising the fuel tanks of wealthy SUV owners, the administration redirected funds into direct cash transfers for millions of vulnerable households, subsidised credit funds for micro and small enterprises, and enhanced wage awards for civil servants.

Fourth is infrastructure expansion and energy independence. By operationalising local refining through naira-crude agreements and launching massive national infrastructure projects—such as the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, Sokoto-Badagry Superhighway, and nationwide rail networks—Nigeria is building the physical backbone required for single-digit inflation and sustained industrial growth.

Sophistication Over Demagoguery

Atiku Abubakar’s attempt to equate complex economic governance with an exam paper copied by a "dull student" insults the Nigerian electorate. Nigerians understand that chronic economic ailments built over thirty years cannot be cured by populist slogans or 30-day electioneering promises.

The alternative Atiku offers—resurrecting opaque subsidy regimes under the guise of "production subsidies" without the crude volumes to back them—is the exact road to ruin that almost brought Nigeria to its knees before May 2023. It represents the old way of doing business: short-term palliative bribes funded by unsustainable national debt, leading directly to scarcity, currency collapse, and fiscal bankruptcy.

President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s administration has chosen the hard, courageous, and necessary path. By coupling market deregulation with targeted price-smoothing mechanisms, strategic reserves, rapid CNG rollout, and disciplined fiscal management, the administration is laying a permanent foundation for sustainable prosperity.

The Nigerian electorate is far too sophisticated to trade long-term national economic security for Atiku’s shallow, short-term demagoguery.

Dr Sunday Dare is Special Adviser to the President on Media and Public Communications

text:
Governor Alex Otti is not highly admired by civil servants in Abia State, as they claim he is constantly auditing every ministry and agency. He runs the state's bureaucracy like a business, to the anger of those who see government jobs as a source of free money. He withholds salary for every default. 

But others praise him for conducting the most transparent employment exercises; my friend received an offer from Abia State University and his first salary—which he said was even higher than what was stated in his employment letter—without paying anyone or knowing anyone. I have met and know many people who secured teaching jobs in primary and secondary schools without paying bribes, which was the norm previously. 

The physical aesthetics of Aba have not improved much, but the roads are way better and the environment is cleaner. The brash brushing culture still remains; people run in front of Keke Napep. There are no marked pedestrian crossings.

There is this calm. The generator noise has almost disappeared from all the clothing-making areas in Kent, York, Tennant, Cameron, Azikiwe or Pounds Road; even St. Michael's is quiet now.

There is a predictable pattern in electricity supply; even when the supply is interrupted, people wait patiently for it to return because it is going to be restored. It has been raining for an hour now and is continuing as I type this, but we have power.

Lastly, I think he is investing in more citizen-centered infrastructure [the schools with running water, the hospitals with electricity and consumables, the developments outside the urban areas] rather than "legacy projects." The results of these will be evident in years to come, not immediately.
