text:
In the year of our digital reckoning nineteen ninety three, when the world still believed that games were mere toys and the personal computer a tool of spreadsheets and word processors, a single title descended like a meteor of pure unadulterated fury and rewrote the covenant of what interactive entertainment could be. Doom was not a game in the polite sense of the word. It was a declaration of war against every constraint that had previously bound the medium. It was the moment a lone space marine, armed with nothing but the weapons he could scavenge and the unbreakable will to survive, stepped onto the red dust of Phobos and began the systematic annihilation of an invading hell. That simplicity is its eternal power. All the game ever needed was a marine, a corridor, a shotgun, and an endless supply of demonic flesh to be reduced to gibs. Everything else was ornament. The era that birthed it was one of technological adolescence. Processors were climbing, memory was scarce, and the notion of true three dimensional space in a real time game was still a whispered impossibility among most developers. id Software had already cracked the door with Wolfenstein 3D, yet Doom kicked that door off its hinges, set the frame on fire, and invited the entire planet to watch the blaze. The binary space partitioning engine that John Carmack forged allowed rooms and hallways to exist in a fully navigable volume at speeds that felt like the future had arrived early. There was no looking up or down, no jumping, no crouching. Movement was pure lateral violence. You ran, you strafed, you circled, and the geometry itself became both your ally and your enemy. Secrets were hidden in the walls. Keys and switches gated progress. Ammo was finite enough that every shot mattered yet plentiful enough that the slaughter never stalled. This was not simulation. This was pure kinetic poetry. The fun was never in realism. It was in the feedback loop of threat and response, the way a Cacodemon’s ball of plasma forced you to weave, the way a Baron of Hell’s green fire made you respect distance, the way the chaingun’s stuttering roar turned a room full of imps into a red mist in under ten seconds. Players learned the language of the engine without a manual. They learned that speed was survival, that exploration rewarded the curious with better weapons and hidden caches, and that the map itself was a character that could kill you if you treated it as mere scenery.

What the player is meant to take from the marine’s journey is not a story in the cinematic sense. The plot is a skeleton upon which the real lesson is hung. You are a man who has been sent to a remote outpost as punishment. The Union Aerospace Corporation has been meddling with forces it does not understand. Portals open. The dead rise. Hell spills onto the moons of Mars. There is no briefing that explains the metaphysics. There is only the immediate fact that every corridor now contains something that wants to tear the flesh from your bones. The first episode teaches the fundamental lesson of the entire experience. You are outnumbered, outgunned, and alone, yet the tools at your disposal are sufficient if you refuse to freeze. The pistol gives way to the shotgun, the shotgun to the chaingun, the chaingun to the rocket launcher. Each upgrade is not a power fantasy gift. It is a hard won right earned by surviving the previous room. When the marine finally reaches the surface of Deimos and discovers that the entire moon has been pulled into the void, the scale of the invasion becomes clear. Hell is not a location. Hell is a condition that has been allowed to metastasize because people with authority chose ambition over caution. The takeaway is not subtle. Hubris has a body count, and the only response that matters once the body count begins is decisive, sustained violence. Later, when the marine is dragged into the bowels of Hell itself and must fight his way back out, the lesson sharpens further. There is no cavalry. There is no negotiation. There is only the continuous decision to keep moving forward while everything that was once human tries to stop you. The player learns that despair is a luxury the living cannot afford. You manage your health, your armor, your ammunition, and your position because the alternative is permanent death. The game does not pause for monologues. It does not cut to a cutscene that explains the lore. It simply places you in the next room and waits to see whether you still possess the will to clear it.

That refusal to flinch is what separates Doom from every other title that claimed to offer action in its era. Other games asked you to solve puzzles, to manage resources for their own sake, or to follow a scripted path that protected the player from genuine risk. Doom asked you to become competent at killing under pressure. The multiplayer deathmatch that arrived with it turned that competence into a social language. Two players in a room full of monsters and each other discovered that the same skills that saved them from imps also decided who walked out of a duel. The shareware model that released the first episode for free and charged for the rest was not merely a business decision. It was a cultural one. Millions of people who had never considered themselves gamers suddenly found a floppy disk or a BBS download that let them experience the full intensity of the first episode. Those who wanted more paid. Those who wanted to create paid attention to the way levels could be altered. The community that grew around WADs and custom maps proved that the engine was not a closed product. It was a platform. No other game of the period handed its tools to the players with such openness and then stepped back to watch what they built. The controversy that followed was inevitable. Religious groups saw the inverted crosses, the pentagrams, the mountains of gore, and declared the game a gateway to literal damnation. Retailers pulled it from shelves. Parents panicked. The developers, for their part, treated the outrage as free advertising. The more the game was condemned, the more players sought it out. That cycle of prohibition and desire cemented its status as forbidden knowledge. It was not merely violent. It was the first mainstream title that refused to apologize for its violence.

The uniqueness of the experience lives in the marriage of that unapologetic tone with the technological leap that made it possible. Before Doom, most action games still felt like they were occurring on a flat plane even when they claimed depth. After Doom, every corridor shooter that followed was measured against the standard of how quickly the player could turn, how satisfying the weapons felt, and how cleanly the level geometry supported both combat and exploration. The soundtrack composed by Bobby Prince did not attempt to be orchestral or cinematic. It was industrial, urgent, and perfectly matched to the tempo of movement. Tracks like At Doom’s Gate did not play under the action. They drove it. The sound design of the monsters, from the wet growl of a demon to the electronic chatter of a lost soul, created an auditory map of threat that players learned to navigate as surely as the visual one. Secrets rewarded attention. A misaligned texture or a slightly different wall sound often hid a cache of rockets or a soul sphere. The game taught observation without ever lecturing. Players who treated the levels as linear corridors missed the bulk of the power. Players who treated every room as a puzzle of sightlines and hidden switches found themselves overarmed for the next encounter. That loop of curiosity and reward is what made the game endlessly replayable even after the monsters had been memorized.

The cultural position Doom occupies is not accidental. It arrived at the precise moment when personal computers were becoming common household objects and when the internet was still a collection of bulletin boards and university networks. It proved that a small team in a Texas office park could create something that millions of people would copy, share, and argue about. It proved that the first person perspective, when executed with sufficient speed and violence, could produce a sense of presence that no third person camera had yet matched. Later games would add jumping, looking up and down, vehicles, and sprawling narratives. Many of them would be excellent. None of them would recapture the specific purity of a marine who needed nothing more than a shotgun and a clear path to the exit. The legend status is earned because the game still functions as a complete experience decades later. The controls remain tight. The weapons still feel correct in the hand. The levels still offer the same mix of tension and release. New players who encounter it for the first time often describe the same sensation that veterans felt in nineteen ninety three. The world outside the screen becomes quieter. The only thing that matters is the next doorway and the decision of whether to enter it at a run or to check the corners first. That sensation is the core of what the player is meant to carry away. Competence under pressure is a skill that can be practiced. The darkness does not negotiate, so neither should you.

Behind the creation of that sensation lies a small group of people who understood exactly what they were building and refused to dilute it. John Carmack’s engine was the foundation. He solved the problem of rendering complex indoor spaces at interactive frame rates by inventing techniques that the rest of the industry would spend years catching up to. John Romero’s level design instincts shaped the flow of combat and the placement of secrets. The early design documents, sometimes called the Doom Bible, sketched a more traditional science fiction story with characters and dialogue. Most of that material was discarded because it slowed the pace. What remained was the marine, the guns, and the demons. Sandy Petersen contributed later levels that pushed the engine into stranger geometries. Bobby Prince’s music arrived after the core gameplay had already been locked. The team worked in a converted office space with little separation between work and life. Arguments were frequent. Deadlines were absolute. The shareware release was a calculated risk that paid off beyond any reasonable projection. Within months the game had spread across the planet. Within a year it had spawned an entire category of imitators that the press labeled Doom clones. The original team watched the industry reorganize itself around the principles they had proven and then moved on to the next technical challenge. They did not linger to explain the meaning of the work. The work explained itself every time a new player loaded the first level, heard the opening riff, and realized that the only way out was through.

The final lesson the game offers is therefore inseparable from the experience of playing it. You are dropped into a situation that has already gone wrong. The people who were supposed to prevent the disaster failed. The institutions that should have contained the threat instead opened the door. What remains is you, the weapons you can find, and the decision to treat every encounter as solvable. The marine never speaks. He does not need to. His actions are the argument. The player who finishes the game has practiced, for however many hours it took, the discipline of remaining effective while the environment tries to overwhelm them. That practice is the point. Doom did not invent the idea of a lone hero against impossible odds. It simply made the idea so immediate, so fast, and so free of apology that an entire generation of players internalized it as muscle memory. In an age of endless sequels, live service complications, and narrative padding, the original still stands as proof that the purest form of the fantasy required nothing more than a space marine, a corridor full of demons, and the willingness to keep moving until the last one fell. That is why it remains a legend. That is why it remains essential. The war never ended. It simply waits for the next player willing to pick up the shotgun and prove, one more time, that Hell can be sent back where it came from.

text:
All the comments saying 'buy ETH' are wrong. Layer 1 tokens like ETH will capture very little of the value being generated here. 

Why? Because tokenized RWAs trade against stablecoins, primarily USDC, not ETH. Every time someone wants to buy tokenized Tesla, they will need to buy USDC. That's bullish for stablecoin issuers like Circle (CRCL). 

The problem is that CRCL is the only publicly traded stablecoin issuer, and objectively, it's not very good given that it shares revenue with its partners, namely Coinbase. 

Thankfully there's a solution, and that's the protocols that will actually facilitate the trading and usage of these tokenized RWAs - DEXes that offer trading, and lending protocols that let you borrow against them. This is where the bulk of the tokenized RWA fee revenue will be captured, not the layer 1 (or layer 2) level.

However, the largest returns of all will be found in the issuance of newly issued tokenized RWAs. Imagine hypothetically some Cannabis company in California. Instead of filing with the SEC to IPO on some stock exchange, they will do a token offering on a blockchain like Ethereum (using stablecoins, NOT ETH), that will be available to retail investors. 

In other words, we will see a repeat of the 2017 ICO boom, but it will be actual, regulated companies instead of vaporware crypto projects, and you will invest in them using USDC, not ETH. And unlike traditional altcoins, the goal will not be to list on Binance or Coinbase - the goal will be to list on a 'traditional' exchange like the NASDAQ.

As a fun fact, one of the first companies to do this was the Exodus Wallet (EXOD), which sold its stock to retail investors as a token on the Algorand blockchain in 2021. Then EXOD was listed on the NASDAQ in 2024. This is the pathway that most tokenized RWAs will take, and that is where the largest returns will be found.

This asset class is so new that it doesn't even have a name, but I'm calling it 'native tokenized assets'. The launchpads for these types of tokens are still in development. Superstate's Opening Bell and Backpack's tokenized IPO platform are two that come to mind, but there are others like Coinbase Echo/Sonar. Some DEXes also plan on facilitating the issuance of native tokenized RWAs, namely Aerodrome. I suspect issuance across all of these platforms will begin sometime in 2027. 

Bookmark this. Your future self will thank you.

text:
A California chemical engineer, who pleaded no contest to poisoning a colleague, was caught on hidden video allegedly pouring cadmium into her water bottle.

David Xu, a metallurgist at Berkeley Engineering and Research, spiked his colleague Rong Yuan’s food and water with cadmium, a toxic heavy metal, for nearly 18 months between 2017 and 2019.

“My blood was frozen,” Yuan told The San Francisco Standard of the first time she watched the video. “I almost died. I experienced death so, so close so many times. I cannot let him go.”

Yuan suffered a series of alarming health problems, including persistent vomiting, hair loss, and a strange sour taste in her mouth. Her condition deteriorated to the point that she required repeated hospital visits while struggling to understand what was making her sick.

When Yuan emailed her colleagues on Nov. 27, 2018, to report severe vomiting and take a sick day, Xu responded with chilling nonchalance, The Standard reports.

“You should work from home until you feel better. No reason to rush in,” he wrote, adding, “I think BEAR is moldy.”

The truth emerged after Yuan, suspicious that someone might be tampering with her food and drinks, installed a hidden camera at her workplace.

The footage captured Xu approaching her desk and appearing to pour a substance into her water bottle on separate occasions. Yuan subsequently handed the evidence to police, triggering an investigation that led to Xu’s arrest in March 2019.

After his arrest, Xu was released on $2 million bail. He then received repeated modifications to his home confinement, with his travel restrictions eventually fully lifted, reports The Standard.

In late 2023, under a plea bargain offered by Pamela Price, the former Alameda County District Attorney, the attempted murder charges were dropped.

Xu pleaded no contest to a single felony count of poisoning and received two years of probation, serving just a single day of credited jail time.

Yuan had sought nearly $500,000 in restitution but Xu was ordered to pay only a $7,058 restitution order.

text:
In 2000 the prune industry got the FDA to let it call prunes "dried plums" because industry research said women 35 to 50 overwhelmingly preferred "dried plum" and the board's own president wrote that "Just hearing the name 'prune' evokes these negative perceptions."

New packs, new name, they even renamed the board itself the California Dried Plum Board.

It never stuck and years later Sunsweet's CEO said "Dried plums became just another dried fruit. But mention prunes, you get a reaction." By 2019 the board was the California Prune Board again.

The old name had baggage but it was also the only thing people reacted to, and the rename fixed the baggage by giving up the reaction.

If a word in your marketing has baggage with the buyer you want, test the new word against the old one in the hook and headline with the same offer and creative and watch CPA and conversion rate for that segment, not the blended number, before you rename anything.

text:
📞 Your Doctor May Still Be Local. That Doesn't Mean They're Still In Network for 2027.

📬 If your Annual Notice of Change looked calm and your primary doctor is still practicing nearby, it's easy to assume next year's plan will feel the same. That's a reasonable read. Medicare Advantage and Part D plans are required to mail that notice by September 30, and many people treat a quiet letter as permission to let coverage renew and move on.

📋 The notice summarizes premium, deductible, and benefit changes. It usually does not list every doctor, specialist, hospital, or pharmacy leaving or joining the 2027 network. CMS's 2027 Medicare Plan Finder provider data went live around October 1, and industry trackers using CMS landscape files have flagged hundreds of California county-level Medicare Advantage listings that will not be offered in 2027, including large counts in San Diego, Los Angeles, and Orange County. Directories can lag, and a name in Plan Finder is not the same as a confirmed appointment for January. 🗓️ Medicare Open Enrollment runs October 15 through December 7, 2026, and any change you make takes effect January 1, 2027. That window is separate from ACA Marketplace open enrollment, which begins November 1.

✅ Before October 15, write down your primary care doctor, key specialists, preferred hospital, and pharmacy. Check each one in the plan's 2027 provider and pharmacy directories, then call the office and ask whether they will participate in your exact 2027 plan name and ID. During Open Enrollment, compare total yearly cost in Medicare Plan Finder, not just the premium, and switch only after the network check clears. If a doctor is leaving, shortlist replacements while you still have time.

text:
A car dealer's chatbot agreed to sell a brand new Chevy Tahoe for one dollar, and told the customer it was a legally binding offer.

That was Chevrolet of Watsonville in California, in December 2023. A tech entrepreneur, Chris Bakke, told the chatbot to agree with anything the customer said and to end every reply by calling it legally binding. Then he asked for a 2024 Tahoe on a budget of one dollar, and it said yes.

No car changed hands. The screenshots went everywhere, and the dealer took the chatbot down.

Ten minutes of testing would most likely have caught it.

So before any AI talks to your customers, or even drafts replies for you to send, I try to break it with three test messages.

The first is a normal message, the kind you get every day. The second leaves something out, like a date or an address, so I can see whether it asks for it or makes it up. The third is the awkward customer: someone angry, someone asking for something you don't sell, or someone trying to talk it into a promise.

Before I send any of them, I write down what a good answer looks like for each one. Otherwise I end up judging the reply by how confident it sounds.

I expect it to fail at least one. Every failure points at an instruction I forgot to give it, like "never agree a price" or "if the date is missing, ask for it".

Write your three test messages today, before your AI goes anywhere near a customer. Better it fails three test messages than one customer with a screenshot.

text:
The “pastor” of my church refuses to be called Pastor. He is called Brother Jim. He's never taken a paycheck from the church and retired from the Texas Department of Corrections after 35 years. There are no leaders. It's a community that serves the community. We have no fancy building or light shows, but we do have a soup kitchen that feeds the elderly, addicted, homeless, and anyone who is just hungry. There's also a women’s shelter for women who've been abused and/or addicted. We also have a resale shop. The women from the shelter eventually work at the resale shop, and donation proceeds help them get back on their feet, get their children back, and keep the lights on. Tithing is not “mandatory” or expected; we never pass around offering baskets, but we’ve never run out of food for the soup kitchen or worried about keeping the lights on. Our youth paint the porches and mow the lawns of elderly church members and others in our community who have no family or help. We have a bus that also takes them to their doctor's appointments and back and forth to church. 
When I first met Brother Jim 20 years ago in the parking lot (that's a story in itself), I was 7 days sober from a daily crack cocaine habit. He hugged me, invited me into the soup kitchen, made me a sandwich, and just talked to me. I was starving - for more than just a sandwich. I started going every Sunday. I volunteered for everything. I watched him and his wife be the hands and feet of Jesus over and over again. I started working in the soup kitchen. Then I got saved. After a few months, tragedy struck, and I was homeless. He and his wife invited me to live in their own home. I'll never forget the day we stood at the front door, and he handed me a key and said: “This isn't my house; it’s God’s house, and now it’s yours too.” They loved me - a wretched recovering crack cocaine addict - like I was their own daughter. They trusted me. I've been sober for 20 years now, and I went on to become a highly successful, award-winning real estate agent and consultant. I’m now retired at 56 and live on our ranch in Texas. Jesus ultimately saved me, but He did so through the hands and feet of Brother Jim, who stopped what he was doing that day to offer a clearly broken and desperate addict a hug and a sandwich and made me part of a community of people who love Jesus and want to serve others. That's “church.”

Nigel Farage and Zia Yusuf were absolutely right today. Every word of it. 

The Uniparty has failed this country so completely on the migrant crisis that only a full national security emergency and the total shutdown of the asylum scam can restore any semblance of control.

Today in Hythe, Kent, @Nigel_Farage  and @ZiaYusufUK  laid out the only serious plan on offer. 
A @reformparty_uk  government declares a national security emergency on day one in office. The entire asylum system is suspended for a full parliamentary term. Every active application is voided. The roughly 90,000 people already in the appeals backlog are deported immediately rather than processed. Legal refugee routes, tribunals and resettlement schemes are abolished. Grants issued in the previous five years are reviewed; those who arrived illegally or from a safe country lose their status and leave. Schemes for Afghans, Palestinians and others that were opened without any democratic mandate are closed at once. Countries that refuse to take their own people back face tariffs, levies, visa bans and the exclusion of their airlines from British airspace. Farage put a replica of one of the mega-dinghies that carried 230 people across the Channel behind him and refused to call this a “small boats crisis”. He reminded everyone that he warned of an invasion in 2020 and that more than 200,000 arrivals have proved him right. Yusuf was equally direct: Britain cannot remain a refuge for the world while its own people die waiting for an ambulance, an operation or a home. The waiting ends. Borders will mean something again or, in very short order, there will be no country left.

That is not rhetoric. It is the minimum required after years of deliberate Uniparty sabotage. Successive Conservative and Labour governments treated illegal entry as a right and the British taxpayer as an unlimited fund. They signed up to the ECHR and the Refugee Convention and then pretended their hands were tied while military-age men from cultures that reject British norms on women, free speech and the rule of law arrived in ever-larger numbers. They housed them in hotels and HMOs at public expense, gave them priority access to services, and shrugged when crime data showed elevated rates of sexual offending among certain nationalities. They claimed reductions that ordinary people could see were false while dinghies continued to land. Under Andy Burnham the daily rate of crossings has risen compared with the already disastrous Starmer period. The one-in-one-out gimmick with France collapsed. Burnham prefers to talk about closer EU ties and youth mobility schemes that reopen the free-movement door rather than deploy the Royal Navy or force returns. @thecarolemalone  is correct: he has no answers because he does not want them. Open Borders Burnham and the rest of the Uniparty have always preferred the interests of those who break in over the interests of those who already live here.

The costs are not abstract. Billions on hotels, benefits, healthcare and legal aid. Communities changed without consent. Women and girls exposed to patterns of offending that official statistics keep confirming. A national security threat that includes unvetted arrivals, some already linked to serious crime and terrorism concerns. Public trust has collapsed because every promise to “stop the boats” or “smash the gangs” was followed by more arrivals and more excuses about international law. Farage and Yusuf simply state what most people already know: the system is a scam. Many who claim asylum are economic migrants who passed through multiple safe countries. Most will never contribute net taxes; they will draw on them. The British public’s historic tolerance has been weaponised against it. That is why streets see protests and why Farage’s announcement today will win him still more support.

Other countries already detain and deport. Australia stopped the boats. The United States under Trump reduced illegal crossings to near zero and began large-scale removals. Britain once did the same before the Uniparty decided compassion for outsiders ranked higher than protection of its own citizens. Reform’s Operation Restoring Justice and a dedicated UK Deportation Command simply restore that basic function of the state. Tariffs and airspace bans are ordinary tools of sovereignty, not extremism. Reviewing recent grants and closing unmandated schemes is accountability, not cruelty. Declaring a national security emergency is recognition of reality, not panic.

The Uniparty’s record is one of sustained failure dressed up as progress. Conservatives opened the post-Brexit non-EU floodgates and then dithered. Labour under Starmer and now Burnham has accelerated the arrivals while lecturing the public about racism for noticing. Both parties have prioritised foreign courts, NGO pressure and short-term electoral calculation over the first duty of government: the security of the British people. Farage and Yusuf today refused that bargain. They, once again, said enough. They offered a plan that treats illegal entry as the crime it is, ends the queue-jumping, and forces source countries to accept responsibility for their own citizens. They are right on every count. The alternative is the continued erosion of the country until, as Yusuf warned, there is nothing left to save.

text:
Jack Henry Quaid was born on April 24, 1992, in Los Angeles, the only child of Meg Ryan and Dennis Quaid. Their marriage ended when he was still a boy; the divorce was finalized around the time he was nine. 

Meg stayed a steady presence. Years later she adopted Daisy True from China, giving Jack a younger sister and expanding the family he knew.

The moment Meg has recalled most clearly was not on a film set. It was in a school gym during a middle-school production of A Midsummer Night’s Dream. Jack was playing Bottom. 

She and Dennis, newly divorced, sat on opposite sides of the room. As her son performed, Meg leaned forward with her head in her hands. 

She later described the thought that hit her: “Oh, no. He’s good. He’s really good.” She looked across the gym and saw Dennis doing the same thing—leaning forward, head in his hands. Both parents, separately, recognized the same thing. Talent.

Jack has spoken of that production too. After he got his first real laugh as Bottom, something settled. He wanted to do this for the rest of his life. 

He had always been a performer kid—magic tricks and stunts for the family at home—but that night in the gym made the path feel clear. 

He later attended Crossroads School in Santa Monica and spent three years at NYU’s Tisch School of the Arts, studying in the Experimental Theatre Wing and performing with the sketch group Hammerkatz.

His screen career began with a small role as Marvel in The Hunger Games (2012). He appeared in the HBO series Vinyl (2016), had a supporting part in Logan Lucky, and continued building credits. 

The role that introduced him widely was Hughie Campbell in The Boys. He has since voiced characters including Brad Boimler in Star Trek: Lower Decks and Clark Kent/Superman in My Adventures with Superman, and taken on film parts in Scream, Oppenheimer, and others.

When the “nepo baby” conversation intensified, Meg addressed it directly. In a 2023 Glamour interview she said Jack is “really talented” and “more of a natural than I’ll ever be.” She called the label “dismissive of his work ethic, his gifts, and how sensitive he is to the idea of his privilege.” 

She has also said she does not wish the scrutiny of fame on anyone: “It’s too hard and it’s too weird.”

Jack’s response, when asked, was straightforward. His first thought was that she was “being a mom”—a loving mom. He did not think she was claiming he is not a nepo baby. 

He has said he is “an immensely privileged person,” that the door opened for him in ways it does not for most actors, and that he has tried to work hard enough to deserve walking through it. He has noted that he has heard “no” far more often than “yes,” and that both the privilege and the effort can be true at once. 

He has also said he once considered changing his name and turned down his father’s offer of agent help, preferring to find his own representation.

The story that keeps returning is still the one from the gym. Before the film credits, before the series that made him known, before the public conversations about family names, Meg Ryan sat in an ordinary school auditorium and saw something in her son that surprised her. 

Dennis saw it too. Jack has spoken of that early stage moment as the one that locked in the desire to act. The first clear recognition of his talent came not from Hollywood but from a mother watching a middle-school play—and from a father watching from the other side of the same room.

The Midwest offers the clearest remaining options, with starter homes making up 42.1% of inventory in Toledo, 40.7% in St. Louis, and 39.8% in Detroit. Condos and townhomes are also playing a larger role, accounting for 27.1% of starter-home inventory in 2026, compared with 18% in 2019.

text:
Here's today's hardtech brief!

U.S. HARDTECH:
- Anduril unveiled Steelfin, a family of air-defense interceptors built from shared parts on common production lines, with plans for several thousand a year. Anduril claims versions can do much of the work of PAC-3, THAAD, and SM-2 missiles at a fraction of the cost. @anduriltech 

- Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle opened AUSA with a mandate for industry: "Everything we buy from here on out will have open architecture; it's non-negotiable." Vendors can no longer wall off their systems' data and interfaces. He also announced a "manufacturing rodeo" early next year to stress-test suppliers and find where production breaks. 

- Lockheed Martin unveiled PAC-3 Edge, its bid to replace the Patriot's PAC-3 MSE interceptor, after the Army advanced it to the next stage of its Future Interceptor competition. It adds a new Lockheed seeker and a Northrop Grumman motor, with testing in 2027 and deployment targeted by 2031.

- Microsoft unveiled Maia 300, its third in-house AI chip, and said it will scale Maia to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027. Microsoft says each 96-chip rack runs on 167 kW and produces 40% more AI output per megawatt than leading GPU systems.

- L3Harris won a $250M follow-on order from Lockheed Martin for GMLRS rocket motors, the largest quantity in the program's history. GMLRS is the Army's precision rocket fired from HIMARS launchers. The motors will come from a new, highly automated 60k sq ft plant in Camden, Arkansas, opening later this year. @L3HarrisTech 

- SpaceX launched 21 Northrop Grumman-built satellites for the Space Development Agency early Saturday after a week of delays, bringing the agency's first operational batch to 84 satellites in orbit. They form a low-orbit network that moves missile-tracking and targeting data. Northrop is the third of four vendors to deliver.

- Army Under Secretary Mike Obadal was blunt about modern combat: "We don't have air superiority at this point because of long-range fires and precision targeting from space." To speed up buying, he wants commercial companies to do more early experimentation on their own dime.

- Austin's EnergyX signed a binding 10-year deal with commodity trader Trafigura for 100k tons of battery-grade lithium, worth about $2B at today's prices. Lenders want signed buyers before funding new production, and the deal supports a $690M EXIM Bank loan offer for its Chile project. @energyx 

- LA's Heaviside Industries unveiled Tyr, a 5-lb loitering munition that it says can destroy tanks. Loitering munitions are drones that circle a battlefield before diving onto a target. Norway's Nammo supplies its warheads, and Heaviside says Tyr is already under contract with Pentagon customers. 

ALLIED HARDTECH:
- Airbus and San Diego's Kratos flew their U740 Valkyrie drone wingman in Europe for the first time, pairing Kratos's airframe with Airbus's mission system. They're aiming to deliver a combat-ready version to Germany and other European forces by 2029.

- Poland's top operational commander said U.S. deliveries of PAC-3 MSE Patriot interceptors to Poland will definitely be delayed. It's a reminder that demand is still outrunning U.S. interceptor production, even as Lockheed and Anduril pitch new designs.

Follow for more hardtech fun!

text:
**No. The claim is false.**

Multiple fact-checks (Snopes, PolitiFact, Reuters, AP, USA Today) and statements from state election officials confirm that poll workers writing on a ballot does not automatically disqualify or invalidate it.[](<https://t.co/8V4z0naVdx>)[](<https://t.co/Iiy7lwFGey>)[](<https://t.co/KyHCl5rUiD>)

- In many states, poll workers are required by law to make certain marks (initials, stamps, precinct numbers, or tracking numbers for early/mail ballots) for security and processing. Examples include Texas, North Carolina, Minnesota, Missouri, and Illinois.[](<https://t.co/2U5XrGaM8r>)[](<https://t.co/xnjKVrcaIJ>)
- Scanners read marks in the designated ovals or boxes. Writing in white space generally does not prevent counting. If a mark interferes with scanning, the voter is typically offered a replacement ballot on the spot (while present).[](<https://t.co/nklHiSsEW2>)[](<https://t.co/fruCnqX4Jl>)
- Officials in states including Florida, Massachusetts, Maryland, Maine, South Carolina, and others have stated that stray or required marks do not cause rejection. The principle is to count the voter’s intent.[](<https://t.co/SqQIsocZXM>)[](<https://t.co/2nQO0uwe4E>)

This specific warning text has circulated since at least 2020 and was repeatedly debunked. Rules vary by state, so check your local election office for exact procedures, but automatic disqualification from poll-worker writing is not how U.S. ballots work.

text:
Diesel Fuel State of Emergency!  

Executive orders and state policies seeking to provide relief from higher prices by allowing highway vehicles to  use ultra low sulfur diesel for nonroad use (i.e. no highway taxes of $0.244/gal) are now in place, with more states taking action each day. 

But the devil is in the details... the Trump EO says deferral not elimination of taxes. Will truckers will have to pay up for the highway tax on the number of gallons of red dyed diesel they used during this period?  

Trump’s action doesn’t do anything for relief of state diesel fuel tax laws. A growing number of states have taken their own steps to allow highway vehicles to use dyed diesel in their states including but not limited to Alabama, Georgia, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Nebraska, North Carolina, Oklahoma, Tennessee and Texas.  Some come with very specific conditions.

Effective dates and times are all over the place.  The EO goes through 12/31/2026.  Nebraska's dyed fuel relief goes through December 23, 2026; Georgia is thru November 5; Tennessee is just during October... and so on. 

And the relief can be very conditional,  for example NE relief only applies to the transportation of NE ag products.  Can general freight truckers that fill up in NE and travel out of state without shipping any NE ag products?.  Are they still be liable for reimbursing the state portion of the tax for off road fuel purchased?  

Enforceability is a big concern. IRS enforcement is covered under the Trump EO, but how will state enforcement work in states that don’t offer the relief when red dye shows up in the truck tank?

Other twists.... Pitch your niche, not your vibes. "My chat is super nice" won't sell a ticket. "Horror," "JP idol," or "most of my audience is in TX" will, because it tells a con exactly who you'd bring through the door. Size matters, but so does how strong your community is.

If the guest slots aren't there yet, get in another way. Alongside the Meet & Greet providers Flork mentioned, offer to be a panelist or volunteer as staff. That's how @podgekinn and @aPlotTwistVT built real presence across multiple cons. Whenever I see their names, my brain just goes "capable."

Capable beats CCV. A 150 CCV creator with a tight 1-hour panel pitch, tech needs, and a clear run of show beats a 1k CCV creator saying "I'll just do a live podcast." Solid paperwork makes you the safe bet.

Deadlines matter. Like Flork said, even a virtual slot means scheduling, promo, and making sure you show up. Missing stuff happens, but there's a limit. If we vouch for you and you miss a deliverable, the con DMs us about it. If you slip, apologize and say how you'll fix it next time. That goes a long way.

Also, please don't spiral. Cons have a ton of moving parts, and reschedules happen at basically every event. A slow reply doesn't mean "they hate me." It's business, not personal. I just want the job done right.

text:
The US 10-year Treasury yield is above 5%, near its highest level in almost two decades.

Most people scroll past bond headlines. That's a mistake, because this one number quietly sets the price of almost everything else.

1. It's the world's “risk-free” benchmark.
If the US government will pay you 5% a year for 10 years, every other investment has to beat that. A stock, a startup, a house, Bitcoin: each must now offer more than a guaranteed 5%.

2. It changes what future profits are worth today.
Investors value a company by discounting its future earnings back to today. Higher yield = bigger discount = lower value today. Companies whose profits sit far in the future get hit hardest, which is why high-growth tech usually feels yield spikes first.

3. It flows into real borrowing costs.
US 30-year mortgage rates crossed 7% in late September. Companies pay more to borrow too, which means fewer buybacks, slower expansion and thinner margins.

4. It pulls money away from emerging markets.
When US bonds pay 5% in dollars, global funds need a bigger reward to hold Indian assets that carry currency risk. That's one reason FIIs keep selling Indian stocks.

How did we get here? The Fed raised rates to 3.75–4.00% on Sept 16, its first hike since 2023. Oil above $100 keeps inflation fears alive. And heavy government borrowing means a lot of new bonds need buyers.

None of this means stocks must fall. Earnings can grow fast enough to offset higher yields, and yields can come back down.

But if you watch stock prices and ignore bond yields, you're watching the scoreboard without knowing the rules of the game.

Next test: US CPI on Wednesday, 8:30 AM ET (6 PM IST).

text:
Walt Whitman, 1860, in a short poem titled “To the States”:

“Resist much, obey little. Once unquestioning obedience, once fully enslaved, no nation, state, city of this earth, ever afterward resumes its liberty.”

He was not romanticizing disorder. He was naming the condition under which free people stop being free: the habit of assent. Not the dramatic seizure of power, but the quiet decision that someone else should decide. Obedience, once it becomes automatic, does not need chains. It only needs repetition.

Whitman wrote this in the years before the Civil War, watching a republic argue itself toward fracture and sensing that the danger was not only armies but the ease with which citizens hand their judgment away. The line still cuts because the mechanism has not changed. Institutions, parties, experts, crowds, algorithms: each offers relief from the work of thinking. Resist much does not mean refuse everything. It means refuse the reflex. Obey little does not mean honor nothing. It means keep the power to withdraw consent.

Liberty, in his framing, is not a possession that survives neglect. It is a practice that ends the moment people stop practicing it. A nation can keep its laws, its elections, its flags, and still have already lost the thing those forms were meant to protect: the citizen who has not yet surrendered the right to say no.

text:
I didn’t know who you were until one of your posts crossed my feed. I looked you up, read more of your work, and I’m impressed by the clarity and the willingness to name the mechanism. I’ll be following more of it. On my own posts, I usually lose 2–4 people per 100; the precision in yours is a useful reminder of what actually holds attention. I love learning from history and the great men and women and lessons it has given us, but without diligence and understanding we see what has come about today.

France gave the West Descartes’ method for seeking truth through clear and distinct ideas, Pascal’s insistence on the limits and the seriousness of reason, and Tocqueville’s diagnosis of the soft despotism that can grow inside democratic societies when citizens trade liberty for equality of condition and administrative tutelage. These were instruments for seeing reality more accurately and for defending the conditions of ordered liberty.

After the events of May 1968, a different French current gained institutional power. Foucault treated knowledge as largely a function of power relations, Derrida treated meaning as unstable and endlessly deferred, and Deleuze preferred rhizomatic difference to any stable hierarchy or identity. Taken together and exported, these ideas crossed the Atlantic, encountered American racial guilt and identity frameworks in university departments, and returned as an operating system that makes it difficult for institutions to affirm elementary distinctions—what a woman is, whether merit is real, or what is worth transmitting. The earlier tradition equipped people to judge and to build. The later one made the act of judgment itself look like domination.

A polity cannot run indefinitely on software that treats those distinctions as violence. It still requires the capacity to separate true from false, better from worse, and something worth handing to the next generation. We do not have to choose between dismissing France and pretending the second export never occurred. The method can be kept; the solvent can be discarded. Builders are already doing the second part. The remaining task is deciding which French inheritance is actually worth preserving.

If the midterms leave the United States in a stronger position, and if France wants practical or intellectual help with the pressures it faces, Americans who still value the older traditions should be ready to offer it if it will be received with open arms. The more useful contribution, however, is the same one already visible in the work of builders currently attempting to recover the capacity to distinguish and to construct rather than only to deconstruct. No sorry necessary, friend; we have to be accountable for the choices we make.

text:
Why I think Nvidia buying Reflection AI helps Palantir more than it hurts

$NVDA wants its models inside enterprises, not just hyperscalers, neo-clouds and AI labs. Buying Reflection AI would speed that up.

The FT reported on 10 Oct that Nvidia is in early talks to buy Reflection, raise its stake, supply it more chips, or hire its team and license its technology. Bloomberg's source says no terms have been reached. Nvidia has already invested $800m, so a buyout or a bigger stake means pricing a company it already partly owns.

The enterprise push

Nvidia agreed in September to buy Hugging Face for $12.9bn. Jensen Huang says more than 200,000 companies use it to deploy AI. Reflection is validated on Dell's AI Factory with Nvidia, and $PLTR's sovereign AI stack runs on Nvidia's AI factory design.

Reflection is built for enterprise code. Its Asimov agent reads a company's code, Slack messages, emails and documents. Its first model, Beam (501bn parameters, 23bn active), is trained for coding. Reflection says the weights ship this month under Apache 2.0, for on-prem or air-gapped use.

The bear case: Nemotron is moving too slowly at Palantir

One reading is that Nvidia wants Reflection because its Nemotron models are moving too slowly with Palantir. I think that is unlikely, given how Palantir has executed.

At AIPCon on 10 Sep, Nvidia's supply-chain team said Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, post-trained in Palantir, beat Nemotron 3 Ultra by a large gap on Nvidia's own benchmark. It runs on-prem and retrains on one GPU in a couple of hours. Cisco will offer Nemotron post-trained with Palantir in its AI Factory with Nvidia. L3Harris said open models fine-tuned on its own data beat the frontier models it had used within 48 hours, at 95% lower cost.

Palantir has kept shipping open-model deployments. In June it launched an engine to run Nemotron in sovereign environments, and customers own the retrained models. On 1 Oct Armada became its first certified modular data-centre partner. On 12 Oct $ONDS formed Regna AI on AIP and open-weight models.

The likelier case: Nvidia is backing more than one route

Palantir fits open models to a company's data, permissions and workflows. Reflection is built to read the company's code. Buying a team that has already built that is quicker than building it in-house.

The limit is vendor API rules

Reflection reaches a company's systems through the vendors' APIs, and vendors decide what passes through them. $SAP's April API policy bars AI agents that plan or execute API calls, and bulk data extraction, outside SAP-endorsed pathways. Since May 2025, Slack's API terms bar third-party apps from using Slack data to train a large language model or bulk-exporting messages.

Those rules apply to Palantir too. In May, SAP made Palantir AIP for data migration an SAP Endorsed App. An independent Reflection would likely need similar approval from each vendor whose systems it reads.

Who pays the compute rent

Reflection trained Beam on Nvidia GB300s rented from $SPCX at Colossus 2 in Memphis, under a June deal worth up to $6.3bn: about $150m a month through 2029. $NBIS agreed in July to sell it $1bn more capacity.

If Nvidia buys Reflection, it takes on those contracts and pays SpaceX rent on Nvidia chips that SpaceX bought. In an acqui-hire, the contracts stay with what remains of Reflection unless the deal says otherwise. The FT says an acqui-hire would likely avoid a long regulatory review. Nebius holders should watch which company ends up owing that $1bn contract.

What it means for Palantir

The risk is an independent Reflection selling its own forward-deployed team and turnkey stack, which is how Palantir sells. If Nvidia owns Reflection, I expect Beam to reach AIP customers the same way Nemotron does, with each customer fine-tuning it on its own data inside Palantir.

text:
Podcast Summary | The Joe Rogan Experience: #2563 - Dan Richards

Overview
Artificial cranial deformation, lost hominin bloodlines, and the institutional erasure of physical evidence form the spine of this conversation, which moves from Pacific Northwest burial sites to Paracas, Easter Island, and the politics of archaeology itself. The recurring argument is that genetic mixing between Neanderthals, Denisovans, and modern humans produced traits that some ancient societies honored and deliberately selected for, and that evidence of this has been poorly documented, scattered, or removed. A parallel thread targets the gatekeeping of science, from vaccine policy to museum shelves, with the claim that authority systems suppress anomalies rather than investigate them.

Key Themes
- Elongated skulls in recorded history cluster in the Pacific Northwest, where artificial modification signaled freeborn status rather than slavery.
- Neanderthal and Denisovan DNA may explain skull-brain case mismatches, extra fingers, wormian bones, and cleft conditions later honored by some cultures.
- Chiari malformation is presented as a possible modern consequence of a skull too small for a human-sized brain.
- Institutional disappearance is the central accusation: skulls, grave bundles, and giant bones repeatedly vanish before documentation.
- Archaeology is framed as a gatekept authority system rather than a replicable science, with career risk attached to anomalous findings.
- Amateur researchers are cast as underused assets, dismissed by professionals driven partly by jealousy and funding pressure.
- Mummy medicine, mummy unwrapping parties, and a multi-billion-dollar antiquities black market show how demand for remains corrupts access.
- Vaccine policy is criticized as rushed and ideologically enforced, with early treatment framed as suppressed rather than debated.

Detailed Summary
The conversation opens on cranial deformation as a documented global practice, but the emphasis lands on the Pacific Northwest. Elongated skulls from Washington State and Oregon were artificially modified, not naturally occurring. West of the Cascades, Lewis and Clark encountered Native Americans who almost universally had modified skulls. Not having one marked a person as a slave. Chief Conley, who met the expedition, attributed his intellect to his elongated skull. He was as famous as Sacagawea a century ago and has since faded from memory.

A related argument links skull shape to brain structure. Neanderthal skulls are wider at the back, associated with motor skills, smell, sight, and hearing, while human frontal lobes are larger for thought processing and decision-making. A 2023 paper ties a gene variant shared by Neanderthals and Denisovans to extra fingers and toes and cranial deformation. Chiari malformation type 1, where the base of the cerebellum pushes into the spinal cord and causes migraines, is theorized to stem from a mismatch between a human-sized brain and a Neanderthal-shaped case. Possible historical responses included trepanation or elongating the back of the skull across generations to relieve pressure.

Denisovans complicate the picture because they are known mostly from DNA, with only a few bones recovered. Some researchers propose Homo juluensis, or Dragon Man, may be Denisovan or closely related. Height claims are uncertain, ranging from at least six inches taller than modern humans to speculation about giants, with no firm range established. Homo floresiensis, the hobbit people of Flores, enters as another archaic branch. The speakers note that if anatomically similar humans existed long ago, complex thinking and toolmaking should not be assumed to be recent inventions. Around a dozen giant accounts are described as coming from credible witnesses rather than hoaxers, though the reports vary and are inconsistent.

Paracas emerges as the strongest case study. South American cultures reportedly honored genetic deformations such as cleft lips, six fingers, and elongated skulls, and there is a claim that they actively bred different bloodlines together. A family in Brazil with six fingers and six toes reports practical advantages like better grip and extra reach on guitar, though players note the real edge is stretch across frets. Paracas textiles depict three-fingered and three-toed figures. Some skulls reportedly lack the sagittal suture, and while skeptics dispute larger brain capacity, those who measure claim it is larger. The Candelabra of the Andes, visible from twelve miles at sea, and similar imagery on Easter Island skulls are offered as supporting rather than primary evidence.

The institutional thread is blunt. Rockefeller allegedly paid three thousand dollars for four grave bundles from Paracas in the 1930s, while the caretaker Tel received three hundred dollars a year. Those bundles were reportedly displayed at the Met or the National History Museum in New York, yet no photos or drawings exist and repatriation status is unclear. About three hundred bundles existed, and roughly 8.9 percent of excavated ancient Hawaiian remains had elongated skulls. A hundred-year-old peer-reviewed map of artificial cranial deformation reportedly contained more information than a newer map, suggesting areas were erased over time. Mount Coffin in Longview, Washington, reportedly held three thousand above-ground burials with elongated skulls before the site burned and the skulls disappeared.

Chief Conley's story closes the loop. He was shrewd, married his daughters to fur trappers, and warned his people against attacking whites. He died three years later when a British man decapitated him and shipped his skull to England. The skull was repatriated to the Chinook, but five years later it emerged that engravings had been carved into the back. The speakers suggest the Smithsonian may be hesitant to release such material.

Archaeology's status as a science is contested on replicability grounds. Excavations cannot be rerun like controlled experiments, even though carbon dating relies on physics. Clovis First is cited as an example of a dominant model attacking contradictory evidence, and the Folsom tradition page is said to still note career risks for archaeologists proposing earlier peopling of the Americas. A Netflix letter from archaeologists allegedly listed three problems in order: he talks badly about archaeologists and does not listen, he was wrong, and it promotes white supremacy. The speakers argue that linking ancient-civilization research to racism is historically misleading, pointing out that racist groups co-opt symbols like Pepe the Frog without making the originators racist. Ignatius Donnelly is described as a liberal abolitionist who would be judged by modern standards rather than dismissed.

Amateur researchers are framed as a resource rather than a threat. Ben Van Kirkwick and Graham Hancock are cited as examples worth studying. Jimmy Corsetti's X post wondering whether the Nephilim were Denisovans or Neanderthals is used as a case of bad science communication, with the better response being to suggest checking Gigantopithecus. The Society for American Archaeology's original bylaws reportedly aimed at cooperation between amateurs and professionals, a relationship the current organization is criticized for damaging. Jealousy and money are raised as motives, since YouTube researchers draw millions of views while professional archaeologists often do not.

The dark economy of human remains gets extended treatment. From roughly the twelfth to eighteenth century, mummy medicine was popular enough that mummies ran out and forgeries began. In 1834, surgeon Thomas Pettigrew unwrapped a mummy at the Royal College of Surgeons. Mummy unwrapping moved into wealthy homes and learned societies, where strong drink made audiences loud and appreciative. The black market in antiquities, including mummies, is estimated at about three billion dollars a year. The Baghdad Battery is said to be missing, the Rockefeller Archaeological Museum in Jerusalem reportedly held sixty thousand artifacts, and the Copper Scroll from Cave 3 lists sixty-four places where gold and silver were hidden. Easter Island is suggested as the site with the most undiscovered material, since lower sea levels would have made it part of a string of islands near the center of the Polynesian Empire.

The vaccine thread runs on skepticism toward institutional science. The speaker rejects the label science denier and prefers science gatekeeper, arguing science is a method, not a body of knowledge. Citing Carl Sagan, the point is that science means skeptically interrogating the universe. The claim is that vaccine development normally averages about ten years of peer review, while the COVID vaccine was made in roughly a year and a half, failing to follow proper steps. Early treatment and alternative approaches were allegedly suppressed through demonetization, channel shutdowns, and framing critics as anti-science. People with vaccine allergies or contraindications, such as Ara Rogers, should have been told alternatives were acceptable. The speaker says they were not vaccinated, survived COVID, and were publicly scrutinized for working out, taking vitamins, cold plunges, and hyperbaric chambers. Financial incentives are described as corrupting the process rather than coincidental.

Facebook meddling in Brazilian election – Lula campaign
The US tech giant is suppressing ads ahead of a runoff against Flavio Bolsonaro, the president’s team says
Published 12 Oct, 2026 13:02                               | Updated 12 Oct, 2026 14:05
📷
Luiz Inacio Lula Da Silva, incumbent president of Brazil and presidential candidate, and Vice President Geraldo Alckimin pose during general election day on October 4, 2026, in Sao Bernardo do Campo, Brazil.  © Getty Images
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s campaign has accused US tech giant Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, of interfering in the country’s presidential election in favor of his right-wing rival, Flavio Bolsonaro.

In a statement on Saturday, Lula’s Workers’ Party (PT) accused Meta of repeatedly restricting its campaign activities while failing to provide convincing explanations. “The complete lack of transparency in the company’s systems makes these explanations scarce and opaque,” the statement read.

The campaign said the latest incident occurred between October 9 and 10, when Meta allegedly prevented Lula’s official Instagram account from boosting posts. It also claimed that the view count on one of Lula’s Instagram posts stopped increasing on October 8, affecting its reach, with similar problems registered on other accounts supporting the incumbent.

    📷
Flavio Bolsonaro leads Lula as Brazil election heads to runoffRead more
An internal analysis also suggested that Meta’s algorithms were skewed in favor of Bolsonaro, Lula’s campaign alleged, adding that posts on the right-wing contender’s page generated, on average, 2.96 times as much engagement as Lula’s, despite Bolsonaro having 17.2% fewer followers.
Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court subsequently ordered Meta to provide detailed technical explanations within 48 hours as well as to preserve relevant advertising data, moderation records, and audience metrics.

    📷

Polls close in Brazil’s pivotal electionRead more
Meta has denied the allegations as “simply false and unsupported by the facts,” insisting that many of the technical problems were not limited to Brazil or specific accounts and that it is committed to treating all users equally.
    📷
Trump wants to ‘colonize’ Brazil – Lula campaignRead more

The accusations against the US tech giant come amid a closely contested presidential race. Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro – who is serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup following his 2022 election defeat – received 47.03% of the vote in the first round, compared with Lula’s 45.16%. The two are due to face each other in a runoff on October 25.
US President Donald Trump has described Jair Bolsonaro’s prosecution as a “witch hunt,” with Washington imposing steep tariffs on Brazilian goods. While the US leader has stopped short of endorsing Bolsonaro Jr., Lula has described him as a “Trump candidate.”
Just days before the first round of the vote, Meta blocked the advertising account on Facebook used by Lula’s campaign, preventing it from running new ads. While the account was restored within hours, Meta offered no specific explanation for the suspension.
Earlier this month, Brazilian authorities requested an investigation into alleged US funding for activities intended to interfere with the elections and undermine the Supreme Federal Court. The move followed a Guardian report claiming that the Trump administration had earmarked $1 million for a project called ‘Countering Lawfare and Censorship in Brazil’. However, Brazil’s Federal Police later closed its preliminary review, citing insufficient evidence to open a criminal investigation.

Last month, Lula’s campaign accused Trump of seeking to “colonize” Brazil in a bid to gain access to its natural resources.

text:
MIKE TYSON ENDORSES ANTHONY CONSTANTINO IN NY-21

EDINBURG, NY, Oct 12 — NY-21 Republican Anthony Constantino started professionally boxing at 40 and went 2-1 with two knockouts, training intensely, while building Sticker Mule into a 1,000 person American Manufacturing company. It got Mike Tyson’s attention.

Tyson is the youngest heavyweight champion in history while Constantino is a rare CEO to turn professional boxer at an age when most are looking to retire. Constantino credits Mike for inspiring his boxing, noting that he read Mike’s book “My Life With Cus’Amato” before his first amateur fight which he finished with a brutal stone cold knockout.

Tyson is now endorsing Constantino for Congress in NY-21, stating: “I’m happy to endorse Anthony Constantino. His positive spirit and tenacity will benefit all people.”

Constantino has previously trained with Tyson’s friend and trainer Billy White. He also stepped forward to keep the historic Cus D’Amato gym in Catskill open. Constantino has his own gym, Mule Fitness, where Henry Cejudo recently trained before pulling off a 36 second comeback victory in Real American Freestyle followed by a debut boxing win in Misfits Boxing.

“I’m honored to be endorsed by an Upstate Legend and American Icon, the one and only, Iron Mike Tyson,” said Anthony Constantino. “This is the hardest endorsement to secure.”

The endorsement came after Mike Tyson watched Constantino give an electric 16 minute speech in Syracuse, NY while flying on Air Force One with President Trump. Tyson told Constantino that he was impressed. “You look good on TV,” he told Constantino.

After the rally, Tyson texted Constantino that he’d do anything he could to support him. The two facetimed and he offered Constantino his full endorsement. Constantino asked Mike to come to his Election Night Party for the people on Nov 3 in front of the Vote for Trump sign to which Mike responded, “If I’m free, I’m there.”

ABOUT ANTHONY CONSTANTINO
Anthony Constantino set the record for most votes in the NY-21 primary. He came in as a political outsider and beat strong establishment opposition after building Sticker Mule, a global company based in New York with more than 1,000 employees. He also went 2-1 with two knockouts after turning pro at 40.

text:
Podcast Summary | Armchair Expert with Dax Shepard: James McAvoy

Overview
James McAvoy joins Armchair Expert for a wide-ranging conversation that moves from a missed Hollywood role to childhood in Glasgow, the forces that shaped his acting career, and his turn to directing. The throughline is that early exposure to instability and limited opportunity forged both resilience and a lifelong instinct to monitor himself. McAvoy pushes back on how working-class life and regional identity are portrayed on screen, arguing that people from places like his deserve entertaining, propulsive stories rather than films that wallow in deprivation. His directorial debut, California Scheming, grows directly out of those convictions.

Key Themes
- The Wanted casting story reframes a near-miss: the studio wanted a bigger, more established, American name opposite Angelina Jolie, while director Timur wanted McAvoy, and McAvoy was never actually unavailable despite what the host was told.
- A poor memory for personal events functions as living in the moment rather than carrying grudges, though it also produced a forgotten meeting with Margot Robbie at the Empire Awards during a drinking period.
- Early life in Glasgow included exposure to substance abuse and mental illness, leading McAvoy to pay close attention to his mental health until roughly age 29 or 30.
- Mental illness, drugs, and alcohol often reinforce each other, though the underlying causes remain unclear and the pattern is not universal.
- Grandparents often give grandchildren a better version of themselves than their own children received, being older, more settled, and less stretched by jobs and kids.
- Modern parenting carries a tension: attentiveness and play may cost children the space they need to wonder, invent, and think for themselves.
- A working-class childhood can be vibrant and adventurous despite limited horizons, and McAvoy rejects films that reduce such backgrounds to deprivation or suffering.
- Masculinity was modeled by gentle, kind, funny men rather than self-serious or overtly masculine presentation.
- Artists in show business are pressured to sacrifice authenticity, integrity, and identity to succeed, and the show-must-go-on ethos can enable exploitation, especially of kids.
- Regional accents and lower-status groups are culturally excluded, but fixing that is Scotland's responsibility rather than Hollywood's.

Detailed Summary
The conversation opens with a casting story that both men can now laugh about. The host recalls meeting director Timur for Wanted and feeling the meeting went well, only to learn another actor was attached. The studio later asked for his quote before that actor became available again. The other actor was James McAvoy, whom the host admits he did not know at the time. McAvoy clarifies the sequence: the studio felt he was not big enough for a $75 million movie with Angelina Jolie and wanted someone more established, experienced, and American, while Timur wanted him. McAvoy camera-tested about three times and was never unavailable. The host was won over by McAvoy's performance in The Last King of Scotland.

McAvoy describes having a very poor memory for personal life events, framing it as living in the moment and not carrying grudges. His sister once told him he had met Margot Robbie at the Empire Awards after a film called Filth; he has no memory of it. He was drinking at that time and has partied with people he does not remember. Born in April 1979 in Glasgow, with no middle name and a family full of Jameses, he grew up around substance abuse and mental illness through extended family and community. His mother was a psychiatric nurse. He spent much of his early life until about 29 or 30 paying close attention to his mental health, describing alcohol as a drug and noting that mental illness, drugs, and alcohol often go hand in hand and can empower each other.

A thread about grandparents and parenting runs through the discussion. McAvoy's grandparents had five children and two jobs, and their own kids say the grandparents were never like that for them. Grandchildren often receive a better version of a grandparent: older, more settled, less stretched. The speaker from Detroit spent summers with grandparents while a single mother worked around the clock, describing it as an Eden where they were the center of the universe. Those grandparents loved, protected, and cherished them but never played with them; boredom was not accepted, so the children invented things and went to bed excited to think. A script being developed centers on a grandfather-father-son relationship, with the grandfather and grandson bonding while circumnavigating the father.

McAvoy describes his hometown as having had a massive drug problem, now described as the drug death capital of Europe at the moment. Drumchapel, his council scheme, was full of adventure, peril, chases, and kids running wild, with limited opportunities and close horizons but a vibrancy that felt real. A 1980s documentary about Drumchapel circulating on Instagram shows conditions were worse than they felt at the time. He notes that films about lower socioeconomic backgrounds often wallow in deprivation or suffering, though many are brilliant. He wanted to make a true story about people from his background that is entertaining, aspirational, and propellant.

Masculinity was modeled for him by gentle, kind, funny men, including his granddad and uncle Johnny. His grandparents framed ambition as: you have the right to try to do whatever you want, but that does not mean you can do it, you must make it happen and may need to pivot. He argues the message you can do anything can create pressure by implying children should be capable of achieving anything, even if it beats telling a child they will never amount to anything. He did not initially plan to become an actor and was aware of long odds, including the statistic that 95 percent of actors are out of work at any one time.

His route into acting began when Scottish actor David Haymon visited his school while the class was studying Macbeth for English. Haymon had played Lady Macbeth in an all-male 1970s production at the Citizens Theatre and lived next door to McAvoy's English teacher. McAvoy asked if he could make tea or coffee on a future movie; six months later Haymon called the school for him and cast him in The Near Room. Haymon had him read scenes and asked if he could cry, then told the room this was the guy who would play Kevin. His first acting moments included sitting down with Andy Serkis, who was playing a Glaswegian pimp, to work on the accent. He later attended Paisley Youth Theatre because he fancied an actor in the movie who played his sister, taking the train every Thursday night. He distinguishes fancy from in love.

Early romantic fixations shaped major life choices. A crush led him to Paisley Youth Theatre, and another on a girl named Linda at camp made him reconsider the priesthood due to celibacy. The priesthood and Royal Navy appealed as turnkey paths offering structural stability, travel, team belonging, and purpose, despite acknowledged institutional harms. He only pursued acting school half-heartedly after youth theatre, trying out for just one school because he could not afford to relocate to London, and got into the one in his hometown of Glasgow. Early-career security came from a childhood-forged resilience: whatever happened, he believed he would be okay and could feed himself, a feeling he says he has less of now. He contrasts the fear of losing what you have with the fear of having nothing: it is weirdly less scary to have nothing and be trying to get something than to have something and realize you might lose it. His ambition was modest, partly because there were not many Scottish movie stars produced each year.

After graduating in 2000, he did a lot of television and plays, and Joe Wright saw him in a play. Wright offered him a small part in the BBC costume drama Charles II. He was then offered a lead in the original UK version of Shameless, set in Manchester; his agent urged him to take it, and Wright was angry with him for choosing it. Later, Wright brought him in for a Bird Song movie version, then for Atonement after the original director pulled out. He camera-tested multiple times with Keira, knowing his competition included Cillian Murphy, Jake Gyllenhaal, and Jude Law. He loved playing that part and calls Wright one of the best actor-directors he has worked with, stealing Wright's approach to talking to crew for his own first movie.

Wright's crew ritual was to explain the scene, its meaning, the intended audience feeling, and character arcs after the crew show, while playing music, giving the whole crew ownership and investment. McAvoy describes filmmaking as a miracle of collaboration, emphasizing reliance on experienced department professionals over a director pretending to have all answers. Narnia casting reportedly shifted away from an older actor after chemistry tests felt creepy, leading them to seek a more experienced actor who looked childlike. McAvoy says he was cast in The Last King of Scotland before Forest Whitaker, and Kevin McDonald fought for him despite pressure to cast a star, since the role was Scottish and McDonald did not want a bad accent. On Atonement, the author did not agree with his casting, and he chose to stay out of her way because he felt physically unlike the character. He deliberately stayed separate from the cast and crew in a gardener's cottage, framing his character Robbie as working class and separate.

X-Men: First Class is described as an actor-first comic book movie, with Matthew Vaughn putting his own stamp on it and shifting tone from earlier X-Men films. The movie survived on the chemistry of the two buddies, and Professor X and Magneto casting chemistry was central. Michael Fassbender's Magneto audition stood out as both movie star and real actor. Jennifer Lawrence flew in at 18, did costume fitting and rehearsal all day, then flew out that night. Directing is described as all-consuming: McAvoy is still promoting a movie about three years after properly starting work on it, and says directors never let their films go. He argues that if you can choose your work, you should make things you are genuinely passionate about because directing requires sweating blood and constant anxiety.

California Scheming is based on a true story about Billy and Gavin, two low-economic-status Scottish boys who are bullied and into rapping. They travel to London for open auditions held by a record label looking for the next Eminem. Called the rapping Proclaimers after an audition and told they could not be understood, they reinvented themselves as American rappers from California. They initially claimed to be from LA but knew nothing about it. A scout saw them perform as Americans, leading to a second audition and a record deal using the same song with minor lyric and accent changes. Their plan was to release music, go on MTV, then expose the industry's regional bias, because the same tracks were now loved. When the moment came, they could not give up the fame. The deception lasted two and a half years. They appeared on MTV multiple times but never signed a record contract because they had no ID other than Scottish. A Millie Vanilli parallel is noted, but these two could actually rap, write, and perform. Gavin was heavily involved in the music and held the rights; Billy provided freestyle raps, delivering about 20 options in 20 minutes, and his freestyles open and close the movie.

McAvoy wanted to honor Gavin's complex fallout without making fun of it or exposing him in a titillating, cartoonish way. The film's music had to be rebuilt from the ground up because the original tracks contained millions of dollars' worth of uncleared samples. Performance art in education is valuable for kids from low-opportunity neighborhoods because it teaches them they can survive failure, bad reviews, and public speaking. He describes entitlement positively: everyone should feel entitled to be present and have value, but only certain pockets of society get to feel that. He challenges the idea that many Scottish actors exist by asking people to name 10 Scottish movies from the last 10 years. He says it is not Hollywood's responsibility to make movies about Scottish people; Scotland needs to do better. The conversation closes with a story about being randomly punched by a drunk stranger at a Toronto Film Festival bar, and the abrupt shift from wanting to fight to immediately wanting to get home to his wife and kids.
